articles.title: ARACNE recovers tree networks exactly
articles.statement:
**ARACNE recovers tree networks exactly** (Margolin et al. 2006, Theorem 1): if the true
network `T` is a tree whose edges all carry mutual information above `I₀`, and the strict
data-processing inequality holds on every separated triple, then ARACNE returns `T`. Strictness
is the explicit form of the paper's exclusion of exact cancellations; with equality ARACNE can
keep an indirect edge (see the tests).

articles.title: No false positives
articles.statement:
If the true network `T` is a tree and `I a b < min (I a c) (I c b)`
whenever `c` separates `a` from `b` in `T`, then every edge ARACNE keeps is an edge of `T`.

articles.title: ARACNE gene network reconstruction
articles.statement:
The network ARACNE reconstructs from symmetric pairwise mutual informations `I` with
independence threshold `I₀` and DPI tolerance zero (Margolin et al. 2006): `{i, k}` is an edge
iff `i ≠ k`, `I₀ < I i k`, and no third gene `j` with `I₀ < I i j` and `I₀ < I j k` has
`I i k < min (I i j) (I j k)`.

articles.title: No false negatives
articles.statement:
If the true network `T` is a forest whose edges all carry mutual
information above `I₀`, and `I a b ≤ min (I a c) (I c b)` whenever `c` separates `a` from `b` in
`T` (every walk from `a` to `b` visits `c`), then ARACNE keeps every edge of `T`.

articles.title: Chow–Liu trees survive ARACNE
articles.statement:
**Chow–Liu trees survive ARACNE** (Margolin et al. 2006, Theorem 2): a spanning tree `T` of
maximum total weight `∑_{{i, k} ∈ T} I i k` among all spanning trees, whose edges all carry
mutual information above `I₀`, is a subnetwork of the ARACNE network.

articles.title: The ChromHMM update maximizes `Q(· | θ)`
articles.statement: **The ChromHMM update maximizes `Q(· | θ)`** over all valid product-Bernoulli HMMs.

articles.title: One ChromHMM step on rich data
articles.statement: One ChromHMM step, on rich data.

articles.title: Factored update is below one
articles.statement: The factored update is below one when both counts are positive.

articles.title: Positivity of the factored update
articles.statement: The factored update is positive when both counts are.

articles.title: Factored per-mark update
articles.statement: The factored (per-mark) update `ones j / (ones j + zeros j)`.

articles.title: Positivity of the ChromHMM joint weight
articles.statement: The ChromHMM joint weight is positive.

articles.title: ChromHMM joint weight of a state path and mark vectors
articles.statement: The EM model of ChromHMM: the joint weight of a state path and a sequence of mark vectors.

articles.title: EM log-likelihood as a sum of HMM log-likelihoods
articles.statement: The EM log-likelihood is the sum of the HMM log-likelihoods of the sequences.

articles.title: The log-likelihood is monotone along the ChromHMM iterates
articles.statement: **The log-likelihood is monotone along the ChromHMM iterates.**

articles.title: Each ChromHMM step does not decrease the log-likelihood
articles.statement: **Each ChromHMM step does not decrease the log-likelihood.**

articles.title: The ChromHMM update is a valid parameter
articles.statement: **The ChromHMM update is a valid parameter** on rich data.

articles.title: The ChromHMM M-step
articles.statement:
The Baum-Welch initial and transition updates, and the factored
emission update `prob s j = markOnes / (markOnes + markZeros)`.

articles.title: The factored update in posterior form
articles.statement:
`markOnes s j` is the posterior expected number
of bins in state `s` at which mark `j` is present.

articles.title: Expected number of bins in a state with a mark present
articles.statement: The expected number of bins in state `s` with mark `j` present.

articles.title: Expected number of bins in a state with a mark absent
articles.statement: The expected number of bins in state `s` with mark `j` absent.

articles.title: Weight of binary vectors with a mark present
articles.statement: The weight `∑ o with o j = true, c o` of the binary vectors with mark `j` present.

articles.title: ChromHMM parameters
articles.statement:
ChromHMM parameters: initial and transition weights, and the presence probability of each
mark in each state.

articles.title: Rich data for the ChromHMM M-step
articles.statement:
Data on which the ChromHMM M-step is valid: a sequence, a transition, and every mark both
present and absent somewhere.

articles.title: Product of Bernoulli distributions sums to one
articles.statement:
A product of Bernoulli distributions sums to one over the binary vectors, for every
parameter vector `p` (the identity is algebraic: `∏ j, (p j + (1 - p j)) = 1`).

articles.title: The factored update maximizes the expected log-likelihood
articles.statement:
**The factored update maximizes the expected log-likelihood** over all products of
Bernoulli distributions with parameters in `(0, 1)`, for nonnegative weights `c` in which every
mark is both present and absent with positive weight.

articles.title: Expected product-Bernoulli log-likelihood splits over marks
articles.statement:
The expected log-likelihood of weighted binary vectors under a product of Bernoulli
distributions with parameters in `(0, 1)` splits over the marks.

articles.title: Valid ChromHMM parameters give a valid HMM
articles.statement: A valid ChromHMM parameter is a valid HMM.

articles.title: HMM of ChromHMM parameters
articles.statement: The HMM of ChromHMM parameters: emissions are products of Bernoulli distributions.

articles.title: Valid HMM built from a valid ChromHMM parameter
articles.statement: The valid HMM of a valid ChromHMM parameter.

articles.title: Parameter space of ChromHMM
articles.statement: The parameter space of ChromHMM.

articles.title: Valid ChromHMM parameters
articles.statement:
Valid parameters: positive initial and transition distributions, mark probabilities in
`(0, 1)`.

articles.title: Weight of binary vectors with a mark absent
articles.statement: The weight `∑ o with o j = false, c o` of the binary vectors with mark `j` absent.

articles.title: De Bruijn multigraph of a string
articles.statement:
The de Bruijn multigraph of `s` (Pevzner–Tang–Waterman 2001) as its list of edge
occurrences: one edge per `k`-mer occurrence, in order of position.

articles.title: De Bruijn edge of a k-mer
articles.statement:
The edge of the de Bruijn multigraph contributed by a `k`-mer `w`: from its prefix
`(k-1)`-mer `w.dropLast` to its suffix `(k-1)`-mer `w.tail`.

articles.title: Efficient executable computation of k-mers
articles.statement:
Executable form of `kmers`: the suffixes of `s` are generated once by `List.tails`, so the
cost is `O(|s| · k)` rather than the `Θ(|s|²)` of recomputing `s.drop i` for every `i`. The
compiler uses it in place of `kmers` (`kmers_eq_kmersImpl`).

articles.title: Every Eulerian trail spells a string with the same `k`-mer multiset
articles.statement:
**Every Eulerian trail spells a string with the same `k`-mer multiset** (`2 ≤ k`): if `W` is a
walk of `(k-1)`-mers whose steps are a permutation of the edge occurrences of the de Bruijn
multigraph of `s`, then the `k`-mers of the spelled string are a permutation of those of `s`.
(The empty walk is allowed: it is a trail only when `s` has no `k`-mers, and spells `[]`.)

articles.title: The k-mers of a string
articles.statement:
The `k`-mers of `s` in order of position: the length-`k` windows `(s.drop i).take k`
for `i + k ≤ |s|`.

articles.title: The (k-1)-mer walk of a string spells the string
articles.statement: The `(k-1)`-mer walk of `s` spells `s` back (`2 ≤ k`, `k - 1 ≤ |s|`).

articles.title: String spelled by a walk of (k-1)-mers
articles.statement:
The string spelled by a walk of `(k-1)`-mers: the first vertex followed by the last letter of
each later vertex.

articles.title: The `k`-mer walk of `s` is an Eulerian trail
articles.statement:
**The `k`-mer walk of `s` is an Eulerian trail** of its de Bruijn multigraph: its steps are a
permutation of the edge occurrences, each traversed once.

articles.title: The `(k-1)`-mer walk of `s` traverses the de Bruijn multigraph in order
articles.statement:
Its steps are
exactly the edges contributed by the `k`-mers of `s`, one per occurrence, in order of position.

articles.title: Elimination
articles.statement:
When some event survives, event `j` gets probability zero iff
`N j ≤ α`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the GPS M-step update
articles.statement: The update is nonnegative.

articles.title: GPS M-step formula when every event survives
articles.statement: When every event survives, the update is `(N j - α) / ∑ k, (N k - α)`.

articles.title: GPS M-step keeps positive probability exactly on surviving events
articles.statement: When some event survives, event `j` keeps positive probability iff `α < N j`.

articles.title: GPS M-step at zero sparseness is the ordinary mixture M-step
articles.statement:
With `α = 0` and nonnegative counts the update is the ordinary mixture M-step
`N j / ∑ N`.

articles.title: The GPS M-step with component elimination
articles.statement: `π j = max (N j - α) 0 / ∑ k, max (N k - α) 0`.

articles.title: The M-step of the restructured model
articles.statement:
When every remaining event survives
(`α < N j` for all `j`), the update maximizes the GPS expected complete-data log penalized
likelihood over the positive probability vectors.

articles.title: Expected penalized complete-data log-likelihood of GPS
articles.statement:
The expected complete-data log penalized likelihood of GPS, up to an additive constant:
`∑ j, (N j - α) log (π j)` (the expected log-likelihood `∑ j, N j log (π j)` plus the log of the
negative Dirichlet prior). Meaningful for positive `π`.

articles.title: GPS M-step update sums to one when some event survives
articles.statement: The update sums to one when some event survives.

articles.title: Total surviving weight is positive iff some event survives
articles.statement: The total surviving weight is positive iff some event has `α < N j`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of surviving weights
articles.statement: Surviving weights are nonnegative.

articles.title: Surviving weight of a GPS event
articles.statement:
The surviving weight `max (N j - α) 0` of event `j`, for expected read counts `N` and
sparseness parameter `α`.

articles.title: Truncated and penalized objectives agree when every event survives
articles.statement: When every event survives, the penalized and truncated objectives agree.

articles.title: The update is an upper bound for the truncated objective
articles.statement:
**The update is an upper bound for the truncated objective** over the positive
probability vectors (derived characterization of the elimination rule). Upper-bound
statement only: this does not prove the value at `mStep` is the supremum (no
approximation or `sSup` theorem is given). When elimination occurs `mStep` itself is not
a positive vector (eliminated coordinates are zero), so it is the boundary point on the
face where eliminated coordinates vanish, not a maximizer inside the positive simplex.

articles.title: Truncated GPS objective
articles.statement: The truncated objective `∑ j, max (N j - α) 0 * log (π j)`.

articles.title: Exact depth law (count form)
articles.statement:
For `L ≤ G`, base `x` is covered by exactly `k` reads for
`N.choose k * L ^ k * (G - L) ^ (N - k)` of the start tuples.

articles.title: Exact coverage count
articles.statement:
For `L ≤ G`, base `x` is uncovered by all `N` reads for exactly
`(G - L) ^ N` of the `G ^ N` start tuples.

articles.title: Read covering a base of a circular genome
articles.statement:
A read of length `L` starting at position `s` of a circular genome of length `G` covers base
`x` when `x` is one of `s, s + 1, …, s + L - 1 (mod G)`, i.e. `(x - s) mod G < L`.

articles.title: Depth of coverage of a base
articles.statement: The depth of coverage of base `x`: the number of reads covering it.

articles.title: Expected number of no-successor reads (exact)
articles.statement:
For `0 < G` and `L ≤ G`, the
expected number of reads with no successor is `N (1 - (L - 1) / G) ^ (N - 1)`.
The `0 < G` hypothesis is essential: at `G = 0` and `N > 0`, the right-hand expression is
`N` while the sum of totalized normalized counts is zero.

articles.title: Read with no successor
articles.statement:
Read `j` has no successor when no other read starts in the `L - 1` positions after it,
`starts j + 1, …, starts j + L - 1 (mod G)` (reads starting at the same position are not
successors of each other). In Lander and Waterman's terms such a read is counted as ending
an island, but several no-successor reads can lie in one island, so this is not the island
count.

articles.title: Exact depth law
articles.statement:
The depth at a fixed base is binomial with `N` trials and success
probability `L / G`, for `L ≤ G`.

articles.title: Normalized count agrees with the totalized uniform measure
articles.statement:
`normalizedCount` agrees with Mathlib's totalized uniform measure on all start tuples.
This measure is a probability law only when the sample space is nonempty.

articles.title: Exact uncovered probability
articles.statement:
**Exact uncovered probability** (Clarke–Carbon, Lander–Waterman, circular genome):
`(1 - L / G) ^ N` for `L ≤ G`.

articles.title: Normalized count of read start tuples
articles.statement:
The totalized normalized count `|E| / G ^ N` of a set of start tuples.
For `0 < G`, this is the probability when the `N` start positions are independent and uniform
on `Fin G`. If `G = 0` and `N > 0`, the sample space is empty and this value is zero, so it is
not a probability law. For `N = 0`, there is one empty start tuple, even when `G = 0`.

articles.title: Count of no-successor reads (exact)
articles.statement:
For `L ≤ G`, summed over the
reads, the number of start tuples in which read `j` has no successor is
`N * G * (G - (L - 1)) ^ (N - 1)`. This counts no-successor reads, not island ends:
a start tuple can have several no-successor reads in one island.

articles.title: The coverage depth tends to Poisson(`c`)
articles.statement:
Under the hypotheses of
`tendsto_normalizedCount_uncovered`, the probability that a given base is covered by exactly `k`
reads tends to `e^{-c} c^k / k.factorial`.

articles.title: Lander–Waterman limit for the uncovered fraction
articles.statement:
With read length `L` fixed, genome
lengths `G N ≥ L`, and coverage `N L / G_N → c` as the number of reads `N → ∞`, the probability
that a given base is uncovered tends to `e^{-c}`.

articles.title: Complementary base pairing of two positions
articles.statement: Positions `i` and `j` of `s` both lie in `s` and carry complementary bases.

articles.title: Counting semiring
articles.statement:
The number of secondary structures on `n` points with minimum
hairpin `m`, when every pair of positions may pair, is Waterman's number `S_m(n)`.

articles.title: Additive base-pair energy model
articles.statement:
An **additive base-pair energy model**: the free energy of a structure is the sum of the
energies `e i j` of its base pairs (in the same units as `RT`).

articles.title: McCaskill's algorithm
articles.statement:
**McCaskill's algorithm** (inside part): over the sum-product semiring `ℝ` with Boltzmann
weights `exp (-e i j / RT)`, the inside value of the whole sequence is the partition function.
This is an algebraic identity valid for every real `RT`.

articles.title: Inside value sums the weights of all secondary structures
articles.statement: The inside value of the whole sequence sums the weights of all its secondary structures.

articles.title: Inside algorithm
articles.statement:
The inside recursion sums the weights of all secondary structures
supported in the interval `[i, i + len)`, over any commutative semiring.

articles.title: Tropical semiring
articles.statement:
With every base pair weighted `-1` in the min-plus semiring
`MinTropical (WithTop ℤ)` (addition `min`, multiplication `+`), a structure with `k` pairs has
weight `-k`, so the inside value of the whole sequence is minus the Nussinov maximum number of
base pairs.

articles.title: Inside recursion
articles.statement:
**Inside recursion** over a commutative semiring `R`: `inside pair m s w i len` is the
weighted sum over the secondary structures supported in the interval `[i, i + len)` (proved in
`inside_eq_sum`). Base `i` is either unpaired, or paired with `i + 1 + k` for some `k ≥ m`
with `CanPair pair s i (i + 1 + k)`, which contributes `w i (i + 1 + k)` times the inside
values of the enclosed interval `[i + 1, i + 1 + k)` and of the outer interval
`[i + k + 2, i + len + 1)`.

articles.title: Membership in the set of secondary structures
articles.statement: `structures` is exactly the set of secondary structures on `s`.

articles.title: Total structure weight is at least one
articles.statement:
For nonnegative weights the total weight of all structures is at least `1`, the weight of
the empty structure; so the denominator of `pairProb` is positive.

articles.title: Outside algorithm
articles.statement:
**Outside algorithm** (McCaskill 1990): for a candidate pair `(i, j)` (`i + m < j` and
`CanPair pair s i j`), the outside value times the pair's weight times the inside value of the
enclosed interval `[i + 1, j)` sums the weights of all secondary structures containing
`(i, j)`.

articles.title: Outside recursion
articles.statement:
**Outside recursion** (McCaskill 1990) over a commutative semiring `R`, for a sequence of
length `n = s.length`: `outside pair m s w i j` is the weighted sum of the parts outside the
pair `(i, j)` of all structures containing it (proved in `outside_mul_eq_sum`). Either no pair
encloses `(i, j)`, leaving independent structures on `[0, i)` and `[j + 1, n)`, or there is a
unique innermost enclosing pair `(a, b)` (`a < i`, `j < b < n`), contributing the outside value
of `(a, b)`, its weight, and the inside values of `[a + 1, i)` and `[j + 1, b)`.

articles.title: McCaskill's base-pair probabilities
articles.statement:
For a candidate pair `(i, j)`,
`P(i, j) = outside(i, j) · w(i, j) · inside(i + 1, j) / inside(0, n)`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of base-pair probabilities
articles.statement: Base-pair probabilities are nonnegative for nonnegative weights.

articles.title: Base-pair probability
articles.statement:
The **base-pair probability** `P(i, j)`: the total weight of the structures containing the
pair `(i, j)`, divided by the total weight `Z` of all structures. For nonnegative weights `Z ≥ 1`
(the empty structure has weight `1`), so the denominator is positive; for Boltzmann weights this
is the probability of `(i, j)` under the Boltzmann distribution on structures.

articles.title: McCaskill partition function of RNA secondary structures
articles.statement:
The **partition function** `Z = ∑_S exp (-E(S) / RT)` over all secondary structures `S`
on `s` with minimum hairpin `m`, for the additive energy `e` at thermal energy `RT`
(physically `0 < RT`; the identities below hold for every real `RT`).

articles.title: Secondary structures within an interval
articles.statement:
The secondary structures on `s` (`IsStructure pair m s`) all of whose pairs lie in the
interval `[i, i + len)`.

articles.title: Set of all secondary structures of a sequence
articles.statement: All secondary structures on `s` with minimum hairpin `m` (see `mem_structures`).

articles.title: Each base pairs at most once
articles.statement:
For nonnegative weights, the probabilities that base `i`
pairs with some later base `j` or some earlier base `j` sum to at most `1`
(`∑_j (P(i, j) + P(j, i)) ≤ 1`).

articles.title: Waterman numbers with no hairpin constraint are Motzkin numbers
articles.statement:
For `m = 0` (no hairpin constraint) Waterman's numbers are the Motzkin numbers
`M(n) = ∑_k C(n, 2k) C(k)`: the number of non-crossing partial matchings on `n` points.

articles.title: Waterman's recursion
articles.statement:
**Waterman's recursion** for the number `S_m(n)` of secondary structures on `n` points
with minimum hairpin `m` when every pair is allowed: `S(0) = 1` and
`S(n + 1) = S(n) + ∑_{m ≤ k < n} S(k) S(n - 1 - k)` (Waterman 1978; Stein–Waterman 1979).
For `m = 0` these are the Motzkin numbers (`watermanNumber_zero_eq_motzkinNumber`); for `m = 1`
the Stein–Waterman numbers `1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 17, 37, …` (OEIS A004148).

articles.title: Weight of a secondary structure
articles.statement: The weight of a structure: the product of the weights of its base pairs.

articles.title: Soundness bound
articles.statement: Every secondary structure has at most `nussinov pair m s` pairs.

articles.title: Optimality
articles.statement:
Some secondary structure has exactly `nussinov pair m s` pairs, so the
recursion computes the maximum number of pairs over all non-crossing structures.

articles.title: RNA secondary structure
articles.statement:
A secondary structure on `s` (Nussinov et al. 1978): a finite set of base pairs `(i, j)`,
each closing a hairpin with at least `m` unpaired positions strictly inside (`i + m < j`), joining
complementary bases (`pair s[i] s[j]`, which also puts both positions inside `s`), with every
position in at most one pair and no two pairs crossing (`i < k < j < l`).

articles.title: Maximum of a list of natural numbers
articles.statement: The largest of a list of naturals (`0` for the empty list).

articles.title: The Nussinov recursion
articles.statement:
The first base `a` of `a :: rest` is either unpaired, or paired
with `rest[k]` for some `k ≥ m` with `pair a rest[k]`, splitting the rest into the enclosed part
`rest.take k` and the outer part `rest.drop (k + 1)`. Exponential-time specification; the usual
`O(n³)` table memoizes it on the intervals of `s`.

articles.title: Circular edge-covering walk
articles.statement: A circular edge-covering walk: a nonempty closed walk through every edge.

articles.title: Subwalk of a circular walk
articles.statement:
`w` is a subwalk of the circular walk `A`: it is read off `A` from some start position,
wrapping around (possibly several times).

articles.title: Safe walks are omnitigs
articles.statement:
Safe walks are omnitigs (Theorem 1, (1) ⇒ (2)), when a circular edge-covering walk exists
(otherwise every walk is vacuously safe).

articles.title: Omnitig
articles.statement:
Omnitig (Tomescu–Medvedev, Definition 5): for all `1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ t` (`t + 1 = w.length`),
no path from `v_j = src e_j` to `v_i = src e_i` has first edge `≠ e_j` and last edge
`≠ e_{i-1}`.

articles.title: Path in a directed multigraph
articles.statement:
A path: a nonempty walk whose nodes `src e₀, tgt e₀, …, tgt e_ℓ` are distinct, except that
the first and last node may coincide.

articles.title: Omnitigs are safe walks
articles.statement: Omnitigs are safe (Theorem 1, (2) ⇒ (1)).

articles.title: Safe walk in a multigraph
articles.statement: Safe walk: a subwalk of every circular edge-covering walk.

articles.title: Walk in a directed multigraph
articles.statement: A list of edges is a walk when consecutive edges are incident (head to tail).

articles.title: Directed multigraph
articles.statement: A directed multigraph given by the source and target of each edge.

articles.title: Adjacent-similarity score of a leaf order
articles.statement: The score of a leaf order: the sum of the similarities of adjacent leaves.

articles.title: Correctness of the optimal leaf ordering recursion
articles.statement:
**Correctness of the optimal leaf ordering recursion** (Bar-Joseph, Gifford and
Jaakkola 2001): the dynamic program computes, for every end pair `(i, j)`, the best score of
a leaf order of `t` starting at `i` and ending at `j`.

articles.title: Bar-Joseph–Gifford–Jaakkola dynamic program for leaf ordering
articles.statement:
The dynamic program of Bar-Joseph, Gifford and Jaakkola: `bestEnds S t i j` is computed
from the tables of the two children, trying both child orders.

articles.title: Dendrogram as a leaf-labeled binary tree
articles.statement:
A rooted binary tree whose leaves are labeled by `α`: the shape of a dendrogram
(merge heights are irrelevant for leaf ordering).

articles.title: Joining two subtree orders at an adjacent leaf pair
articles.statement:
One side of the recursion: the left part ranges over orders of a subtree with leaves `Ll`
and best-score table `Ml`, the right part over a subtree with leaves `Lr` and table `Mr`; the
two are joined at the adjacent pair `(k, l)`.

articles.title: Leaves of a dendrogram
articles.statement: The leaves of a dendrogram, left to right.

articles.title: A dendrogram with m internal nodes has $2^m$ leaf orders
articles.statement: A dendrogram with `m` internal nodes has `2 ^ m` leaf orders (one per flip pattern).

articles.title: Number of internal nodes of a dendrogram
articles.statement: The number of internal (merge) nodes.

articles.title: Optimal leaf-ordering score with fixed end leaves
articles.statement:
The best score among the leaf orders of `t` that start with `i` and end with `j`
(`⊥` if there is none).

articles.title: Optimal leaf-ordering score via the dynamic program
articles.statement: The optimal leaf-ordering score is the best `bestEnds` value over end pairs of leaves.

articles.title: Optimal leaf-ordering score is finite
articles.statement: Every dendrogram has a leaf order, so the optimal score is a real number.

articles.title: Optimal leaf-ordering score
articles.statement: The best score among the leaf orders of `t` (never `⊥`: `optScore_ne_bot`).

articles.title: Leaf orderings of a dendrogram
articles.statement:
The leaf orders obtained by choosing, at each internal node, which child is drawn first.
Each choice pattern contributes one entry, so the list has `2 ^ numInternal t` entries.

articles.title: Leaf orders are permutations of the leaves
articles.statement: Every leaf order of `t` is a permutation of its leaves.

articles.title: Scaling and rounding error
articles.statement:
Rounding `c · W` to integers changes the rescaled score of
every site by at most `w / (2c)`.

articles.title: Background likelihood of a sequence
articles.statement:
The likelihood `∏ₖ q (x k)` of a sequence of length `m` under the background of independent
letters with law `q`.

articles.title: Boltzmann position weight matrix
articles.statement: The Boltzmann PWM `q b e^{-λ ε i b} / Zᵢ` of an energy matrix `ε`.

articles.title: The both-strand score is invariant under reverse complementing the sequence
articles.statement:
**The both-strand score is invariant under reverse complementing the sequence**, for an
involutive complement.

articles.title: Both-strand convolution score
articles.statement:
The both-strand score: the larger of the max-pooled responses of `W` and of its reverse
complement.

articles.title: The convolution response is the PWM score of the window
articles.statement: **The convolution response is the PWM score of the window.**

articles.title: The reverse-complement filter scans the other strand
articles.statement:
On a sequence of length `m + w`,
its response at window `i ≤ m` is the response of `W` on the reverse complement at window
`m - i`.

articles.title: Translation equivariance
articles.statement:
Dropping the first letter shifts the responses by one
window.

articles.title: Convolution filter response at a window
articles.statement:
The response of a convolution (cross-correlation) filter `W` of width `w` on the one-hot
encoded sequence `x` at the window starting at `i`:
`∑ k, ∑ b, W k b * oneHot (x (i + k)) b`.

articles.title: Coverage condition for motif columns
articles.statement:
Every letter can occur in every motif column: for each column `i` and letter `b` some
sequence has `b` at offset `i` of some possible occurrence. This keeps the M-step positive.

articles.title: The M-step maximizes the EM objective
articles.statement:
**The M-step maximizes the EM objective** over PWMs with positive entries and normalized
columns: for every `θ'`, `Q(θ' | θ) ≤ Q(mStep θ | θ)` (Gibbs' inequality per column).

articles.title: Max pooling returns the best PWM hit
articles.statement: Some window attains the max-pooled output.

articles.title: Karlin–Altschul `λ`
articles.statement:
**Karlin–Altschul `λ`** (Karlin and Altschul 1990): if the expected score under a positive
background distribution is negative and some score is positive, there is a unique `λ > 0` with
`∑ pₐ p_b e^{λ s_{ab}} = 1`.

articles.title: Positivity of expected motif counts
articles.statement: Under `Covers`, every expected count is positive.

articles.title: Expected letter counts in motif columns
articles.statement:
The expected count of letter `b` in motif column `i` under the posteriors at `θ`:
`∑ₘ ∑_z P(z | xₘ, θ) [start z = some j ∧ xₘ (j + i) = b]`.

articles.title: Information content is a Kullback–Leibler divergence
articles.statement:
For laws `P ≪ Q`, the information
content of `P` against `Q` is `KL(P ‖ Q) / log 2`, Mathlib's `klDiv` in bits.

articles.title: Information content is nonnegative
articles.statement:
**Information content is nonnegative** (Gibbs' inequality) for a column distribution and a
positive background distribution.

articles.title: A DNA column carries at most two bits
articles.statement:
For a four-letter alphabet (DNA) and the uniform background, a column carries between `0`
and `2` bits.

articles.title: Information content is at most the log of the alphabet size
articles.statement: Against the uniform background, a column carries at most `log₂ |α|` bits.

articles.title: Information content against the uniform background
articles.statement:
**Information content against the uniform background** (Schneider et al. 1986):
`log₂ |α| - H(p)`, the maximal entropy minus the column entropy.

articles.title: Information content of a position weight matrix column
articles.statement:
The information content `∑_b p b log₂ (p b / q b)` (in bits) of a PWM column `p` against
the background `q` (Schneider et al. 1986). Letters with `p b = 0` contribute `0`.

articles.title: Columns of the Boltzmann matrix are distributions
articles.statement: Each column of the Boltzmann PWM is a distribution.

articles.title: Target frequencies form a distribution on pairs
articles.statement: At a root of `pairMGF p s λ = 1` the target frequencies form a distribution on pairs.

articles.title: Every window's PWM score is at most the max-pooled output
articles.statement: Every window's PWM score is at most the max-pooled output.

articles.title: The motif likelihood is nondecreasing along the EM iterates
articles.statement: **The motif likelihood is nondecreasing along the EM iterates.**

articles.title: Log-odds are affine in the energies
articles.statement:
`log (p i b / q b) = -λ ε i b - log Zᵢ` for the
Boltzmann PWM.

articles.title: Log-odds matrix of a site model
articles.statement:
The log-odds matrix `log (p i b / q b)` of a site model against a background (natural
logarithm).

articles.title: M-step for position weight matrices
articles.statement: The M-step: normalized expected letter counts, `θ' i b = c i b / ∑_{b'} c i b'`.

articles.title: Filter responses read only positions within the sequence length
articles.statement: The responses only read the positions `< m + w` of a sequence of length `m + w`.

articles.title: Max pooling the reverse-complement filter equals max pooling `W` on the reverse complement
articles.statement:
**Max pooling the reverse-complement filter equals max pooling `W` on the reverse
complement.**

articles.title: Bias and ReLU commute with max pooling
articles.statement:
Pooling `max (conv + β) 0` over the windows
gives `max (maxPool + β) 0`.

articles.title: Global max pooling
articles.statement: **Global max pooling** over the `m + 1` windows of a sequence of length `m + w`.

articles.title: Joint likelihood with no motif occurrence
articles.statement: With no occurrence, the joint is the prior times the background likelihood.

articles.title: The joint is the window model
articles.statement:
For a positive background and an occurrence at `j`, the
joint is the prior times the product of `θ (k - j)` inside the window and `q` outside.

articles.title: Joint likelihood of a sequence and a motif occurrence
articles.statement:
The joint likelihood of a sequence `x` and a latent occurrence `z` with prior `prior z` and
start `start z` (`none`: no occurrence): background letters outside the window, site-model letters
inside. One occurrence per sequence (OOPS) is `Z = Fin (n + 1)`, `start = some`, `prior` uniform;
zero or one (ZOOPS) is `Z = Option (Fin (n + 1))`, `start = id`, `prior none = 1 - γ` and
`prior (some j) = γ / (n + 1)` for a fixed `γ`. The background `q` is a fixed parameter.

articles.title: Positivity of the motif model
articles.statement: The motif model is positive for a positive background and a positive prior.

articles.title: Motif model as an EM model
articles.statement: The motif model as an EM model on `PosPWM`.

articles.title: One-hot encoding of a letter
articles.statement: The one-hot encoding of a letter: `oneHot a b = 1` if `b = a` and `0` otherwise.

articles.title: Exact p-values
articles.statement:
`pValue q M t = ∑_{s : score M s ≥ t} ∏ᵢ q (s i)`, the background
probability `P_q(score M ≥ t)` when `q` is a distribution.

articles.title: Exact p-value of a score threshold
articles.statement: The exact p-value of the score threshold `t`, summed over the computed distribution.

articles.title: Moment generating function of a pair score
articles.statement:
The moment generating function `∑ₐ ∑_b pₐ p_b e^{λ s_{ab}}` of a pair score under independent
letters with law `p`.

articles.title: Positivity of the column partition function
articles.statement: The partition function of a positive background is positive.

articles.title: Column partition function of an energy matrix
articles.statement:
The column partition function `Z = ∑_b q b e^{-λ ε b}` of energies `ε` at inverse
temperature `λ`.

articles.title: Positive position weight matrices
articles.statement: PWMs with positive entries and columns summing to `1`: the EM parameter space.

articles.title: The E-step in closed form
articles.statement:
The posterior of the occurrence `z` is proportional to its
prior times the likelihood ratio of its window (Lawrence and Reilly 1990; Bailey and Elkan
1995).

articles.title: Reverse-complement filter
articles.statement: The reverse-complement filter: `rcFilter W k b = W (Fin.rev k) (comp b)`.

articles.title: Reverse complement of a sequence prefix
articles.statement:
The reverse complement of the length-`L` prefix of `x`: position `j < L` holds the complement
of `x (L - 1 - j)`.

articles.title: The relative entropy of the target frequencies
articles.statement:
**The relative entropy of the target frequencies** (Altschul 1991):
`λ ∑ q_{ab} s_{ab} = ∑ q_{ab} log (q_{ab} / (pₐ p_b))`, which is nonnegative.

articles.title: The column recursion computes the exact score distribution
articles.statement:
`scoreDist q M t` is
`∑_{s : score M s = t} ∏ᵢ q (s i)`, for every `q`. When `q` is a distribution this is the
background probability of the score `t` (the weights sum to `1` by `sum_bgLik`).

articles.title: Background score distribution of an integer matrix
articles.statement:
The background distribution of the score of an integer matrix `M`, computed column by column
from the point mass at `0` (Staden 1989; Touzet and Varré 2007).

articles.title: Every such score matrix is a log-odds matrix
articles.statement:
**Every such score matrix is a log-odds matrix** (Karlin and Altschul 1990):
`s_{ab} = log (q_{ab} / (pₐ p_b)) / λ` for every `λ > 0`; at the Karlin–Altschul root the
`q_{ab}` form a distribution (`isDist_targetFreq`), the implicit target frequencies.

articles.title: Log-odds score of a selected site is its scaled energy up to a constant
articles.statement: The log-odds score of a selected site is `-λ E(s)` up to the constant `∑ᵢ log Zᵢ`.

articles.title: The log-odds score is a log-likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
**The log-odds score is a log-likelihood ratio** (Staden 1989; Stormo 2000): for positive
site model and background, `score (logOdds p q) s = log (siteLik p s / bgLik q s)`.

articles.title: One column step of the score-distribution recursion
articles.statement:
One column of the score-distribution recursion: from the distribution `d` of the score of
the first columns, the distribution after adding a column `c` with background `q`,
`∑_b q b · (d shifted by c b)`.

articles.title: Score of a site under a position weight matrix
articles.statement: The score `∑ᵢ W i (s i)` of a site `s` of width `w` under a position weight matrix `W`.

articles.title: Berg–von Hippel
articles.statement:
Boltzmann selection of background sites with an additive energy yields
the product site model with columns `boltzmannPWM`. This is an identity for every `q`
(both sides vanish when some `Zᵢ = 0`); it is a statement about laws for positive `q`.

articles.title: Law of energy-selected background sites
articles.statement:
The law of background sites selected with weight `e^{-λ E(s)}` for the additive energy
`E s = score ε s = ∑ᵢ ε i (s i)`: `q(s) e^{-λ E(s)} / ∑_{s'} q(s') e^{-λ E(s')}`.

articles.title: Site likelihood under a column-independent model
articles.statement:
The likelihood `∏ᵢ p i (s i)` of a site under the product (column-independent) site model
`p`.

articles.title: Sequence position of a motif column
articles.statement:
The position `j + i` of motif column `i` for a motif starting at `j`, in a sequence of
length `n + w` (so `n + 1` possible starts).

articles.title: Background likelihoods form a distribution
articles.statement: The background law of independent letters is a distribution on sequences.

articles.title: Thresholding the log-odds score is most powerful
articles.statement:
**Thresholding the log-odds score is most powerful** (Neyman–Pearson): a test `φ` of the
background (null) against the site model whose background size is at most that of the
threshold test `score > t` has at most its power.

articles.title: The expected log-odds score is the total information content
articles.statement:
Under the site model,
`E[score] = log 2 · ∑ᵢ IC(pᵢ ‖ q)`. This is an identity for every `q` (both sides use the same
logarithms); it is an expected log-likelihood ratio for a positive background.

articles.title: Product site likelihoods form a distribution
articles.statement: A product of column distributions is a distribution on sites.

articles.title: The target score is positive
articles.statement:
At the Karlin–Altschul root `λ > 0`, the expected score
`∑ q_{ab} s_{ab}` under the target frequencies is positive.

articles.title: Implicit target frequencies of a score matrix
articles.statement: The implicit target frequencies `q_{ab} = pₐ p_b e^{λ s_{ab}}` of a score matrix.

articles.title: Window of a sequence starting at a position
articles.statement: The window of length `w` of `x` starting at `i`.

articles.title: Likelihood ratio of a motif window
articles.statement:
The likelihood ratio of the window at `j` under the site model `θ` against the background
`q`, and `1` when there is no motif occurrence.

articles.title: Window of a sequence at a given start
articles.statement: The window of width `w` of `x` starting at `j`.

articles.title: Joint probability of class and features in naive Bayes
articles.statement:
The joint probability of class `c` (`true` = damaging) and feature values `x`:
`π ∏ P_D(x_j)` or `(1 - π) ∏ P_B(x_j)`.

articles.title: Log-likelihood ratio of a feature value
articles.statement: The log-likelihood ratio `log (P_D(v) / P_B(v))` of value `v` of feature `j`.

articles.title: Two-class naive Bayes model
articles.statement:
A two-class naive Bayes model: class *damaging* has prior `prior ∈ (0, 1)`, class *benign*
the complement; each feature `j` takes values in the finite type `X j` with class-conditional
probabilities `damaging j` and `benign j`, assumed positive; features are conditionally
independent given the class. The tables are estimated from training data.

articles.title: Naive-Bayes posterior
articles.statement:
The posterior probability of *damaging* is the logistic function
of the score.

articles.title: Naive Bayes posterior is strictly monotone in the score
articles.statement: The posterior is strictly monotone in the score.

articles.title: Monotonicity in a feature value
articles.statement:
Let feature `j` carry a numerical value `g v` (for
example a PSIC-difference bin) such that its likelihood ratio `P_D(v) / P_B(v)` is monotone in
`g v`. With the other features fixed, the posterior is monotone in `g`.

articles.title: Naive Bayes posterior probability of damage
articles.statement:
The posterior probability that the variant is damaging given feature values `x`
(Bayes' rule on the joint law).

articles.title: Profile log-odds score of a residue
articles.statement:
The profile log-odds score `log (p a / q a)` of residue `a`: `p` is the position-specific
profile probability (estimated from aligned homologs), `q` the background probability.
Meaningful for `p a, q a > 0`; otherwise Lean's `log 0 = 0` and `x / 0 = 0` give junk.

articles.title: PSIC difference as a log ratio of likelihood ratios
articles.statement: The PSIC difference is the log of the ratio of the two residues' likelihood ratios.

articles.title: Positivity criterion for the PSIC difference
articles.statement:
The PSIC difference is positive iff the wild type is more enriched in the profile, relative
to background, than the mutant.

articles.title: PSIC score difference of a substitution
articles.statement:
The PSIC score difference of a substitution from the wild-type residue `wt` to the mutant
residue `mt`: `profileScore p q wt - profileScore p q mt`.

articles.title: Naive Bayes score
articles.statement: The naive-Bayes score: prior log-odds plus the features' log-likelihood ratios.

articles.title: Naive Bayes joint law is a probability law
articles.statement: The joint law of class and features is a probability law.

articles.title: Gibbs' inequality for the profile score
articles.statement:
If `p` and `q` are probability vectors and
`q` is positive, the expected score under the profile, `∑ p a log (p a / q a)` (the
Kullback–Leibler divergence), is nonnegative.

articles.title: Expected profile score under the background is nonpositive
articles.statement:
If `p` and `q` are probability vectors and `p` is positive, the expected score under the
background, `∑ q a log (p a / q a)`, is nonpositive.

articles.title: The score is a log-likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
For a sequence `s` over independent positions with
profiles `p j` and background `q` (all positive), the summed profile score is the log of the
likelihood ratio `∏ p_j(s_j) / ∏ q(s_j)` of the profile model against the background.

articles.title: Bound at an intermediate point, sum form
articles.statement:
For integers $a$, $d$, $t$ and $w$, if
$|a| \le w$, $|a + d| \le w$ and $0 \le t \le d$, then $|a + t| \le w$.

Used for runs of alignment columns that consume only letters of the first sequence, where the
offset difference grows.

articles.title: Bound at an intermediate point, difference form
articles.statement:
For integers $a$, $d$, $t$ and $w$,
if $|a| \le w$, $|a - d| \le w$ and $0 \le t \le d$, then $|a - t| \le w$.

Used for the gap phases of an alignment, where the offset difference interpolates between its
start and end values.

articles.title: Alignment score is at most minus the number of gap columns
articles.statement:
With nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at most `-1`, an alignment scores at most
minus its number of gap columns.

articles.title: The diagonal alignment stays in the band
articles.statement:
Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x$, $y$
be lists of lengths $m$ and $n$. If $|i - j| \le w$ and $|(i + m) - (j + n)| \le w$, then the
band check of the diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true.

The match phase keeps the offset difference and the gap phases interpolate it.

articles.title: A passing band check bounds the final offset
articles.statement:
Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$A$ be an alignment. If the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true, then
$|(i + p) - (j + q)| \le w$, where $p$ and $q$ are the numbers of columns of $A$ whose first,
respectively second, entry is present.

articles.title: Columns using only the first sequence stay in the band
articles.statement:
Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $x$ be a list of length $n$, and let $A$ be the alignment with one column for each element
$a$ of $x$, in order, with first entry $a$ and empty second entry. If $|i - j| \le w$ and
$|(i + n) - j| \le w$, then the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset
$(i, j)$ is true.

articles.title: Columns using only the second sequence stay in the band
articles.statement:
Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $y$ be a list of length $n$, and let $A$ be the alignment with one column for each element
$b$ of $y$, in order, with empty first entry and second entry $b$. If $|i - j| \le w$ and
$|i - (j + n)| \le w$, then the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset
$(i, j)$ is true.

articles.title: An alignment with few gap columns stays in the band from its start
articles.statement:
Along every prefix, the offset difference is at most the starting difference plus the number
of gap columns: an alignment starting at `(i, j)` stays in the band of width `w` as soon as
`|i - j| + gapColumns A ≤ w`.

articles.title: Band check from a starting offset
articles.statement:
Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$ be a band width. For natural
numbers $i$, $j$ and an alignment $A$, the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$
is true exactly when every prefix $P$ of $A$ (including the empty prefix and $A$ itself)
satisfies $|(i + p) - (j + q)| \le w$, where $p$ and $q$ are the numbers of columns of $P$
whose first, respectively second, entry is present.

articles.title: Banded alignment is exact when some optimal alignment is banded
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an
integer substitution score on an alphabet, $g$ an integer gap score and $w \in \mathbb{N}$ a
band width. For sequences $x$ and $y$ over the alphabet, if some alignment of $x$ and $y$ is
banded with width $w$ and has score (under $\sigma$ and $g$) equal to the Needleman–Wunsch
score of $x$ and $y$, then the banded score of $x$ and $y$ (under $\sigma$, $g$ and width $w$)
is defined and equals their Needleman–Wunsch score.

articles.title: The banded optimum is exact
articles.statement:
**The banded optimum is exact** when the optimal score is at least `-w` (optimal cost at
most `w`), for nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at most `-1`: some optimal
alignment exists and, by the band lemma, it is `w`-banded.

articles.title: The banded score is at most the Needleman–Wunsch score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an integer
substitution score on an alphabet, $g$ an integer gap score and $w \in \mathbb{N}$ a band
width. For sequences $x$ and $y$ over the alphabet and an integer $s$, if the banded score of
$x$ and $y$ (under $\sigma$, $g$ and width $w$) is defined and equals $s$, then $s$ is at most
the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: No banded score when the lengths differ by more than the band width
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be
an integer substitution score on an alphabet, $g$ an integer gap score and $w \in \mathbb{N}$ a
band width. For sequences $x$ and $y$ over the alphabet, of lengths $m$ and $n$, with
$w < |m - n|$, the banded score of $x$ and $y$ (under $\sigma$, $g$ and width $w$) is undefined:
no alignment of $x$ and $y$ is banded with width $w$.

articles.title: The banded score is defined when the lengths are close
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score
$\sigma$, assigning an integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to each pair of letters $a$, $b$, an integer gap
score $g$ and a band width $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If two sequences $x$ and $y$ have lengths differing
by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$, then the banded alignment score of $x$
and $y$ (for $\sigma$, $g$ and $w$) is defined: it equals some integer $s$.

articles.title: Banded alignment score
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score $\sigma$, assigning an integer
$\sigma(a, b)$ to each pair of letters $a$, $b$, an integer gap score $g$ and a band width
$w \in \mathbb{N}$. The banded alignment score of two sequences $x$ and $y$ is the maximum, over
all valid alignments of $x$ and $y$ that are banded with width $w$, of the (integer) alignment
score with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. It has no value (it is the empty optional value) when no
such alignment exists.

articles.title: Diagonal alignment
articles.statement:
For sequences $x = x_1 \dots x_m$ and $y = y_1 \dots y_n$, let
$k = \min(m, n)$. The diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ consists of the columns
$(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_k, y_k)$, which pair letters by position whether or not they are equal,
followed by one column for each remaining letter of the longer sequence, in order, pairing that
letter with a gap.

articles.title: Number of gap columns of an alignment
articles.statement: The number of gap columns of an alignment: columns with exactly one letter.

articles.title: The diagonal alignment is a valid alignment
articles.statement:
For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the diagonal
alignment of $x$ and $y$ is a valid alignment of $x$ and $y$: none of its columns consists of two
gaps, and deleting the gaps from its first and second rows gives $x$ and $y$ respectively.

articles.title: The diagonal alignment is banded
articles.statement:
Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If two sequences $x$ and $y$
have lengths differing by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$, then the diagonal
alignment of $x$ and $y$ is banded with width $w$.

articles.title: Banded alignments force close lengths
articles.statement:
Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If $A$ is a valid alignment
of sequences $x$ and $y$ and $A$ is banded with width $w$, then the lengths of $x$ and $y$ differ
by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$.

articles.title: An alignment with at most w gap columns is w-banded
articles.statement: An alignment with at most `w` gap columns is `w`-banded.

articles.title: The band lemma
articles.statement:
**The band lemma** (Ukkonen 1985): with nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at
most `-1`, every alignment scoring at least `-w` (cost at most `w`) is `w`-banded.

articles.title: Banded alignments
articles.statement:
Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. An alignment $A$ is banded with width $w$ when,
for every prefix of $A$ (including the empty prefix and $A$ itself), the number of columns of
that prefix with a letter in the first row and the number with a letter in the second row
differ by at most $w$.

articles.title: Linear gaps as affine gaps, from any gap state
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution
score and $g$ an integer. If the gap-open cost and the gap-extend cost both equal $g$, then for
every alignment $A$ and every gap state $p$, the affine-gap score of $A$ started from state $p$,
with substitution score $\sigma$, equals the alignment score of $A$ with substitution score
$\sigma$ and gap penalty $g$.

articles.title: Affine-gap score from a gap state
articles.statement:
Fix an integer substitution score $\sigma$, an integer
gap-open cost $o$ and an integer gap-extend cost $e$. The affine-gap score of an alignment started
from a gap state $p$ is the sum of its column scores, computed left to right while carrying a gap
state that starts at $p$ and is updated after each column. The empty alignment scores $0$. A
column pairing an element $a$ of the first sequence with an element $b$ of the second scores
$\sigma(a, b)$ and sets the state to $\mathrm{none}$. A column pairing an element of the first
sequence with a gap has kind $\mathrm{gapX}$, and a column pairing a gap with an element of the
second sequence has kind $\mathrm{gapY}$; such a column scores $e$ if the carried state equals its
kind and $o$ otherwise, and sets the state to its kind. A column of two gaps scores $0$ and sets
the state to $\mathrm{none}$.

The column of two gaps cannot occur in a valid alignment; it is scored as a no-op.

articles.title: Linear gaps are affine gaps with equal costs
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution
score and $g$ an integer. If the gap-open cost and the gap-extend cost both equal $g$, then for
every alignment $A$, the affine-gap score of $A$ with substitution score $\sigma$ equals the
alignment score of $A$ with substitution score $\sigma$ and gap penalty $g$.

articles.title: Gotoh is optimal
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score, $o$ an integer gap-open
cost and $e$ an integer gap-extend cost. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ and every valid alignment
$A$ of $x$ and $y$, the affine-gap score of $A$ is at most the Gotoh score of $x$ and $y$, both
taken with $\sigma$, $o$ and $e$.

articles.title: The table is an upper bound
articles.statement:
Every alignment of `xs` and `ys` has affine-gap score at
most `gotohTab`.

articles.title: Affine-gap alignment score
articles.statement:
Given an integer substitution score $\sigma$, an integer
gap-open cost $o$ and an integer gap-extend cost $e$, the affine-gap score of an alignment is its
affine-gap score from a gap state, started from the state $\mathrm{none}$ (no open gap run).

articles.title: Specification of a Gotoh table cell
articles.statement:
The specification of a cell: the three continuation values `(M, X, Y)` of the suffix pair
`(xs, ys)`, given that the previous column was a match, a gap in `ys`, or a gap in `xs`.

articles.title: Gotoh is attained
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score, $o$ an integer gap-open
cost and $e$ an integer gap-extend cost. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ there is a valid alignment
$A$ of $x$ and $y$ whose affine-gap score equals the Gotoh score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with
$\sigma$, $o$ and $e$.

articles.title: The table is attained
articles.statement: Some alignment of `xs` and `ys` has affine-gap score `gotohTab`.

articles.title: The first row
articles.statement: `firstRow ys` holds the cells of `([], t)` for the suffixes `t` of `ys`.

articles.title: Gotoh table row of the empty first suffix
articles.statement:
The row of the suffix `[]` of `xs`: the cells of `([], t)` for the suffixes `t` of `ys`,
longest first, each one gap column in `xs` more than the next.

articles.title: Gap cost
articles.statement:
Given an integer gap-open cost $o$, an integer gap-extend cost $e$ and gap states
$p$ (of the previous column) and $c$ (of the current gap column), the cost of the current column
is $e$ if $p = c$ (the column continues a run) and $o$ otherwise (it opens a run).

articles.title: Adding a column to a gap run
articles.statement:
For an integer gap-open cost $o$, an integer gap-extend cost
$e$, gap states $p$ and $c$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the gap cost of a column in state $c$ after
state $p$, plus the cost of a run of $k$ columns in state $c$ that follows state $c$, equals the
cost of a run of $k + 1$ columns in state $c$ that follows state $p$.

articles.title: Cost of a gap run
articles.statement:
Given an integer gap-open cost $o$, an integer gap-extend cost $e$, gap
states $p$ (of the column before the run) and $c$ (of the run's columns) and a length
$k \in \mathbb{N}$, the cost of a run of $k$ gap columns is $k e$ if $p = c$ (the run continues
an open run); otherwise it is $0$ for $k = 0$ and $o + (k - 1) e$ for $k \ge 1$.

articles.title: Gap states
articles.statement:
A gap state is one of three values: $\mathrm{none}$, $\mathrm{gapX}$ and
$\mathrm{gapY}$. The affine-gap score and the Gotoh recursion carry one as the kind of the previous
column: $\mathrm{gapX}$ after a column pairing an element of the first sequence with a gap,
$\mathrm{gapY}$ after a column pairing a gap with an element of the second sequence, and
$\mathrm{none}$ otherwise, including before the first column.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded Gotoh recursion
articles.statement:
Fix an integer-valued scoring function $\sigma$ on pairs of
letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend penalties $g_o$ and $g_e$. A gap state records what
the previous alignment column was: a match ($\mathrm{none}$), a gap in the second sequence
($\mathrm{gapX}$) or a gap in the first sequence ($\mathrm{gapY}$). For gap states $p$, $q$ let
$c(p, q)$ be the gap cost, $g_e$ if $p = q$ and $g_o$ otherwise. Write $\varepsilon$ for the
empty sequence and $a \cdot u$ for the sequence with first letter $a$ followed by $u$. For fuel
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, sequences $u$, $v$ and a gap state $p$, the integer $G_n(u, v, p)$ is defined
by recursion on $n$: $G_0(u, v, p) = 0$, $G_{n+1}(\varepsilon, \varepsilon, p) = 0$,
$G_{n+1}(\varepsilon, b \cdot v, p) = c(p, \mathrm{gapY}) + G_n(\varepsilon, v, \mathrm{gapY})$,
$G_{n+1}(a \cdot u, \varepsilon, p) = c(p, \mathrm{gapX}) + G_n(u, \varepsilon, \mathrm{gapX})$,
and $G_{n+1}(a \cdot u, b \cdot v, p)$ is the maximum of $\sigma(a, b) + G_n(u, v, \mathrm{none})$,
$c(p, \mathrm{gapX}) + G_n(u, b \cdot v, \mathrm{gapX})$ and
$c(p, \mathrm{gapY}) + G_n(a \cdot u, v, \mathrm{gapY})$.

With fuel at least the sum of the two lengths this is the Gotoh dynamic program; with less fuel
the base case $G_0 = 0$ cuts the recursion short.

articles.title: First-column recurrence for the continuation after a gap in the second sequence
articles.statement:
Fix an
integer-valued scoring function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend
penalties $g_o$ and $g_e$. For sequences $u$, $v$ let $N(u, v)$, $X(u, v)$ and $Y(u, v)$ be the
Gotoh continuation values when the previous column was a match, a gap in $v$ and a gap in $u$
respectively, and write $a \cdot u$ for the sequence with first letter $a$ followed by $u$. For
all letters $a$, $b$ and sequences $u$, $v$, the value $X(a \cdot u, b \cdot v)$ is the maximum
of $N(u, v) + \sigma(a, b)$, $X(u, b \cdot v) + g_e$ and $Y(a \cdot u, v) + g_o$.

articles.title: Continuation after a gap in the second sequence, empty first sequence
articles.statement:
Fix a scoring
function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend penalties $g_o$ and
$g_e$, and let $X(u, v)$ be the Gotoh continuation value of sequences $u$, $v$ when the previous
column was a gap in $v$. For every sequence $v$ of length $k$, the value $X(\varepsilon, v)$,
where $\varepsilon$ is the empty sequence, is the cost of one freshly opened gap run of length
$k$: it is $0$ if $k = 0$ and $g_o + (k - 1) g_e$ if $k \ge 1$.

articles.title: Continuation after a gap in the second sequence, empty second sequence
articles.statement:
Fix a scoring
function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend penalties $g_o$ and
$g_e$, and let $X(u, v)$ be the Gotoh continuation value of sequences $u$, $v$ when the previous
column was a gap in $v$. For every sequence $u$ of length $k$, the value $X(u, \varepsilon)$,
where $\varepsilon$ is the empty sequence, equals $k \, g_e$: the open gap run is extended by
$k$ columns.

articles.title: Gotoh continuation value after a gap in the second sequence
articles.statement:
Fix an integer-valued
scoring function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend penalties $g_o$
and $g_e$. For sequences $u$ and $v$, the value $X(u, v)$ is the fuel-bounded Gotoh recursion on
$u$ and $v$, run with fuel equal to the sum of their lengths and started in the gap state where
the previous column was a gap in $v$.

It is the best affine-gap score of an alignment of $u$ with $v$ scored from that state. It is a
continuation value, not an endpoint-restricted matrix: the next column may be a match or either
gap, and the previous state only makes a next gap in $v$ cost $g_e$ instead of $g_o$.

articles.title: First-column recurrence for the continuation after a gap in the first sequence
articles.statement:
Fix an
integer-valued scoring function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend
penalties $g_o$ and $g_e$. For sequences $u$, $v$ let $N(u, v)$, $X(u, v)$ and $Y(u, v)$ be the
Gotoh continuation values when the previous column was a match, a gap in $v$ and a gap in $u$
respectively, and write $a \cdot u$ for the sequence with first letter $a$ followed by $u$. For
all letters $a$, $b$ and sequences $u$, $v$, the value $Y(a \cdot u, b \cdot v)$ is the maximum
of $N(u, v) + \sigma(a, b)$, $X(u, b \cdot v) + g_o$ and $Y(a \cdot u, v) + g_e$.

articles.title: Continuation after a gap in the first sequence, empty first sequence
articles.statement:
Fix a scoring
function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend penalties $g_o$ and
$g_e$, and let $Y(u, v)$ be the Gotoh continuation value of sequences $u$, $v$ when the previous
column was a gap in $u$. For every sequence $v$ of length $k$, the value $Y(\varepsilon, v)$,
where $\varepsilon$ is the empty sequence, equals $k \, g_e$: the open gap run is extended by
$k$ columns.

articles.title: Continuation after a gap in the first sequence, empty second sequence
articles.statement:
Fix a scoring
function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend penalties $g_o$ and
$g_e$, and let $Y(u, v)$ be the Gotoh continuation value of sequences $u$, $v$ when the previous
column was a gap in $u$. For every sequence $u$ of length $k$, the value $Y(u, \varepsilon)$,
where $\varepsilon$ is the empty sequence, is the cost of one freshly opened gap run of length
$k$: it is $0$ if $k = 0$ and $g_o + (k - 1) g_e$ if $k \ge 1$.

articles.title: Gotoh continuation value after a gap in the first sequence
articles.statement:
Fix an integer-valued
scoring function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend penalties $g_o$
and $g_e$. For sequences $u$ and $v$, the value $Y(u, v)$ is the fuel-bounded Gotoh recursion on
$u$ and $v$, run with fuel equal to the sum of their lengths and started in the gap state where
the previous column was a gap in $u$.

It is the best affine-gap score of an alignment of $u$ with $v$ scored from that state. It is a
continuation value, not an endpoint-restricted matrix: the next column may be a match or either
gap, and the previous state only makes a next gap in $u$ cost $g_e$ instead of $g_o$.

articles.title: First-column recurrence for the continuation after a match
articles.statement:
Fix an
integer-valued scoring function $\sigma$ on pairs of letters and integer gap-open and gap-extend
penalties $g_o$ and $g_e$. For sequences $u$, $v$ let $N(u, v)$, $X(u, v)$ and $Y(u, v)$ be the
Gotoh continuation values when the previous column was a match, a gap in $v$ and a gap in $u$
respectively, and write $a \cdot u$ for the sequence with first letter $a$ followed by $u$. For
all letters $a$, $b$ and sequences $u$, $v$, the value $N(a \cdot u, b \cdot v)$ is the maximum
of $N(u, v) + \sigma(a, b)$, $X(u, b \cdot v) + g_o$ and $Y(a \cdot u, v) + g_o$.

articles.title: Gotoh value against an empty first sequence
articles.statement:
Let $g_o$ and $g_e$ be the gap-open and
gap-extend scores. For every sequence $y$ of length $n$, the Gotoh value with no open gap run of
the empty sequence against $y$ equals the score of a freshly opened run of $n$ gaps in the first
sequence: $0$ if $n = 0$, and $g_o + (n - 1) g_e$ if $n \ge 1$.

articles.title: Gotoh value against an empty second sequence
articles.statement:
Let $g_o$ and $g_e$ be the gap-open and
gap-extend scores. For every sequence $x$ of length $n$, the Gotoh value with no open gap run of
$x$ against the empty sequence equals the score of a freshly opened run of $n$ gaps in the second
sequence: $0$ if $n = 0$, and $g_o + (n - 1) g_e$ if $n \ge 1$.

articles.title: Gotoh value with no open gap run
articles.statement:
Given a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap-open score
$g_o$ and a gap-extend score $g_e$, this is the value of the Gotoh dynamic program on sequences
$x$ and $y$ when no gap run is open (the previous column was a match, or there is no previous
column): the best affine-gap score of an alignment of $x$ and $y$, where a match column pairing
$a$ with $b$ scores $\sigma(a, b)$ and a gap column scores $g_e$ if it continues a run of gaps in
the same sequence and $g_o$ otherwise.

It is a continuation value, not an endpoint-restricted matrix: the first column may be a match
or either gap.

articles.title: The rows of the table
articles.statement:
The row of `xs` holds `cellSpec xs t` for every suffix `t` of
`ys`, longest first.

articles.title: Gotoh table row of a suffix of the first sequence
articles.statement:
The row of the suffix `xs` (of the first sequence) of the table, computed from the rows of
its shorter suffixes.

articles.title: Gotoh with equal gap scores is Needleman–Wunsch
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score
and $g$ an integer. If the gap-open and gap-extend scores both equal $g$, then for all sequences
$x$ and $y$ the Gotoh score (optimal affine-gap alignment score) of $x$ and $y$ equals the
Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$ with substitution score $\sigma$ and gap score $g$.

articles.title: Gotoh score
articles.statement:
For a substitution score $\sigma$ and gap-open and gap-extend scores $g_o$
and $g_e$, the Gotoh score of sequences $x$ and $y$ is the Gotoh value of $x$ against $y$ with no
open gap run, since no gap run is open before the first column.

It is the optimal affine-gap alignment score of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: The table computes the optimal affine-gap score
articles.statement: **The table computes the optimal affine-gap score** (Gotoh 1982): `gotohTab = gotohScore`.

articles.title: Gotoh table with equal gap costs gives the Needleman–Wunsch score
articles.statement:
With `gapOpen = gapExtend = gap`, the Gotoh table computes the linear-gap Needleman–Wunsch
score.

articles.title: The Gotoh table
articles.statement: The `M` value of the cell `(xs, ys)`.

articles.title: Prepending a column with a gap in the second sequence
articles.statement:
If $A$ is a valid alignment of
sequences $x$ and $y$, then for every element $a$, the alignment obtained by prepending to $A$ the
column that pairs $a$ with a gap is a valid alignment of $a x$ (the sequence $x$ with $a$
prepended) and $y$.

articles.title: Prepending a column with a gap in the first sequence
articles.statement:
If $A$ is a valid alignment of
sequences $x$ and $y$, then for every element $b$, the alignment obtained by prepending to $A$ the
column that pairs a gap with $b$ is a valid alignment of $x$ and $b y$ (the sequence $y$ with $b$
prepended).

articles.title: Prepending a match column
articles.statement:
If $A$ is a valid alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$, then for
all elements $a$ and $b$, the alignment obtained by prepending to $A$ the column that pairs $a$
with $b$ is a valid alignment of $a x$ and $b y$ (the sequences $x$ and $y$ with $a$ and $b$
prepended).

articles.title: Removing a leading column with a gap in the second sequence
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an alignment, $a$
an element and $x$, $y$ sequences. If prepending to $A$ the column that pairs $a$ with a gap gives
a valid alignment of $a x$ (the sequence $x$ with $a$ prepended) and $y$, then $A$ is a valid
alignment of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Removing a leading column with a gap in the first sequence
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an alignment, $b$
an element and $x$, $y$ sequences. If prepending to $A$ the column that pairs a gap with $b$ gives
a valid alignment of $x$ and $b y$ (the sequence $y$ with $b$ prepended), then $A$ is a valid
alignment of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Removing a leading match column from a valid alignment
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be elements,
let $xs$ and $ys$ be sequences, and let $A$ be an alignment. If the alignment whose first column
is the match column $(a, b)$, followed by the columns of $A$, is a valid alignment of the
sequence $a$ followed by $xs$ and the sequence $b$ followed by $ys$, then $A$ is a valid
alignment of $xs$ and $ys$.

articles.title: One row of the table
articles.statement:
From the row of the suffix `xs`, `nextRow` computes the row of
`a :: xs`: the cells `cellSpec (a :: xs) t` for the suffixes `t` of `ys`, longest first.

articles.title: Gotoh table row from the previous row
articles.statement:
The row of `a :: xs` from the row `prev` of `xs`, over the remaining suffixes of `ys`, longest
first; each cell uses the cell to its right in the same row. A row `prev` that is too short gives
junk cells (this does not happen for rows of the table, `nextRow_eq`).

articles.title: Gotoh cell recurrence against an empty second suffix
articles.statement: The cell of `(a :: xs, [])` from the cell `o` of `(xs, [])`: one more gap column in `ys`.

articles.title: Gotoh cell recurrence from diagonal, upper and left cells
articles.statement:
The cell of `(a :: xs, b :: ys)` from the cells `diag` of `(xs, ys)`, `up` of `(xs, b :: ys)`
and `left` of `(a :: xs, ys)`: a match continues from `M`, a gap in `ys` from `X` (extending if
the previous column was one), a gap in `xs` from `Y`.

articles.title: Hirschberg reconstruction with enough fuel attains the optimum
articles.statement:
Fix a type $\alpha$, a
substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$.
For every fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all lists $xs$, $ys$ over $\alpha$ with
$|xs| + |ys| \le n$, the alignment score of the Hirschberg reconstruction of $xs$ and $ys$ with
fuel $n$ equals the Needleman–Wunsch score of $xs$ and $ys$.

articles.title: Hirschberg reconstruction attains the Needleman–Wunsch optimum
articles.statement:
Fix a type $\alpha$, a
substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$.
For all lists $xs$, $ys$ over $\alpha$, the alignment score of the Hirschberg alignment of $xs$
and $ys$ equals the Needleman–Wunsch score of $xs$ and $ys$.

articles.title: The base-case alignment is optimal
articles.statement:
Fix a type $\alpha$, a substitution score
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$. For all lists
$xs$, $ys$ over $\alpha$ with $|xs| \le 1$ and $|ys| \le 1$, the alignment score of the
base-case alignment of $xs$ and $ys$ equals the Needleman–Wunsch score of $xs$ and $ys$.

articles.title: The argmax over $\{0, \dots, n\}$ is at most $n$
articles.statement:
For every function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the argmax of $f$ over
$\{0, \dots, n\}$ is at most $n$.

articles.title: The argmax over $\{0, \dots, n\}$ maximizes the function there
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$, let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $m$ be the argmax of $f$ over
$\{0, \dots, n\}$. Then $f(k) \le f(m)$ for every $k \le n$.

articles.title: Argmax over an initial segment
articles.statement:
For a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the argmax of $f$ over $\{0, \dots, n\}$ is the least $k \le n$ such that
$f(j) \le f(k)$ for all $j \le n$.

It is computed as the first maximizer of $f$ on the list $[0, 1, \dots, n]$, which is never
empty.

articles.title: Every cut of the first list extends to an optimal split
articles.statement:
Fix a type $\alpha$, a
substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$.
Write $S(u, v)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of lists $u$, $v$, and $u_{\lt m}$ for the first
$m$ elements of $u$ and $u_{\ge m}$ for the rest. For all lists $xs$, $ys$ over $\alpha$ and
every $m \le |xs|$, there is $k \le |ys|$ with
$S(xs_{\lt m}, ys_{\lt k}) + S(xs_{\ge m}, ys_{\ge k}) = S(xs, ys)$.

articles.title: Every cut of the second list extends to an optimal split
articles.statement:
Fix a type $\alpha$, a
substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$.
Write $S(u, v)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of lists $u$, $v$, and $u_{\lt m}$ for the first
$m$ elements of $u$ and $u_{\ge m}$ for the rest. For all lists $xs$, $ys$ over $\alpha$ and
every $m \le |ys|$, there is $k \le |xs|$ with
$S(xs_{\lt k}, ys_{\lt m}) + S(xs_{\ge k}, ys_{\ge m}) = S(xs, ys)$.

articles.title: Hirschberg reconstruction on lists of length at most one
articles.statement:
Fix a type $\alpha$, a
substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$.
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all lists $xs$, $ys$ over $\alpha$ with $|xs| \le 1$ and
$|ys| \le 1$, the Hirschberg reconstruction of $xs$ and $ys$ with fuel $n + 1$ is the
base-case alignment of $xs$ and $ys$.

articles.title: Hirschberg reconstruction splits the longer first list
articles.statement:
Fix a type $\alpha$, a
substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$.
Write $H_n(u, v)$ for the Hirschberg reconstruction of lists $u$, $v$ with fuel $n$, $S(u, v)$
for their Needleman–Wunsch score, and $u_{\lt m}$, $u_{\ge m}$ for the first $m$ elements of $u$
and the rest. Let $xs$, $ys$ be lists over $\alpha$ that are not both of length at most $1$,
with $|ys| < |xs|$. Put $h = \lfloor |xs| / 2 \rfloor$ and let $k$ be the least maximizer over
$\{0, \dots, |ys|\}$ of $j \mapsto S(xs_{\lt h}, ys_{\lt j}) + S(xs_{\ge h}, ys_{\ge j})$. Then
for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $H_{n+1}(xs, ys)$ is the concatenation of
$H_n(xs_{\lt h}, ys_{\lt k})$ and $H_n(xs_{\ge h}, ys_{\ge k})$.

articles.title: Hirschberg recursion step splitting the second sequence
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score
$\sigma$ assigning an integer to each pair of letters and an integer gap score $g$, and write
$\mathrm{NW}$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score. For a sequence $s$, write $s_{\lt j}$ for its first
$j$ letters and $s_{\ge j}$ for the remaining letters. Let $x$, $y$ be sequences with
$|y| \ge |x|$ that do not both have length at most $1$, let $m = \lfloor |y|/2 \rfloor$, and
let $k$ be the first index $j \in \{0, \dots, |x|\}$ that maximizes
$\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt j}, y_{\lt m}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge j}, y_{\ge m})$. Then for every natural
number $n$, the Hirschberg reconstruction of $x$ and $y$ with fuel $n + 1$ is the
concatenation of the Hirschberg reconstruction of $x_{\lt k}$ and $y_{\lt m}$ with fuel $n$ and the
Hirschberg reconstruction of $x_{\ge k}$ and $y_{\ge m}$ with fuel $n$.

articles.title: Hirschberg reconstruction with fuel
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score $\sigma$ assigning an
integer to each pair of letters and an integer gap score $g$, and write $\mathrm{NW}$ for the
Needleman–Wunsch score. For a sequence $s$, write $s_{\lt j}$ for its first $j$ letters and
$s_{\ge j}$ for the remaining letters. The Hirschberg reconstruction of sequences $x$ and $y$
with fuel $n$ is the alignment defined by recursion on $n$. With fuel $0$ it is the empty
alignment. With fuel $n + 1$: if $|x| \le 1$ and $|y| \le 1$, it is the base-case alignment
of $x$ and $y$; otherwise, if $|y| \ge |x|$, let $m = \lfloor |y|/2 \rfloor$ and let $k$ be
the first index $j \in \{0, \dots, |x|\}$ that maximizes
$\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt j}, y_{\lt m}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge j}, y_{\ge m})$, and the result is the
concatenation of the reconstructions with fuel $n$ of $x_{\lt k}$ and $y_{\lt m}$ and of $x_{\ge k}$
and $y_{\ge m}$; otherwise, let $m = \lfloor |x|/2 \rfloor$ and let $k$ be the first index
$j \in \{0, \dots, |y|\}$ that maximizes
$\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt m}, y_{\lt j}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge m}, y_{\ge j})$, and the result is the
concatenation of the reconstructions with fuel $n$ of $x_{\lt m}$ and $y_{\lt k}$ and of $x_{\ge m}$
and $y_{\ge k}$.

Hirschberg's alignment algorithm runs this reconstruction with fuel $|x| + |y|$.

articles.title: Hirschberg's alignment algorithm
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score $\sigma$ assigning an integer
to each pair of letters and an integer gap score $g$. The Hirschberg alignment of sequences $x$
and $y$ is the Hirschberg reconstruction of $x$ and $y$ with fuel $|x| + |y|$.

articles.title: Hirschberg reconstruction with enough fuel is valid
articles.statement:
For every substitution score
$\sigma$ assigning an integer to each pair of letters, integer gap score $g$, natural number
$n$ and sequences $x$, $y$ with $|x| + |y| \le n$, the Hirschberg reconstruction of $x$ and
$y$ with fuel $n$ is a valid alignment of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Hirschberg reconstruction is valid
articles.statement:
For every substitution score $\sigma$ assigning an
integer to each pair of letters, integer gap score $g$ and sequences $x$, $y$, the Hirschberg
alignment of $x$ and $y$ is a valid alignment of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: The base-case alignment is valid
articles.statement:
For every substitution score $\sigma$ assigning an
integer to each pair of letters, integer gap score $g$ and sequences $x$, $y$ with
$|x| \le 1$ and $|y| \le 1$, the base-case alignment of $x$ and $y$ is a valid alignment of
$x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Hirschberg split identity, splitting the first sequence
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score
$\sigma$ assigning an integer to each pair of letters and an integer gap score $g$, and write
$\mathrm{NW}$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score. For a sequence $s$, write $s_{\lt j}$ for its first
$j$ letters and $s_{\ge j}$ for the remaining letters. Let $x$, $y$ be sequences and
$m \le |x|$, and let $k$ be the first index $j \in \{0, \dots, |y|\}$ that maximizes
$\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt m}, y_{\lt j}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge m}, y_{\ge j})$. Then
$\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt m}, y_{\lt k}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge m}, y_{\ge k}) = \mathrm{NW}(x, y)$.

articles.title: Hirschberg split identity, splitting the second sequence
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score
$\sigma$ assigning an integer to each pair of letters and an integer gap score $g$, and write
$\mathrm{NW}$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score. For a sequence $s$, write $s_{\lt j}$ for its first
$j$ letters and $s_{\ge j}$ for the remaining letters. Let $x$, $y$ be sequences and
$m \le |y|$, and let $k$ be the first index $j \in \{0, \dots, |x|\}$ that maximizes
$\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt j}, y_{\lt m}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge j}, y_{\ge m})$. Then
$\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt k}, y_{\lt m}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge k}, y_{\ge m}) = \mathrm{NW}(x, y)$.

articles.title: Needleman–Wunsch score of two single letters
articles.statement:
For every substitution score $\sigma$
assigning an integer to each pair of letters, integer gap score $g$ and letters $a$, $b$, the
Needleman–Wunsch score of the one-letter sequences $[a]$ and $[b]$ is
$\max(\sigma(a, b), g + g)$: the better of matching $a$ with $b$ and gapping both.

articles.title: Base-case alignment for Hirschberg
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score $\sigma$ assigning an
integer to each pair of letters and an integer gap score $g$, and write a column as a pair
whose missing entry, a gap, is marked $\bot$. The base-case alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$
is the empty alignment if both are empty; the single column $(\bot, b)$ if $x$ is empty and
$y = [b]$; the single column $(a, \bot)$ if $x = [a]$ and $y$ is empty; if $x = [a]$ and
$y = [b]$, it is the single column $(a, b)$ when $\sigma(a, b) \ge 2g$ and the two columns
$(a, \bot)$, $(\bot, b)$ otherwise; and it is the empty alignment when $x$ or $y$ has length
at least $2$.

articles.title: A split of the first sequence scores at most the Needleman–Wunsch optimum
articles.statement:
Let
$\sigma$ be an integer-valued substitution score on an alphabet, let $g$ be an integer gap
score, and write $\mathrm{NW}(x, y)$ for the optimal Needleman–Wunsch global alignment score
of sequences $x$ and $y$ under $\sigma$ and $g$. For sequences $x$, $y$ and natural numbers
$m$, $k$, let $x_{\lt m}$ be the first $m$ letters of $x$ (all of $x$ if $m$ is at least its
