length) and $x_{\ge m}$ the remaining letters, and define $y_{\lt k}$ and $y_{\ge k}$ likewise.
Then $\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt m}, y_{\lt k}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge m}, y_{\ge k}) \le \mathrm{NW}(x, y)$.

articles.title: A split of the second sequence scores at most the Needleman–Wunsch optimum
articles.statement:
Let
$\sigma$ be an integer-valued substitution score on an alphabet, let $g$ be an integer gap
score, and write $\mathrm{NW}(x, y)$ for the optimal Needleman–Wunsch global alignment score
of sequences $x$ and $y$ under $\sigma$ and $g$. For sequences $x$, $y$ and natural numbers
$k$, $m$, let $x_{\lt k}$ be the first $k$ letters of $x$ (all of $x$ if $k$ is at least its
length) and $x_{\ge k}$ the remaining letters, and define $y_{\lt m}$ and $y_{\ge m}$ likewise.
Then $\mathrm{NW}(x_{\lt k}, y_{\lt m}) + \mathrm{NW}(x_{\ge k}, y_{\ge m}) \le \mathrm{NW}(x, y)$.

The bound holds because optimal alignments of the two halves concatenate to an alignment of
$x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Score of an induced pairwise alignment
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ assign an integer score to each
pair of letters and let $g$ be an integer gap score. For a multiple alignment $A$ of $k$
sequences and rows $i, j < k$, the score (with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$) of the pairwise
alignment induced by $A$ on rows $i$ and $j$ equals the sum, over all columns $c$ of $A$, of the
column score of the pair $(c_i, c_j)$.

articles.title: Sum-of-pairs score of a column
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ assign an integer score to each pair of
letters and let $g$ be an integer gap score. For a column $c$ of a multiple alignment of $k$
sequences, which gives each row $r < k$ either a letter or a gap $c_r$, the sum-of-pairs score of
$c$ is $\sum_{i < j < k} s(c_i, c_j)$, where $s$ is the pairwise column score: $\sigma(a, b)$ for
letters $a$ and $b$, $g$ for a letter against a gap, and $0$ for two gaps.

articles.title: Every family of sequences has a multiple alignment
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and
every family of $k$ sequences $s_0, \dots, s_{k-1}$ whose lengths sum to at most $n$, there is a
valid multiple alignment of $s_0, \dots, s_{k-1}$.

The bound $n$ is the parameter of the induction in the proof, which removes the first letter of
one nonempty sequence; taking $n$ to be the total length shows that every finite family of
sequences has a valid multiple alignment.

articles.title: Letters of the first row of an induced alignment
articles.statement:
For a multiple alignment $A$ of $k$
sequences and rows $i, j < k$, deleting the gaps from the first row of the pairwise alignment
induced by $A$ on rows $i$ and $j$ gives the same sequence as deleting the gaps from row $i$ of
$A$.

articles.title: Letters of the second row of an induced alignment
articles.statement:
For a multiple alignment $A$ of $k$
sequences and rows $i, j < k$, deleting the gaps from the second row of the pairwise alignment
induced by $A$ on rows $i$ and $j$ gives the same sequence as deleting the gaps from row $j$ of
$A$.

articles.title: Induced pairwise alignments are valid
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a valid multiple alignment of sequences
$s_0, \dots, s_{k-1}$. Then for all rows $i, j < k$, the pairwise alignment induced by $A$ on rows
$i$ and $j$ is a valid pairwise alignment of $s_i$ and $s_j$.

articles.title: Induced alignments have no all-gap column
articles.statement:
For a multiple alignment $A$ of $k$ sequences
and rows $i, j < k$, no column of the pairwise alignment induced by $A$ on rows $i$ and $j$ is a
gap in both rows.

articles.title: Induced pairwise alignment
articles.statement:
Given a multiple alignment $A$ of $k$ sequences and rows
$i, j < k$, the pairwise alignment induced by $A$ on rows $i$ and $j$ is obtained by keeping, for
each column $c$ of $A$ in order, the pair $(c_i, c_j)$, and dropping the columns in which both
$c_i$ and $c_j$ are gaps.

articles.title: Valid multiple alignment
articles.statement:
A multiple alignment $A$ of $k$ rows is a valid multiple
alignment of sequences $s_0, \dots, s_{k-1}$ when no column of $A$ consists only of gaps and, for
every $i < k$, deleting the gaps from row $i$ of $A$ gives $s_i$.

articles.title: The SP score is the sum of the induced pairwise scores
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ assign an integer
score to each pair of letters and let $g$ be an integer gap score. For every multiple alignment
$A$ of $k$ sequences, the sum-of-pairs score of $A$ equals the sum, over all pairs of rows
$i < j < k$, of the score of the pairwise alignment induced by $A$ on rows $i$ and $j$.

articles.title: The sum-of-pairs score is bounded by the pairwise optima
articles.statement:
Fix a score
$\sigma(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for each pair of letters $a, b$ of an alphabet $\alpha$ and a gap
score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$. Let $s_0, \dots, s_{k-1}$ be sequences over $\alpha$ and let $A$ be a
valid multiple alignment of them: no column of $A$ consists only of gaps, and deleting the gaps
from row $i$ of $A$ leaves $s_i$. Then the sum-of-pairs score of $A$ under $\sigma$ and $g$ is at
most $\sum_{0 \le i < j < k} \mathrm{NW}(s_i, s_j)$, where $\mathrm{NW}(s_i, s_j)$ is the optimal
global (Needleman–Wunsch) alignment score of $s_i$ and $s_j$ under $\sigma$ and $g$.

articles.title: Sum-of-pairs score
articles.statement:
Fix a score $\sigma(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for each pair of letters
$a, b$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$. For two entries $x, y$, each a letter or a gap, let
$s(x, y) = \sigma(x, y)$ if both are letters, $s(x, y) = g$ if exactly one is a gap, and
$s(x, y) = 0$ if both are gaps. The sum-of-pairs score of a multiple alignment $A$ of $k$
sequences is the sum, over the columns $c$ of $A$, of $\sum_{0 \le i < j < k} s(c_i, c_j)$,
where $c_i$ is the entry of $c$ in row $i$.

articles.title: Multiple alignments
articles.statement:
A multiple alignment with $k$ rows over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a
finite list of columns, each of which assigns to every row $i \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ either a
letter of $\alpha$ or a gap. No condition ties the rows to given sequences.

articles.title: Pairs of rows
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the finite set of all pairs $(i, j)$ with
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ and $i < j$, so that each unordered pair of distinct rows appears
exactly once.

articles.title: Every alignment weighs at most the Viterbi value
articles.statement: **Every alignment weighs at most the Viterbi value.**

articles.title: Joint weight of sequences and an alignment's state path
articles.statement:
The joint weight of the sequences and the state path of an alignment `A` (the path visits
`colState c` for each column `c`): the product of the transition and emission weights along the
path, from the begin state to the end state.

articles.title: Every alignment weighs at most the max recursion
articles.statement: **Every alignment weighs at most the max recursion** (nonnegative weights).

articles.title: Weight of an alignment read by an automaton
articles.statement:
The weight of an alignment read from control state `q`: the product of the column weights
along the alignment, then the final weight.

articles.title: Weighted alignment automaton
articles.statement:
A weighted automaton reading an alignment of a sequence over `α` with a sequence over `β`
column by column with a control state in `Q`: the weight of reading a column in a control
state, the next control state, and the final weight of a control state. Weights are in `R`.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded enumeration of two-alphabet alignments
articles.statement:
All alignments of `xs : List α` with `ys : List β`, by fuel recursion on the first column
(the same recursion as `Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.alignmentsAux`, for two alphabets). Implementation
detail: use `alignmentsOf`, whose fuel `xs.length + ys.length + 1` is enough.

articles.title: Alignments of two nonempty sequences by first column
articles.statement: The alignments of two nonempty sequences, by their first column.

articles.title: Alignments of a nonempty sequence with the empty one
articles.statement: The alignments of a nonempty sequence with the empty one.

articles.title: Two-alphabet alignments agree with single-alphabet alignments
articles.statement: On one alphabet, `alignmentsOf` is `Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.alignments`.

articles.title: Alignments of the empty sequence with a nonempty one
articles.statement: The alignments of the empty sequence with a nonempty one.

articles.title: All alignments of sequences over two alphabets
articles.statement:
All alignments of a sequence over `α` with a sequence over `β`: lists of columns
`Option α × Option β` with no `(none, none)` column whose rows filter to `xs` and `ys`
(`mem_alignmentsOf`), each listed once (`nodup_alignmentsOf`). For `β = α` this is
`Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.alignments` (`alignmentsOf_eq_alignments`).

articles.title: Independence-model weight of a sequence pair
articles.statement:
The independence-model weight for `xs` and `ys` (Durbin et al., chapter 4):
`η² (1 - η)^(|xs| + |ys|) ∏ q xs ∏ q ys`. This is a probability when `q` is a
normalized nonnegative distribution and `0 < η < 1`, as required by `LinearGapLogOdds`.

articles.title: Pair HMM state emitting an alignment column
articles.statement:
The state that emits an alignment column: `M` for `(some a, some b)`, `X` for
`(some a, none)`, `Y` for `(none, some b)` (and `M`, unused, for the invalid `(none, none)`).

articles.title: Emission weight of an alignment column
articles.statement: The emission weight of an alignment column (`0` for the invalid `(none, none)`).

articles.title: The Viterbi value is attained
articles.statement: **The Viterbi value is attained** by an alignment: the Viterbi alignment.

articles.title: The max recursion is attained
articles.statement: **The max recursion is attained** by an alignment.

articles.title: Memoryless pair HMM
articles.statement:
The pair HMM's transition weights do not depend on the current state: every transition into
an emitting state `s` (from the begin state or from any emitting state) has weight `π s`, and
every transition into the end state has weight `τ`.

articles.title: The pair-HMM recursion computes the total weight
articles.statement:
The sum over all alignments of
`xs` and `ys` of the joint weight of the sequences and the alignment.

articles.title: Total weight of a sequence pair under a pair HMM
articles.statement:
The total weight `P(xs, ys)` of a pair HMM: the total weight of all state paths that emit
`xs` and `ys` (`likelihood_eq_sum`), by the first-column recursion.

articles.title: Hypotheses of the linear-gap log-odds correspondence
articles.statement:
The hypotheses of the log-odds correspondence: a memoryless pair HMM with normalized
positive transition and emission probabilities, normalized positive background frequencies
and `0 < η < 1`, whose per-column log-odds scores against the independence model are the
integer scores `σ a b` (aligned pair) and `gap` (gap column).

articles.title: Log-odds of one alignment
articles.statement:
For a memoryless pair HMM, the log-odds of an alignment
against the independence model is its linear-gap alignment score plus `log (τ / η²)`.

articles.title: Log-odds Viterbi is linear-gap Needleman–Wunsch
articles.statement:
For a memoryless pair HMM whose
per-column log-odds scores are `σ a b` and `gap`, the log-odds Viterbi score against the
independence model is the Needleman–Wunsch score with substitution scores `σ` and linear gap
score `gap`, plus the length term `log (τ / η²)`.

articles.title: Max recursion on two nonempty sequences
articles.statement: The max recursion on two nonempty sequences.

articles.title: Max recursion with an empty second sequence
articles.statement: The max recursion when the second sequence is empty.

articles.title: Max recursion with an empty first sequence
articles.statement: The max recursion when the first sequence is empty.

articles.title: Max recursion on two empty sequences is the final weight
articles.statement: The max recursion on two empty sequences is the final weight.

articles.title: Max-recursion alignment value from a control state
articles.statement:
The max-recursion value of an alignment of `xs` and `ys` read from control state `q`, by
the first-column recursion (`alignWeight_le_maxDP`, `exists_alignWeight_eq_maxDP`). It is the
largest alignment weight only when the weights are nonnegative; in general it is the value of
the recursively chosen alignment.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded max recursion over alignments
articles.statement: The max recursion with fuel. Implementation detail: use `maxDP`.

articles.title: Membership in `alignmentsOf` is validity
articles.statement:
No `(none, none)` column, and the rows filter
to the two sequences.

articles.title: Each alignment is listed once
articles.statement: **Each alignment is listed once.**

articles.title: Nonnegative weights of a pair HMM
articles.statement:
Nonnegative transition weights into emitting states and nonnegative emission weights (the
transitions into the end state may have any sign: the Viterbi bound does not need them).

articles.title: Nonnegative column weights of an alignment automaton
articles.statement:
Nonnegative column weights. The final weights may have any sign: the max recursion bounds
every alignment weight without that (`alignWeight_le_maxDP`).

articles.title: Pair hidden Markov model
articles.statement:
A pair HMM over the alphabet `α` with weights in `R` (Durbin et al., chapter 4): the
transition weights from the silent begin state (`start`) and between emitting states (`trans`),
to the silent end state (`stop` from an emitting state, `startStop` for the empty alignment),
and the emission weights of the three emitting states.

articles.title: Emitting states of a pair HMM
articles.statement:
The emitting states of a pair HMM: `M` emits an aligned pair, `X` a letter of the first
sequence only, `Y` a letter of the second sequence only.

articles.title: Sum recursion on two nonempty sequences
articles.statement: The sum recursion on two nonempty sequences.

articles.title: Sum recursion with an empty second sequence
articles.statement: The sum recursion when the second sequence is empty.

articles.title: The sum recursion is the sum over alignments
articles.statement: **The sum recursion is the sum over alignments.**

articles.title: Sum recursion with an empty first sequence
articles.statement: The sum recursion when the first sequence is empty.

articles.title: Sum recursion on two empty sequences is the final weight
articles.statement: The sum recursion on two empty sequences is the final weight.

articles.title: Total alignment weight by first-column recursion
articles.statement:
The total weight of all alignments of `xs` and `ys` read from control state `q`, by the
first-column recursion (`sumDP_eq_sum`).

articles.title: Fuel-bounded sum recursion over alignments
articles.statement:
The sum recursion with fuel (the fuel bounds the recursion depth). Implementation detail:
use `sumDP`, whose fuel `xs.length + ys.length + 1` is enough.

articles.title: Nonnegative pair HMM gives a nonnegative alignment automaton
articles.statement: A pair HMM with nonnegative weights is a nonnegative alignment automaton.

articles.title: Pair HMM as an alignment automaton
articles.statement:
The pair HMM as an alignment automaton: the control state is the previous HMM state
(`none` for the begin state).

articles.title: Viterbi value of a pair HMM
articles.statement:
The Viterbi value of a pair HMM: the max-recursion value for `xs`, `ys`. It is the
largest joint weight over alignments when the HMM weights are nonnegative
(see `alignProb_le_viterbi`).

articles.title: Needleman–Wunsch is optimal
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a
substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ over
$\alpha$ and every valid alignment $A$ of $x$ and $y$, the score of $A$ with respect to
$\sigma$ and $g$ is at most the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Reversal preserves alignment score
articles.statement:
For every substitution score
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and alignment $A$, the
alignment obtained by listing the columns of $A$ in reverse order has the same score as $A$.

articles.title: Score of an alignment
articles.statement:
Given a substitution score $\sigma$, which assigns an integer
$\sigma(a, b)$ to all letters $a, b \in \alpha$, and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, the score of
an alignment $A$ over $\alpha$ is the sum, over all columns of $A$, of the score of the column
with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.

articles.title: Alignment
articles.statement:
An alignment over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a finite list of columns, where
each column is a pair $(u, v)$ and each of $u$ and $v$ is either a letter of $\alpha$ or a gap.

Whether an alignment is valid for two given sequences is a separate condition.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded enumeration of alignments
articles.statement:
Given a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sequences
$x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, this lists alignments column by column from the front. With fuel $0$
the list is empty. With fuel $n + 1$: two empty sequences give the single empty alignment; if
only $y$ is nonempty, with first letter $b$ and rest $y'$, each alignment of $x$ and $y'$ with
fuel $n$ is preceded by the column pairing a gap with $b$; if only $x$ is nonempty, with first
letter $a$ and rest $x'$, each alignment of $x'$ and $y$ with fuel $n$ is preceded by the
column pairing $a$ with a gap; and if both are nonempty, $x$ with first letter $a$ and rest $x'$
and $y$ with first letter $b$ and rest $y'$, the list consists of the alignments of $x'$ and
$y'$ preceded by the column $(a, b)$, then those of $x'$ and $y$ preceded by the column pairing
$a$ with a gap, then those of $x$ and $y'$ preceded by the column pairing a gap with $b$, each
computed with fuel $n$.

With fuel at least $|x| + |y| + 1$ the fuel never runs out before both sequences are used up;
with less fuel some alignments are missing from the list.

articles.title: The list of all alignments
articles.statement:
For sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, this is the list
produced by the fuel-bounded enumeration of alignments of $x$ and $y$ with fuel
$|x| + |y| + 1$.

This fuel suffices: an alignment belongs to the list exactly when it is a valid alignment of
$x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Score of an alignment column
articles.statement:
Given a substitution score $\sigma$, which assigns an
integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to all letters $a, b \in \alpha$, and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, a
column pairing letters $a$ and $b$ scores $\sigma(a, b)$, a column pairing a letter with a gap
(on either side) scores $g$, and a column with a gap on both sides scores $0$.

articles.title: Needleman–Wunsch is attained
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a
substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ over
$\alpha$ there is a valid alignment $A$ of $x$ and $y$ whose score with respect to $\sigma$ and
$g$ equals the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: The suffix maximum is attained
articles.statement:
For a substitution score
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and sequences $x$
and $y$ over $\alpha$, there is a suffix pair $(x', y')$ of $x$ and $y$, that is, a suffix $x'$
of $x$ and a suffix $y'$ of $y$, whose Needleman–Wunsch score equals the suffix maximum of $x$
and $y$.

articles.title: Infix pairs
articles.statement:
For sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, the list of infix pairs of $x$ and
$y$ is obtained by going through each prefix $p$ of $x$ and each prefix $q$ of $y$ and, for each
such $(p, q)$, listing all pairs $(x', y')$ of a suffix $x'$ of $p$ and a suffix $y'$ of $q$.

So $(x', y')$ occurs in the list exactly when $x'$ is a contiguous block of $x$ and $y'$ is a
contiguous block of $y$; a pair may occur more than once.

articles.title: Extending an alignment by a letter of the second sequence
articles.statement:
If $A$ is an alignment of
sequences $x$ and $y$ and $b$ is a letter, then $A$ followed by the column with a gap in the
first row and $b$ in the second row is an alignment of $x$ and of $y$ followed by $b$.

articles.title: Extending an alignment by a letter of the first sequence
articles.statement:
If $A$ is an alignment of
sequences $x$ and $y$ and $a$ is a letter, then $A$ followed by the column with $a$ in the
first row and a gap in the second row is an alignment of $x$ followed by $a$ and of $y$.

articles.title: Concatenation of alignments
articles.statement:
If $A_1$ is an alignment of sequences $x_1$ and $y_1$, and
$A_2$ is an alignment of sequences $x_2$ and $y_2$, then the concatenation of $A_1$ and $A_2$ is
an alignment of the concatenation of $x_1$ and $x_2$ and the concatenation of $y_1$ and $y_2$.

articles.title: Reversing an alignment
articles.statement:
For a list of columns $A$ and sequences $x$ and $y$, $A$ is an
alignment of the reversal of $x$ and the reversal of $y$ if and only if the reversal of $A$ (its
columns in reverse order) is an alignment of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Valid alignment of two sequences
articles.statement:
A list $A$ of columns, each a pair of optional letters,
is an alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$ when no column has both entries empty, the letters
present in the first entries of the columns, read in order, form $x$, and the letters present in
the second entries, read in order, form $y$.

articles.title: Maximum of an integer list with floor zero
articles.statement:
For a list $l$ of integers, this is the
largest of $0$ and the entries of $l$; in particular the empty list gives $0$.

It is used to define the suffix maximum, the local score and the Smith–Waterman score.

articles.title: The local score equals the Smith–Waterman score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an integer-valued
substitution score on letters and let $g$ be an integer gap score with $g \le 0$. Then for all
sequences $x$ and $y$, the local score of $x$ and $y$ (the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over
pairs of infixes) equals their Smith–Waterman score (the maximum terminal-cell score over pairs
of prefixes).

The proof uses that an infix is a suffix of a prefix and that the terminal cell is a maximum
over pairs of suffixes.

articles.title: Upper bounds on the local score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score, $g$ an
integer gap score, $x$ and $y$ sequences and $c$ an integer. If the Needleman–Wunsch score of
every pair $(x', y')$ with $x'$ an infix of $x$ and $y'$ an infix of $y$ is at most $c$, then the
local score of $x$ and $y$ is at most $c$.

articles.title: Local alignment score
articles.statement:
For an integer substitution score $\sigma$, an integer gap score
$g$ and sequences $x$ and $y$, the local score of $x$ and $y$ is the maximum of the
Needleman–Wunsch score of $(x', y')$ over all pairs of an infix $x'$ of $x$ and an infix $y'$ of
$y$ (contiguous and possibly empty).

articles.title: The enumerated alignments are exactly the valid ones
articles.statement:
For sequences $x$ and $y$ and a
list $A$ of columns, $A$ occurs in the enumerated list of all alignments of $x$ and $y$ if and
only if $A$ is an alignment of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Remaining cells of a Needleman–Wunsch table row
articles.statement:
The cells `F[i+1][j+1], F[i+1][j+2], …` of a row from the remaining letters `b :: ys` of the
second sequence, the remaining cells `up :: prev` of the previous row, the previous row's cell
`diag` to the upper left and the cell `left` just computed. A previous row that is too short ends
the row early (this does not happen for rows of the table, `nextRow_eq`).

articles.title: One row of the table
articles.statement:
From the row of the prefix `px`, `nextRow` computes the row of
`px ++ [a]`: the cells `nwScore (px ++ [a]) py` for the prefixes `py` of `ys`, shortest first.

articles.title: Next row of the Needleman–Wunsch table
articles.statement:
The row of the table for the prefix extended by `a`, from the previous row: the first cell is
one more gap than the previous row's first cell, then the recurrence left to right.

articles.title: Row-by-row filling of the Needleman–Wunsch table
articles.statement:
The rows of the table, filled top to bottom over the letters of the first sequence; the
result is the last row. Row `0` is `F[0][j] = j * gap`.

articles.title: The last row of the table
articles.statement:
**The last row of the table** is `F[|xs|][j] = nwScore xs (ys.take j)`: the cells
`nwScore xs py` over the prefixes `py` of `ys`, shortest first.

articles.title: Last row of the Needleman–Wunsch table
articles.statement: The last row `F[|xs|][·]` of the Needleman–Wunsch table.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded Needleman–Wunsch recursion
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, and write $|x|$ for
the length of a sequence $x$ and $ax$ for the sequence with first element $a$ followed by $x$.
For a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$, the value
$N_n(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}$ is defined by $N_0(x, y) = 0$, by $N_{n+1}(x, y) = g\,|y|$ if $x$ is
empty and $N_{n+1}(x, y) = g\,|x|$ if $y$ is empty, and by

$$N_{n+1}(ax, by) = \max\bigl(N_n(x, y) + \sigma(a, b),\ N_n(x, by) + g,\ N_n(ax, y) + g\bigr).$$

The Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$ is $N_{|x|+|y|}(x, y)$; this fuel suffices because every
recursive call shortens the pair. This is an exponential-time specification, not a memoized
table.

articles.title: The Needleman–Wunsch recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a
substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score, and write $N(x, y)$ for the
Needleman–Wunsch score of sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$ with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. For all
letters $a, b \in \alpha$ and sequences $x, y$, writing $ax$ for the sequence with first element
$a$ followed by $x$,

$$N(ax, by) = \max\bigl(N(x, y) + \sigma(a, b),\ N(x, by) + g,\ N(ax, y) + g\bigr).$$

articles.title: Infix pairs score at most the local score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$
be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. If $(x', y')$ is an infix pair of
sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, that is, $x'$ is a suffix of a prefix of $x$ and $y'$ is a
suffix of a prefix of $y$, then the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ and $y'$ is at most the local
score of $x$ and $y$, both with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.

articles.title: Appending to the first sequence loses at most one gap
articles.statement:
Let
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score, $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap
score, and write $N(x, y)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$ with
respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. For all sequences $x, y$ and every letter $a \in \alpha$, writing
$xa$ for $x$ with $a$ appended at the end, $N(x, y) + g \le N(xa, y)$.

An optimal alignment of $x$ and $y$ followed by the gap column pairing $a$ with nothing is an
alignment of $xa$ and $y$.

articles.title: Appending to the second sequence loses at most one gap
articles.statement:
Let
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score, $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap
score, and write $N(x, y)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$ with
respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. For all sequences $x, y$ and every letter $b \in \alpha$, writing
$yb$ for $y$ with $b$ appended at the end, $N(x, y) + g \le N(x, yb)$.

An optimal alignment of $x$ and $y$ followed by the gap column pairing nothing with $b$ is an
alignment of $x$ and $yb$.

articles.title: Suffix pairs score at most the suffix maximum
articles.statement:
Let
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap
score. If $(x', y')$ is a suffix pair of sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, that is, $x'$ is a
suffix of $x$ and $y'$ is a suffix of $y$, then the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ and $y'$ is at
most the suffix maximum of $x$ and $y$, both with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.

articles.title: Suffix pairs score at most the terminal Smith–Waterman cell
articles.statement:
Let
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \le 0$ a gap score. If
$x'$ is a suffix of a sequence $x$ and $y'$ is a suffix of a sequence $y$ over $\alpha$, then the
Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ and $y'$ is at most the terminal Smith–Waterman cell score of $x$
and $y$, both with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.

articles.title: Aligning the empty sequence with a sequence
articles.statement:
For every substitution score
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and sequence $y$ over
$\alpha$ of length $|y|$, the Needleman–Wunsch score of the empty sequence and $y$ with respect to
$\sigma$ and $g$ is $g\,|y|$: one gap per letter.

articles.title: Aligning a sequence with the empty sequence
articles.statement:
For every substitution score
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and sequence $x$ over
$\alpha$ of length $|x|$, the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and the empty sequence with respect to
$\sigma$ and $g$ is $g\,|x|$: one gap per letter.

articles.title: Needleman–Wunsch is reversal-invariant
articles.statement:
Reversing both sequences preserves the
optimal global score.

articles.title: The Needleman–Wunsch recurrence, end-peeling
articles.statement:
Let
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap
score, and write $N(x, y)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$ with
respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. For all sequences $x, y$ and letters $a, b \in \alpha$, writing $xa$
for the sequence $x$ followed by the letter $a$,

$$N(xa, yb) = \max\bigl(N(x, y) + \sigma(a, b),\ N(x, yb) + g,\ N(xa, y) + g\bigr).$$

articles.title: Needleman–Wunsch score
articles.statement:
Given a type $\alpha$, a substitution score
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, the
Needleman–Wunsch score $\mathrm{NW}(xs, ys)$ of two lists over $\alpha$ is defined by recursion
on their total length: if one of the lists is empty, it is $g$ times the length of the other;
and for lists $a\,xs$ and $b\,ys$ with heads $a$, $b$ and tails $xs$, $ys$,

$$\mathrm{NW}(a\,xs, b\,ys) = \max\bigl(\mathrm{NW}(xs, ys) + \sigma(a, b),
\ \mathrm{NW}(xs, b\,ys) + g,\ \mathrm{NW}(a\,xs, ys) + g\bigr).$$

By the Needleman–Wunsch optimality theorem, this is the optimal global alignment score of the
two lists.

articles.title: The table computes the optimal global alignment score
articles.statement:
**The table computes the optimal global alignment score** (Needleman–Wunsch 1970), for every
substitution score `σ` and gap score `gap`.

articles.title: The Needleman–Wunsch table
articles.statement: Its last cell `F[|xs|][|ys|]`.

articles.title: Pairs of prefixes
articles.statement:
For lists $xs$ and $ys$, the list of all pairs $(p, q)$ where $p$ is
a prefix of $xs$ and $q$ is a prefix of $ys$, the empty lists and $xs$, $ys$ themselves
included.

articles.title: Appending an element preserves suffixes
articles.statement:
If a list $s$ is a suffix of a list $xs$,
then for every element $a$, the list $s$ with $a$ appended at the end is a suffix of $xs$ with
$a$ appended at the end.

articles.title: The suffix maximum is at most the terminal Smith–Waterman cell
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a
substitution score and $g \le 0$ an integer gap score. For all lists $xs$ and $ys$, the
maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over all pairs of a suffix of $xs$ and a suffix of $ys$ is at
most the terminal Smith–Waterman cell score of $xs$ and $ys$.

articles.title: Upper bounds on the suffix maximum
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score, $g$ an integer
gap score, $xs$ and $ys$ lists and $y$ an integer. If every pair $(u, v)$ with $u$ a suffix of
$xs$ and $v$ a suffix of $ys$ has Needleman–Wunsch score at most $y$, then the maximum
Needleman–Wunsch score over all such suffix pairs is at most $y$.

articles.title: Suffix maximum of Needleman–Wunsch scores
articles.statement:
Given a substitution score $\sigma$ and an
integer gap score $g$, the suffix maximum of lists $xs$ and $ys$ is the maximum of the
Needleman–Wunsch scores of all pairs $(u, v)$ with $u$ a suffix of $xs$ and $v$ a suffix of
$ys$.

The maximum is taken with floor $0$, which changes nothing, since the pair of empty suffixes
scores $0$.

articles.title: Suffixes of a list with an element appended
articles.statement:
If $s$ is a suffix of the list obtained by
appending an element $a$ at the end of a list $xs$, then either $s$ is empty, or there is a
suffix $s'$ of $xs$ such that $s$ is $s'$ with $a$ appended at the end.

articles.title: Pairs of suffixes
articles.statement:
For lists $xs$ and $ys$, the list of all pairs $(u, v)$ where $u$ is
a suffix of $xs$ and $v$ is a suffix of $ys$, the empty lists and $xs$, $ys$ themselves
included.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded Smith–Waterman recursion
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, and write $ax$ for
the sequence with first element $a$ followed by $x$. For a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sequences
$x, y$ over $\alpha$, the value $F_n(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}$ is defined by $F_0(x, y) = 0$, by
$F_{n+1}(x, y) = 0$ if $x$ or $y$ is empty, and by

$$F_{n+1}(ax, by) = \max\bigl(0,\ F_n(x, y) + \sigma(a, b),\ F_n(x, by) + g,
\ F_n(ax, y) + g\bigr).$$

This is an exponential-time specification, not a memoized table.

articles.title: For nonpositive gaps, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell is the best suffix-pair score
articles.statement:
For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap score $g \le 0$ and all sequences $x$ and $y$, the
terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(x, y)$ equals the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over all pairs
of a suffix of $x$ and a suffix of $y$ (the empty suffixes included).

articles.title: The Smith–Waterman recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score,
and for a sequence $s$ and a letter $c$ write $sc$ for $s$ followed by $c$. For all sequences
$x$ and $y$ and all letters $a$ and $b$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H$ satisfies

$$H(xa, yb) = \max\bigl(0,\ H(x, y) + \sigma(a, b),\ H(x, yb) + g,\ H(xa, y) + g\bigr).$$

articles.title: The terminal cell is at most the suffix maximum
articles.statement:
For every substitution score $\sigma$,
every gap score $g$ of either sign and all sequences $x$ and $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman
cell $H(x, y)$ is at most the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over all pairs of a suffix of $x$
and a suffix of $y$.

Only the reverse inequality needs $g \le 0$.

articles.title: Each prefix-pair cell is at most the Smith–Waterman score
articles.statement:
For a substitution score
$\sigma$, a gap score $g$, sequences $x$ and $y$, a prefix $p$ of $x$ and a prefix $q$ of $y$,
the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(p, q)$ is at most the Smith–Waterman score of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: The terminal cell vanishes when the first sequence is empty
articles.statement:
For a substitution score
$\sigma$, a gap score $g$ and every sequence $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell of the empty
sequence and $y$ is $0$.

articles.title: The terminal cell vanishes when the second sequence is empty
articles.statement:
For a substitution score
$\sigma$, a gap score $g$ and every sequence $x$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell of $x$ and the
empty sequence is $0$.

articles.title: The terminal Smith–Waterman cell is nonnegative
articles.statement:
For every substitution score $\sigma$,
every gap score $g$ and all sequences $x$ and $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(x, y)$
satisfies $H(x, y) \ge 0$.

articles.title: The terminal Smith–Waterman cell
articles.statement:
Given a substitution score $\sigma(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}$
for letters $a, b$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, and writing $sc$ for a sequence $s$
followed by a letter $c$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(x, y)$ of two sequences $x$ and
$y$ is the integer defined by $H(x, y) = 0$ when $x$ or $y$ is empty, and

$$H(xa, yb) = \max\bigl(0,\ H(x, y) + \sigma(a, b),\ H(x, yb) + g,\ H(xa, y) + g\bigr)$$

for all sequences $x, y$ and letters $a, b$. It is the entry $H(|x|, |y|)$ of the
Smith–Waterman dynamic-programming table.

For $g \le 0$ it equals the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over pairs of suffixes of $x$ and $y$;
for $g > 0$ it can be strictly smaller (for one-letter sequences with $\sigma = -100$ and
$g = 1$ the cell is $1$, while the alignment with two gap columns scores $2$). It is not the
optimal local alignment score over all positions; that is the Smith–Waterman score, the maximum
of this cell over all pairs of prefixes.

articles.title: Bounding the Smith–Waterman score by its cells
articles.statement:
For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap
score $g$, sequences $x$ and $y$ and an integer $c$, if the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(p, q)$
is at most $c$ for every prefix $p$ of $x$ and every prefix $q$ of $y$, then the Smith–Waterman
score of $x$ and $y$ is at most $c$.

articles.title: The Smith–Waterman score
articles.statement:
Given a substitution score $\sigma$ and a gap score $g$, the
Smith–Waterman score of two sequences $x$ and $y$ is the maximum of the terminal Smith–Waterman
cell $H(p, q)$ over all pairs of a prefix $p$ of $x$ and a prefix $q$ of $y$ (the empty prefixes
included).

For $g \le 0$ this is the optimal local alignment score, the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over
pairs of infixes; for $g > 0$ it can be smaller.

articles.title: The suffix maximum is nonnegative
articles.statement:
For every scoring function
$\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, every gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and all lists
$x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, the suffix maximum of $x$ and $y$ (the largest Needleman–Wunsch score,
under $\sigma$ and $g$, of a suffix of $x$ against a suffix of $y$) is at least $0$, since the
pair of empty suffixes scores $0$.

articles.title: Consensus columns of a profile HMM
articles.statement: The consensus columns `[1, …, L]`.

articles.title: The Viterbi value is attained
articles.statement:
Some path (alignment of `x` to the profile) has
weight equal to the Viterbi value. Under nonnegative weights this attained value is the
largest path weight (`pathProb_le_viterbi`); without that hypothesis attainment alone
does not imply maximality.

articles.title: Forward computes the total path weight
articles.statement:
The sum, over all alignments of `x` to the
columns `[1, …, L]` (all paths through the model emitting `x`, each once), of the path
weights.

articles.title: Forward value of a sequence under a profile HMM
articles.statement:
The forward value of a sequence `x`: the total weight of all paths through the model that
emit `x` (`forward_eq_sum`), by the recursion on one residue and one column.

articles.title: HMMER Plan 7 restrictions
articles.statement:
HMMER's Plan 7 restrictions (Eddy 1998): no delete-to-insert and no insert-to-delete
transitions, and no insert states at node `0` (the begin state) or node `L`.

articles.title: Nonnegative weights of a profile HMM
articles.statement:
Nonnegative transition and emission weights (the transitions to the end state may have any
sign: the Viterbi bound does not need them).

articles.title: Every path weighs at most the Viterbi value
articles.statement: **Every path weighs at most the Viterbi value.**

articles.title: Weight of a path through a profile HMM
articles.statement:
The weight of a path through the model, given as an alignment `A` of the sequence to the
columns: the product of its transition and emission weights from the begin state to the end
state.

articles.title: Profile hidden Markov model
articles.statement:
A profile HMM with `L` consensus columns over the alphabet `α`, with weights in `R`.
`trans k s t` is the weight of a transition from the state of type `s` at node `k`
(`0 ≤ k ≤ L`; node `0` is the begin state, read as type `M`) to a state of type `t`: to `M`
or `D` at node `k + 1`, or to `I` at node `k`. `stop s` is the weight of the transition from the
state of type `s` at node `L` to the end state.

articles.title: State types of a profile HMM node
articles.statement: The state types of a profile HMM node: match, insert, delete.

articles.title: Pseudocount emission estimates are positive
articles.statement:
With positive pseudocounts, every residue gets a positive emission estimate, including
residues absent from the column.

articles.title: Pseudocount emission estimate of a match state
Pseudocount emission estimates sum to one
articles.statement: With positive pseudocounts, the estimated emissions sum to one.

articles.title: Nonnegative profile HMM gives a nonnegative alignment automaton
articles.statement: A profile HMM with nonnegative weights is a nonnegative alignment automaton.

articles.title: Profile HMM as an alignment automaton
articles.statement:
The profile HMM as an alignment automaton reading alignments of a sequence to the columns
`[1, …, L]`. The control state is the type of the previous state and the current node (the last
column consumed); it starts at `(M, 0)`, the begin state. Reading `(some a, some j)` visits `M j`,
`(some a, none)` visits the insert state of the current node, `(none, some j)` visits `D j`; the
invalid column `(none, none)` has weight `0`.

articles.title: Viterbi value of a sequence under a profile HMM
articles.statement:
The Viterbi value of a sequence `x`: the value selected by the max recursion
(`pathProb_le_viterbi`, `exists_pathProb_eq_viterbi`). Under nonnegative weights it is the
largest weight of a path through the model emitting `x`.

articles.title: The fitting score is attained
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap
score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ there is an infix $l$ of $y$ such that the
Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) equals the fitting score of
$x$ against $y$.

articles.title: The overlap score is attained
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap
score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ there is an overlap pair $(x', y')$ of $x$ and $y$ such
that the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ against $y'$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) equals the
overlap score of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: The fitting score is at most the local score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score
and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the fitting score of $x$ against $y$ is at
most the local score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.

Every fitting candidate, all of $x$ against an infix of $y$, is an infix pair.

articles.title: Upper bounds on the fitting score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score, $g$ a gap
score, $x$ and $y$ sequences and $b$ an integer. If the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against
every infix of $y$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) is at most $b$, then the fitting score of $x$
against $y$ is at most $b$.

articles.title: Fitting score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. The fitting
score of a sequence $x$ against a sequence $y$ is the maximum, over all infixes $l$ of $y$
(including the empty one), of the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ with $\sigma$ and
$g$: the best global alignment score of $x$ against a substring of $y$.

The empty infix is always a candidate, so the maximum is attained. Unlike the overlap score,
the fitting score is not floored at $0$: it can be negative when every fitting alignment
scores negatively.

articles.title: Infixes
articles.statement:
The infixes of a sequence $y$ are its contiguous substrings: the sequences
$l$ such that $y$ is the concatenation of $s$, $l$ and $t$ for some sequences $s$ and $t$,
including the empty sequence and $y$ itself. They are listed as the suffixes of the prefixes
of $y$, so the list can contain repetitions.

articles.title: Infix scores are at most the fitting score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and
$g$ a gap score. If $l$ is an infix of a sequence $y$, then for every sequence $x$ the
Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ is at most the fitting score of $x$ against $y$,
both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.

articles.title: Overlap-pair scores are at most the overlap score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution
score and $g$ a gap score. If $(x', y')$ is an overlap pair of sequences $x$ and $y$, then the
Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ against $y'$ is at most the overlap score of $x$ and $y$, both
taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.

articles.title: Overlap pairs
articles.statement:
The overlap pairs of sequences $x$ and $y$ are the pairs $(x', y')$ in
which $x'$ is a suffix of $x$ and $y'$ is a prefix of $y$, or $x'$ is a prefix of $x$ and
$y'$ is a suffix of $y$. Prefixes and suffixes include the empty sequence and the whole
sequence; the pairs are listed with the suffix–prefix pairs first, and the list can contain
repetitions.

articles.title: The overlap score is at most the local score
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score
and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the overlap score of $x$ and $y$ is at
most the local score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.

Every overlap pair is an infix pair.

articles.title: Upper bounds for the overlap score
articles.statement:
Fix a substitution score $\sigma$ and a gap score
$g$, and sequences $s$ and $t$. If an integer $b$ is at least the Needleman–Wunsch score of
every overlap pair of $s$ and $t$ (a suffix of $s$ with a prefix of $t$, or a prefix of $s$
with a suffix of $t$), then the overlap score of $s$ and $t$ is at most $b$.

articles.title: The overlap score is nonnegative
articles.statement:
For every substitution score $\sigma$, gap
score $g$ and sequences $s$ and $t$, the overlap score of $s$ and $t$ is at least $0$.

The pair of two empty sequences is an overlap pair, and its score is $0$.

articles.title: Overlap alignment score
articles.statement:
Given a substitution score $\sigma$ and a gap score $g$, the
overlap score of sequences $s$ and $t$ is the maximum, with floor $0$, of the Needleman–Wunsch
scores of the overlap pairs of $s$ and $t$: the pairs $(s', t')$ where $s'$ is a suffix of $s$
and $t'$ a prefix of $t$, or $s'$ is a prefix of $s$ and $t'$ a suffix of $t$.

The pair of two empty sequences is an overlap pair with score $0$, so the floor never changes
the value: this is the best alignment score of a suffix of one sequence against a prefix of the
other.

articles.title: The floored list maximum is nonnegative
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of integers, the maximum of
$L$ with floor $0$ (which is $0$ for the empty list) is at least $0$.

articles.title: Auxiliary row computation for the Smith–Waterman table
articles.statement:
The cells `H[i+1][j+1], H[i+1][j+2], …` of a row from the remaining letters `b :: ys` of the
second sequence, the remaining cells `up :: prev` of the previous row, the previous row's cell
`diag` to the upper left and the cell `left` just computed. A previous row that is too short ends
the row early (this does not happen for rows of the table, `nextRow_eq`).

articles.title: One row of the table
articles.statement:
From the row of the prefix `px`, `nextRow` computes the row of
`px ++ [a]`: the cells `H[i+1][j] = swCellScore σ gap (px ++ [a]) py` for the prefixes `py` of
`ys`, shortest first.

articles.title: Next row of the Smith–Waterman table
articles.statement:
The row of the table for the prefix extended by `a`, from the previous row: `H[i+1][0] = 0`,
then the recurrence left to right.

articles.title: Row-by-row filling of the Smith–Waterman table
articles.statement:
The Smith–Waterman table, filled row by row over the remaining letters of the first sequence:
`row` is the current row and `best` the largest cell of the earlier rows.

articles.title: The table computes the optimal local alignment score
articles.statement:
**The table computes the optimal local alignment score** (Smith–Waterman 1981, `gap ≤ 0`):
`swTab` is the maximum, over all pairs of infixes of `xs` and `ys` (including the empty ones,
which give the floor `0`), of their optimal global alignment score `nwScore`.

articles.title: The table computes the Smith–Waterman score
articles.statement:
`swTab` is the largest cell
`swCellScore σ gap px py` over all pairs of prefixes.

articles.title: The Smith–Waterman table
articles.statement:
The largest cell of the `(|xs| + 1) × (|ys| + 1)` table, with
the zero row `H[0][j] = 0` to start.

articles.title: Alignment score is the negated linear-penalty cost
articles.statement: Scores are negated costs.

articles.title: Cost of an alignment column under linear gap penalties
articles.statement: The cost of one alignment column.

articles.title: Cost of an alignment under linear gap penalties
articles.statement: The cost of an alignment: the sum of its column costs.

articles.title: The wavefront algorithm computes the optimal alignment cost
articles.statement:
The end cell is reached by
some score `s' ≤ s` iff `s` is at least the optimal Needleman–Wunsch cost.

articles.title: Exactness of the wavefront alignment algorithm
articles.statement:
The wavefront algorithm is exact: the end cell is reached by some score `s' ≤ s` iff some
alignment of `xs` and `ys` costs at most `s`. Hence the least such `s` is the optimal cost.

articles.title: Fuelled extension of matches along a diagonal
articles.statement: Follow matching letters along diagonal `k` from offset `h`, with fuel.

articles.title: Linear gap penalties
articles.statement: Linear gap penalties: match `0`, mismatch `mismatch ≥ 1`, each gap column `gap ≥ 1`.

articles.title: Largest valid offset on a diagonal
articles.statement: The largest valid offset on diagonal `k`: `h ≤ |ys|` and `v = h - k ≤ |xs|`.

articles.title: Substitution score from linear gap penalties
articles.statement:
The substitution score in the maximization convention of `nwScore`: `0` for a match and
`-mismatch` for a mismatch (the gap score is `-gap`).

articles.title: Match extension (slide) along a diagonal
articles.statement: The match extension ("slide") along diagonal `k` from offset `h`.

articles.title: Fuelled wavefront recurrence
articles.statement:
The wavefront recurrence with fuel (fuel `s + 1` suffices; see `wavefront`).
`none` stands for an unreachable diagonal. Offsets proposed by an operation are clamped to the
largest valid offset of the target diagonal before sliding.

articles.title: Completeness of the wavefront algorithm
articles.statement:
Completeness: every alignment of a pair of prefixes is dominated on its diagonal by the
wavefront of its exact cost.

articles.title: Soundness of the wavefront algorithm
articles.statement:
Soundness: a wavefront offset is a valid cell of its diagonal, reachable by an alignment
of the corresponding prefixes with cost at most `s`.

articles.title: Furthest-reaching wavefront offset
articles.statement: The furthest-reaching offset of score `s` on diagonal `k = h - v`.

articles.title: Branches of a loop closed by a base pair
articles.statement:
The branches of the loop closed by `p` in `P`: the pairs of `P` strictly inside `p` that
are not strictly inside another pair of `P` strictly inside `p`.

articles.title: Strict enclosure of one base pair by another
articles.statement: `q` lies strictly inside the pair `p`: `p.1 < q.1` and `q.2 < p.2`.

articles.title: Unique loop decomposition
articles.statement:
In a secondary structure every pair is either an exterior
branch or a branch of exactly one pair of the structure (and not both): each pair is shared by
the loop it closes and exactly one enclosing loop, possibly the exterior loop.

articles.title: Every position has a unique innermost strict container
articles.statement:
**Every position has a unique innermost strict container** (not loop membership): a
position `x` either lies strictly inside no pair, or there is a unique pair `p` with
`p.1 < x < p.2` such that no branch of `p` has `x` strictly inside it. This is an
innermost-container assignment, not the conventional loop decomposition of positions:
endpoints are excluded from the loop they close (a position `x = q.1` or `x = q.2` is
assigned to the loop of which `q` is a branch, never to the loop closed by `q`), and no
`x < s.length` hypothesis is assumed, so positions outside the sequence fall in the
first (exterior) case. In particular do not read this as saying loops uniquely decompose
positions; see `existsUnique_closing_pair` for the closing-pair side of the convention.

articles.title: Exterior branches of a secondary structure
articles.statement: The exterior branches of `P`: the pairs not strictly inside any pair of `P`.

articles.title: Free energy of a structure in the loop model
articles.statement:
The free energy of a structure in the loop model: the sum of the energies of the loops
closed by its pairs (the exterior loop contributes `0`).

articles.title: Energy of the loop closed by a base pair
articles.statement:
The energy of the loop closed by `p = (i, j)` in `P`: a hairpin with no branch, a stack,
bulge or interior loop with one branch `(k, l)`, and the affine multiloop energy
`a + b · r + c · u` with `r ≥ 2` branches and `u = (j - i - 1) - ∑ (l - k + 1)` unpaired
bases.

articles.title: A pair with no branch closes a hairpin loop
articles.statement: A pair with no branch closes a hairpin loop.

articles.title: A pair with one branch closes a stack, bulge or interior loop
articles.statement:
A pair with exactly one branch `q` closes a stack, bulge or interior loop with inner pair
`q`.

articles.title: A pair with two or more branches closes a multiloop
articles.statement: A pair with at least two branches closes a multiloop with the affine energy.

articles.title: Nearest-neighbor loop energy model
articles.statement:
A loop (nearest-neighbor) energy model: energies of hairpin loops closed by `(i, j)`, of
stacks, bulges and interior loops closed by `(i, j)` with inner pair `(k, l)`, and the affine
multiloop parameters `a` (per multiloop), `b` (per branch) and `c` (per unpaired base). The
exterior loop has energy `0`. Units: free energy, e.g. kcal/mol.

articles.title: Zuker exterior-loop recursion
articles.statement:
The exterior-loop recursion on the prefix `[0, len)`: `W(0) = 0` and
`W(len + 1) = min (W(len), min_{i ≤ len} W(i) + V(i, len + 1 - i))` (the last base is unpaired,
or closes an exterior branch `(i, len)`).

articles.title: Zuker's algorithm
articles.statement:
**Zuker's algorithm** (Zuker and Stiegler 1981; Zuker and Sankoff 1984), here with the affine
multiloop energy of Jaeger, Turner and Zuker (1989): the Zuker recursion computes the minimum
free energy over all secondary structures on `s` with minimum hairpin `m`, for any real loop
energies (of either sign). The minimum ranges over a finite set that contains the empty
structure, so it is never `⊤`.

articles.title: Minimum free energy is at most zero
articles.statement:
The minimum free energy is at most `0`, the energy of the open chain (the empty
structure).

articles.title: Zuker minimum free energy
articles.statement: Zuker's minimum free energy of `s`: the exterior recursion on the whole sequence.

articles.title: Zuker's recursion
articles.statement:
**Zuker's recursion** on the interval `[i, i + len)`, with `j = i + len - 1`, returning
`(V, WM)`:
* `V = ⊤` unless `(i, j)` can close a loop (`i + m < j`, `CanPair pair s i j`); otherwise `V` is
  the least of the hairpin energy `hairpin i j`, the interior-loop energies
  `interior i j k l + V(k, l)` over `i < k < l < j`, and the multiloop energies
  `a + WM(i + 1, u) + WM(u + 1, j - 1)` over `i < u < j - 1`;
* `WM` (a multiloop fragment with at least one branch, charging `b` per branch and `c` per
  unpaired base) is the least of `V + b`, `WM(i + 1, j) + c` (base `i` unpaired),
  `WM(i, j - 1) + c` (base `j` unpaired) and `WM(i, u) + WM(u + 1, j)` over `i ≤ u < j`.
Intervals are written by start and length.

articles.title: The binomial family is TP2
Maximum-likelihood cancer cell fraction
articles.statement:
The continuous maximum-likelihood CCF `ĉ = min 1 (a / (n κ))` for the allelic-fraction
slope `κ = α / (α q + 2 (1 - α))`. Landau et al. (2013) use the grid posterior; this continuous
maximizer over `[0, 1]` is derived here.

articles.title: The clonal call is a read-count threshold
articles.statement:
For every CCF threshold `t` and posterior
level `γ` there is `a₀` such that, for `a ≤ n`, the mutation is called clonal iff `a₀ ≤ a`
(`a₀ = n + 1` when no count is called clonal).

articles.title: Grid model for the cancer cell fraction
articles.statement:
Hypotheses on the CCF grid model: purity `0 < α ≤ 1`, copy number `q > 0`, grid in
`[0, q]` and within the defining CCF bound `≤ 1`, a nonnegative prior, and one grid point
of positive prior weight whose allelic fraction lies strictly inside `(0, 1)` (this makes
every posterior well defined).

articles.title: Clonal call for a mutation
articles.statement: Landau et al.'s clonal call: `P(CCF > t | a) > γ` (they take `t = 0.95`, `γ = 0.5`).

articles.title: The continuous CCF MLE
articles.statement:
For `0 < α ≤ 1`, `q ≥ 1`, `a ≤ n` and `0 < n`, the likelihood
`c ↦ Binom(a | n, f(c))` on `[0, 1]` is maximized at `ĉ = min 1 (a / (n κ))`.

articles.title: The clonal call is upward closed in the read count
articles.statement: **The clonal call is upward closed in the read count.**

articles.title: Positivity of the grid posterior normalizer
articles.statement:
In a grid model every posterior normalizer `∑_k π_k Binom(a | n, f(grid k))`, `a ≤ n`,
is positive.

articles.title: Monotone likelihood ratio implies stochastically larger posteriors
articles.statement:
If the kernels
`L` (data `x`) and `L'` (data `x'`) satisfy the TP2 inequality `L' i L j ≥ L i L' j` whenever
`c j ≤ c i`, then for a nonnegative prior every posterior tail `P(c > t)` is at least as large
under `L'` as under `L` (both normalizers positive).

articles.title: The CCF posterior is stochastically increasing in the read count
articles.statement:
**The CCF posterior is stochastically increasing in the read count** (Landau et al. 2013
with the monotone-likelihood-ratio argument): `P(CCF > t | a) ≤ P(CCF > t | a')` for
`a ≤ a' ≤ n`.

articles.title: Posterior probability that the cancer cell fraction exceeds a threshold
articles.statement:
Landau et al.'s posterior probability that the CCF exceeds `t`, given `a` of `n` reads,
purity `α`, copy number `q`, a prior `prior` on the grid points `grid k`:
`∑_{grid k > t} π_k Binom(a | n, f(grid k)) / ∑_k π_k Binom(a | n, f(grid k))`, with
`f(c) = α c / (α q + 2 (1 - α))`.

articles.title: Posterior tail probability on a grid
articles.statement:
Posterior probability that the parameter `c i` exceeds `t`, for prior weights `prior` and
likelihoods `lik i` of the observed data: `∑_{c i > t} prior i lik i / ∑_i prior i lik i`.

articles.title: Binomial probabilities vanish above n
articles.statement: Binomial probabilities vanish above `n`.

articles.title: The binomial likelihood is unimodal in `p`, decreasing part
articles.statement:
For `a ≤ n` and
`a / n ≤ p ≤ p' ≤ 1`, `Binom(a | n, p') ≤ Binom(a | n, p)`.

articles.title: The binomial likelihood is unimodal in `p`, increasing part
articles.statement:
For `a ≤ n` and
`0 ≤ p ≤ p' ≤ a / n`, `Binom(a | n, p) ≤ Binom(a | n, p')`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of binomial probabilities
articles.statement: Binomial probabilities are nonnegative for `0 ≤ p ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Positivity of binomial probabilities
articles.statement: Binomial probabilities are positive on `{0, …, n}` for `0 < p < 1`.

articles.title: Binomial probability mass function
articles.statement:
The binomial probability `C(n, i) p^i (1 - p)^(n - i)` of `i` successes in `n` trials, as a
function of `i : ℕ`. It vanishes for `i > n` (the binomial coefficient is zero there, so the
truncated subtraction `n - i` is harmless).

articles.title: Upper bound on the critical count
articles.statement: The critical count is at most `n + 1` (for `FPR ≥ 0`).

articles.title: Positivity of the critical count
articles.statement: The critical count is positive when `FPR < 1`.

articles.title: Critical count of the mutation detection test
articles.statement:
Carter's critical count `k = min {m | P(m) ≤ FPR}` for the null success probability
`p₀ = ε / 3` (Online Methods, before Eq. 9).

articles.title: Minimality of the critical count
articles.statement: Minimality of the critical count: `FPR < P(k - 1)` (for `0 ≤ FPR < 1`).

articles.title: Detection power as a mixture of tail probabilities
articles.statement:
The power is the mixture `(1 - d) P_f(X ≥ k) + d P_f(X ≥ k - 1)` of two tail
probabilities.

articles.title: Power increases with the allelic fraction
articles.statement:
`Pow(n, f) ≤ Pow(n, f')` for
`0 ≤ f ≤ f' ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Exact size
articles.statement:
**Exact size** (Carter et al. 2012, Eq. 9 with the randomization at `k - 1`): under the
null `f = p₀` the rejection probability is exactly `FPR`, for `0 ≤ FPR < 1`.

articles.title: Power decreases with local copy number
articles.statement:
**Power decreases with local copy number** at the ABSOLUTE allelic fraction, for a clonal
mutation of multiplicity `0 ≤ s ≤ q ≤ q'` (Carter et al. 2012, Eqs. 2, 9, 10).

articles.title: Power increases with multiplicity
articles.statement:
**Power increases with multiplicity** at the ABSOLUTE allelic fraction, for
`0 ≤ s ≤ s' ≤ q` (Carter et al. 2012, Eqs. 2, 9).

articles.title: Power increases with purity
articles.statement:
**Power increases with purity** at the ABSOLUTE allelic fraction `α s / (α q + 2 (1 - α))`
of a clonal mutation of multiplicity `0 ≤ s ≤ q` (Carter et al. 2012, Eqs. 2, 9, 10).

articles.title: Power of the randomized mutation detection test
articles.statement:
The power `Pow(n, f) = P_f(X ≥ k) + d Binom(k - 1 | n, f)` of the exact-size randomized
test (Carter et al. 2012, Eq. 9, with the randomization at `k - 1`; see the module doc).

articles.title: The randomization is a probability
Randomization probability of the detection test
articles.statement: The randomization probability `d = (FPR - P(k)) / (P(k - 1) - P(k))` of Eq. 9.

articles.title: Binomial probabilities sum to one
articles.statement: The binomial law sums to one (the binomial theorem), for every real `p`.

articles.title: Binomial upper tail is decreasing
articles.statement: `m ↦ P(m)` is antitone for `0 ≤ p ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Critical count meets the false-positive bound
articles.statement: The critical count meets the false-positive bound: `P(k) ≤ FPR` (for `FPR ≥ 0`).

articles.title: Recursion for the binomial upper tail
articles.statement: One step of the tail recursion: `P(m) = Binom(m | n, p) + P(m + 1)`.

articles.title: Binomial upper tail as one minus a lower sum
articles.statement: Carter's form of the tail: `P(m) = 1 - ∑_{i < m} Binom(i | n, p)`, for every `m`.

articles.title: Binomial upper tail beyond n is zero
articles.statement: `P(m) = 0` for `m > n`.

articles.title: Binomial tails increase with the success probability
Nonnegativity of binomial tail probabilities
articles.statement: Tail probabilities are nonnegative for `0 ≤ p ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Tail gap at the critical count
articles.statement: The gap `P(k - 1) - P(k)` is the null probability of the boundary point `k - 1`.

articles.title: Binomial upper tail from zero is one
articles.statement: `P(0) = 1`, for every real `p`.

articles.title: Binomial upper tail probability
articles.statement:
The binomial upper tail `ℙ_p(X ≥ m) = ∑_{m ≤ i ≤ n} C(n, i) p^i (1 - p)^(n - i)`, Carter's
`P(m)` with `p = ε / 3`.

articles.title: GeneGISTIC null
articles.statement:
**GeneGISTIC null** (Mermel et al. 2011): permuting the per-sample minima of all running
windows of `n + 1` markers gives, at every window `i`, the law of a sum of independent draws
of one window minimum per sample.

articles.title: The GISTIC permutation null is the law of a sum of independent per-sample draws
articles.statement:
(Mermel et al. 2011): the probability of the score `g` is the fraction of the `M ^ S` marker
choices with that score, whatever the marker `m`.

articles.title: Convolution step
articles.statement:
Adding sample `S` convolves the null of the first `S` samples with
the empirical law of the new sample, `P_{S+1}(g) = ∑_v (1 / M) P_S(g - x_S(v))`.

articles.title: GISTIC null with no samples is a point mass at zero
articles.statement: With no samples the null is the point mass at `0`.

articles.title: GISTIC permutation null distribution
articles.statement:
The GISTIC permutation null at marker `m`: the probability that `∑ j, x j (σ j m) = g`
when the permutations `σ j` of the markers are independent and uniform.

articles.title: Permuted GISTIC score at a marker
articles.statement: The permuted score at marker `m`: `∑ j, x j (σ j m)`.

articles.title: Count of marker choices with a given score
articles.statement:
The number of marker choices `u : Fin S → Fin M` (one marker per sample) with
`∑ j, x j (u j) = g`.

articles.title: Window minimum over consecutive markers
articles.statement:
The minimum of `y` over the window of `n + 1` consecutive markers starting at `i`
(GeneGISTIC's per-sample gene-level value for a gene covering those markers).

articles.title: Number of amplified copies
articles.statement: The number of original copies amplified by the event (`desc i ≥ 2`).

articles.title: Copy-neutral LOH
articles.statement: **Copy-neutral LOH** (`2 + 0`): `t = 2 E₂ / (E₁ + 2 E₂)`, for `μ ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity
articles.statement: Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity `1 + 1 → 2 + 0`: one copy duplicated, the other lost.

articles.title: Identifiability
articles.statement:
If some copy is amplified, two parameter pairs `(μ, t)`, `(μ', t')`
with `μ, μ' ≠ 0` and the same expected multiplicity spectrum are equal.

articles.title: Expected number of mutations of a given multiplicity
articles.statement:
Expected number of mutations of multiplicity `m`:
`μ t #{i | desc i = m} + [m = 1] μ c₁ (1 - t)` (per-copy rate `μ`, event at time `t` of the
normalized history `[0, 1]`).

articles.title: Positive copy number after an amplifying event
articles.statement: An event that amplifies some copy leaves a positive copy number.

articles.title: Copy number after a copy-number event
articles.statement: The copy number `c₁ = ∑ i, desc i` after the event.

articles.title: Copy-number gain history
articles.statement:
A single copy-number event on a region: `copies` original copies, of which copy `i` has
`desc i` copies after the event (`0` if lost, `2` if duplicated).

articles.title: The mutation rate from the spectrum
Single gain
articles.statement: **Single gain** (`2 + 1`): `t = 3 E₂ / (E₁ + 2 E₂)`, for `μ ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Single-copy gain
articles.statement: A single-copy gain `1 + 1 → 2 + 1`: one copy duplicated, the other kept.

articles.title: Expected count of mutations on amplified copies
articles.statement:
The mutations of multiplicity at least two number `μ t #{i | desc i ≥ 2}` in expectation:
they all arose before the event, on an amplified copy.

articles.title: The multiplicity-weighted total is time-invariant
articles.statement:
`∑_m m E_m = μ c₁`, summing over
all multiplicities up to a bound `B ≥ max(1, max_i desc i)`.

articles.title: The timing closed form
articles.statement:
When some copy is amplified and `μ ≠ 0`,
`t = c₁ ∑_{m ≥ 2} E_m / (#{i | desc i ≥ 2} ∑_m m E_m)`.

articles.title: Whole-genome doubling
articles.statement: **Whole-genome doubling** (`2 + 2`): `t = 2 E₂ / (E₁ + 2 E₂)`, for `μ ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Whole-genome doubling event
articles.statement: Whole-genome doubling of a diploid region `1 + 1 → 2 + 2`.

articles.title: Data-fit term of the ARD-NMF objective
articles.statement: The data-fit term `D_1(V | W H) = ∑_{f,n} d(v_fn | (W H)_fn)`.

articles.title: Lower bound on the relevance update
articles.statement: The relevance never falls below its floor `b / c` (`W, H ≥ 0`, `c > 0`).

articles.title: Generalized Kullback–Leibler divergence
articles.statement:
The Kullback–Leibler `β = 1` divergence `d(x | y) = x log (x / y) - x + y` (Tan–Févotte,
Eq. 4). With Mathlib's `0 * log _ = 0` it gives `d(0 | y) = y`, the correct value; `y > 0` is
needed when `x > 0`.

articles.title: The `H` update is monotone
articles.statement:
**The `H` update is monotone** (Tan–Févotte 2013, §IV-B, `β = 1`): it does not increase
`D_1(V | W H) / φ + ∑ h_kn / λ_k`, for `φ > 0`, `λ > 0`, `V ≥ 0`, `W ≥ 0` with no zero row, and
`H > 0` entrywise.

articles.title: H-dependent part of the ARD-NMF objective
articles.statement:
The `H`-dependent part `D_1(V | W H) / φ + ∑_{k,n} h_kn / λ_k` of the `ℓ₁`-ARD objective
(Tan–Févotte, Eq. 20, `β = 1`).

articles.title: The `W` update is monotone
articles.statement:
It does not increase
`D_1(V | W H) / φ + ∑ w_fk / λ_k`, for `φ > 0`, `λ > 0`, `V ≥ 0`, `H ≥ 0` with no zero column,
and `W > 0` entrywise (the transpose of `objectiveH_updateH_le`).

articles.title: W-dependent part of the ARD-NMF objective
articles.statement:
The `W`-dependent part `D_1(V | W H) / φ + ∑_{f,k} w_fk / λ_k` of the `ℓ₁`-ARD objective
(Tan–Févotte, Eq. 20, `β = 1`).

articles.title: Reconstruction matrix in nonnegative matrix factorization
articles.statement: The reconstruction `(W H)_fn = ∑_k w_fk h_kn`.

articles.title: Pruning
articles.statement:
**Pruning** (Tan–Févotte, §IV-D): the relevance equals its floor `b / c` exactly when the
`k`-th column of `W` and the `k`-th row of `H` are zero (`W, H ≥ 0`, `c > 0`).

articles.title: The relevance update is the exact minimizer
articles.statement:
**The relevance update is the exact minimizer** (Tan–Févotte, §IV-C): for `A > 0` and
`c > 0`, `λ ↦ A / λ + c log λ` attains its minimum over `λ > 0` at `λ = A / c`.

articles.title: The minimizer is unique
articles.statement: If `λ > 0` does as well as `A / c`, then `λ = A / c`.

articles.title: Relevance update in ARD-NMF
articles.statement:
The relevance update `λ_k = (‖w_k‖₁ + ‖h_k‖₁ + b) / c` (Tan–Févotte, Eq. 33, `ℓ₁` prior;
`c = F + N + a + 1`).

articles.title: A pruned entry stays pruned
articles.statement:
The multiplicative update maps a zero entry of `H` to
zero.

articles.title: ARD multiplicative update of H
articles.statement:
The `ℓ₁`-ARD multiplicative update of `H` for `β = 1` (Tan–Févotte, Eq. 32, Algorithm 2):
`h_kn ← h_kn (∑_f w_fk v_fn / (W H)_fn) / (∑_f w_fk + φ / λ_k)`.

articles.title: A pruned entry stays pruned
articles.statement:
The multiplicative update maps a zero entry of `W` to
zero.

articles.title: ARD multiplicative update of W
articles.statement:
The `ℓ₁`-ARD multiplicative update of `W` for `β = 1` (Tan–Févotte, Algorithm 2):
`w_fk ← w_fk (∑_n v_fn h_kn / (W H)_fn) / (∑_n h_kn + φ / λ_k)`.

articles.title: `N_β` exists
articles.statement:
For every target power `β < 1` there is a cohort size beyond which the
power is at least `β` (Lawrence et al. 2014 take `β = 0.9`).

articles.title: Driver genes raise the per-patient mutation probability
articles.statement:
A driver mutated above background raises the per-patient probability:
`p₀ < p₀ + r (1 - m)` for `r > 0` and `m < 1`.

articles.title: Background mutation probability lies in (0, 1)
articles.statement:
The background probability is a probability below one: `0 ≤ p₀ < 1` for
`0 ≤ μ f_g < 1` and `L ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Background mutation probability per patient
articles.statement:
Background probability `p₀ = 1 - (1 - μ f_g)^(3L/4)` that a patient carries at least one
non-silent background mutation in a gene of `L` coding bases (Lawrence et al. 2014).

articles.title: Signal mutation probability per patient
articles.statement:
Signal probability `p₁ = p₀ + r (1 - m)` for a gene mutated in a fraction `r` of patients
above background, with miss rate `m` (Lawrence et al. 2014).

articles.title: Saturation power of the binomial gene discovery test
articles.statement:
Power of the one-sided binomial test of Lawrence et al. (2014): the probability, when each
of `N` patients is mutated with probability `p₁`, of observing a count `x` whose background
p-value `ℙ_{p₀}(X ≥ x)` is at most `γ`.

articles.title: Power tends to one
articles.statement:
For `0 ≤ p₀ < p₁ ≤ 1` and any level `γ > 0`, the power of the
binomial test tends to `1` as the number of patients grows.

articles.title: Purity and ploidy are identifiable from the slope and intercept of Eq. 1
articles.statement:
The map
`(α, τ) ↦ (α / D, 2 (1 - α) / D)` is a bijection from `{0 < α ≤ 1, 0 < τ}` onto
`{0 < b, 0 ≤ δ < 1}`.

articles.title: Genome doubling
articles.statement:
Doubling every copy number and the ploidy and replacing the purity by
`α / (2 - α)` reproduces every copy ratio (the `m = 2` case of `copyRatio_scale`).

articles.title: Eq. 1 is affine in `q`
articles.statement: `R = (α / D) q + 2 (1 - α) / D`, for all real arguments.

articles.title: Ploidy-scaling non-identifiability, copy ratios
articles.statement:
Scaling every copy number and the
ploidy by `m > 0` and the purity to `α / (m - (m - 1) α)` leaves every copy ratio of Eq. 1
unchanged.

articles.title: Relative copy ratio
articles.statement:
Relative copy ratio `R = (α q + 2 (1 - α)) / (α τ + 2 (1 - α))` of a locus with copy number
`q`, purity `α` and cancer-cell ploidy `τ` (Carter et al. 2012, Eq. 1).

articles.title: Ploidy-scaling non-identifiability, germline allelic fractions
articles.statement:
**Ploidy-scaling non-identifiability, germline allelic fractions** (Eq. 11): with copy
number and germline multiplicity both scaled by `m > 0` and the purity rescaled, the allelic
fraction is unchanged.

articles.title: Expected allelic fraction of a germline variant
articles.statement:
Expected allelic fraction `((1 - α) + α g) / (α q + 2 (1 - α))` of a heterozygous germline
variant present in `g` copies per cancer cell at a locus of copy number `q` (Carter et al.
2012, Eq. 11).

articles.title: Copy-ratio intercept
articles.statement:
The copy-ratio intercept `2 (1 - α) / D` of Eq. 1 (Carter et al. 2012), the copy ratio of a
homozygously deleted locus.

articles.title: Positivity of the mixture copy number
articles.statement: The mixture copy number is positive in the biological domain `0 ≤ α ≤ 1`, `0 < q`.

articles.title: Average absolute copy number of a tumor sample
articles.statement:
Average absolute copy number `α q + 2 (1 - α)` of a locus with copy number `q` in the cancer
cells, in a sample of purity `α` whose normal cells are diploid (Carter et al. 2012). With
`q = τ` this is the sample ploidy `D` of Eq. 1; with the local copy number it is `D_s` of
Eq. 2.

articles.title: Ploidy from copy-ratio slope and intercept
articles.statement:
Inverse of Eq. 1, ploidy: `τ = (1 - δ) / b` for the slope `b` and intercept `δ`, when
`0 < α ≤ 1` and `0 < τ`.

articles.title: Purity from copy-ratio slope and intercept
articles.statement:
Inverse of Eq. 1, purity: `α = 2 b / (2 b + δ)` for the slope `b` and intercept `δ`, when
`0 < α ≤ 1` and `0 < τ`.

articles.title: Positivity of the rescaled purity denominator
articles.statement:
The denominator `m - (m - 1) α = m (1 - α) + α` of the rescaled purity is positive for
`m > 0` and `0 ≤ α ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Rescaled purity lies in (0, 1)
articles.statement:
The rescaled purity is again a purity: `0 ≤ α / (m - (m - 1) α) ≤ 1` for `m > 0` and
`0 ≤ α ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Rescaled purity differs from the original purity
articles.statement:
The rescaled solution is a genuinely different purity: for `0 < α < 1` and `m ≠ 1`,
`α / (m - (m - 1) α) ≠ α`.

articles.title: Rescaled purity
articles.statement:
The purity `α / (m - (m - 1) α)` that, together with all copy numbers multiplied by `m`,
reproduces the copy ratios and allelic fractions of purity `α` (derived from Carter et al.
2012, Eqs. 1, 2, 11).

articles.title: Copy-ratio slope
articles.statement:
The copy-ratio slope `α / D` of Eq. 1 (Carter et al. 2012), the copy ratio of one extra
copy per cancer cell.

articles.title: Somatic allelic fraction decreases with copy number
articles.statement:
The somatic allelic fraction decreases with the local copy number (`0 ≤ α ≤ 1`,
`0 ≤ s`, `0 < q ≤ q'`).

articles.title: Allelic fractions are determined by the copy-ratio slope
articles.statement:
**Allelic fractions are determined by the copy-ratio slope** (Carter et al. 2012, Eq. 2):
`α s / D_s = (α / D) s / R`, whenever `D ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Somatic allelic fraction is at most one
articles.statement:
A somatic allelic fraction is at most one when the multiplicity does not exceed the copy
number (`s ≤ q`).

articles.title: Somatic allelic fraction increases with multiplicity
articles.statement: The somatic allelic fraction increases with the multiplicity (`0 ≤ α ≤ 1`, `0 < q`).

articles.title: Somatic allelic fraction increases with purity
articles.statement: The somatic allelic fraction increases with the purity (`0 ≤ s`, `0 < q`).

articles.title: Nonnegativity of somatic allelic fractions
articles.statement: Somatic allelic fractions are nonnegative in the biological domain.

articles.title: Ploidy-scaling non-identifiability, somatic allelic fractions
articles.statement:
**Ploidy-scaling non-identifiability, somatic allelic fractions** (Eq. 2): with copy
number and multiplicity both scaled by `m > 0` and the purity rescaled, the allelic fraction is
unchanged.

articles.title: Expected allelic fraction of a somatic mutation
articles.statement:
Expected allelic fraction `α s / (α q + 2 (1 - α))` of a clonal somatic point mutation with
multiplicity `s` (copies per cancer cell) at a locus of copy number `q` (Carter et al. 2012,
Eq. 2; Eq. 10 is `s = 1`).

articles.title: Calibrated copy ratios have mean `1`
articles.statement:
If the segment weights `w` sum to one and the
ploidy is the weighted mean copy number `τ = ∑ w q`, the weighted mean copy ratio is `1`
(Carter et al. 2012, Methods: "correctly calibrated copy-ratio data always has mean = 1").

articles.title: Eigenvalues of Kingman's block-counting generator
articles.statement: The eigenvalues of the block-counting generator, `-(k.choose 2)`.

articles.title: Right eigenvector equation for the block-counting generator
articles.statement: The columns of `blockCountingRightEigen n` are right eigenvectors: `G V = V D`.

articles.title: Generator of Kingman's block-counting process
articles.statement:
The rate matrix of Kingman's block-counting (pure-death) process on `{0, …, n}`: `k`
lineages become `k - 1` at rate `k.choose 2`, time in units of `M = 2N` generations.

articles.title: Left eigenvector equation for the block-counting generator
articles.statement: The rows of `blockCountingLeftEigen n` are left eigenvectors: `W G = D W`.

articles.title: Left and right eigenvector matrices are mutually inverse
articles.statement: The left and right eigenvector matrices are mutually inverse: `W V = 1`.

articles.title: Left eigenvectors of Kingman's block-counting generator
articles.statement:
Left eigenvectors of the block-counting generator, as rows: row `0` is the indicator of
state `0`, and for `1 ≤ k` row `k` has entries `(2k-1) (-1)^{k-j} j^{(k-1)} / (j! (k-j)!)` for
`j ≤ k` and `0` for `j > k`; the eigenvalue is `-(k.choose 2)`.

articles.title: Right eigenvectors of Kingman's block-counting generator
articles.statement:
Right eigenvectors of the block-counting generator, as columns: column `k` has entries
