articles.title: Covariance of coalescence times at two linked loci
articles.statement:
The covariance `Cov(T_A, T_B) = (ρ + 18) / (ρ² + 13 ρ + 18)` of the coalescence times at two
loci of two sequences sampled linked (Hudson 1983; Kaplan & Hudson 1985).

articles.title: Positivity of the two-locus moment denominator
articles.statement: The denominator `ρ² + 13 ρ + 18` is positive for `ρ ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Common denominator of the two-locus moments
articles.statement: The common denominator `ρ² + 13 ρ + 18` of the two-locus moments.

articles.title: Hill–Robertson / Ohta–Kimura, first row
articles.statement:
On the simplex,
`L D² = -(3 + ρ + 8ν) D² + D (1 - 2p)(1 - 2q) + p (1 - p) q (1 - q)` (for all real `ρ`, `ν`).

articles.title: Hill–Robertson / Ohta–Kimura, second row
articles.statement:
On the simplex,
`L (D z) = 4 D² - (5 + ρ/2 + 8ν) D z` with `z = (1 - 2p)(1 - 2q)`.

articles.title: Hill–Robertson / Ohta–Kimura, third row
articles.statement:
On the simplex,
`L Π = D z - (2 + 8ν) Π + ν (p (1 - p) + q (1 - q))`; for `ν = 0` the three rows close.

articles.title: Drift of gamete frequencies matches recombination
articles.statement:
Without mutation the drift of a gamete frequency is `2 N` times its per-generation change
under `Linkage.recombine` when `ρ = 4 N r`.

articles.title: Generator of the two-locus Wright–Fisher diffusion
articles.statement:
The generator of the two-locus Wright–Fisher diffusion on polynomials in the gamete
frequencies, time in units of `2 N` generations, `ρ = 4 N r`, symmetric mutation at rate `ν` per
locus in each direction (`ν = θ / 2`, `θ = 4 N u`):
`L f = ½ ∑ x_g (δ_{gh} - x_h) ∂_g ∂_h f + ∑ (-(ρ/2) ε_g D + ν (x_{g'} + x_{g''} - 2 x_g)) ∂_g f`.

articles.title: Rate matrix of the two-locus coalescent
articles.statement:
The rate matrix of the two-locus ancestral process of a sample of two, with time in units of
`2 N` generations and `ρ = 4 N r`: coalescence at rate `1` for every pair of ancestral lineages,
recombination at rate `ρ / 2` for every lineage ancestral at both loci.

articles.title: States of the two-locus ancestral process
articles.statement: The states of the two-locus ancestral process of a sample of two sequences.

articles.title: Positivity of component Bayes factors
articles.statement: Every component Bayes factor is positive.

articles.title: Bayes factor of a component statistic
articles.statement:
The Bayes factor of component `i` at the observed value: the ratio of its score
function under selection to its score function under neutrality.

articles.title: CMS score as a ratio of joint densities
articles.statement: The CMS score is the ratio of the two joint densities.

articles.title: Composite of multiple signals (CMS) score
articles.statement: The CMS score: the product of the component Bayes factors.

articles.title: Composite selection score model
articles.statement:
A composite-score model (Grossman et al. 2010): a prior probability `prior` that the site
is under selection, and for each of the `k` component statistics a positive score function
`sel` under selection and `neut` under neutrality (unnormalized densities: only positivity is
assumed). Conditionally on the hypothesis the components are independent, which is what
makes the joint scores the products below. The Bayes/posterior reading of `posterior`
requires the additional normalization hypothesis of `sum_joint_eq_one`.

articles.title: Escape probability vanishes only at the swept site
articles.statement: No lineage escapes at the swept site itself, and nowhere else.

articles.title: Escape profile determines sweep location and strength
articles.statement:
The escape-probability profile determines the sweep location and its strength. Positivity
of one of the two strength parameters is enough: the location is the unique zero of that
profile, and the strengths then agree by injectivity of `exp`.

articles.title: Probability of escaping a selective sweep
articles.statement:
The probability that a lineage at position `y` escapes a sweep located at `x`, with
compound strength parameter `α > 0`: `1 - exp (-α |y - x|)` (Kim and Stephan 2002;
Nielsen et al. 2005). The parameter `α` is proportional to the recombination rate per unit
distance divided by the selection coefficient.

articles.title: Additivity of evidence on the log-odds scale
articles.statement:
On the log scale the evidence is additive: the log posterior odds are the log prior odds
plus the sum of the log Bayes factors of the component statistics.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the mixing weight of a two-component mixture
articles.statement: A mixture of two distinct laws determines its mixing weight.

articles.title: Posterior probability is strictly increasing in the CMS score
articles.statement:
The posterior probability is a strictly increasing function of the CMS score, so the two
rankings of sites agree.

articles.title: Posterior odds equal prior odds times the CMS score
articles.statement:
Bayes-rule identity for conditionally independent components: the posterior odds of
selection are the prior odds times the CMS score. This is an algebraic identity for the
normalized score; it is a genuine Bayes rule only under the normalization hypothesis of
`sum_joint_eq_one`.

articles.title: Normalized composite score
articles.statement:
The normalized composite score: the normalized ratio of the products of the
component score functions. This is the posterior probability of selection given the
observed component values when the score functions are normalized densities
(see `sum_joint_eq_one` for the normalization hypothesis).

articles.title: Normalization of the composite score model
articles.statement:
The model is a probability model: with normalised component score functions (each a
density with respect to a common base measure), the joint distribution of the
observations sums to one. This is the validity hypothesis that makes `posterior` a
genuine Bayes posterior.

articles.title: Identifiability of sweep parameters from frequency spectra
articles.statement:
Identifiability of the sweep parameters from the per-site frequency spectra. If the
neutral spectrum `f` and the post-sweep spectrum `g` differ, and two sweep parameter pairs
give the same mixture at every position, then the parameters coincide. This is what the
composite likelihood of SweepFinder maximises over.

articles.title: Exchangeable pair of statistics
articles.statement:
The pair of statistics `(X, Y)` is exchangeable under `μ`: the joint law is unchanged by
swapping the two coordinates. This is an additional calibration assumption for a two-group
haplotype test, stronger than the ordinary neutral null.
Defined as `IdentDistrib` of the two orderings, so the measurability of the joint laws is
part of the hypothesis rather than restored separately in each theorem.

articles.title: Exchangeability is preserved by a common measurable map
articles.statement: Applying the same measurable function to both statistics preserves exchangeability.

articles.title: Difference of an exchangeable pair has a symmetric law
articles.statement: The difference of an exchangeable pair has a symmetric law.

articles.title: Two-sided rejection region splits into equal tails
articles.statement: A two-sided rejection region splits into two tails of equal probability.

articles.title: Equal tails of the log ratio of an exchangeable pair
articles.statement: For positive statistics, the log ratio — the XP-EHH form — has equal tails.

articles.title: Equal tails of the ratio of an exchangeable pair
articles.statement:
The same statement for the ratio itself, the form used for relative EHH: the probability
that the ratio exceeds `c` equals the probability that it falls below `1 / c`.

articles.title: Equal tails of the difference of an exchangeable pair
articles.statement:
Equal tails: the upper tail of `X - Y` at `t` has the same probability as the lower tail
at `-t`.

articles.title: Symmetry of the XP-EHH law under exchangeability
articles.statement:
Under exchangeability, the XP-EHH score has a symmetric law: the two tails of the
two-sided test carry the same probability.

articles.title: XP-EHH in star-genealogy sweep models
articles.statement:
XP-EHH computed from two star-genealogy sweep models with the same recombination rate is
the log ratio of the two ages, with the opposite sign to `ihs`.

articles.title: Cross-population extended haplotype homozygosity (XP-EHH)
articles.statement:
The cross-population extended haplotype homozygosity score (Sabeti et al. 2007): the log
ratio of the integrated haplotype homozygosities of the same core region in two populations.
Both arguments must be positive for the score to be meaningful. Outside that domain
`Real.log` is totalized by Mathlib, not by the stated junk value: `Real.log 0 = 0` and
`Real.log (-x) = Real.log x`, so for example `xpehh (-2) 1 = log 2`.

articles.title: Uniform bound on the expected site-frequency spectrum
articles.statement:
The expected number of sites with `i` derived copies in a sample of `n`, `1 ≤ i < n`, is
bounded uniformly in the selection coefficient: `|E ξ_i(σ)| ≤ |θ| C(n, i)`.

articles.title: Frequency density averaged over a distribution of fitness effects
articles.statement:
The Poisson-random-field frequency density averaged over the distribution of fitness
effects `μ`: `∫ φ_σ(x) dμ(σ)`.

articles.title: DFE spectrum is additive in the measure
articles.statement: The spectrum is additive in the (finite) DFE.

articles.title: Spectrum under a point-mass DFE is the single-selection spectrum
articles.statement: A DFE concentrated on one selection coefficient gives the single-`σ` spectrum.

articles.title: Mixture identity
articles.statement:
For a finite measure `μ` of selection coefficients and a segregating
class `1 ≤ i < n`, the DFE-averaged spectrum is the binomial sampling integral of the
DFE-averaged frequency density:
`∫ E ξ_i(σ) dμ(σ) = ∫₀¹ C(n, i) x ^ i (1 - x) ^ (n - i) (∫ φ_σ(x) dμ(σ)) dx`.

articles.title: Site-frequency spectrum under the gamma DFE
articles.statement: The spectrum under the gamma DFE as an integral against the gamma law of the strength.

articles.title: DFE spectrum is homogeneous in the measure
articles.statement: The spectrum is homogeneous in the DFE.

articles.title: Site-frequency spectrum under a distribution of fitness effects
articles.statement:
The expected unfolded site-frequency spectrum under the distribution of fitness effects
`μ` (a law on the scaled selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns`): `∫ E ξ_i(σ) dμ(σ)`, where each new
mutation draws its own `σ` from `μ`.

articles.title: No mutation is beneficial under the gamma DFE
articles.statement: Under the gamma DFE no mutation is beneficial.

articles.title: Rescaling a gamma DFE divides its rate
articles.statement:
Rescaling a gamma DFE by `c > 0` (for example from `s` to `σ = 2Ns`, `c = 2N`) keeps the
shape and divides the rate by `c`.

articles.title: Fraction of mutations in a strength interval under the gamma DFE
articles.statement:
The fraction of new mutations whose strength `-σ` lies in `(c₁, c₂]`, `0 ≤ c₁ ≤ c₂`, is
`(Γ(a, r c₁) - Γ(a, r c₂)) / Γ(a)`.

articles.title: Fraction of strongly deleterious mutations
articles.statement:
Under the gamma DFE the fraction of new
mutations with `σ < -c`, `c ≥ 0`, is the gamma tail `Γ(a, r c) / Γ(a)`.

articles.title: Gamma distribution of fitness effects
articles.statement:
The gamma distribution of fitness effects (Boyko et al. 2008): the scaled selection
coefficient is `σ = -T` with `T ~ Gamma(a, r)`, shape `a > 0` and rate `r > 0` (scale `1 / r`),
so new mutations are deleterious with mean strength `a / r`.

articles.title: Derivative of the Poisson log-likelihood
articles.statement:
The derivative of the log-likelihood in the parameter `ψ`, when the means `E_i(ψ)` are
positive and differentiable at `ψ`: `∑ (k_i / E_i(ψ) - 1) · DE_i(ψ)`.

articles.title: Integrability of the expected spectrum in the selection coefficient
articles.statement:
For `1 ≤ i < n`, the expected spectrum `E ξ_i(σ)` is integrable in `σ` against every
finite measure.

articles.title: Mean selection coefficient under the gamma DFE
articles.statement: The mean scaled selection coefficient under the gamma DFE is `-a / r`.

articles.title: Gamma DFE is a probability measure
articles.statement: The gamma DFE is a probability law.

articles.title: The Poisson-random-field log-likelihood
articles.statement:
For independent Poisson counts with positive
means `E_i`, the log-probability of the observed counts `k` is `poissonLogLik E k`.

articles.title: Probability of a count vector under independent Poisson laws
articles.statement:
The joint law of independent Poisson counts with means `E_i` gives the count vector `k`
the probability `∏ e^{-E_i} E_i ^ {k_i} / (k_i!)`.

articles.title: Profile maximum in `θ`
articles.statement:
With means `E_i = θ f_i` linear in the mutation parameter,
positive `f_i` and at least one count, every `θ > 0` has likelihood at most that of
`θ̂ = ∑ k_i / ∑ f_i`.

articles.title: Poisson log-likelihood of counts
articles.statement:
The Poisson log-likelihood `∑ (k_i log E_i - E_i - log k_i!)` of counts `k_i` with means
`E_i`. Meaningful for `E_i > 0`; at `E_i = 0` Lean's `log 0 = 0` gives a junk value.

articles.title: Score equations
articles.statement:
If `ψ` maximizes the Poisson log-likelihood over a parameter set `S`
that is a neighborhood of `ψ`, and the means are positive and differentiable at `ψ`, then
`∑ (k_i / E_i(ψ) - 1) · DE_i(ψ) = 0`.

articles.title: Variance of the selection coefficient under the gamma DFE
articles.statement: The variance of the scaled selection coefficient under the gamma DFE is `a / r ^ 2`.

articles.title: Conditional upper-tail p-value of the Ewens–Watterson test
articles.statement:
The **conditional upper-tail p-value** of a statistic `T` of the allelic partition: the
conditional probability, given the observed number of alleles `K(π)`, that `T` is at least
its observed value `T π`. It is written with the cycle-type weights and so does not involve
`θ` (by `ewensCondProb_eq` it is the conditional tail probability for every `θ > 0`).

articles.title: Positivity of the cycle-type weight
articles.statement: The cycle-type weight is positive.

articles.title: Number of permutations with a given cycle type
articles.statement:
The number of permutations of `n` letters with cycle type `π`,
`w(π) = n! / ∏ j, j ^ (a j) * (a j)!` with `a j = π.parts.count j` (Cauchy's formula).

articles.title: The Ewens–Watterson conditional law
articles.statement:
**The Ewens–Watterson conditional law** (Ewens 1972; Watterson 1978): for `θ > 0`,
`P(π | K = K(π)) = w(π) / |s(n, K(π))| = n! / (|s(n, k)| ∏ j, j ^ (a j) (a j)!)`.

articles.title: `K` is sufficient for `θ`
articles.statement:
**`K` is sufficient for `θ`** (Ewens 1972): for `θ > 0`, the conditional law of the
allelic partition given the number of alleles is `w(π) / ∑_{K(π') = K(π)} w(π')`, which does
not depend on `θ`.

articles.title: Ewens conditional probability given the number of alleles
articles.statement:
The conditional probability of the allelic partition `π` given that the number of alleles
is `K = K(π) = π.parts.card`, under the Ewens sampling formula with parameter `θ`.

articles.title: Factorization of the Ewens sampling formula
articles.statement:
**Factorization of the Ewens sampling formula** (Ewens 1972):
`P_θ(π) = θ ^ K(π) / θ^{(n)} * w(π)`, with `K(π) = π.parts.card` the number of alleles.

articles.title: Sample homozygosity of an allelic partition
articles.statement:
The **sample homozygosity** `F(π) = ∑_i (n_i / n)²`, the sum over the alleles of the
squared sample frequencies (Watterson 1978); `n_i` ranges over the parts of `π`.

articles.title: Law of the number of alleles
articles.statement:
**Law of the number of alleles** (Ewens 1972):
`P_θ(K = k) = |s(n, k)| θ ^ k / θ^{(n)}`. As an identity between the defining sums it holds
for every real `θ`; it is a probability for `θ > 0`.

articles.title: Probability of a given number of alleles under the Ewens formula
articles.statement:
The probability `P_θ(K = k)` that a sample of `n` genes carries exactly `k` distinct
alleles under the Ewens sampling formula.

articles.title: Conditional validity of the Ewens–Watterson test
articles.statement:
For `θ > 0`, every number of alleles
`k` and every level `t ≥ 0`, the conditional probability given `K = k` that the conditional
upper-tail p-value of `T` is at most `t` is at most `t`.

articles.title: Validity of the Ewens–Watterson test
articles.statement:
**Validity of the Ewens–Watterson test** (Watterson 1978): for every `θ > 0` and every
level `t ≥ 0`, the Ewens probability that the conditional upper-tail p-value of `T` is at most
`t` is at most `t`. With `T = homozygosity` this is the test against excess homozygosity, with
`T = -homozygosity` the test against a deficit of homozygosity.

articles.title: Cauchy's count by number of cycles
articles.statement:
The cycle-type weights of the partitions of `n`
into `k` parts sum to the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind `|s(n, k)|`.

articles.title: Validity of a discrete upper-tail p-value
articles.statement:
For nonnegative masses `q` on a finite set
`s` and a statistic `T`, the upper-tail p-value `p x = ∑_{y ∈ s, T x ≤ T y} q y` satisfies
`∑_{x ∈ s, p x ≤ t} q x ≤ t` for every `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Concordant haplotype pairs sharing a core allele
articles.statement:
The number of ordered pairs of distinct haplotypes of `C` whose core alleles (under
`core`) agree and whose windows of radius `d` agree. The extended haplotype includes the
core, so pairs carrying different core alleles are never concordant, even when their
outward windows match.

articles.title: Concordant haplotype pairs at a given radius
articles.statement:
The number of ordered pairs of distinct haplotypes of `C` whose windows of radius `d`
agree.

articles.title: EHH is nonincreasing in the radius
articles.statement: EHH is nonincreasing in the radius: widening the window can only break ties.

articles.title: Extended haplotype homozygosity with core-allele labels
articles.statement:
Extended haplotype homozygosity with core-allele labels: the probability that two
distinct haplotypes drawn from `C` without replacement share both their core allele and
their window of radius `d`. For a set `C` of carriers of a single core allele this is the
same count as `ehh`; for a pooled set `D` carrying several core alleles it excludes the
cross-core pairs that plain `ehh` would wrongly count as concordant.

articles.title: EHH as homozygosity of window-type counts
articles.statement:
EHH as the sampling-without-replacement homozygosity of the partition of `C` into window
types: `EHH(d) = ∑_t c_t (c_t - 1) / (#C (#C - 1))`, where `c_t` is the number of haplotypes of
`C` with window `t`. This is the form in which EHH is usually defined.

articles.title: EHH is zero for a set of at most one haplotype
articles.statement: Outside the domain `2 ≤ #C` the definition returns the junk value `0`.

articles.title: EHH at radius zero equals one
articles.statement: At radius `0` every pair of haplotypes agrees, so `EHH(0) = 1`.

articles.title: Extended haplotype homozygosity (EHH)
articles.statement:
Extended haplotype homozygosity at radius `d` of the haplotype set `C`: the probability
that two distinct haplotypes drawn from `C` without replacement agree at all `d` sites nearest
the core (Sabeti et al. 2002). For `#C ≤ 1` the denominator vanishes and the junk value `0` is
returned; every statement below that needs the probabilistic reading assumes `2 ≤ #C`.

articles.title: Mean no-recombination probability under the neutral coalescent
articles.statement:
Averaging over the pair coalescence time `T₂`, which is exponential of rate `1` in units of
`2N` generations under the neutral coalescent, the probability that no recombination falls on
the pair's genealogy within distance `d` is `1 / (1 + ρ d)`. In a mutation-free model, since
a recombined lineage can still carry an identical haplotype, this is a lower bound for
`E[EHH(d)]`; without that assumption the bound is not established.

articles.title: Criterion for relative EHH to exceed one
articles.statement:
With a positive reference EHH, the relative EHH exceeds `1` exactly when the core allele's
haplotypes are the more homozygous ones.

articles.title: No-recombination probability decays with distance
articles.statement: The no-recombination probability decays in the distance from the core.

articles.title: Probability of no recombination on a pair's genealogy
articles.statement:
The probability that no recombination falls on the genealogy of a pair of lineages within
genetic distance `d` of the core, given that the pair coalesces at time `t` (time in units of
`2N` generations, `ρ = 4Nr` the scaled recombination rate per site): the two lineages carry
recombination events at total rate `ρ * d` until they coalesce.

In a mutation-free model this is a lower bound for the probability that the two haplotypes
are identical over the window — no recombination then implies identical windows, while a
recombined lineage may still carry the same alleles — so it is a lower bound for the
expected EHH, not its value. Without the mutation-free assumption the bound is not
established: mutations on either descendant branch can make the haplotypes differ even
with no recombination.

articles.title: Relative extended haplotype homozygosity (REHH)
articles.statement:
Relative extended haplotype homozygosity: the core-labelled EHH of the core-allele
carriers `C` divided by the core-labelled EHH of the pooled set `D` of haplotypes carrying
the other core alleles. The denominator counts only pairs sharing a core allele, so
cross-core pairs never inflate it. This is the statistic of the long-range haplotype test
(Sabeti et al. 2002). It is a junk value `0` when the denominator vanishes;
`one_lt_rehh_iff` assumes a positive denominator.

articles.title: Equality of haplotype windows
articles.statement:
Two haplotypes have the same window of radius `d` exactly when they agree at every site
`k < d`.

articles.title: Haplotype window around the core
articles.statement:
The window of radius `d` of haplotype `i`: its alleles at the `d` sites closest to the
core, in the direction indexed by `ℕ`.

articles.title: HKA expected divergence
articles.statement: HKA's expected divergence `θ (T + (1 + f) / 2)`.

articles.title: Positivity of the HKA divergence variance
articles.statement: HKA's divergence variance is positive for `θ > 0`, `T ≥ 0`, `f > -1`.

articles.title: HKA variance of the divergence
articles.statement: HKA's variance of the divergence, `θ (T + (1 + f) / 2) + (θ (1 + f) / 2)²`.

articles.title: True parameters solve the HKA estimating equations
articles.statement: The true parameters solve HKA's estimating equations at the expected counts.

articles.title: HKA's estimating equations
articles.statement:
**HKA's estimating equations** (Hudson, Kreitman & Aguadé 1987) for parameters
`θ i`, `T`, `f` given the counts: the totals over loci of polymorphism in `A`, in `B` and of
divergence match their expectations, and at each locus the total of the three counts matches
its expectation. (Only `L - 1` of the per-locus equations are independent of the totals.)

articles.title: HKA expected number of segregating sites
articles.statement:
HKA's expected number of segregating sites `θ C(n)` in a sample of `n` genes with scaled
mutation rate `θ` (use `f θ` for species `B`).

articles.title: Positivity of the HKA polymorphism variance
articles.statement: HKA's variances are positive in the biological domain: `θ > 0`, `n ≥ 2`.

articles.title: HKA variance of the number of segregating sites
articles.statement: HKA's variance of the number of segregating sites, `θ C(n) + θ² C₂(n)`.

articles.title: Hudson–Kreitman–Aguadé statistic
articles.statement:
The **HKA statistic** for `L` loci with polymorphism counts `SA i`, `SB i`, divergences
`D i`, parameters `θ i`, `T`, `f` and sample sizes `nA`, `nB`: the sum over loci of the
squared standardized deviations of the three counts from their HKA expectations.

articles.title: Expected divergence
articles.statement:
**Expected divergence** (Hudson, Kreitman & Aguadé 1987): if the ancestral coalescence time
`τ` is exponential with rate `2 / (1 + f)` and, given the genealogy σ-algebra `m`, the
divergence `D` has conditional mean `θ (T + τ)`, then `E D = θ (T + (1 + f) / 2)`
(for `f > -1`). No integrability hypothesis on `D` is needed: if `D` were not integrable its
conditional expectation would be `0` (Mathlib's convention), and the hypothesis would force
`θ = 0`, where the identity reads `0 = 0`.

articles.title: The HKA statistic has mean `3 L` at the true parameters
articles.statement:
If every count is square
integrable with the HKA mean and variance (as derived above under the neutral model), with
`θ i > 0`, `T ≥ 0`, `f > 0` and `nA, nB ≥ 2`, then `E X² = 3 L`.

articles.title: Variance of the divergence
articles.statement:
**Variance of the divergence** (Hudson, Kreitman & Aguadé 1987): under the hypotheses of
`integral_hkaDivergence`, if moreover `D` is square integrable with conditional variance
`θ (T + τ)` given `m` (as for a Poisson count), then
`Var D = θ (T + (1 + f) / 2) + (θ (1 + f) / 2)²`.

articles.title: Adaptive proportion estimator equals one minus the neutrality index
articles.statement: `α̂ = 1 - NI`, for all real counts (the junk values of division agree).

articles.title: `α̂` at the expected counts is the proportion of adaptive substitutions
articles.statement: (Smith & Eyre-Walker 2002): `1 - (E D_s E P_n) / (E D_n E P_s) = A / E D_n`.

articles.title: Smith–Eyre-Walker estimator of adaptive substitutions
articles.statement:
The Smith–Eyre-Walker estimator of the proportion of adaptive nonsynonymous
substitutions, `α̂ = 1 - (D_s P_n) / (D_n P_s)`.

articles.title: Proportion of adaptive nonsynonymous substitutions
articles.statement: The proportion of nonsynonymous substitutions that are adaptive, `α = A / E D_n`.

articles.title: Expected nonsynonymous fixed differences
articles.statement: Expected nonsynonymous fixed differences `E D_n = λ_D f₀ L_n + A`.

articles.title: Expected synonymous fixed differences
articles.statement: Expected synonymous fixed differences `E D_s = λ_D L_s`.

articles.title: Expected nonsynonymous polymorphisms
articles.statement: Expected nonsynonymous polymorphisms `E P_n = θ_P f₀ L_n`.

articles.title: Expected synonymous polymorphisms
articles.statement: Expected synonymous polymorphisms `E P_s = θ_P L_s`.

articles.title: Expected-count model of the McDonald–Kreitman table
articles.statement:
Expected counts of the MK table without a slightly deleterious class (see the module
docstring): synonymous and nonsynonymous mutational targets `Ls`, `Ln`, neutral fraction `f₀`
of nonsynonymous mutations, polymorphisms and neutral fixed differences per unit of neutral
target `polyRate`, `divRate` (`θ_P`, `λ_D` in the module docstring), and `A` expected adaptive
substitutions.

articles.title: Neutrality index
articles.statement: The neutrality index `NI = (P_n / P_s) / (D_n / D_s)`.

articles.title: The MK null is neutrality
articles.statement:
The proportions of nonsynonymous changes among expected
fixed differences and expected polymorphisms agree iff there are no adaptive substitutions.

articles.title: Consistency of `α̂` over loci
articles.statement:
Let `Dn i, Ds i, Pn i, Ps i` be the counts at locus
`i`; suppose each of the four sequences consists of pairwise independent, identically
distributed, integrable variables whose means are the expected counts of `M` (the loci are
exchangeable copies of the model). Then almost surely `α̂` computed from the counts summed over
the first `m` loci converges to `α = A / E D_n` as `m → ∞`.

articles.title: Sweep trajectory solves the logistic equation
articles.statement: The logistic equation: `x'(t) = s x(t) (1 - x(t))`.

articles.title: One-sided iHH in the star-genealogy model
articles.statement:
In the star-genealogy model the one-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity is
`1 / (2 r T)`.

articles.title: Two-sided iHH in the star-genealogy model
articles.statement:
In the star-genealogy model the two-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity is
`1 / (r T)`.

articles.title: Two-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity
articles.statement:
The two-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity of Voight et al.: the sum of the
one-sided integrals in the two chromosome directions.

articles.title: One-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity
iHS as the log ratio of genealogy ages
articles.statement:
In the star-genealogy model the integrated haplotype score is the log ratio of the two
ages, so the recombination rate cancels.

articles.title: iHS is negative exactly when the derived allele is younger
articles.statement:
The integrated haplotype score is negative exactly when the derived allele's star
genealogy is the younger one, i.e. when the derived allele swept faster.

articles.title: Integrated haplotype score (iHS)
articles.statement:
The integrated haplotype score of Voight et al. (2006): the log ratio of the integrated
haplotype homozygosities of the ancestral and the derived allele, whose star genealogies have
ages `T_A` and `T_D`. The factor of two between the one-sided and two-sided integrals
cancels in this ratio.

articles.title: Duration of a complete deterministic sweep
articles.statement:
A complete sweep in a population of `N` diploids, from a single copy `1 / (2N)` to
`1 - 1 / (2N)`, takes exactly `(2 / s) log (2N - 1)` generations in the deterministic logistic
model. (The familiar `(2 / s) log (2Ns)` is the conditional expected duration of the
corresponding stochastic sweep, a different quantity.)

articles.title: Positivity of the sweep duration
articles.statement: The time to reach a higher frequency is positive.

articles.title: Duration of a logistic sweep between two frequencies
articles.statement:
The time the logistic trajectory with selection coefficient `s` takes to go from frequency
`a` to frequency `b`: `(1/s) log (b (1 - a) / (a (1 - b)))`, the difference of the logits
divided by `s`.

articles.title: Star-genealogy EHH decays with window length
articles.statement: Haplotype homozygosity decays with the window length.

articles.title: Star-genealogy EHH as a squared Poisson zero probability
articles.statement:
The star-genealogy EHH is the square of the probability that a Poisson number of
recombination events with mean `r d T` on one lineage is zero.

articles.title: Power-law EHH after a complete sweep
articles.statement:
Combining the exact sweep duration with the star-genealogy decay: after a complete sweep
of a favourable allele with selection coefficient `s` in a population of `N` diploids, the
extended haplotype homozygosity at genetic distance `d` is the power law
`(2N - 1) ^ (-(4 r d / s))`.

articles.title: EHH in the star-genealogy sweep model
articles.statement:
The probability that two carriers of a swept allele are identical over a window of genetic
length `d`, in the star-genealogy model of Voight et al. (2006): all carriers coalesce at the
start of the sweep, a time `T` ago, and the pair is identical exactly when neither of its two
lineages recombined, each at rate `r * d` per unit time.

articles.title: Sweep trajectory stays strictly between 0 and 1
articles.statement: The trajectory stays strictly between `0` and `1`.

articles.title: Sweep trajectory reaches its target at the sweep duration
articles.statement:
`sweepDuration s a b` is the exact time at which the trajectory started at `a` reaches
`b`.

articles.title: Logistic trajectory of a selective sweep
articles.statement:
The logistic trajectory of a favourable allele with genic selection coefficient `s`,
starting from frequency `x₀`: the solution of `x' = s x (1 - x)` with `x 0 = x₀`
(Maynard Smith and Haigh 1974).

articles.title: Level of the Chebyshev test
articles.statement:
If Tajima's numerator `π - S / a₁` is square integrable
with mean `0` and variance `c₁ θ₀ + c₂ θ₀² > 0` (as under the standard neutral model, by
`KingmanTimes.integral_tajimaNumerator` and `KingmanTimes.variance_tajimaNumerator`), then for
every `α > 0` the test rejects with probability at most `α`.

articles.title: Positivity of Tajima's $c_1$ for at least four genes
Tajima's $c_1$ vanishes for three genes
articles.statement: For three genes `c₁ = 0`.

articles.title: Tajima's $c_1$ vanishes for two genes
articles.statement: For two genes `c₁ = 0`.

articles.title: Positivity of Tajima's $c_2$ for at least four genes
articles.statement: `c₂ = b₂ - (n + 2) / (a₁ n) + a₂ / a₁² > 0` for `n ≥ 4`.

articles.title: Tajima's $c_2$ vanishes for three genes
articles.statement: For three genes `c₂ = 0`.

articles.title: Tajima's $c_2$ vanishes for two genes
articles.statement: For two genes `c₂ = 0`.

articles.title: Chebyshev test of neutrality
articles.statement:
The rejection region of the **Chebyshev test of neutrality** at level `α` and hypothesized
`θ₀`: `|π - S / a₁| ≥ √((c₁ θ₀ + c₂ θ₀²) / α)`.

articles.title: Tajima's `D`
articles.statement:
**Tajima's `D`** (Tajima 1989) for a sample of `n` genes with mean number of pairwise
differences `π` and `S` segregating sites:
`D = (π - S / a₁) / √(e₁ S + e₂ S (S - 1))`. It is meaningful for `n ≥ 4` and `S ≥ 1`
(`tajimaVarEstimator_pos`); otherwise Lean's junk values for `x / 0` and `√` of a nonpositive
number apply.

articles.title: Positivity of the denominator of Tajima's D
articles.statement:
The denominator of Tajima's `D` is well defined: `e₁ S + e₂ S (S - 1) > 0` for `n ≥ 4` and
`S ≥ 1`.

articles.title: Convex order
articles.statement:
`g₁ ≤cx g₂` if `∫ φ dg₁ ≤ ∫ φ dg₂` for every convex `φ : ℝ → ℝ` that is
integrable under both laws (Shaked–Shanthikumar 2007, §3.A).

articles.title: Euler–Lotka
articles.statement:
Under the hypotheses of `renewal_exp_iff`, exponential growth at rate
`r` solves the renewal equation iff `R = 1 / M_g(-r)`.

articles.title: Renewal equation for exponential growth
articles.statement:
For `c ≠ 0`, the exponential
`b(t) = c e^{r t}` solves `b(t) = R ∫ b(t - a) g(da)` for every `t` iff `R M_g(-r) = 1`.
This is meaningful when `a ↦ e^{-r a}` is `g`-integrable; otherwise Lean's integral and
`M_g(-r)` are both `0` and both sides of the equivalence are false.

articles.title: Fixed generation interval
articles.statement: **Fixed generation interval** `T`: `R = e^{r T}` (for all real `r`, `T`).

articles.title: Exponential generation interval
articles.statement:
**Exponential generation interval** with mean `T > 0` (rate `1 / T`): for `r T > -1`,
`R = 1 + r T` (Wallinga–Lipsitch 2007, eq. 3.1).

articles.title: Gamma generation interval
articles.statement:
**Gamma generation interval** with shape `α > 0` and rate `β > 0`: for `r > -β`,
`R = (1 + r / β)^α`.

articles.title: Jensen bound
articles.statement:
If the generation interval has finite mean `T̄ = ∫ a g(da)` and finite
`M_g(-r)`, then `R ≤ e^{r T̄}` (any real `r`); Wallinga and Lipsitch (2007, §3) note that the
fixed interval gives this upper bound.

articles.title: More spread lowers `R`
articles.statement:
If `g₁ ≤cx g₂` and both have finite `M(-r)`, then
`R(g₂) ≤ R(g₁)` at growth rate `r` (any real `r`). In particular, among generation intervals
with a given mean, the fixed interval maximizes `R`.

articles.title: Positivity of the reproductive number
articles.statement: The reproductive number is positive when `M_g(-r)` is finite.

articles.title: Reproductive number from growth rate and generation interval
articles.statement:
The **reproductive number** implied by growth rate `r` and generation-interval law `g`:
`R = 1 / M_g(-r)` (Wallinga–Lipsitch 2007, eq. 2.9).

articles.title: Threshold theorem (Kermack–McKendrick 1927)
articles.statement:
If initially `I(0) > 0`, with `γ > 0` and
`N > 0`, the number of infectives initially increases, `I'(0) > 0`, iff
`R₀ S(0) / N > 1` with `R₀ = β / γ`.

articles.title: Final-size equation (Kermack–McKendrick 1927)
articles.statement:
If the population is `N = S + I + R`,
nobody is removed initially (`R(0) = 0`), `γ ≠ 0`, `S(t) → S∞` and the epidemic dies out
(`I(t) → 0`), then `S∞ = S(0) e^{-R₀ (N - S∞) / N}` with `R₀ = β / γ`.

articles.title: Final-size relation (Kermack–McKendrick 1927)
articles.statement:
If along a solution (`γ ≠ 0`)
`S(t) → S∞` and `R(t) → R∞` as `t → ∞`, then `S∞ = S(0) e^{-R₀ (R∞ - R(0)) / N}` with
`R₀ = β / γ`. See `final_size_eq` for the classical form.

articles.title: Solution of the Kermack–McKendrick SIR system
articles.statement:
`(S, I, R)` solves the Kermack–McKendrick SIR system with transmission rate `β`, removal
rate `γ` and population size `N` for all times `t ≥ 0`:
`S' = -β S I / N`, `I' = β S I / N - γ I`, `R' = γ I`.

articles.title: Conserved quantity behind the final-size relation
articles.statement:
For `γ ≠ 0`, the quantity
`S(t) e^{R₀ R(t) / N}` (`R₀ = β / γ`) is constant along a solution on `[0, ∞)`.

articles.title: Conservation of the population
articles.statement:
Along a solution, `S + I + R` is constant on
`[0, ∞)`.

articles.title: `R₀ > 1` gives an unstable mode
articles.statement:
**`R₀ > 1` gives an unstable mode** (van den Driessche–Watmough 2002, proof of Theorem 2).
If `F` is entrywise nonnegative and `V` is a nonsingular M-matrix, then `F - V` has an
eigenvalue with positive real part iff `R₀ = ρ(F V⁻¹) > 1`.

articles.title: Threshold theorem, instability half, spectral form
articles.statement:
**Threshold theorem, instability half, spectral form** (van den Driessche–Watmough 2002,
Theorem 2). With `F ≥ 0` and `V` a nonsingular M-matrix, if `R₀ = ρ(F V⁻¹) > 1` then the
Jacobian `[[F - V, 0], [C, D]]` at the disease-free equilibrium has an eigenvalue with positive
real part (whatever `C` and `D`).

articles.title: Threshold theorem, stability half, conditional decay form
articles.statement:
**Threshold theorem, stability half, conditional decay form** (van den Driessche–Watmough
2002, Theorem 2). Let `x₀` be an equilibrium of `x' = f(x)` on `ℝ^{ι ⊕ κ}` (infected
compartments `ι`, the others `κ`), with `f` differentiable at `x₀` and Jacobian
`[[F - V, 0], [C, D]]` as in their Lemma 1, where `F ≥ 0`, `V` is a nonsingular M-matrix and
`D` is Hurwitz. If `R₀ = ρ(F V⁻¹) < 1`, then every solution defined on all of `[0, ∞)`
starting near `x₀` decays exponentially. The statement concerns only solutions defined on all of `[0, ∞)`, so it is not by itself local exponential stability.

articles.title: Hurwitz criterion for block lower-triangular matrices
articles.statement:
A block lower-triangular real matrix `[[A, 0], [C, D]]` is Hurwitz iff both diagonal
blocks are.

articles.title: `R₀` as a threshold for the linearized infected subsystem
articles.statement:
**`R₀` as a threshold for the linearized infected subsystem** (van den Driessche–Watmough
2002, proof of Theorem 2). If `F` is entrywise nonnegative and `V` is a nonsingular M-matrix,
then every eigenvalue of `F - V` has negative real part iff `R₀ = ρ(F V⁻¹) < 1`.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a block lower-triangular matrix
articles.statement:
The complex eigenvalues of a block lower-triangular real matrix `[[A, 0], [C, D]]` are
those of `A` together with those of `D`.

articles.title: Basic reproduction number of the next-generation matrix
articles.statement:
The **basic reproduction number** `R₀ = ρ(F V⁻¹)`: the spectral radius (largest modulus of
a complex eigenvalue) of the next-generation matrix `F V⁻¹` (van den Driessche–Watmough 2002,
Eq. (4)). It is meaningful when `V` is invertible (for a nonsingular M-matrix it is).

articles.title: Comparison principle for Galton–Watson extinction
articles.statement:
If the offspring generating
functions satisfy `f₂ ≤ f₁` on `[0, 1]`, then the extinction probabilities satisfy
`q₂ ≤ q₁`.

articles.title: Superspreading raises the extinction probability
articles.statement:
**Superspreading raises the extinction probability** (Lloyd-Smith et al. 2005): at a
fixed mean `R ≥ 0`, the probability `q_k` that the outbreak started by one case goes extinct
is nonincreasing in the dispersion `k > 0`.

articles.title: Generating-function identity
Negative-binomial extinction probability is the least fixed point
articles.statement:
The extinction probability of the negative-binomial epidemic is the least fixed point of
`G_k` in `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Negative-binomial offspring law is a probability measure
articles.statement: The negative-binomial offspring law is a probability measure (`k > 0`, `R ≥ 0`).

articles.title: Negative-binomial offspring distribution
articles.statement: The negative-binomial offspring law as a measure on `ℕ`.

articles.title: Monotonicity in the dispersion
articles.statement:
For `R ≥ 0`, `s ∈ [0, 1]` and `0 < k₁ ≤ k₂`,
`G_{k₂}(s) ≤ G_{k₁}(s)`; equivalently `k ↦ k log (1 + x / k)` is nondecreasing for `x ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Negative-binomial law with dispersion one is geometric
articles.statement: `k = 1` is the geometric offspring law: `G_1(s) = 1 / (1 + R (1 - s))`.

articles.title: Negative-binomial probability generating function
articles.statement: The **negative-binomial generating function** `G_k(s) = (1 + (R / k) (1 - s))^{-k}`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the negative-binomial probabilities
articles.statement: The negative-binomial probabilities are nonnegative for `k > 0`, `R ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Negative-binomial offspring probabilities
articles.statement:
The **negative-binomial offspring probability** with mean `R` and dispersion `k`:
`P(Z = n) = C(k + n - 1, n) p^k (1 - p)^n` with `p = k / (k + R)` (Lloyd-Smith et al. 2005).
Meaningful for `k > 0`, `R ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Generating function of the negative-binomial law in closed form
articles.statement: The generating function of the negative-binomial offspring law is `nbPgf` on `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Poisson limit
articles.statement: As `k → ∞`, `G_k(s) → e^{-R (1 - s)}` (for all real `R`, `s`).

articles.title: Rate of the Ablowitz–Zeppetella wave
articles.statement: The rate `κ = √(r / (6 D))` of the Ablowitz–Zeppetella wave.

articles.title: Speed of the Ablowitz–Zeppetella wave
articles.statement: The Ablowitz–Zeppetella speed `c = 5 √(r D / 6)` (`5 / √6` when `D = r = 1`).

articles.title: Derivative of the Ablowitz–Zeppetella profile
articles.statement: The derivative of the Ablowitz–Zeppetella profile, `-2 κ C e^{κ z} (1 + C e^{κ z})⁻³`.

articles.title: Ablowitz–Zeppetella wave profile
articles.statement: The Ablowitz–Zeppetella profile `U(z) = (1 + C exp (κ z))⁻²`.

articles.title: Kolmogorov–Petrovsky–Piskunov: fronts exist at every speed `c ≥ 2 √(r D)`
articles.statement:
**Kolmogorov–Petrovsky–Piskunov: fronts exist at every speed `c ≥ 2 √(r D)`**, and they are
strictly decreasing.

articles.title: Time derivative of a traveling wave
articles.statement: Time derivative of the wave `u(x, t) = U(x - c t)`: `∂u/∂t = -c U'(x - c t)`.

articles.title: Space derivative of a traveling wave
articles.statement: Space derivative of the wave: `∂u/∂x = U'(x - c t)`.

articles.title: Traveling wave solves the Fisher–KPP equation
articles.statement:
Second space derivative of the wave; with `hD : D ≠ 0` it gives the PDE
`-c U' = D U'' + r U (1 - U)`, i.e. `∂u/∂t = D ∂²u/∂x² + r u (1 - u)`.

articles.title: The Ablowitz–Zeppetella front
articles.statement:
For `D, r, C > 0`, `(1 + C exp (z √(r / (6 D))))⁻²` is a
front of speed `5 √(r D / 6)`.

articles.title: Traveling front of the Fisher–KPP equation
articles.statement:
A traveling front of speed `c`: a wave profile with `0 < U < 1`, `U → 1` at `-∞` and
`U → 0` at `+∞`.

articles.title: Traveling-wave profile of the Fisher–KPP equation
articles.statement:
`U` is a traveling-wave profile of speed `c` for `∂u/∂t = D ∂²u/∂x² + r u (1 - u)`: it is
twice differentiable with first derivative `U'` and `U'' = -(c U' + r U (1 - U)) / D`, which for
`D ≠ 0` is the profile equation `D U'' + c U' + r U (1 - U) = 0`.

articles.title: No traveling wave with `c² < 4 r D`
articles.statement:
If `D, r > 0` and `c² < 4 r D`, a wave profile
tending to `0` at `+∞` is not eventually positive. (This excludes `|c| < 2 √(r D)`, not
`c < 2 √(r D)` for negative `c`.)

articles.title: Minimal speed of Fisher–KPP traveling fronts
articles.statement: A front of speed `c` needs `c² ≥ 4 r D`; for `c ≥ 0` this is `c ≥ 2 √(r D)`.

articles.title: Ablowitz–Zeppetella speed exceeds the minimal front speed
articles.statement: The Ablowitz–Zeppetella speed exceeds the minimal speed: `2 √(r D) < 5 √(r D / 6)`.

articles.title: Positivity of the decay length
articles.statement: The decay length is positive for positive `D` and `k`.

articles.title: Decay length of a morphogen gradient
articles.statement:
The decay length `λ = √(D / k)` of a morphogen with diffusion coefficient `D` and linear
degradation rate `k` (both positive in the model).

articles.title: Diffusion coefficient over squared decay length equals degradation rate
articles.statement: `D / λ² = k`.

articles.title: Uniqueness
articles.statement:
Every bounded steady state with source flux `j` is the exponential
profile on `[0, ∞)`.

articles.title: Slope of the morphogen profile
articles.statement: The profile has slope `c'(x) = -c(x)/λ`.

articles.title: Exponential profile is a bounded steady state
articles.statement: The exponential profile is a bounded steady state with source flux `j`.

articles.title: Bounded steady state of the synthesis–diffusion–degradation model
articles.statement:
A bounded steady state of the synthesis–diffusion–degradation model on `[0, ∞)`, with
`c' = dc/dx`: `D c'' = k c` for `x > 0`, `c` and `c'` continuous up to the source, source flux
`-D c'(0) = j`, and `c` bounded on `[0, ∞)`.

articles.title: French-flag regions
articles.statement:
A cell at `x` is at or above threshold `θ` iff it lies within the
boundary `x_θ`: `θ ≤ c(x) ↔ x ≤ x_θ`.

articles.title: French-flag boundary
articles.statement:
For positive parameters and threshold `θ`, `c(x) = θ` exactly at
`x = x_θ = λ log(c(0)/θ)`.

articles.title: Morphogen profile is strictly decreasing
articles.statement: The profile is strictly decreasing in `x` for a positive source.

articles.title: Profile equals the threshold at the French-flag boundary
articles.statement: The profile equals `θ` at the boundary `x_θ`.

articles.title: Steady-state exponential morphogen profile
articles.statement:
The steady-state gradient `c(x) = (j / √(D k)) e^{-x/λ}`, `λ = √(D / k)`, for source flux
`j` at `x = 0`. Meaningful for `D, k > 0`.

articles.title: Source amplitude in terms of the decay length
articles.statement: `√(D k) = D / λ`, so the source amplitude is `c(0) = j λ / D`.

articles.title: Boundary shift
articles.statement:
Scaling the source flux by `a > 0` moves every French-flag boundary by
`λ log a`.

articles.title: Doubling the source flux shifts boundaries by $\lambda \log 2$
articles.statement:
Doubling the source flux shifts every French-flag boundary away from the source by exactly
`λ log 2`.

articles.title: French-flag boundary position for a threshold
articles.statement:
The French-flag boundary for threshold `θ`: `x_θ = λ log(c(0) / θ)`, where
`c(0) = j / √(D k)`. Meaningful for `D, k, j, θ > 0`; it is negative when `θ > c(0)` (no cell
is above threshold).

articles.title: Discriminant of the dispersion polynomial
articles.statement: The discriminant `(d_v f_u + d_u g_v)² - 4 d_u d_v det J` of the dispersion polynomial.

articles.title: Lower end of the unstable wavenumber band
articles.statement:
Lower end `q₋ = (S - √Δ) / (2 d_u d_v)` of the unstable band of squared wavenumbers, where
`S = d_v f_u + d_u g_v` and `Δ = bandDiscriminant` (meaningful when `0 < Δ`, `d_u, d_v > 0`).

articles.title: Upper end of the unstable wavenumber band
articles.statement:
Upper end `q₊ = (S + √Δ) / (2 d_u d_v)` of the unstable band of squared wavenumbers
(meaningful when `0 < Δ`, `d_u, d_v > 0`).

articles.title: Critical wavenumber at the Turing bifurcation threshold
articles.statement:
At the bifurcation threshold `d_v f_u + d_u g_v = 2 √(d_u d_v det J)` the critical
squared wavenumber is `k_c² = √(det J / (d_u d_v))` and `h(k_c²) = 0`.

articles.title: Squared critical wavenumber
articles.statement:
The squared critical wavenumber `k_c² = (d_v f_u + d_u g_v) / (2 d_u d_v)`, the minimizer
of the dispersion polynomial (meaningful for `d_u, d_v > 0`; division by zero gives `0`).

articles.title: Determinant of the Gierer–Meinhardt Jacobian
articles.statement: `det J = b` for the Gierer–Meinhardt Jacobian (`a + 1 ≠ 0`, `b ≠ 0`).

articles.title: Determinant of the mode matrix is the dispersion polynomial
articles.statement: `det (J - k² D) = h(k²)`.

articles.title: Determinant of the Schnakenberg Jacobian
articles.statement: `det J = (a + b)²` for the Schnakenberg Jacobian (`a + b ≠ 0`).

articles.title: Diffusion matrix of a two-species system
articles.statement: The diffusion matrix `D = diag(d_u, d_v)` of a two-species reaction-diffusion system.

articles.title: Critical squared wavenumber minimizes the dispersion polynomial
articles.statement: The critical squared wavenumber minimizes the dispersion polynomial over all real `q`.

articles.title: Minimum value of the dispersion polynomial
articles.statement:
The value of the dispersion polynomial at its minimizer:
`h(k_c²) = det J - (d_v f_u + d_u g_v)² / (4 d_u d_v)`.

articles.title: Dispersion polynomial is negative exactly on the unstable band
articles.statement:
For `d_u, d_v > 0`, the dispersion polynomial is negative exactly on the open band
`(q₋, q₊)`, which is nonempty iff the discriminant is positive.

articles.title: Dispersion polynomial
articles.statement:
The dispersion polynomial `h(q) = d_u d_v q² - (d_v f_u + d_u g_v) q + det J`, so that
`det (J - k² D) = h(k²)` (`det_modeMatrix`).

articles.title: Turing's criterion for diffusion-driven instability
articles.statement:
For `d_u, d_v > 0` and `0 < det J`, the dispersion polynomial is negative at some
`q ≥ 0` iff `2 √(d_u d_v det J) < d_v f_u + d_u g_v`.

articles.title: Routh–Hurwitz for `2 × 2` matrices
articles.statement:
A real `2 × 2` matrix has a complex eigenvalue with
positive real part iff its trace is positive or its determinant is negative.

articles.title: Turing's criterion
articles.statement:
If the steady state is stable without diffusion
(`tr J < 0`, `0 < det J`) and `d_u, d_v > 0`, some Fourier mode is unstable iff
`d_v f_u + d_u g_v > 2 √(d_u d_v det J)`.

articles.title: Large domains pattern
articles.statement:
Under Turing's criterion, every long enough interval `[0, L]` has
an unstable Neumann mode.

articles.title: Long intervals have a squared Neumann wavenumber in any given band
articles.statement:
Every long enough interval has a squared Neumann wavenumber inside a given nonempty open band
`(qlo, qhi)` with `0 < qhi`: there is `L₀ > 0` such that for all `L ≥ L₀` some `(n π / L)²` lies
in `(qlo, qhi)`.

articles.title: Only finitely many Neumann modes are unstable
articles.statement: Only finitely many Neumann modes are unstable on `[0, L]` (for `d_u, d_v, L > 0`, any `J`).

articles.title: Dispersion relation
articles.statement:
The Fourier mode `e^{μ t} cos(k x) v` is a classical solution of
the linearized system `w_t = D w_xx + J w` iff `(J - k² D) v = μ v`.

articles.title: Complex Fourier mode
articles.statement:
The complex Fourier mode `w(t, x) = e^{μ t} cos(k x) v` with growth rate `μ`, wavenumber `k`
and amplitude vector `v`. (The real part of a complex solution of the real linear system is a
real solution.)

articles.title: Jacobian of the Gierer–Meinhardt kinetics at its steady state
articles.statement:
The Jacobian of the Gierer–Meinhardt kinetics at its steady state,
`[[b (1 - a) / (1 + a), -(b / (a + 1))²], [2 (a + 1) / b, -1]]`.

articles.title: Gierer–Meinhardt steady state is an equilibrium
articles.statement:
`((a + 1) / b, ((a + 1) / b)²)` is a steady state of the Gierer–Meinhardt kinetics when
`a + 1 ≠ 0` and `b ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Steady state of the Gierer–Meinhardt kinetics
articles.statement:
The homogeneous steady state `(u₀, v₀) = ((a + 1) / b, ((a + 1) / b)²)` of the
Gierer–Meinhardt kinetics (meaningful for `b ≠ 0`, `a + 1 ≠ 0`).

articles.title: Turing instability of the Gierer–Meinhardt kinetics
articles.statement:
With `d_u = 1`, `d_v = d > 0`,
`0 < a + 1`, `0 < b` and `b (1 - a) < 1 + a` (stable without diffusion), some Fourier mode is
unstable iff `2 √(d b) < d b (1 - a) / (1 + a) - 1`.

articles.title: Gierer–Meinhardt activator-inhibitor kinetics
Neumann modes have zero flux at the boundary
articles.statement:
The Neumann mode `cos(k_n x)` has zero flux at both ends of `[0, L]`: the `x`-derivative of
the Fourier mode with wavenumber `k_n = n π / L` vanishes at `x = 0` and `x = L`.

articles.title: Classical solution of the linearized reaction-diffusion system
articles.statement:
`w` is a classical solution of the linearized reaction-diffusion system
`w_t = D w_xx + J w` on `ℝ × ℝ`: `w(t, ·)` is twice differentiable with first and second
derivatives `wx`, `wxx`, and `w(·, x)` is differentiable with the prescribed time derivative.

articles.title: Mode instability iff the dispersion polynomial is negative
articles.statement: If `tr J < 0` and `d_u, d_v ≥ 0`, mode `k` is unstable iff `h(k²) < 0`.

articles.title: A Fourier mode grows iff `J - k² D` has an eigenvalue with positive real part
articles.statement: **A Fourier mode grows iff `J - k² D` has an eigenvalue with positive real part.**

articles.title: Instability criterion for a Fourier mode via trace and determinant
articles.statement: Mode `k` is unstable iff `0 < tr (J - k² D)` or `det (J - k² D) < 0`.

articles.title: Finite domain
articles.statement:
On `[0, L]` with Neumann boundary conditions, if `tr J < 0` and
`d_u, d_v > 0`, mode `n` is unstable iff `k_n² = (n π / L)²` lies in the unstable band
`(q₋, q₊)` (which requires a positive discriminant).

articles.title: Critical wavenumber is unstable under Turing's criterion
articles.statement:
Under Turing's criterion the critical wavenumber `k_c = √(k_c²)` is itself unstable (and
`0 < k_c²`).

articles.title: Linearly unstable Fourier mode
articles.statement:
The Fourier mode of wavenumber `k` is *linearly unstable*: the mode matrix `J - k² D` has
a complex eigenvalue `μ` with `0 < Re μ`.

articles.title: Computation of the Gierer–Meinhardt Jacobian at the steady state
articles.statement:
The Jacobian matrix of the Gierer–Meinhardt kinetics at the steady state is
`giererMeinhardtJacobian a b`.

articles.title: Computation of the Schnakenberg Jacobian at the steady state
articles.statement:
The Jacobian matrix of the Schnakenberg kinetics at the steady state is
`schnakenbergJacobian a b`.

articles.title: The inhibitor diffuses faster
articles.statement:
In the activator-inhibitor sign pattern (`u` is the
activator, `0 < f_u`; then `g_v < 0` follows from `tr J < 0`), diffusion-driven instability of a
kinetically stable state forces `d_u < d_v`.

articles.title: Mode matrix of a linearized reaction-diffusion system
articles.statement:
The mode matrix `J - k² D` governing the Fourier mode of wavenumber `k` of the linearized
system `w_t = D w_xx + J w`, where `J` is the Jacobian of the kinetics at the steady state
(convention: `J i j` is the partial derivative of the `i`-th reaction term with respect to the
`j`-th species, so `J = [[f_u, f_v], [g_u, g_v]]`).

articles.title: `f_u` and `g_v` have opposite signs
articles.statement:
If the steady state is stable without diffusion
and `d_u, d_v ≥ 0`, diffusion-driven instability forces `f_u g_v < 0`.

articles.title: Neumann wavenumber on an interval
articles.statement:
The Neumann wavenumber `k_n = n π / L` of the mode `cos(n π x / L)` on `[0, L]`.
Meaningful only for `0 < L`; at `L = 0` the totalized division gives `0`, so every
labeled Neumann mode collapses to the homogeneous mode.

articles.title: Fourier mode is largest at the origin
articles.statement: `‖w(t, 0)‖` is the amplitude of the mode: `‖w(t, x)‖ ≤ ‖w(t, 0)‖` for every `x`.

articles.title: Amplitude of a Fourier mode
articles.statement: The amplitude of a Fourier mode: `‖w(t, 0)‖ = e^{Re μ · t} ‖v‖`.

articles.title: Small domains admit no pattern
articles.statement:
If the first nonhomogeneous mode already lies beyond the
band, `q₊ ≤ (π / L)²`, then no Neumann mode is unstable on `[0, L]`.

articles.title: Homogeneous mode is stable for stable kinetics
articles.statement:
The homogeneous mode `k = 0` is stable when the kinetics are stable (`tr J < 0`,
`0 < det J`).

articles.title: Jacobian of the Schnakenberg kinetics at its steady state
articles.statement:
The Jacobian of the Schnakenberg kinetics at its steady state,
`[[(b - a) / (a + b), (a + b)²], [-2 b / (a + b), -(a + b)²]]`.

articles.title: Schnakenberg steady state is an equilibrium
articles.statement: `(a + b, b / (a + b)²)` is a steady state of the Schnakenberg kinetics when `a + b ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Steady state of the Schnakenberg kinetics
articles.statement:
The homogeneous steady state `(u₀, v₀) = (a + b, b / (a + b)²)` of the Schnakenberg
kinetics (meaningful for `a + b ≠ 0`; at `a + b = 0` the division gives the junk `v₀ = 0`).

articles.title: Turing instability of the Schnakenberg kinetics
articles.statement:
**Turing instability of the Schnakenberg kinetics** (Murray 2003, ch. 2). With
`d_u = 1`, `d_v = d > 0`, `0 < a + b` and `b - a < (a + b)³` (stable without diffusion), some
Fourier mode is unstable iff `2 √d (a + b)² < d (b - a) - (a + b)³`.

articles.title: Schnakenberg reaction kinetics
articles.statement:
Schnakenberg's reaction terms `(f, g) = (a - u + u² v, b - u² v)` as a map on
`x = (u, v) : Fin 2 → ℝ`, with source rates `a, b` (biologically `a, b > 0`).

articles.title: Fourier mode grows unboundedly iff its growth rate is positive
articles.statement: A nonzero Fourier mode grows without bound iff its growth rate has positive real part.

articles.title: Stability of the Gierer–Meinhardt steady state without diffusion
articles.statement:
The Gierer–Meinhardt steady state is stable without diffusion iff `b (1 - a) < 1 + a`
(for `0 < a + 1`; then `0 < det J = b` for `0 < b`).

articles.title: Trace of the mode matrix
articles.statement: `tr (J - k² D) = tr J - k² (d_u + d_v)`.

articles.title: Stability of the Schnakenberg steady state without diffusion
articles.statement:
The Schnakenberg steady state is stable without diffusion iff `b - a < (a + b)³`
(for `0 < a + b`; then `0 < det J` automatically).

articles.title: Diffusion-driven instability (Turing 1952)
articles.statement:
If the steady state is stable without
diffusion (`tr J < 0`, `0 < det J`), `d_u, d_v ≥ 0`, and `det (J - k² D) < 0`, then the
homogeneous mode is stable while mode `k` is unstable.

articles.title: Turing condition in squared form
articles.statement:
The Turing condition in squared form: `2 √(d_u d_v det J) < S` iff `0 < S` and
`4 d_u d_v det J < S²`, where `S = d_v f_u + d_u g_v`. This holds for all real inputs: when
`d_u d_v det J < 0`, `Real.sqrt` returns `0` and both sides reduce to `0 < S`.

articles.title: The first join of neighbor joining on a perturbed tree metric joins a cherry
articles.statement:
Under the
hypotheses of `exists_adj_adj_of_qCriterion_min_of_abs_sub_lt`, any pair of clusters that
neighbor joining run on `D` may join from the initial singletons consists of two taxa with a
common neighbor.

articles.title: Robust cherry lemma for neighbor joining
articles.statement:
The selection step of Atteson's theorem
(Atteson 1999), with a proof after Mihaescu, Levy & Pachter (2009, Theorem 16). Let `d` be
the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths
`w` and at least four taxa, and let `μ` be a lower bound on the lengths of the internal edges
(edges with no taxon at either end). Let `D` be a symmetric dissimilarity with zero diagonal
such that `|D x y - d x y| < μ / 2` for all distinct taxa.
If the distinct taxa `x, y` minimize the Q-criterion of `D` over all pairs of distinct
singleton clusters at the start of neighbor joining, then `ι x` and `ι y` have a common
neighbor: they form a cherry. The bound is sharp: with `≤ μ / 2` a non-cherry can tie
(see the tests).

articles.title: Neighbor joining averages up to row shifts
articles.statement:
Along every run of neighbor joining on a
symmetric dissimilarity `d` with zero diagonal there are weights `α s` (nonnegative, supported
on `s`, summing to `1`) and row terms `κ s` such that the cluster dissimilarity vanishes on the
diagonal and `D s t = ∑ x, ∑ y, α s x * α t y * d x y - κ s - κ t` for distinct current
clusters. Joining `a, b` takes `α (a ∪ b) = (α a + α b) / 2` and
`κ (a ∪ b) = (κ a + κ b + D a b) / 2`.

articles.title: Robust cherry lemma for split systems
articles.statement:
The selection step of Atteson's theorem
(Atteson 1999), with a proof after Mihaescu, Levy & Pachter (2009, Theorem 16).
Let `A e` (`e : E`) be a compatible binary system of splits with positive weights `w`,
containing every trivial split and closed under complement, on at least four taxa, and let
`d x y` be half the total weight of the indices whose side separates `x` and `y`. Let `μ` be
a lower bound on the weight of every internal split (both sides with at least two taxa). If
`D` is symmetric, vanishes on the diagonal, and `|D x y - d x y| < μ / 2` for all distinct
`x, y`, then a pair of distinct taxa minimizing the Q-criterion
`(|X| - 2) D x y - ∑_z D x z - ∑_z D y z` is a side of the split system.

articles.title: Atteson's theorem: neighbor joining has `ℓ∞` radius `1/2`
articles.statement:
**Atteson's theorem: neighbor joining has `ℓ∞` radius `1/2`** (Atteson 1999). Let `d` be
the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths
`w`, let `μ` be a lower bound on the lengths of its internal edges (edges with no taxon at
either end), and let `D` be a symmetric dissimilarity with zero diagonal such that
`|D x y - d x y| < μ / 2` for all distinct taxa. Then every complete run of neighbor joining on
`D` (stopped with at most three clusters) forms exactly the splits of the internal edges of the
tree: a set of taxa `A` or its complement is a formed cluster if and only if `A` is the set of
taxa on the `a`-side of an edge `{a, b}` with both endpoints internal.

## Sources

- Atteson (1999); stated as Theorem 2 of Mihaescu, Levy and Pachter (2009). `NJRun` uses the Studier–Keppler update. The proof was written for this formalization: up to row shifts, which do not change the pairs neighbor joining selects, the cluster dissimilarity of a run is an average of `D` (`NJRun.exists_avg`), so its errors against the tree metric of the current clusters stay below `μ / 2`, and the cherry step `exists_eq_pair_of_qCriterion_min_of_abs_sub_lt` applies at every join.

articles.title: The shifting lemma
articles.statement:
**The shifting lemma** (Mihaescu, Levy & Pachter 2009, Lemma 4): if `D'` agrees with `D` on
the diagonal of `S` and `D' s t = D s t + f s + f t` for distinct `s, t ∈ S`, then the
Q-criterion of every pair of distinct clusters drops by the same amount `2 ∑_{c ∈ S} f c`, so
both have the same minimizing pairs.

articles.title: Codon as a triple of nucleotides
articles.statement: A codon: three nucleotides, each in `Fin 4` (order `A, C, G, T`).

articles.title: `dN / dS = ω`
articles.statement:
**`dN / dS = ω`** in the Goldman–Yang model with sites counted under `ω = 1` (derived;
see the module docstring for the site definition), provided `ρ_S(1) > 0` and `ρ_N(1) > 0`.

articles.title: Nonsynonymous substitution rate per nonsynonymous site (dN)
articles.statement: The nonsynonymous rate per nonsynonymous site, `dN = ρ_N(ω) / N`.

articles.title: Synonymous substitution rate per synonymous site (dS)
articles.statement: The synonymous rate per synonymous site, `dS = ρ_S(ω) / S`.

articles.title: Positions at which two codons differ
articles.statement: The positions at which two codons differ.

articles.title: Dependence of Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities on ω
articles.statement:
The nonsynonymous exchangeabilities are linear in `ω`, the synonymous ones do not
involve it.

articles.title: Symmetry of Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities
articles.statement: The Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities are symmetric.

articles.title: Goldman–Yang codon exchangeability
articles.statement:
The **Goldman–Yang exchangeability** between codons `i` and `j`: `0` unless they differ at
one position; otherwise `κ` for a transition (`1` for a transversion), times `ω` if the amino
acid changes.

articles.title: Off-diagonal entries of the Goldman–Yang rate matrix
articles.statement: Off the diagonal the Goldman–Yang rate is `gyExchange i j * π j`.

articles.title: Goldman–Yang codon rate matrix
articles.statement:
The **Goldman–Yang rate matrix** (Goldman & Yang 1994): the GTR matrix with codon
frequencies `π` and exchangeabilities `gyExchange`.

articles.title: The Goldman–Yang chain is reversible
articles.statement:
It is in detailed balance with its codon
frequencies.

articles.title: Goldman–Yang matrix is a rate matrix
articles.statement:
With nonnegative frequencies, `κ ≥ 0` and `ω ≥ 0`, the Goldman–Yang matrix is a rate
matrix.

articles.title: Symmetry of single-position codon changes
articles.statement: Differing at exactly one position is symmetric.

articles.title: Codons differing at exactly one position
articles.statement: Two codons differ at exactly one position.

articles.title: Symmetry of transition codon changes
articles.statement: Being a transition change is symmetric.

articles.title: Codon change consisting of transitions
articles.statement: Every differing position is a transition (same parity: `A ↔ G` or `C ↔ T`).

articles.title: Nonsynonymous rate is linear in ω
articles.statement: The nonsynonymous rate is linear in `ω`: `ρ_N(ω) = ω ρ_N(1)`.

articles.title: Positivity of the nonsynonymous rate
articles.statement:
`ρ_N(1) > 0` if the frequencies are nonnegative, `κ > 0`, and some nonsynonymous single
change joins two codons of positive frequency.

articles.title: Stationary rate of nonsynonymous substitutions
articles.statement:
The stationary **rate of nonsynonymous substitutions** per codon,
`ρ_N = ∑_{aa i ≠ aa j} π_i Q_ij`. This is the stationary rate when
`∑ i, π i = 1`; for unnormalized weights it is scaled by `(∑ i, π i) ^ 2`.

articles.title: Number of nonsynonymous sites per codon
articles.statement:
The number of **nonsynonymous sites** per codon, counted under `ω = 1`:
`N = 3 ρ_N(1) / (ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1))`.

articles.title: Synonymous rate does not depend on ω
articles.statement: The synonymous rate does not depend on `ω`: `ρ_S(ω) = ρ_S(1)`.

articles.title: Positivity of the synonymous rate
articles.statement:
`ρ_S(1) > 0` if the frequencies are nonnegative, `κ > 0`, and some synonymous single
change joins two codons of positive frequency.

articles.title: Stationary rate of synonymous substitutions
articles.statement:
The stationary **rate of synonymous substitutions** per codon,
`ρ_S = ∑_{i ≠ j, aa i = aa j} π_i Q_ij`. This is the stationary rate when
`∑ i, π i = 1`; for unnormalized weights it is scaled by `(∑ i, π i) ^ 2`.

articles.title: Synonymous and nonsynonymous sites sum to three
articles.statement: There are three sites per codon: `S + N = 3` when `ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1) ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Number of synonymous sites per codon
articles.statement:
The number of **synonymous sites** per codon, counted under `ω = 1`:
`S = 3 ρ_S(1) / (ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1))`.

articles.title: Isomorphic trees have the same clusters
articles.statement: Isomorphic trees have the same clusters.

articles.title: Cluster set of a tree seen from a leaf
articles.statement:
The clusters of all vertices seen from the leaf labeled `a`. (The cluster of the leaf `a`
itself is the set of all other taxa, which is also the cluster of its neighbor.)

articles.title: Cluster of a vertex seen from a leaf
articles.statement:
The **cluster** of a vertex `v` seen from the leaf labeled `a`: the taxa `x ≠ a` whose leaf
lies beyond `v`, i.e. `v` is on the path from the leaf `a` to the leaf `x`.

articles.title: Every binary hierarchy is a cluster set of a tree
articles.statement:
Every binary hierarchy on the taxa other than `a` is the cluster set, seen from the leaf
`a`, of some unrooted binary phylogenetic tree (vertices: the leaf `a` and the members of the
hierarchy; each member is joined to the smallest member strictly containing it).

articles.title: Clusters of an unrooted tree form a binary hierarchy
articles.statement:
The clusters of a tree seen from a leaf form a binary hierarchy on the other taxa
(Semple & Steel 2003, Section 3.1).

articles.title: Binary hierarchy restricted below a member is a binary hierarchy
articles.statement: The members of a binary hierarchy below a member form a binary hierarchy.

articles.title: Binary hierarchy on a finite set
articles.statement:
A **binary hierarchy** on a finite set `S`: a family of nonempty subsets of `S` containing
`S` and every singleton, any two members nested or disjoint, and every member with at least two
elements the disjoint union of two members. These are the cluster systems of the rooted binary
phylogenetic trees on `S` (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 3.1).

articles.title: Clusters determine an unrooted binary tree
articles.statement:
Two trees with the same clusters seen from the leaf `a` are isomorphic: the clusters
determine the tree.

articles.title: Isomorphism of unrooted binary phylogenetic trees
articles.statement:
Two unrooted binary phylogenetic trees are **isomorphic** when some graph isomorphism maps
the leaf with each label to the leaf with the same label.

articles.title: Every planar binary tree has a leaf
articles.statement: Every planar tree has at least one leaf.

articles.title: Leaf labels of a planar binary tree
articles.statement: The multiset of leaf labels.

articles.title: The number of binary hierarchies
articles.statement:
On a nonempty finite set `S` there are
`(2 |S| - 3)‼` binary hierarchies, as many as rooted binary phylogenetic trees on `S`: a tree
corresponds to the leaf sets of its subtrees.

articles.title: Schröder's count of rooted binary phylogenetic trees
articles.statement:
On `n ≥ 1` labeled taxa there are
`(2 n - 3)‼ = 1 · 3 · 5 ⋯ (2 n - 3)` rooted binary phylogenetic trees (`1` tree for `n = 1`
and `n = 2`, `3` for `n = 3`, `15` for `n = 4`). For `n = 1` the natural-number subtraction
gives `2 - 3 = 0` and `0‼ = 1`, the conventional value `(-1)‼ = 1` of the formula; the empty
set of taxa (excluded here) has no tree (`isEmpty_rootedBinaryTree_empty`).

## Sources

- Semple & Steel (2003), Proposition 2.1.4.

articles.title: Number of unrooted binary phylogenetic trees
articles.statement:
The count `(2 n - 5)‼` of unrooted binary phylogenetic trees holds from `n = 2` taxa on:
for `n = 2` the single tree is one edge and `2 · 2 - 5 = 0` in `ℕ`, `0‼ = 1` (the conventional
value `(-1)‼ = 1`). For `n ≤ 1` there is no tree while the formula gives `1`.

articles.title: The number of unrooted binary phylogenetic trees
articles.statement:
On `n ≥ 3` labeled taxa there are
`(2 n - 5)‼ = 1 · 3 ⋯ (2 n - 5)` unrooted binary phylogenetic trees up to label-preserving
isomorphism.

## Sources

- Semple & Steel (2003), Proposition 2.1.4. Proves the deferred entry `nat_card_unrootedBinaryTree`.

articles.title: Planar drawings of rooted binary trees on a taxon set
articles.statement:
The planar drawings of rooted binary trees on the taxa `X`: planar trees whose leaves are
labeled by `X`, each taxon labeling exactly one leaf.

articles.title: Planar rooted binary tree with labeled leaves
articles.statement:
A planar rooted binary tree with leaves labeled by `α`: a leaf `leaf a`, or an internal
vertex `node l r` with left subtree `l` and right subtree `r` (the children are ordered).

articles.title: Unrooted binary trees correspond to binary hierarchies
articles.statement:
Unrooted binary phylogenetic trees up to label-preserving isomorphism correspond to the
binary hierarchies on the taxa other than `a`, by their clusters seen from the leaf `a`.

articles.title: Rooted binary phylogenetic tree
articles.statement:
The **rooted binary phylogenetic trees** on the taxa `X`: planar drawings with leaf set `X`
modulo exchanging the two children of internal vertices, i.e. rooted binary trees with
unordered children and leaves labeled bijectively by `X`, up to label-preserving isomorphism.

articles.title: Swap of the children of an internal vertex
articles.statement: One swap: exchange the two children of one internal vertex (anywhere in the tree).

articles.title: Unrooted binary phylogenetic tree
articles.statement:
An **unrooted binary phylogenetic tree** on the taxa `X`: a finite tree `G` on a vertex
type `V` whose degree-one vertices are labeled bijectively by `X` (`label`) and whose other
vertices all have degree three.

articles.title: Binomial upper tail vanishes beyond $n$
articles.statement: `P(X ≥ k) = 0` for `k > n`.

articles.title: The tail is nonincreasing in `k`
articles.statement: **The tail is nonincreasing in `k`** for `p ∈ [0, 1]`.

articles.title: Binomial upper tail at zero equals one
articles.statement: `P(X ≥ 0) = 1`, for every real `p` (the binomial theorem).

articles.title: Upper tail of the binomial distribution
articles.statement:
The upper tail `P(X ≥ k) = ∑_{i = k}^{n} C(n, i) p^i (1 - p)^(n - i)` of the binomial law
`Bin(n, p)`.

articles.title: Branch length score of the empty set is zero
articles.statement: The BLS of the empty set is `0`.

articles.title: Normalized branch length score is at most one for nonnegative lengths
articles.statement: The normalized BLS is at most `1` when the tree has positive total length.

articles.title: Normalized branch length score is nonnegative for nonnegative lengths
articles.statement: The normalized BLS is nonnegative.

articles.title: Normalized branch length score
articles.statement:
The normalized Branch Length Score, `bls S T w / totalLength T w`, as reported by
Kheradpour et al. (a fraction of the total branch length).

articles.title: Branch length score is at most the tree length for nonnegative lengths
articles.statement: The BLS is at most the total branch length.

articles.title: All species give the whole tree
articles.statement:
The BLS of the set of all leaves is the total branch
length.

articles.title: Monotonicity
articles.statement:
With nonnegative edge lengths, more conserving species never lower the
BLS.

articles.title: Branch length score is nonnegative for nonnegative edge lengths
articles.statement: The BLS is nonnegative for nonnegative edge lengths.

articles.title: A single species has BLS `0`
articles.statement: **A single species has BLS `0`** (a motif present in one genome is not conserved).

articles.title: Subadditivity
articles.statement:
For sets of species `S`, `S'` that share a species, the subtree
connecting `S ∪ S'` is at most as long as the two subtrees together.

articles.title: The Branch Length Score
articles.statement:
**The Branch Length Score** (unnormalized): the total branch length of the smallest
subtree of `T` connecting the leaves `S`, as half the sum over the darts of the edge length
times the indicator that `S` meets both sides (`edgeSide`) of the dart's edge.

articles.title: Sum over darts is twice the sum over edges
articles.statement:
A sum over darts of a function of the undirected edge is twice the sum over the edges:
the two darts of each edge contribute equally.

articles.title: The side of a pendant edge is the singleton of its leaf
articles.statement:
The taxa whose leaf is
closer to the leaf vertex than to its neighbor are exactly that leaf's taxon.

articles.title: Constant $n \log R$ term of the SiPhy objective
articles.statement: The `n log R` constant of Eq. 6.

articles.title: The Lagrange multiplier of the `π` update exists and is unique
articles.statement:
For positive `c` and
nonnegative `d` on a nonempty finite alphabet there is exactly one `γ` with `d b + γ > 0` for
all `b` and `∑ b, c b / (d b + γ) = 1`.

articles.title: Time-weighted exchange rate into a state
articles.statement: The time-weighted exchange rate into `b`, `e b = ∑_{a ≠ b} τ a R a b`.

articles.title: The rate update maximizes Eq. 6 over `ω > 0`
articles.statement:
**The rate update maximizes Eq. 6 over `ω > 0`** for a fixed positive `π`, when the expected
number of substitutions `N` and the time-weighted rate `∑ b, e b π b` are positive.

articles.title: The rate update is the unique maximizer
articles.statement:
Any other `ω > 0` gives a strictly smaller
value of Eq. 6.

articles.title: The constraint-vector update is the unique maximizer of Eq. 6
articles.statement:
**The constraint-vector update is the unique maximizer of Eq. 6** over the positive
probability vectors `π` (the rate matrix `ω R π` and the root distribution both use `π`), for
fixed `ω > 0`, positive off-diagonal `R` and positive weights `c`.

articles.title: Eq. 6 for the SiPhy matrix
articles.statement:
For `ω > 0`, positive off-diagonal `R` and positive `π`,
`expectedLogLik = N log ω + ∑_{a ≠ b} n a b log R a b + piObjective c (ω e) π`.

articles.title: The expected complete-data log-likelihood
articles.statement:
**The expected complete-data log-likelihood** of a rate matrix `Q` and root distribution `π`
(Garber et al. 2009, Eq. 6): `∑_{a ≠ b} n a b log Q a b + ∑ a, τ a Q a a + ∑ b, r b log π b`,
for expected substitution counts `n`, expected state durations `τ` and the root posterior `r`.

articles.title: Derivative of the binomial upper tail
articles.statement:
**Derivative of the binomial upper tail** in the success probability: for `1 ≤ k ≤ n`,
`d/dp P(Bin(n, p) ≥ k) = n C(n - 1, k - 1) p^(k-1) (1-p)^(n-k)` at every real `p` (the sum
telescopes).

articles.title: Weight of a state: substitutions into it plus root posterior
articles.statement:
The weight `c b = ∑_{a ≠ b} n a b + r b` of state `b`: substitutions into `b` plus the root
posterior of `b`.

articles.title: `π` is the equilibrium of the SiPhy matrix
articles.statement:
For symmetric `R` it is in detailed balance
with `π`, for every `ω`.

articles.title: SiPhy matrix is a rate matrix
articles.statement: With `ω ≥ 0`, nonnegative `R` and nonnegative `π`, the SiPhy matrix is a rate matrix.

articles.title: Motif conservation score approximation is strictly increasing
articles.statement: The MCS approximation is strictly increasing in the conserved count, for `N ≥ 1` and `p ∈ (0, 1)`.

articles.title: Motif conservation score approximation as a de Moivre–Laplace sum
articles.statement:
The MCS approximation of the number of conserved occurrences among the first `n` is the
de Moivre–Laplace standardized sum.

articles.title: Binomial z-score approximation to the motif conservation score
articles.statement:
The conserved count
`k` of a motif with `N` occurrences, standardized under `Bin(N, p)`:
`(k - N p) / √(N p (1 - p))`. This is an approximation to Xie et al.'s MCS, not their
exact score.

articles.title: The binomial upper tail is nondecreasing in `p` on `[0, 1]`
articles.statement: **The binomial upper tail is nondecreasing in `p` on `[0, 1]`**, for every `n` and `k`.

articles.title: Nonnegative edge lengths of a tree
articles.statement: Edge lengths are nonnegative: every dart's undirected edge has nonnegative length.

articles.title: The SiPhy rate update
articles.statement: **The SiPhy rate update** (Eq. 7, for fixed `π`): `ω = N / ∑ b, e b π b`.

articles.title: The `π` update is the unique maximizer
articles.statement:
**The `π` update is the unique maximizer** of `piObjective c d` over the positive
probability vectors: with `γ` as in `existsUnique_lagrange`, every other positive `π` summing to
one has a strictly smaller objective than `b ↦ c b / (d b + γ)`.
