articles.title: Part of the SiPhy objective depending on the constraint vector
articles.statement:
The part of Eq. 6 that depends on `π` (for fixed `ω`):
`∑ b, (c b * log (π b) - d b * π b)`.

articles.title: The SiPhy constraint-vector update
articles.statement:
**The SiPhy constraint-vector update** (Eq. 8, for fixed `ω`):
`π b = c b / (ω e b + γ)`, with `γ` the Lagrange multiplier of `existsUnique_lagrange`.

articles.title: Leaf set meeting both sides of a tree edge
articles.statement:
Whether the leaf set `S` meets both sides of an edge with leaf set `B` below it, inside a
tree with leaf set `U`: `S ∩ B` and `S ∩ (U \ B)` are nonempty.

articles.title: The SiPhy rate matrix
articles.statement:
**The SiPhy rate matrix** `Q a b = ω R a b π b` for `a ≠ b` (Garber et al. 2009, Eq. 10),
with rows summing to zero: `ω` times the GTR matrix with exchangeabilities `R` and base
frequencies `π`.

articles.title: The binomial upper tail is strictly increasing in `p` on `[0, 1]`
articles.statement: **The binomial upper tail is strictly increasing in `p` on `[0, 1]`** when `1 ≤ k ≤ n`.

articles.title: De Moivre–Laplace for the MCS approximation
articles.statement:
If the conservation indicators of
the occurrences are i.i.d. Bernoulli(`p`) with `0 < p < 1`, then for every `z`,
`P(z ≤ MCS approximation of the first n occurrences)` tends to the standard normal mass of
`[z, ∞)`.

articles.title: Expected total number of substitutions
articles.statement: The expected total number of substitutions `N = ∑_{a ≠ b} n a b`.

articles.title: Total branch length of a tree
articles.statement:
The total branch length: half the sum of the edge lengths over the darts, since each
undirected edge is traversed once in each direction.

articles.title: Brute-force likelihood at a leaf
articles.statement: At a leaf, the brute-force likelihood is the leaf weight.

articles.title: Brute-force likelihood factors over subtrees
articles.statement:
The brute-force likelihood factors over the two subtrees of the root (the distributive law
behind pruning).

articles.title: Brute-force likelihood given the root state
articles.statement:
The likelihood of the leaf data conditioned on root state `s`, by brute force: the sum of
the weights of all labelings of the non-root nodes.

articles.title: Number of labelings of a tree
articles.statement:
There are `|S| ^ (2 · #internal nodes)` labelings (one state for each non-root node), so the
brute-force sum `bruteLik` has exponentially many terms.

articles.title: Labeling of the non-root nodes of a tree
articles.statement:
A labeling of the non-root nodes of a tree by states: at every internal node, the states of
its two children and labelings of the two subtrees.

articles.title: Site likelihood from tabulated partial likelihoods
articles.statement: The site likelihood from the tabulated partial likelihoods at the root.

articles.title: The site likelihood by pruning
articles.statement: `likelihood obs t π = ∑ s, π s * prune obs t s`.

articles.title: Site likelihood of a phylogenetic tree
articles.statement: The site likelihood with root distribution `π`: `∑ s, π s * bruteLik obs t s`.

articles.title: Number of internal nodes of a tree
articles.statement: The number of internal nodes.

articles.title: Number of leaves of a tree
articles.statement: The number of leaves.

articles.title: Felsenstein's pruning algorithm computes the likelihood conditioned on the root state
articles.statement: **Felsenstein's pruning algorithm computes the likelihood conditioned on the root state.**

articles.title: Tabulated pruning computes the pruning recursion
articles.statement: The tabulated algorithm computes the pruning recursion.

articles.title: Tabulated Felsenstein pruning algorithm
articles.statement:
Felsenstein's pruning algorithm, tabulated on the states `Fin n`: the vector of partial
likelihoods of each subtree is computed once, with `O(n²)` operations per internal node.

articles.title: Felsenstein's pruning recursion
articles.statement:
Felsenstein's pruning recursion: the partial likelihood of the subtree `t` given state `s`
at its root.

articles.title: Independent sites
articles.statement:
For an alignment whose sites `k : ι` evolve independently along the
same tree with leaf data `obs k`, the joint likelihood (the sum over all choices of a root state
and a labeling at every site of the product of the per-site weights) is the product of the
per-site likelihoods.

articles.title: Rooted binary tree with transition weights
articles.statement:
A rooted binary tree with leaf labels `L`; an internal node `node P l Q r` carries the
transition weights `P` and `Q` (from the node's state to the child's state) on the edges to its
left child `l` and right child `r`.

articles.title: Weight of a tree labeling
articles.statement:
The weight of a labeling given root state `s`: the product over all edges of the transition
weight from the parent's state to the child's state, times the leaf weight `obs l` at the state
of every leaf `l`.

articles.title: Detailed balance of the Jukes–Cantor chain
articles.statement:
The uniform distribution satisfies detailed balance with the Jukes–Cantor matrix (the
matrix is symmetric), hence is stationary.

articles.title: Kolmogorov forward equation
articles.statement:
**Kolmogorov forward equation** for the Jukes–Cantor model:
`d/dt P(t) = P(t) Q` with `Q = jcRate μ`.

articles.title: The Jukes–Cantor distance correction
articles.statement:
`-(3/4) · log (1 - 4/3 · pDiff μ t i) = μ * t`,
the expected number of substitutions per site along the branch.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor distance
articles.statement:
The Jukes–Cantor distance: the expected number of substitutions per site corresponding to a
proportion `p` of differing sites. Meaningful only for `0 ≤ p < 3/4`; outside that range the
value is Lean's totalized logarithm, not a distance (at `p = 3/4` it is `0`).

articles.title: Invertible Jukes–Cantor eigenbasis
articles.statement: The eigenbasis as a unit, with its explicit inverse.

articles.title: Eigenbasis of the Jukes–Cantor rate matrix
articles.statement:
An eigenbasis of the Jukes–Cantor rate matrix, as columns: the constant vector (eigenvalue
`0`) and three vectors with zero sum (eigenvalue `-4 μ / 3`).

articles.title: The Jukes–Cantor transition matrix is the matrix exponential of the rate matrix
articles.statement: `jcProb μ t = exp (t • jcRateMatrix μ)`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of Jukes–Cantor transition probabilities
articles.statement: The Jukes–Cantor transition probabilities are nonnegative when `0 ≤ μ * t`.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor transition matrix at time zero is the identity
articles.statement: At time `0` the Jukes–Cantor transition matrix is the identity.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor transition probability
articles.statement:
The Jukes–Cantor transition probability from base `i` to base `j` over a branch of length
`t`, with substitution rate `μ`.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor rate matrix as a matrix
articles.statement: The Jukes–Cantor rate matrix as a `Matrix`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of off-diagonal Jukes–Cantor rates
articles.statement: Off-diagonal Jukes–Cantor rates are nonnegative when `0 ≤ μ`.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor rate matrix
articles.statement: The Jukes–Cantor rate matrix: rate `μ / 3` to each other base, `-μ` on the diagonal.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor transition matrix as a stochastic matrix
articles.statement:
The Jukes–Cantor transition matrix over a branch with `0 ≤ μ * t`, packaged as a
`StochasticMatrix` on the four states `Fin (3 + 1)` so that the finite Markov-chain API
(matrix powers, stationarity, detailed balance) applies to it.

articles.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov equation for the Jukes–Cantor chain
articles.statement:
The `n`-step matrix of the Jukes–Cantor chain observed every `t` time units is the
transition matrix over the branch length `n * t` (Chapman–Kolmogorov).

articles.title: Closed form of the Jukes–Cantor difference probability
articles.statement:
The probability that the two ends of a branch differ is `3/4 · (1 - exp (-4 μ t / 3))`,
whatever the starting base.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor difference probability is below 3/4
articles.statement:
The probability that the ends of a branch differ is below the saturation value `3/4`, for
all real `μ` and `t` (it is negative when `μ * t < 0`, see `pDiff_mem_Ico`).

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor difference probability lies in (0, 3/4)
articles.statement:
For `0 ≤ μ * t` the probability that the ends of a branch differ lies in `[0, 3/4)`, the
domain of `jcDistance`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the Jukes–Cantor difference probability
articles.statement: The probability that the ends of a branch differ is nonnegative when `0 ≤ μ * t`.

articles.title: Probability that the ends of a branch differ
articles.statement:
The probability that the two ends of a branch of length `t` carry different bases, given
base `i` at the start.

articles.title: Diagonalization of the Jukes–Cantor rate matrix
articles.statement: Diagonalization of `t • jcRateMatrix μ`.

articles.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov equation
articles.statement: **Chapman–Kolmogorov equation** for the Jukes–Cantor model.

articles.title: Right-hand side of the Jukes–Cantor forward equation in closed form
articles.statement: The right-hand side of the forward equation, in closed form.

articles.title: Rows of the Jukes–Cantor transition matrix sum to one
articles.statement: Each row of the Jukes–Cantor transition matrix sums to `1`.

articles.title: Rows of the Jukes–Cantor rate matrix sum to zero
articles.statement: Each row of the Jukes–Cantor rate matrix sums to `0`.

articles.title: State maximizing a function
articles.statement: A state maximizing `f` (ties broken by choice).

articles.title: Likelihood of Pupko's joint reconstruction
articles.statement: The likelihood of Pupko's reconstruction is `max_s π s * maxPrune obs t s`.

articles.title: Root state of Pupko's reconstruction
articles.statement: The root state of Pupko's reconstruction: it maximizes `π s * maxPrune obs t s`.

articles.title: The argmax state maximizes the function
articles.statement: `argmaxState f` maximizes `f`.

articles.title: The max-product recursion computes the maximal labeling weight
articles.statement:
`maxPrune obs t s` is the
maximum over all labelings `z` of the non-root nodes of `weight obs t s z`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of max-product pruning
articles.statement: With nonnegative weights, `maxPrune` is nonnegative.

articles.title: Max-product pruning recursion
articles.statement:
The max-product (Viterbi) form of Felsenstein's pruning recursion: the largest weight of a
labeling of the subtree `t` given state `s` at its root.

articles.title: Nonnegative transition weights on a tree
articles.statement: All transition weights in the tree are nonnegative.

articles.title: Pupko et al. (2000): joint maximum likelihood
articles.statement:
With nonnegative root, transition and leaf
weights, no root state `s` and labeling `z` of the non-root nodes has larger joint likelihood
`π s * weight obs t s z` than Pupko's reconstruction.

articles.title: Pupko's joint reconstruction
articles.statement: The root state `jointRoot` and the traced labeling.

articles.title: Value at the argmax state is the maximum
articles.statement: The value at `argmaxState f` is the maximum `univ.sup'` of `f`.

articles.title: Pupko's traceback
articles.statement:
Pupko's traceback: given the state `s` of the root of `t`, label each child with a state
maximizing the transition weight times the child's `maxPrune`, and recurse.

articles.title: `maxPrune` bounds the weight of every labeling
articles.statement: **`maxPrune` bounds the weight of every labeling** (nonnegative weights).

articles.title: Nonnegativity of labeling weights
articles.statement: With nonnegative weights, every labeling has nonnegative weight.

articles.title: The traced labeling attains `maxPrune`
articles.statement: No sign condition is needed.

articles.title: Generalized Pauplin coefficient of a cherry tree
articles.statement:
The generalized Pauplin coefficient of the pair of clusters `u, v` in the tree `T_ab`
obtained from the star on `S` by joining `a` and `b`: `1/2` for `{a, b}`; `1/(2(|S| - 2))` when
one of `u, v` is `a` or `b` and the other is not; `1/(|S| - 2)` when neither is. Values on the
diagonal `u = v` are never used.

articles.title: The coefficients give the tree length
articles.statement:
Let `T_ab` carry real edge lengths: `ℓ c` on the
pendant edge of each cluster `c ∈ S` and `m` on the edge between `u` and the center. If `D` is
its path-length dissimilarity (`D a b = ℓ a + ℓ b`, `D x c = ℓ x + m + ℓ c` for `x ∈ {a, b}` and
`c` another cluster, `D c c' = ℓ c + ℓ c'` for two other distinct clusters), then
`cherryLength S D a b = ∑_{c ∈ S} ℓ c + m`.

articles.title: The BME length of a join in terms of the Q-criterion
articles.statement:
For `D` symmetric and zero on the
diagonal of `S`, `|S| ≥ 3` and distinct `a, b ∈ S`:
`cherryLength S D a b = (∑_{u ≠ v ∈ S} D u v + Q(a, b)) / (2 (|S| - 2))`.

articles.title: Balanced minimum-evolution length of a cherry tree
articles.statement:
The balanced minimum-evolution length of `T_ab` for the dissimilarity `D`:
half the sum over ordered pairs of distinct clusters of `cherryCoeff S a b u v * D u v`, which
is `∑_{u<v} cherryCoeff S a b u v * D u v` when `D` is symmetric.

articles.title: Q-minimality is cherry-length minimality at a run state
articles.statement:
At every state of a run on a
symmetric dissimilarity with zero diagonal and at least three clusters, a pair of distinct
clusters minimizes the Q-criterion (the pairs NJ may join) if and only if joining it gives
the smallest `cherryLength`, the BME length of the join tree `T_ab` on the current clusters
for the current cluster dissimilarity `D`. This is the local star identity only: it does not
compare partially resolved trees on all taxa under the original dissimilarity `d`.

articles.title: Minimizing `Q` is minimizing the local star BME length of the join
articles.statement:
The BME length
of `T_ab` on the current clusters for the current cluster dissimilarity `D`. This is the
local star identity; it is not the full Gascuel–Steel comparison on all taxa.

articles.title: Neighbor joining preserves symmetry and zero diagonal
articles.statement:
Along a run of neighbor joining on a symmetric `d` with zero diagonal, the cluster
dissimilarity stays symmetric and vanishes on every current cluster.

articles.title: A two-taxon side forms a cherry
articles.statement:
If a side of the edge `{a, b}` is the pair `{x, y}`, then `a` is a common neighbor of the
leaves `ι x` and `ι y`: they form a cherry.

articles.title: Split decomposition of a tree metric
articles.statement:
The path length between two taxa is half the sum,
over the darts (oriented edges) of the tree, of the lengths of the edges whose split separates
them.

articles.title: A singleton side is a pendant leaf side
articles.statement: A side holding a single taxon `z` is the leaf side of `z`'s pendant edge.

articles.title: The first join of neighbor joining on a tree metric joins a cherry
articles.statement:
On the path-length
metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree with positive edge lengths and at least four taxa,
any pair of clusters that neighbor joining may join from the initial singletons consists of
two taxa with a common neighbor.

articles.title: On a tree metric, a pair of taxa minimizing the Q-criterion is a cherry
articles.statement:
(Saitou & Nei 1987; Studier & Keppler 1988; Bryant 2005). Let `d` be the path-length metric
of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w` and at least four
taxa. If the distinct taxa `x, y` minimize the Q-criterion over all pairs of distinct
singleton clusters at the start of neighbor joining, then `ι x` and `ι y` have a common
neighbor.

articles.title: Cherry lemma for split systems
articles.statement:
For a compatible system of splits with positive weights,
containing every trivial split and binary (every side with at least two taxa is the disjoint
union of two sides), on at least four taxa, a pair maximizing the total `splitGain` is a
side of some split.

articles.title: The path metric on a partition into sides
articles.statement:
Let `S` partition the taxa of a binary
phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w` and path-length metric `d` into
sides of edges. Then there is a system of splits `A e` (`e : E`) of the set of clusters with
positive weights `w' e`, closed under complement, pairwise compatible, binary, and containing
every trivial split, such that
* the weight of every internal split (both sides with at least two clusters) is the length of an
  edge with both endpoints internal;
* a split whose side is `{s, t}` comes from an edge with side `s ∪ t`;
* for taxa `x ∈ s` and `y ∈ t` of distinct clusters, `d x y` is half the total weight of the
  splits separating `s` from `t`, plus a term `ρ s x` depending only on `s` and `x` and a term
  `ρ t y`.
In the construction, the splits are those of the edges that cut no cluster.

articles.title: Initial cluster dissimilarity in neighbor joining
articles.statement:
The dissimilarity between clusters at the start of neighbor joining: on singletons,
`initialDist d {x} {y} = d x y` (only singleton values are used).

articles.title: Binary phylogenetic tree
articles.statement:
`G` with the taxon placement `ι` is a **binary phylogenetic `X`-tree**: `G` is a tree,
`ι` is injective, the leaves (degree-one vertices) are exactly the taxa, and every other
vertex has degree three.

articles.title: Cluster dissimilarity after a neighbor-joining step
articles.statement:
The cluster dissimilarity after joining `a` and `b`: the new cluster `a ∪ b` is at
`(D a c + D b c - D a b) / 2` from every other cluster `c`, and at `0` from itself; other
values are unchanged.

articles.title: Neighbor joining forms the splits of a tree when every join forms a side
articles.statement:
Let `(G, ι)`
be a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree and `D` any dissimilarity. Suppose that whenever a run of
neighbor joining on `D` has reached a partition `S` of the taxa into sides of edges of the tree
(with at least four clusters) and joins two of its clusters, their union is again a side of an
edge. Then every complete run of neighbor joining on `D` (stopped with at most three clusters)
forms exactly the splits of the internal edges of the tree. This reduces the correctness of
neighbor joining on `D` to its selection step.

articles.title: Neighbor joining is exact on tree metrics
articles.statement:
Let `d` be the path-length metric of a
binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w`. Then every complete run
of neighbor joining (stopped with at most three clusters) forms exactly the splits of the
internal edges of the tree: a set of taxa `A` or its complement is a formed cluster if and
only if `A` is the set of taxa on the `a`-side of an edge `{a, b}` with both endpoints
internal.

## Sources

- Saitou & Nei (1987); Studier & Keppler (1988); Gascuel (1994); Bryant (2005). Proves the deferred entry `njRun_splits`.

articles.title: Runs of neighbor joining
articles.statement:
`NJRun d S D C`: some run of neighbor joining on the dissimilarity `d` reaches the cluster
set `S` with cluster dissimilarity `D`, having formed the clusters in `C`. A join is allowed
while at least four clusters remain, for any pair of distinct clusters minimizing
`qCriterion`.

articles.title: Q-criterion of two singleton clusters
articles.statement:
The Q-criterion of two singleton clusters at the start of neighbor joining:
`Q({x}, {y}) = (|X| - 2) d x y - ∑_z d x z - ∑_z d y z`.

articles.title: Neighbor-joining Q-criterion
articles.statement:
The Studier–Keppler form of the neighbor-joining criterion on the cluster set `S`:
`Q(a, b) = (|S| - 2) D a b - ∑_{c ∈ S} D a c - ∑_{c ∈ S} D b c`.

articles.title: Splits of two tree edges are compatible
articles.statement:
In a tree, the splits of any two edges are compatible: one side of the first edge lies
inside one side of the second.

articles.title: Edge side at an internal vertex as a disjoint union
articles.statement:
At an internal vertex `a` with neighbor `b`, the `a`-side of `{a, b}` is the disjoint union
of the far sides of the other two edges at `a`.

articles.title: Leaf side of a pendant edge
articles.statement: The leaf side of a pendant edge holds only the leaf's taxon.

articles.title: Every edge side of a binary phylogenetic tree is nonempty
articles.statement: Every side of every edge of a binary phylogenetic tree holds a taxon.

articles.title: Two sides of a tree edge partition the taxa
articles.statement: In a tree, the two sides of an edge partition the taxa.

articles.title: Taxa on one side of a tree edge
articles.statement:
The taxa on the `a`-side of the edge `{a, b}`: those whose vertex is still joined to `a`
once the edge `{a, b}` is deleted.

articles.title: Contribution of a split to the neighbor-joining score
articles.statement:
The contribution of one split `{A, Aᶜ}` to the neighbor-joining score of the pair `x, y`:
the number of taxa on the far side of the split when `x, y` lie on the same side, and `1`
when the split separates them.

articles.title: The Q-criterion of a split-decomposed dissimilarity
articles.statement:
If `d x y` is half the total
weight of the splits `A e` separating `x` and `y`, then
`(|X| - 2) d x y - ∑_z d x z - ∑_z d y z = -∑ e, w e * splitGain (A e) x y`.

articles.title: The balanced minimum-evolution length of a tree metric is the tree length
articles.statement:
If `d` is the
path-length dissimilarity of `T` on its leaves and `d` is symmetric, `bmeLength T d = length T`.
Symmetry is needed because `bmeLength` averages the two orientations of each pair.

articles.title: Pauplin's formula
articles.statement:
**Pauplin's formula** (Pauplin 2000): the total edge length of a binary tree with real edge
lengths is `∑_{i<j} 2^{1-τ_ij} d_T(i, j)`, the sum over pairs of leaves of the path length
weighted by `2` to the power one minus the number of edges on the path.

articles.title: Balanced minimum-evolution length
articles.statement:
The **balanced minimum-evolution length** of the topology of `T` for a dissimilarity `d`
(Desper and Gascuel 2002): `∑_{i<j} 2^{1-τ_ij} (d(i, j) + d(j, i)) / 2`. It depends on `T`
only through the topological distances `τ_ij`. Each term is symmetrized, so the value does
not depend on the orientation `T.pairs` happens to assign to a pair: swapping the children of
a node, or the two sides of the root edge, leaves `bmeLength` unchanged.

articles.title: Kraft equality
articles.statement:
**Kraft equality** for unrooted binary trees: for every leaf `i` of a tree with distinct leaf
labels, `∑_{j ≠ i} 2^{1-τ_ij} = 1`.

articles.title: Kraft's equality
articles.statement: **Kraft's equality** for a rooted binary tree: `∑_{leaves} 2^{-depth} = 1`.

articles.title: Leaf labels of an unrooted binary tree
articles.statement: The leaf labels (with multiplicity).

articles.title: Leaves of a rooted binary tree with root distances
articles.statement:
The leaves, each with its label, its distance to the root and its number of edges to the
root.

articles.title: Total edge length of an unrooted binary tree
articles.statement: The total length of the edges.

articles.title: Total edge length of a rooted binary tree
articles.statement: The total length of the edges.

articles.title: Leaf pairs of an unrooted binary tree with path lengths
articles.statement:
The unordered pairs of leaves, each with the two labels, the length `d_T(i, j)` of the path
between the two leaves and its number of edges `τ_ij`.

articles.title: Leaf pairs of a rooted binary tree with path lengths
articles.statement:
The unordered pairs of leaves, each with the two labels, the length of the path between the
two leaves and its number of edges.

articles.title: Pauplin coefficient of a pair of leaves
articles.statement: The Pauplin coefficient `2 ^ (1 - τ)` of a pair of leaves at topological distance `τ`.

articles.title: Rooted binary tree with edge lengths
articles.statement:
A rooted binary tree with leaf labels in `X`; `node a l b r` has the child `l` at the end of
an edge of length `a` and the child `r` at the end of an edge of length `b`.

articles.title: Unrooted binary tree with edge lengths
articles.statement:
An unrooted binary tree, rooted at its edge of length `len` that joins the roots of the
rooted binary trees `left` and `right`.

articles.title: Likelihood of an alignment of independent columns
articles.statement:
The likelihood of an alignment of `m` independent columns: the product of the site
likelihoods.

articles.title: Leaf data of an alignment column
articles.statement:
The leaf data of an alignment column `col : L → S`: the indicator of the observed codon at
each leaf.

articles.title: Deciban score as a rescaled natural-log score
articles.statement: Decibans are the natural-log score rescaled by `10 / log 10`.

articles.title: The published PhyloCSF score in decibans
articles.statement:
`10 * log₁₀(L_C / L_N)`, i.e.
`(10 / log 10) * score`, since `log₁₀ x = log x / log 10`.

articles.title: The score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alignment
articles.statement:
**The score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alignment** when all site likelihoods are
positive.

articles.title: Score threshold test for calling an alignment coding
articles.statement:
The threshold test on the score: call the alignment coding (`1`) iff the score exceeds the
cutoff `c`.

articles.title: The PhyloCSF score
articles.statement:
**The PhyloCSF score** (natural-log scale): the sum over the columns of the
log-likelihood ratio of the coding model `(tC, πC)` against the non-coding model
`(tN, πN)`. The published PhyloCSF score is reported in decibans; see `score_decibans`
for the conversion. Thresholds for this `score` are in natural-log units.

articles.title: Site likelihood by Felsenstein's pruning algorithm
articles.statement: Each site likelihood is computed by Felsenstein's pruning algorithm.

articles.title: Likelihood of one alignment column
articles.statement: The likelihood of one alignment column under the model `(t, π)`.

articles.title: PhyloCSF's score threshold test is most powerful for unnormalized weights
articles.statement:
With
positive site likelihoods under both models, a randomized test `φ` whose weighted size under
the non-coding weights is at most that of `scoreTest c` has at most its weighted power under
the coding weights. This is the dominated Neyman–Pearson inequality for the unnormalized
alignment weights `alignLik`; it becomes a statement about statistical size and power only
under additional normalization hypotheses (`∑ A, alignLik = 1` for each model).

articles.title: Statistical consistency of neighbor joining under Jukes–Cantor
articles.statement:
**Statistical consistency of neighbor joining under Jukes–Cantor** (Saitou & Nei 1987;
Atteson 1999), without a robustness hypothesis. Let `(G, ι)` be a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree
with path-length metric `d` for positive edge lengths `w`, whose internal edges have length at
least `m > 0`, and let the sites be pairwise independent and identically distributed, with the
two-leaf marginals of the JC model with rate `μ > 0` and uniform root. Then almost surely, for
all long enough alignments, every complete run of neighbor joining on the JC-corrected
empirical distances returns exactly the splits of the internal edges of the tree.

articles.title: Statistical consistency of neighbor joining under Jukes–Cantor
articles.statement:
**Statistical consistency of neighbor joining under Jukes–Cantor** (Saitou & Nei 1987;
Atteson 1999). Let `(G, ι)` be a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree with path-length metric `d` for
edge lengths `w`, and let the sites be pairwise independent and identically distributed, with
the two-leaf marginals of the JC model with rate `μ` and uniform root: for every path `p` from
`x` to `y`, `ℙ(site x = i, site y = j) = jcPath μ (lengths of p) i j / 4`. If neighbor joining
recovers the tree within some radius `r > 0` of the scaled metric `μ d` (for `μ > 0`, Atteson's
theorem gives `r = μ m / 2`, `m` the shortest internal edge length), then almost surely, for all
long enough alignments, every complete run of neighbor joining on the JC-corrected empirical
distances returns exactly the splits of the internal edges of the tree.

articles.title: Parsimony is inconsistent in the Felsenstein zone
articles.statement:
**Parsimony is inconsistent in the Felsenstein zone** (Felsenstein 1978): if the sites
`σ i` are pairwise independent and identically distributed with the pattern distribution of the
quartet, and `0 ≤ Q < 1/2`, `P ^ 2 > Q (1 - Q)`, then almost surely, for all long enough
alignments, the wrong quartet `AC | BD` has a strictly smaller total Fitch score than the true
quartet `AB | CD` and the third quartet `AD | BC`.

articles.title: Strong law for the p-distances
articles.statement:
For pairwise independent, identically distributed
sites, the empirical p-distance of every pair of taxa converges almost surely to the
probability that the two taxa differ at a site.

articles.title: The Felsenstein zone
articles.statement:
**The Felsenstein zone** (Felsenstein 1978): if `0 ≤ Q < 1/2` and `P ^ 2 > Q (1 - Q)`, the
wrong quartet `AC | BD` has strictly smaller expected parsimony score per site than both the
true quartet `AB | CD` and the third quartet `AD | BC`. The statement is algebraic in `P`; the
model has `0 ≤ P ≤ 1/2`.

articles.title: Expected Fitch parsimony score on a quartet
articles.statement: The expected Fitch parsimony score of one site on the quartet `((a, b), (c, d))`.

articles.title: Reversible continuous-time models give reversible semigroups
articles.statement:
A reversible continuous-time model gives a reversible semigroup: if `π` is in detailed
balance with the generator `Q`, the transition functions `exp (t • Q)` form a reversible
semigroup for `π`.

articles.title: Reversible semigroup of transition matrices
articles.statement:
A family of transition matrices `P t`, indexed by branch length, is a **reversible
semigroup** for the distribution `π`: it satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation and detailed
balance `π a P t a b = π b P t b a`. With rows summing to `1`, detailed balance makes `π`
stationary; the pulley principle uses only the two equations below.

articles.title: JC-corrected distances are path lengths
articles.statement:
**JC-corrected distances are path lengths** (Jukes & Cantor 1969): the JC distance of the
probability that the two ends of a path differ is `μ` times the total branch length.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor corrected empirical distance
articles.statement: The JC-corrected empirical distance `jcDistance (pHat seq n x y)`.

articles.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov along a path
articles.statement:
The JC transition matrix along a path is the
transition matrix of the total length.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor transition matrix along a path
articles.statement:
The JC transition matrix along a path whose branch lengths are listed in `ts`: the product
of the branch transition matrices `jcProb μ t`.

articles.title: Likelihood is invariant under swapping root subtrees
articles.statement: Swapping the two subtrees of the root does not change the likelihood.

articles.title: The root can be pushed to the end of its edge
articles.statement:
With the root on the edge between the
subtrees `l` and `r`, at distances `s` and `t`, the likelihood is that of the root placed at the
root of `l`, with `r` at distance `s + t`.

articles.title: Pulley principle, rerooting
articles.statement:
Let the root sit on the edge between an internal vertex `x`
(at distance `s₁`) and the subtree `C` (at distance `s₂`), where `x` has the subtrees `A` and
`B` at distances `a` and `b`. Moving the root to the edge between `x` and `A`, at distance `u₁`
from `A` and `u₂` from `x` with `u₁ + u₂ = a`, gives the same likelihood: the unrooted tree and
its edge lengths are unchanged (Felsenstein 1981).

articles.title: Pulley principle, sliding
articles.statement:
Moving the root along its edge does not change the
likelihood (Felsenstein 1981).

articles.title: Atteson's radius for the scaled tree metric
articles.statement:
Let `d` be the path-length metric of a
binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w` whose internal edges (no
taxon at either end) have length at least `m`. For `μ > 0`, neighbor joining recovers the tree
within radius `μ m / 2` of the scaled metric `μ d`. This is `njRun_splits_of_abs_sub_lt`
(Atteson 1999) for the edge lengths `μ w`.

articles.title: Neighbor joining recovers a tree within a radius
articles.statement:
Neighbor joining **recovers the tree within radius `r`** of the dissimilarity `d`: every
complete run of neighbor joining on a symmetric dissimilarity `D` with zero diagonal and
`|D x y - d x y| < r` for distinct taxa forms exactly the splits of the internal edges of
`(G, ι)`. Atteson's theorem gives this for the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic tree
with `r` half the shortest internal edge length (`njRecoversWithin_of_le`).

articles.title: Empirical p-distance
articles.statement:
The empirical p-distance of the taxa `x, y` over the first `n` sites of the alignment
`seq` (`seq i x` is the base of taxon `x` at site `i`): the proportion of sites where they
differ.

articles.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance along a chain, one step
articles.statement:
For a Markov chain
`X → Y → Z` with `X` distributed as `p` (positive), transition matrices `A` (nonnegative) and
`B` with unit row sums and nonzero determinants, `d(X, Z) = d(X, Y) + d(Y, Z)`, where
`F_XZ = Π_X A B`, `F_XY = Π_X A` and `F_YZ = Π_Y B` with `Y` distributed as `p A`.

articles.title: LogDet distance of a vertex to itself is zero
articles.statement:
The distance of a vertex to itself is `0`: the joint distribution of `X` with itself is the
diagonal matrix of its (positive) marginal.

articles.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance along a path
articles.statement:
**Additivity of the LogDet distance along a path** (Steel 1994; Lockhart et al. 1994):
for a Markov chain `v₀ → v₁ → ⋯ → v_n` along a path, with positive initial distribution `p`
and nonnegative nonsingular transition matrices `M i` with unit row sums, the LogDet distance
between the ends is the sum of the distances of consecutive vertices. The joint distribution of
`v₀, v_n` is `Π_{v₀} M 0 ⋯ M (n - 1)`, and that of `v_i, v_{i+1}` is `Π_{v_i} M i`, where `v_i`
has distribution `p M 0 ⋯ M (i - 1)`. Under the general Markov model on a tree with positive
marginals and nonsingular matrices, the states along any path form such a chain once the model
is rooted at one end of the path.

articles.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance at a separating vertex
articles.statement:
**Additivity of the LogDet distance at a separating vertex** (Steel 1994; Lockhart et al.
1994; Lake 1994). Let `Y` have distribution `p` (positive) and let `X` and `Z` be conditionally
independent given `Y`, with transition matrices `M` (from `Y` to `X`) and `N` (from `Y` to `Z`)
whose rows sum to `1` and whose determinants are nonzero. The joint distribution matrices are
`F_XY = Mᵀ Π_Y`, `F_YZ = Π_Y N` and `F_XZ = Mᵀ Π_Y N`, and `d(X, Z) = d(X, Y) + d(Y, Z)`. The
identity uses no sign condition on `M` and `N`; with nonnegative entries all logarithms are of
positive numbers (`vecMul_pos`).

articles.title: LogDet (paralinear) distance
articles.statement:
The **LogDet (paralinear) distance** of a joint distribution matrix `F`
(`F i j = ℙ(X = i, Y = j)`): `-log |det F| + (log det Π_X + log det Π_Y) / 2`, where the
diagonal marginal matrices have determinants `∏ i, ∑ j, F i j` and `∏ j, ∑ i, F i j`. It is a
distance only when `det F ≠ 0` and the marginals are positive; otherwise the value is Lean's
totalized logarithm (`log 0 = 0`).

articles.title: Difference of parsimony scores of two quartets
articles.statement:
On four taxa, the parsimony scores of two quartets differ only on informative patterns: the
score on `AB | CD` minus the score on `AC | BD` is `1` on patterns supporting `AC | BD`, `-1` on
patterns supporting `AB | CD`, and `0` otherwise; likewise for `AD | BC`.

articles.title: Fitch parsimony score on a quartet
articles.statement:
The Fitch parsimony score of the site pattern `σ` on the quartet `((a, b), (c, d))`; it is
the small-parsimony score by `Parsimony.fitch_score_eq`.

articles.title: Product of transition matrices along a path
articles.statement:
The product `M 0 * M 1 * ⋯ * M (n - 1)` of the transition matrices along the first `n`
edges of a path.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of site pattern probabilities
articles.statement: The pattern probabilities are nonnegative for change probabilities in `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Probability of a site pattern on a quartet
articles.statement:
The probability of the site pattern `σ` on the quartet, with the uniform root distribution
(the stationary distribution of the symmetric model).

articles.title: Partial likelihoods are invariant under swapping subtrees
articles.statement:
Swapping the two subtrees of a node does not change its partial likelihoods; with
`likelihood_node_comm` this lets the rerooting move `likelihood_reroot` reach either child.

articles.title: Rooted quartet with unit costs
articles.statement: The rooted quartet `((a, b), (c, d))` with unit costs, for Fitch's algorithm.

articles.title: Four-taxon quartet tree model
articles.statement:
The quartet `((A, B), (C, D))` on the taxa `0 = A`, `1 = B`, `2 = C`, `3 = D`, with change
probabilities `pA, pB, pC, pD` on the pendant edges and `pI` on the internal edge. The root
sits at the `AB` end of the internal edge (the edge to the `AB` cherry vertex has change
probability `0`); by the pulley principle its position does not matter.

articles.title: Leaf weights of a site pattern
articles.statement: The leaf weights of a site pattern `σ`: the indicator of the observed state.

articles.title: True split against third split frequency difference
articles.statement:
The true split `AB | CD` against the third split `AD | BC`: the difference of expected
frequencies is `Q (1 - 2 Q) (1 - 2 P)`.

articles.title: Wrong split against third split frequency difference
articles.statement:
The wrong split `AC | BD` against the third split `AD | BC`: the difference of expected
frequencies is `(1 - 2 Q) (P - Q) ^ 2`.

articles.title: Felsenstein (1978), the exact comparison
articles.statement:
With change probability `P` on the long
non-sister branches to `A` and `C` and `Q` on the other three branches, the expected frequency
of patterns supporting the wrong split `AC | BD` exceeds that of the true split `AB | CD` by
`(1 - 2 Q) (P ^ 2 - Q (1 - Q))`, for all real `P, Q`. This is Felsenstein's equations (16)–(17)
(his four-species model has equal probabilities of change `0 → 1` and reversion `1 → 0`).

articles.title: Expected frequency of patterns supporting a split
articles.statement: The expected frequency of the patterns supporting the split `{a, b} | {c, d}`.

articles.title: Site pattern probabilities sum to one
articles.statement: The pattern probabilities sum to `1`, for all parameters.

articles.title: Site pattern supporting a split
articles.statement:
The site pattern `σ` **supports the split** `{a, b} | {c, d}`: `a, b` agree, `c, d` agree,
and the two pairs differ (a parsimony-informative pattern for that split).

articles.title: Symmetric two-state model on a branch
articles.statement:
The **symmetric two-state model** on one branch: the state changes with probability `p`.
As a model, `0 ≤ p ≤ 1/2`.

articles.title: Nonsingular transition matrices preserve positive distributions
articles.statement:
Under a nonnegative, nonsingular transition matrix, a positive distribution stays positive:
every column of `M` has a positive entry. This puts the LogDet logarithms in their domain.

articles.title: Labeling agrees with the observed leaf states
articles.statement: The labeling `x` (with root state `s`) agrees with the observed states `σ` at every leaf.

articles.title: Min-plus cost semiring
articles.statement:
The cost semiring: `MinTropical (WithTop ℕ)`, with `min` as addition and `+` as
multiplication.

articles.title: Total substitution cost of a labeling
articles.statement:
The total substitution cost of a labeling `x` of the non-root vertices of `t` with root
state `s`: the sum over all edges of the cost `untrop (P a b)` from the parent's state `a` to
the child's state `b`.

articles.title: Sankoff's cost is attained
articles.statement:
Sankoff's cost is attained: if it is finite, some labeling that agrees with the leaf states
has exactly this cost. (It is `⊤` exactly when every agreeing labeling uses a forbidden change,
or when `t` is a single leaf whose observed state is not `s`.)

articles.title: Fitch's algorithm computes the small-parsimony score
articles.statement:
On a binary tree with unit costs,
Fitch's count equals the minimum, over root states, of Sankoff's cost.

## Sources

- Fitch (1971); Hartigan (1973).

articles.title: Fitch's root set is the set of optimal root states
articles.statement:
On a binary tree with unit costs, a
root state is in Fitch's set if and only if Sankoff's cost at that state is the minimum.

## Sources

- Hartigan (1973).

articles.title: Fitch's algorithm
articles.statement:
The set of candidate states at the root of the subtree and the number
of changes counted so far. The edge weights of the tree are ignored. Each child is evaluated
once per node, so the recursion makes one call per vertex.

articles.title: Tree with unit costs on every edge
articles.statement: Every edge of the tree carries the unit cost.

articles.title: Tropical leaf weights of observed states
articles.statement:
The leaf weights of the observed states `σ`: the tropical one (cost `0`) at the observed
state and the tropical zero (cost `⊤`) at every other state.

articles.title: Sankoff's algorithm computes the small-parsimony cost
articles.statement:
`sankoff σ t s` is the minimum
total edge cost over all labelings of the non-root vertices that agree with the observed states
at the leaves (with root state `s`).

## Sources

- Sankoff (1975).

articles.title: Sankoff's cost is a lower bound
articles.statement:
Sankoff's cost is a lower bound for the cost of every labeling that agrees with the leaf
states.

articles.title: Sankoff's recursion at a leaf
articles.statement: Sankoff's recursion at a leaf: cost `0` at the observed state, `⊤` elsewhere.

articles.title: Sankoff's recursion at an internal vertex
articles.statement:
Sankoff's recursion at an internal vertex: the cost of state `s` is the sum, over the two
children, of the minimum over the child's state `a` of the edge cost from `s` to `a` plus the
child's cost at `a`.

articles.title: Sankoff's algorithm
articles.statement:
The minimum cost of the subtree `t` given the state `s` at its
root, computed by Felsenstein's pruning recursion over the tropical semiring.

articles.title: Unit substitution cost
articles.statement: The unit cost: `0` for no change and `1` for a change of state.

articles.title: Tropical weight of a labeling equals its edge cost
articles.statement:
The weight of a labeling in the tropical semiring is its edge cost if it agrees with the
leaf states and `⊤` otherwise.

articles.title: Average linkage between clusters
articles.statement: The **average linkage** between two clusters: the mean of `d x y` over `x ∈ C`, `y ∈ D`.

articles.title: Bootstrap support lies in the unit interval
articles.statement: Bootstrap support is a frequency: it lies in `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Bootstrap support
articles.statement:
**Bootstrap support** (Felsenstein 1985) of the split with side `A` away from `a`, for a
tree estimator `est` and an alignment `M` of `m` sites: the fraction of the `m ^ m` site
resamplings with replacement `w : Fin m → Fin m` (uniform draws, whose site counts are
multinomial) for which the tree estimated from the resampled alignment `M ∘ w` has the
cluster `A`. This is the exact bootstrap proportion; Felsenstein's procedure estimates it from a
sample of resamplings.

articles.title: Correctness of BUILD
articles.statement:
**Correctness of BUILD** (Aho, Sagiv, Szymanski & Ullman 1981; Semple & Steel 2003,
Section 6.4): a set `R` of triplets on a nonempty `S`, none of the degenerate form `xx|x` (which
no tree displays and no cut detects), is displayed by a rooted binary phylogenetic tree on `S`
iff for every subset `S'` of at least two taxa the Aho graph of `R` on `S'` is disconnected.
BUILD splits along the components and recurses; the converse direction builds the tree this
way, splitting along any cut.

articles.title: Number of members of a binary hierarchy
articles.statement:
A binary hierarchy on `S` has `2 |S| - 1` members: the `|S|` singletons and `|S| - 1`
internal clusters (stated without subtraction).

articles.title: Split of a binary character
articles.statement: The split of a binary character: the taxa in state `true`.

articles.title: Clusters seen from a leaf are edge sides
articles.statement:
The cluster of a vertex `v` seen from `a` is the side of `v` of the edge from `v` to its
neighbor `p` toward `a`.

articles.title: Compatibility is unchanged by complementing the first split
articles.statement: Compatibility depends only on the split, not on the side used to store it.

articles.title: Compatibility is unchanged by complementing the second split
articles.statement: Compatibility depends only on the split, not on the side used to store it.

articles.title: Compatible clusters are nested or disjoint
articles.statement:
For the sides not containing a fixed taxon `a`, compatibility is being nested or disjoint:
splits seen from a root are clusters.

articles.title: The four-gamete test
articles.statement:
Two binary characters give compatible splits iff they do not
show all four gametes (Buneman 1971; Estabrook, Johnson & McMorris 1976).

articles.title: Edge splits of a tree are pairwise compatible
articles.statement: Any two splits of one tree are compatible.

articles.title: Splits computed from a leaf are pairwise compatible
articles.statement: Any two splits of one tree are compatible.

articles.title: Compatible splits
articles.statement:
The splits `A | Aᶜ` and `B | Bᶜ` are **compatible**: one of `A ∩ B`, `A ∩ Bᶜ`, `Aᶜ ∩ B`,
`Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ` is empty (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 3.1).

articles.title: The two sides of a tree edge are complementary
articles.statement: The two sides of an edge are complementary.

articles.title: Tree displaying a quartet
articles.statement:
`T` **displays the quartet** `xy|zw`: some edge split of `T` has `x, y` on one side and
`z, w` on the other.

articles.title: Cluster system displaying a triplet
articles.statement:
The cluster system `H` **displays** the triplet `xy|z`: some cluster contains `x` and `y`
but not `z`.

articles.title: Side of a tree edge containing a vertex
articles.statement:
The side of the edge `p – v` containing `v`: the taxa whose leaf is closer to `v` than to
`p`.

articles.title: Edge splits of a tree
articles.statement: The **edge splits** of `T`: the sides of all its edges (both sides of every edge).

articles.title: A rooted binary tree is determined by its triplets
articles.statement:
**A rooted binary tree is determined by its triplets** (Semple & Steel 2003, Theorem
6.4.1): two binary hierarchies on `S` displaying the same triplets are equal.

articles.title: Hierarchies are refined by binary trees
articles.statement:
Every family of pairwise nested-or-disjoint
nonempty subsets of a nonempty `S` is contained in a binary hierarchy on `S`, the cluster set of
a rooted binary phylogenetic tree on `S` (Semple & Steel 2003, Proposition 3.5.2 and the
refinement of a rooted tree to a binary one).

articles.title: Perfect phylogeny and the four-gamete condition
The majority-rule consensus tree
articles.statement:
The majority splits are clusters of one unrooted
binary phylogenetic tree (a binary refinement of the majority-rule consensus tree).

articles.title: UPGMA always completes
articles.statement: UPGMA always completes: from the singletons it reaches the single block `univ`.

articles.title: Four-gamete condition for binary characters
articles.statement:
The binary characters `χ` and `ψ` show **all four gametes** `(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)`
on the taxa.

articles.title: Ultrametrics satisfy the four-point condition
articles.statement:
**Ultrametrics satisfy the four-point condition** (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 7.2), so
every ultrametric on a finite set is a tree metric (`IsUltrametric.isTreeMetric`).

articles.title: Cut in the Aho graph
articles.statement:
The **Aho graph** of the triplets `R` on `S'` (vertices `S'`, an edge `x y` for each
`xy|z ∈ R` with `x, y, z ∈ S'`) has a cut: a partition of `S'` into two nonempty parts with no
edge across, i.e. the graph is disconnected.

articles.title: Metric of a dated rooted tree
articles.statement:
`d` is the metric of a **dated rooted tree**, encoded by its clusters: a hierarchy `H` on
the taxa with dates `h` (`0` at the leaves, strictly increasing from a cluster to any cluster
strictly containing it) such that `d x y` is the date of the smallest cluster containing `x`
and `y` (their most recent common ancestor). With edge lengths `(h D - h C) / 2` from each
cluster `C` to its parent `D`, `d x y` is the path length from `x` to `y` and all leaves are
equidistant from the root (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 7.2).

articles.title: A binary hierarchy is a hierarchy
articles.statement: A binary hierarchy is a hierarchy.

articles.title: Pairwise nested-or-disjoint clusters form a hierarchy
articles.statement:
Adding `S` and the singletons to
a family of pairwise nested-or-disjoint nonempty subsets of a nonempty `S` gives a hierarchy.

articles.title: Hierarchy on a finite set
articles.statement:
A **hierarchy** on a finite set `S`: a family of nonempty subsets of `S` containing `S` and
every singleton, any two members nested or disjoint. These are the cluster systems of the rooted
phylogenetic trees on `S` (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 3.5).

articles.title: Perfect phylogeny for a binary character matrix
articles.statement:
`T` is a **perfect phylogeny** for the binary character matrix `M` (taxa by characters):
the split of every non-constant column is a split of `T`, i.e. every character changes state
on exactly one edge.

articles.title: Every ultrametric is a tree metric
articles.statement: Every ultrametric on a finite set is a tree metric (via Buneman's four-point theorem).

articles.title: Ultrametrics are dated tree metrics
articles.statement:
**Ultrametrics are dated tree metrics** (Semple & Steel 2003, Theorem 7.2.5): on a
nonempty finite set of taxa, a dissimilarity satisfies the three-point condition (and is a
metric) iff it is the metric of a dated rooted tree.

articles.title: Ultrametric on taxa
articles.statement:
`d` is an **ultrametric** on the taxa: symmetric, zero exactly on the diagonal, and
satisfying the **three-point condition** `d x z ≤ max (d x y) (d y z)` (equivalently, of the
three distances among any three taxa the two largest are equal).

articles.title: An unrooted binary tree is determined by its quartets
articles.statement:
**An unrooted binary tree is determined by its quartets** (Semple & Steel 2003, Corollary
6.3.8): two trees displaying the same quartets are isomorphic. Already the quartets containing
the taxon `a` suffice; they are the rooted triplets seen from `a`.

articles.title: Majority splits of a family of trees
articles.statement:
The **majority splits** of a finite family of trees `T i`: the clusters, seen from `a`, of
more than half of the trees (repetitions in the family count).

articles.title: Majority splits are compatible
articles.statement:
**Majority splits are compatible** (Margush & McMorris 1981): two clusters each in more than
half of the trees are both clusters of a common tree (pigeonhole), hence nested or disjoint.

articles.title: Clusters seen from a leaf omit that leaf
articles.statement: The clusters seen from `a` do not contain `a`.

articles.title: Bootstrap support above one half means a majority split
articles.statement:
A split has bootstrap support above one half iff it is a majority split of the bootstrap
replicate trees; so the splits with support above one half are pairwise compatible and form
one tree (`exists_tree_majoritySplits_subset`).

articles.title: Symmetry of the Robinson–Foulds distance
articles.statement: The Robinson–Foulds distance is symmetric.

articles.title: Isomorphism invariance of the Robinson–Foulds distance
articles.statement:
The Robinson–Foulds distance is invariant under isomorphism, so it is a metric on the trees
up to isomorphism.

articles.title: Robinson–Foulds distance is independent of the base leaf
articles.statement: The Robinson–Foulds distance does not depend on the leaf used to compute it.

articles.title: Robinson–Foulds distance vanishes exactly on isomorphic trees
articles.statement: The Robinson–Foulds distance vanishes exactly on isomorphic trees (Robinson & Foulds 1981).

articles.title: Maximum of the Robinson–Foulds distance
articles.statement:
On `n ≥ 3` taxa it is at most `2 (n - 3)`, the
number of nontrivial splits of two binary trees (Robinson & Foulds 1981).

articles.title: Robinson–Foulds distance from a tree to itself is zero
articles.statement: The Robinson–Foulds distance from a tree to itself is zero.

articles.title: Triangle inequality for the Robinson–Foulds distance
articles.statement: The Robinson–Foulds distance satisfies the triangle inequality.

articles.title: Robinson–Foulds distance
articles.statement:
The **Robinson–Foulds distance**: the number of splits in exactly one of the two trees.
Each split is counted once, by its side away from the leaf `a` (its cluster seen from `a`);
trivial splits are common to all trees and cancel. The value does not depend on `a`
(`rfDist_eq_rfDist`).

articles.title: Split set from any leaf equals the edge splits
articles.statement: The split set computed from any leaf is the set of edge splits.

articles.title: The split set does not depend on the leaf used to compute it
articles.statement: **The split set does not depend on the leaf used to compute it.**

articles.title: Split set of a tree computed from a leaf
articles.statement:
The split set of `T` computed from the leaf `a`: both sides of every cluster of `T` seen
from `a`. It equals `edgeSplits T` for every `a` (`splitSet_eq_edgeSplits`).

articles.title: Splits-equivalence theorem
articles.statement:
**Splits-equivalence theorem**, binary form (Buneman 1971; Semple & Steel 2003, Theorem
3.1.4): on at least two taxa, a family `F` of proper splits (both sides nonempty) is contained in
the split set of some unrooted binary phylogenetic tree iff its members are pairwise compatible.
The tree is a binary refinement of the tree whose splits are exactly `F` and the trivial ones.

articles.title: Symmetry of split compatibility
articles.statement: Compatibility is symmetric.

articles.title: Rooted triplet
articles.statement: A **rooted triplet** `xy|z`: `x` and `y` are closer to each other than to `z`.

articles.title: Robinson–Foulds distance as half the split symmetric difference
articles.statement:
Each split is counted twice in the symmetric difference of the split sets (once per side),
so the Robinson–Foulds distance is half of it.

articles.title: UPGMA is exact on ultrametrics
articles.statement:
In every UPGMA run on an ultrametric, the recorded
height of two taxa in the same block is their distance. In particular a completed run (one
block) reconstructs `d`, i.e. the dated tree, exactly (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 7.2).

articles.title: States reachable by UPGMA
articles.statement:
The states reachable by **UPGMA** (Sokal & Michener 1958) on `d`: a partition `P` of the
taxa into blocks and the heights `c x y` recorded so far. It starts from the singletons; each
step merges two distinct blocks `C`, `D` of least average linkage (ties broken arbitrarily) and
records `avgDist d C D` as the height at which every `x ∈ C` and `y ∈ D` are joined (the
distance between them in the output tree; their common ancestor sits at half of it).

articles.title: Equal-rates GTR chain is the Jukes–Cantor model
articles.statement:
The equal-rates GTR transition function is the Jukes–Cantor transition probability
`jcProb μ t` (by `JukesCantor.jcProb_eq_exp`).

articles.title: F81 rate matrix
articles.statement: The **F81 rate matrix** (Felsenstein 1981): rate `π j` to every other base `j`.

articles.title: JC69 is the equal-rates GTR model
articles.statement:
Equal base frequencies `1/4` and equal
exchangeabilities `4 μ / 3` give the Jukes–Cantor rate matrix `jcRateMatrix μ`.

articles.title: General time-reversible (GTR) rate matrix
articles.statement:
The **GTR rate matrix** (Tavaré 1986) with base frequencies `π` and exchangeabilities `s`:
`s i j * π j` off the diagonal and minus the off-diagonal row sum on it. The diagonal of `s` is
not used.

articles.title: HKY85 exchangeabilities
articles.statement:
The HKY85 exchangeabilities: `κ` for a transition (indices of equal parity: `A ↔ G`,
`C ↔ T` in the order `A, C, G, T`), `1` for a transversion. The diagonal (also `κ`) is not
used by `gtrRate`.

articles.title: HKY85 with κ = 1 is F81
articles.statement: HKY85 with `κ = 1` is F81.

articles.title: HKY85 rate matrix
articles.statement:
The **HKY85 rate matrix** (Hasegawa–Kishino–Yano 1985) with base frequencies `π` and
transition/transversion ratio `κ`: rate `κ π j` for a transition to `j`, `π j` for a
transversion.

articles.title: Time-reversibility of the GTR chain
articles.statement:
Detailed balance of the GTR transition function with the base frequencies,
`π i P t i j = π j P t j i` for every `t` (time-reversibility of the GTR chain).

articles.title: Detailed balance of the F81 model
articles.statement: F81 is in detailed balance with its base frequencies.

articles.title: GTR is reversible
articles.statement:
With symmetric exchangeabilities, the GTR matrix is in detailed
balance with its base frequencies, `π i Q i j = π j Q j i` (Tavaré 1986).

articles.title: Detailed balance of the HKY85 model
articles.statement: HKY85 is in detailed balance with its base frequencies.

articles.title: F81 matrix is a rate matrix
articles.statement: With nonnegative base frequencies, the F81 matrix is a rate matrix.

articles.title: GTR matrix is a rate matrix
articles.statement:
With nonnegative base frequencies and nonnegative off-diagonal exchangeabilities, the GTR
matrix is a rate matrix (the diagonal `s i i` is not used by `gtrRate`).

articles.title: HKY85 matrix is a rate matrix
articles.statement: With nonnegative base frequencies and `κ ≥ 0`, the HKY85 matrix is a rate matrix.

articles.title: Jukes–Cantor matrix is a rate matrix
articles.statement: For `μ ≥ 0` the Jukes–Cantor matrix is a rate matrix.

articles.title: K80 matrix is a rate matrix
articles.statement: With `κ ≥ 0`, the K80 matrix is a rate matrix.

articles.title: K80 with κ = 1 is the Jukes–Cantor model
articles.statement: K80 with `κ = 1` is JC69 with substitution rate `μ = 3/4`.

articles.title: K80 rate matrix
articles.statement:
The **K80 rate matrix** (Kimura 1980): equal base frequencies `1/4`, rate `κ / 4` for a
transition and `1 / 4` for each transversion.

articles.title: Rows of the GTR rate matrix sum to zero
articles.statement: The rows of the GTR matrix sum to `0`, for all parameters.

articles.title: Base frequencies are stationary for the GTR chain
articles.statement: The base frequencies are stationary for the GTR transition function at every time.

articles.title: Base frequencies are invariant for the GTR generator
articles.statement: The base frequencies are invariant for the GTR generator: `π Q = 0`.

articles.title: Tree metrics satisfy the four-point condition
articles.statement:
**Tree metrics satisfy the four-point condition** (the easy direction of Buneman's
theorem).

## Sources

- Buneman (1974); Semple & Steel (2003), Theorem 7.2.6.

articles.title: Four-point condition
articles.statement: The **four-point condition**: `d x y + d z t ≤ max (d x z + d y t) (d x t + d y z)`.

articles.title: Buneman's four-point theorem
articles.statement:
A symmetric dissimilarity on a finite set that vanishes on
the diagonal is a tree metric if and only if it satisfies the four-point condition.

## Sources

- Buneman (1974); Semple & Steel (2003), Theorem 7.2.6.

articles.title: Buneman's theorem, converse direction
articles.statement:
A symmetric dissimilarity on a finite set that
vanishes on the diagonal and satisfies the four-point condition is a tree metric.

## Sources

- Buneman (1974); Semple & Steel (2003), Theorem 7.2.6.

articles.title: Tree metric
articles.statement:
`d` is a **tree metric**: there are a finite tree `G` on a vertex type `V`, positive edge
lengths `w`, and a placement `ι` of the taxa on vertices such that `d x y` is the total length
of the (unique) path from `ι x` to `ι y`.

articles.title: Eigen's error threshold
articles.statement: In the fixed-`q_L` limit the master sequence persists iff `μ < log σ`.

articles.title: Interior quasispecies equilibrium is at most 1
articles.statement: For `σ > 1` and `Q ≤ 1` the interior equilibrium is at most `1`.

articles.title: Error threshold
articles.statement: For `σ > 1`, the interior equilibrium is positive iff `σ Q > 1`.

articles.title: Interior equilibrium of the master-sequence frequency
articles.statement:
The interior equilibrium `x* = (σ Q - 1) / (σ - 1)` of the master frequency. For
`σ = 1` (no selective advantage) Lean's `x / 0 = 0` gives the junk value `0`; every result
below assumes `1 < σ`.

articles.title: Equilibria of the master-sequence frequency
articles.statement: The equilibria of the master frequency are `0` and `x* = (σ Q - 1)/(σ - 1)`.

articles.title: Master-sequence equation is logistic
articles.statement: The master-sequence equation is logistic: `x' = x ((σ Q - 1) - (σ - 1) x)`.

articles.title: Master-sequence vector field of the single-peak quasispecies
articles.statement:
The master-sequence vector field of the single-peak quasispecies without back mutation:
`x' = σ Q x - (σ x + (1 - x)) x`, where `σ` is the master fitness relative to the mutants and
`Q` the probability of an error-free copy. Meaningful for `σ > 1`, `0 ≤ Q ≤ 1`,
`0 ≤ x ≤ 1`; it is a polynomial and is defined for all reals.

articles.title: Maximal genome length
articles.statement:
For per-site fidelity `0 < q < 1` and `σ > 0`,
`σ q ^ L > 1` iff `L < log σ / (-log q)`.

articles.title: Mutant frequency at the interior equilibrium
articles.statement: The mutant frequency at the interior equilibrium is `1 - x* = σ (1 - Q)/(σ - 1)`.

articles.title: Fixed-`q_L` limit
articles.statement:
With per-site fidelity `q_L = 1 - μ / L`, so that the expected number
of mutations per genome copy is `μ`, the error-free probability is `q_L ^ L → e^{-μ}` and the
master equilibrium converges to `(σ e^{-μ} - 1)/(σ - 1)`.

articles.title: Continuity of the interior equilibrium in the copying fidelity
articles.statement:
The interior equilibrium depends continuously on `Q`, so any sequence of fidelities with
`Q_L → Qlim` has `x*(Q_L) → x*(Qlim)`.

articles.title: Convergence above the threshold
articles.statement:
If `σ > 1`, `σ Q > 1` and `x` solves the master
equation on `[0, ∞)` from a positive master frequency, then `x t → x*`.

articles.title: Loss of the master at or below the threshold
articles.statement:
If `σ > 1`, `σ Q ≤ 1` and `x` solves the
master equation on `[0, ∞)` from a positive master frequency, then `x t → 0`.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the logistic solution
articles.statement:
**Uniqueness of the logistic solution** on `[0, T]`: in the biological domain
(`K > 0`, `x₀ > 0`, `r ≥ 0`), any function continuous on `[0, T]`, with right derivative
`r x (1 - x / K)` on `[0, T)` and `x 0 = x₀`, equals the explicit solution on `[0, T]`.

articles.title: The explicit solution solves the logistic equation
articles.statement:
Wherever the denominator
`K + x₀ (e^{r t} - 1)` is nonzero, `x' = r x (1 - x / K)` (all real parameters, `K ≠ 0`).

articles.title: Positivity of the logistic solution's denominator
articles.statement:
In the biological domain (`K > 0`, `x₀ > 0`, `r t ≥ 0`, or `x₀ ≤ K`) the denominator of the
logistic solution is positive.

articles.title: Logistic transit time from $1/(2N)$ to $1 - 1/(2N)$
articles.statement:
The transit time from `1 / (2N)` to `1 - 1 / (2N)` is `(2 / r) log (2N - 1)`, for
`N ≥ 1` and `r ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Exact deterministic transit time
articles.statement:
Starting from frequency `a ∈ (0, 1)` with `r ≠ 0`,
the logistic frequency reaches `1 - a` at time `(2 / r) log ((1 - a) / a)`.

articles.title: Initial value of the logistic solution
articles.statement: The logistic solution starts at `x₀` (for `K ≠ 0`).

articles.title: Explicit solution of the logistic equation
articles.statement:
Explicit solution of the logistic equation `x' = r x (1 - x / K)` with `x 0 = x₀`:
`K x₀ e^{r t} / (K + x₀ (e^{r t} - 1))`.

articles.title: Log-odds grow linearly
articles.statement:
**Log-odds grow linearly** for a frequency (`K = 1`): for `0 < x₀ < 1` and all `r`, `t`,
`log (x(t) / (1 - x(t))) = log (x₀ / (1 - x₀)) + r t`.

articles.title: Logistic solution is strictly increasing
articles.statement:
For `r > 0` and `0 < x₀ < K` the logistic solution is strictly increasing, so the transit
time of `logistic_transitTime` is the unique time at which `1 - a` is reached.

articles.title: Convergence to the carrying capacity
articles.statement:
For `r > 0` and `x₀ > 0`, `x(t) → K` as
`t → ∞` (the identity needs no sign condition on `K`; biologically `K > 0`).

articles.title: Exponential limit
articles.statement:
For fixed `r`, `x₀`, `t`, the logistic solution tends to the
exponential-growth solution `x₀ e^{r t}` as the carrying capacity `K → ∞`.

articles.title: Positive solutions lie on level curves
articles.statement:
If `(x, y)` solves the Lotka–Volterra system
on `[0, ∞)` and both populations stay positive there, then `V(x t, y t) = V(x 0, y 0)` for
all `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: The coexistence equilibrium minimizes the first integral
articles.statement:
For positive parameters and
`x, y > 0`, `V(γ / δ, α / β) ≤ V(x, y)`.

articles.title: First integral of the Lotka–Volterra system
articles.statement:
The Lotka–Volterra first integral `V(x, y) = δ x - γ log x + β y - α log y` for the
system `x' = α x - β x y`, `y' = δ x y - γ y`. It is meaningful on the open positive quadrant
`x, y > 0`; elsewhere `Real.log` takes junk values (`log 0 = 0`, `log (-x) = log x`).

articles.title: Lotka–Volterra first integral
articles.statement:
If `x' = α x - β x y` and `y' = δ x y - γ y` at time `t`
and `x t, y t > 0`, then `t ↦ V(x t, y t)` has derivative `0` at `t`.

articles.title: Invariance of the faces of the simplex
articles.statement:
For continuous fitness `f`, a strategy absent
at time `0` (`x_i(0) = 0`) stays absent for all `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Evolution of the total frequency under replicator dynamics
articles.statement: The total frequency `∑ x_i` evolves by `(∑ x_i)' = f̄(x) (1 - ∑ x_i)`.

articles.title: Rest points in the interior are equalizers
articles.statement:
If every strategy is present (`x i > 0`),
then `x` is a rest point iff every strategy has fitness equal to the mean fitness.

articles.title: Rest point of the replicator equation
articles.statement: `x` is a rest point of the replicator equation: `x_i (f_i(x) - f̄(x)) = 0` for all `i`.

articles.title: Solution of the replicator equation
articles.statement: `x` solves the replicator equation `x_i' = x_i (f_i(x) - f̄(x))` for all times `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Mean fitness of a population state
articles.statement:
The mean fitness `f̄(x) = ∑ i, x i * f x i` of the population state `x` for the fitness
function `f`.

articles.title: Invariance of the simplex (Hofbauer–Sigmund 1998, §7.1)
articles.statement:
For continuous fitness `f`, a
solution starting in the standard simplex (`x i ≥ 0` for all `i` and `∑ i, x i = 1`) stays in
it for all `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Present strategies stay present
articles.statement:
For continuous fitness `f`, a strategy with positive
frequency at time `0` has positive frequency for all `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Invariance of the simplex hyperplane
articles.statement:
For continuous fitness `f`, a solution with
`∑ x_i(0) = 1` satisfies `∑ x_i(t) = 1` for all `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Mean fitness is unchanged exactly at selection equilibria
articles.statement:
Mean fitness is unchanged by one generation of selection exactly when the allele
frequencies are at an equilibrium of the selection map.

articles.title: Mean fitness stays positive under diploid selection
articles.statement:
Mean fitness stays positive after one generation of diploid viability selection (for
nonnegative frequencies and fitnesses; normalization is not needed).

articles.title: Mean fitness never decreases
articles.statement:
**Mean fitness never decreases** under diploid multi-allele viability selection with random
mating (Mulholland–Smith 1959; Scheuer–Mandel 1959; Kingman 1961).

articles.title: Diploid selection strictly increases mean fitness off equilibria
articles.statement: Away from equilibria, mean fitness strictly increases under diploid viability selection.

articles.title: Wright's formula
articles.statement:
**Wright's formula** (Wright 1937): for two alleles with frequencies `(x, 1 - x)`, one
generation of viability selection changes the frequency of allele `0` by
`Δx = x (1 - x) (dw̄/dx) / (2 w̄)`. The identity is algebraic and holds for every real `x` with
`w̄(x) ≠ 0`; the model domain is `x ∈ [0, 1]` with nonnegative fitnesses.

articles.title: Derivative of two-allele mean fitness
articles.statement:
For two alleles with frequencies `(x, 1 - x)`, the mean fitness
`w̄(x) = x² w₀₀ + x (1 - x) (w₀₁ + w₁₀) + (1 - x)² w₁₁` has derivative `2 (m₀ - m₁)`, twice the
difference of the marginal fitnesses. This holds for every real `x`.

articles.title: Diploid Baum–Eagon mean-fitness inequality, sharp form
articles.statement:
With
nonnegative allele frequencies and genotype fitnesses and positive mean fitness, one generation
of selection raises the log mean fitness by at least twice the relative entropy
`∑ i, p'_i log (p'_i / p_i)` of the new allele frequencies `p'` from the old ones `p`
(Baum–Eagon's argument for the quadratic form `w̄`). Alleles absent before selection stay absent
(`p_i = 0 → p'_i = 0`), so the summands with `p_i = 0` vanish. The inequality does not need
`∑ p = 1`; on the simplex its right side is nonnegative (Gibbs' inequality). This is a
mean-fitness monotonicity inequality, not Fisher's fundamental theorem: Fisher's theorem
concerns the change attributable to selection expressed through additive genetic variance.

articles.title: Closed form above the current frequency
articles.statement:
For `0 < p ≤ x ≤ z < 1` the conditional sojourn
density is the paper's `Ψ₂(z)`; it does not depend on `p`.

articles.title: Closed form below the current frequency
articles.statement:
For `0 < p ≤ z ≤ x < 1` the conditional sojourn
density is the paper's `Ψ₁(z)`; it depends neither on `p` nor on `x`.

articles.title: Maruyama–Kimura conditional sojourn density
articles.statement:
The Maruyama–Kimura conditional sojourn density (the paper's `Ψ_z(p, z)`): given the initial
frequency `p` and the current frequency `x`, the density of mean time spent at frequency `z`
along the path, `Ψ(p, z) Ψ(z, x) / Ψ(p, x)` (Maruyama and Kimura 1975; Kiezun et al. 2013,
Methods). Time in units of `2N` generations.

articles.title: Continuity of the sojourn density in the starting frequency
articles.statement: The sojourn density is continuous in the starting frequency (in particular at `p = x`).

articles.title: Green's representation with selection
articles.statement:
**Green's representation with selection** (Ewens 2004, Chapter 4; the integrated form of the
paper's `-δ(x - p) = s p (1 - p) ∂Ψ/∂p + p (1 - p) / (4N) ∂²Ψ/∂p²`). For continuous `g` and
`p ∈ (0, 1)`, `v(q) = ∫₀¹ Ψ(q, x) g(x) dx` solves `L_σ v = -g` at `p`; with
`integral_selectionGreen_left` and `integral_selectionGreen_right` (`v(0) = v(1) = 0`) this
generalizes `generator_integral_neutralGreen` to `σ ≠ 0`. In the diffusion reading, `v(p)` is the expected value of `∫₀^T g(X_t) dt` up to absorption.

articles.title: Sojourn density solves the backward equation above the target
articles.statement: Above the target frequency: `L_σ Ψ(·, x) = 0` at every `p > x`.

articles.title: Sojourn density solves the backward equation below the target
articles.statement:
Below the target frequency the sojourn density solves the homogeneous backward equation in
its first argument: `L_σ Ψ(·, x) = 0` at every `p < x` (pointwise form of the paper's
`-δ(x - p) = L_σ Ψ(·, x)`).

articles.title: The general Green kernel specializes to Kimura's sojourn density
articles.statement:
For genic selection
`b x = σ x (1 - x)`, `a x = x (1 - x)`, the general Green's function `greenFunction` is
`selectionGreen σ` on `[0, 1] × (0, 1)`. The scale function is `S(y) = u(y) / u'(0)` with
`u = kimuraFixation σ` and `u'(0) = kimuraSlope σ`, since both have derivative `ψ(y) = e^{-2σy}`
and vanish at `0`; substituting that and `S(1) = 1 / u'(0)` into `greenFunction` gives
`selectionGreen`.

articles.title: Right derivative of the sojourn density at the diagonal
articles.statement: Right derivative at the diagonal: `∂_p Ψ(x⁺, x) = -2 u(x) / (x (1 - x))`.

articles.title: Left derivative of the sojourn density at the diagonal
articles.statement:
Left derivative at the diagonal: `∂_p Ψ(x⁻, x) = 2 (1 - u(x)) / (x (1 - x))`. Together with
`hasDerivWithinAt_selectionGreen_Ici` this gives the jump `-2 / (x (1 - x))` of `∂_p Ψ` at
`p = x`, i.e. `L_σ Ψ(·, x) = -δ_x` in the distributional sense.

articles.title: Sojourn density from frequency zero vanishes
articles.statement:
Boundary value at `0`: an absent allele spends no time in `(0, 1)`, so
`∫₀¹ Ψ(0, x) g(x) dx = 0` for every `g`.

articles.title: Sojourn density from frequency one vanishes
articles.statement:
Boundary value at `1`: a fixed allele spends no time in `(0, 1)`, so
`∫₀¹ Ψ(1, x) g(x) dx = 0` for every `g`.

articles.title: Integrability of the sojourn density above the current frequency
articles.statement: `Ψ₂` is integrable on `[x, 1]` for `x ∈ (0, 1)` (it is bounded by `2 / (1 - x)`).

articles.title: Integrability of the sojourn density below the current frequency
articles.statement: `Ψ₁` is integrable on `[0, x]` (it is bounded by `2`).

articles.title: Kimura's fixation probability is less than one
articles.statement: An allele at frequency below `1` is lost with positive probability.

articles.title: Positivity of Kimura's fixation probability
articles.statement: An allele present at positive frequency has positive fixation probability.

articles.title: Positivity of the slope constant in Kimura's formula
articles.statement: The slope constant of Kimura's formula is positive.

articles.title: Mean time as a sum of sojourn times
articles.statement:
**Mean time as a sum of sojourn times** (the identity behind Maruyama and Kimura 1975). For
a jointly measurable family of transition densities `w p x t ≥ 0` on `(0, 1)` satisfying the
Chapman–Kolmogorov equation for positive times,
`∫₀^∞ t w(p, x, t) dt = ∫₀¹ Ψ(p, y) Ψ(y, x) dy` with `Ψ(p, x) = ∫₀^∞ w(p, x, t) dt`, in
`ℝ≥0∞`. Dividing by `Ψ(p, x)` reads `∫₀¹ Ψ(p, y) Ψ(y, x) / Ψ(p, x) dy` (the integral of
`ageDensity` when `Ψ = selectionGreen σ`) as a mean time. The statement is abstract: no
diffusion is constructed, and `w` is not required to be the Wright–Fisher transition density.

articles.title: Hyperbolic form of the sojourn density above the current frequency
articles.statement:
`Ψ₂` in hyperbolic form:
`2 sinh(σ(1 - z))² sinh(σx) / (σ sinh σ sinh(σ(1 - x)) z (1 - z))` for `σ ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Sojourn density above the current frequency via fixation probability
articles.statement:
`Ψ₂` through Kimura's fixation probability:
`Ψ₂(z) = 2 u(x)(1 - u(z))² / ((1 - u(x)) z (1 - z) u'(z))` on `(0, 1)`.

articles.title: Paper units
articles.statement:
The paper's
`Ψ₂(z) = (e^{-γ(1-z)} - 1)(e^{γ(1-z)} - 1)(1 - e^{γx}) / (s z (1 - z)(e^{-γ(1-x)} - 1)(1 - e^{γ}))`,
`γ = 4Ns`, equals `2N · maruyamaAbove (2Ns) x z`.

articles.title: Stronger selection, smaller `Ψ₂`
articles.statement:
For `0 ≤ σ < τ` and `0 < x < z < 1`,
`Ψ₂` at `τ` is strictly below `Ψ₂` at `σ`.

articles.title: Maruyama effect, above the current frequency
articles.statement:
For `σ ≠ 0` and `0 < x < z < 1`,
`Ψ₂(z)` is strictly below its neutral value `2 x (1 - z) / ((1 - x) z)`.

articles.title: Symmetry
articles.statement: `Ψ₂` is the same for `σ` and `-σ`.

articles.title: Sojourn density above the current frequency vanishes at one
articles.statement: At `z = 1` the closed form `Ψ₂` vanishes (a null set for the integral).

articles.title: Positivity of the sojourn density above the current frequency
articles.statement: `Ψ₂` is positive for `0 < x < z < 1`.

articles.title: Closed-form sojourn density above the current frequency
articles.statement:
The paper's closed form `Ψ₂(z)` for `x < z < 1` (Kiezun et al. 2013, Methods), in units of
`2N` generations with `σ = 2Ns`:
`(e^{-2σ(1-z)} - 1)(e^{2σ(1-z)} - 1)(1 - e^{2σx}) /
(σ z (1 - z)(e^{-2σ(1-x)} - 1)(1 - e^{2σ}))`, and its continuous extension
`2 x (1 - z) / ((1 - x) z)` for `σ = 0`.

articles.title: Hyperbolic form of the sojourn density below the current frequency
articles.statement: `Ψ₁` in hyperbolic form: `2 sinh(σz) sinh(σ(1 - z)) / (σ z (1 - z) sinh σ)` for `σ ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Sojourn density below the current frequency via fixation probability
articles.statement:
`Ψ₁` through Kimura's fixation probability: `Ψ₁(z) = 2 u(z)(1 - u(z)) / (z (1 - z) u'(z))`
on `(0, 1)`.

articles.title: Paper units
articles.statement:
With `N` diploid individuals, selection coefficient `s ≠ 0` and time in
generations, the paper prints `Ψ₁(z) = (e^{-γ(1-z)} - 1)(e^{-γz} - 1) / (s z (1 - z)(1 - e^{-γ}))`
with `γ = 4Ns`; it equals `2N · maruyamaBelow (2Ns) z`.

articles.title: Stronger selection, smaller `Ψ₁`
articles.statement:
For `0 ≤ σ < τ` and `z ∈ (0, 1)`,
`Ψ₁` at `τ` is strictly below `Ψ₁` at `σ`.

articles.title: Maruyama effect, below the current frequency
articles.statement:
For `σ ≠ 0`, `Ψ₁(z) < 2`, its neutral
value, for every `z ∈ (0, 1)`.

articles.title: Symmetry
articles.statement: `Ψ₁` is the same for `σ` and `-σ`.

articles.title: Positivity of the sojourn density below the current frequency
articles.statement: `Ψ₁` is positive on `(0, 1)`.

articles.title: Closed-form sojourn density below the current frequency
articles.statement:
The paper's closed form `Ψ₁(z)` for `0 < z < x` (Kiezun et al. 2013, Methods), in units of
`2N` generations with `σ = 2Ns`:
`(e^{-2σ(1-z)} - 1)(e^{-2σz} - 1) / (σ z (1 - z) (1 - e^{-2σ}))`, and its continuous extension
`2` for `σ = 0`. It does not depend on the current frequency `x`.

articles.title: Stronger selection, younger alleles
articles.statement:
**Stronger selection, younger alleles**, for either sign of selection: if `|σ| < |τ|` then
an allele at frequency `x ∈ (0, 1)` under selection `τ` is on average strictly younger than one
under selection `σ`.

articles.title: Stronger selection, younger alleles
articles.statement:
At a fixed frequency `x ∈ (0, 1)`, the mean age is
strictly decreasing in `σ ≥ 0`. Kiezun et al. (2013, Figure 1b) show this numerically from the
closed forms; here it is proved.
