articles.title: Haplotype variance at the first locus
articles.statement: The haplotype variance `V_A = E (X₁ - p)²` at locus `A`.

articles.title: Haplotype variance at the second locus
articles.statement: The haplotype variance `V_B = E (Y₁ - q)²` at locus `B`.

articles.title: Additive variance at a biallelic locus (Falconer & Mackay 1996, ch. 8)
articles.statement:
With
`p = q₁` and `q = 1 - q₁`, `V_A = 2pq (a + d (q - p)) ²`. An algebraic identity, valid for every
real `q₁`; it is a variance for `0 ≤ q₁ ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Additive genetic variance
articles.statement:
The additive genetic variance `V_A = 2 ∑ i p i α i ²`, the variance of the breeding value
`α i + α j`.

articles.title: Average effect of an allele
articles.statement:
The average effect of allele `i`, `α i = ∑ j p j G i j - μ`: the mean value of the genotypes
carrying `i` (the other gene drawn from the population) minus the population mean. This is the
average excess; under Hardy–Weinberg proportions it is Fisher's average effect, the coefficient
of the least-squares additive fit (`domVar_le_sum_sq`).

articles.title: Allele frequencies at a biallelic locus
articles.statement:
Allele frequencies at a biallelic locus: `A₁` (`true`) has frequency `q₁` and `A₂`
(`false`) has frequency `1 - q₁`.

articles.title: Genotypic values at a biallelic locus on Falconer's scale
articles.statement:
Genotypic values at a biallelic locus on Falconer's scale: `A₁A₁ ↦ a`, `A₁A₂ ↦ d`,
`A₂A₂ ↦ -a` (the origin is the midpoint of the homozygotes).

articles.title: Full sibs (Fisher 1918)
articles.statement: `Cov(FS) = V_A / 2 + V_D / 4`.

articles.title: Full-sib covariance of genotypic values
articles.statement:
The covariance of the genotypic values of full sibs: the sire `(i, j)` and the dam
`(k, l)` are unrelated; the first offspring receives `cond b i j` and `cond e k l`, the second,
independently, `cond b' i j` and `cond e' k l`.

articles.title: Half sibs (Fisher 1918)
articles.statement: `Cov(HS) = V_A / 4`.

articles.title: Half-sib covariance of genotypic values
articles.statement:
The covariance of the genotypic values of half sibs: the common parent has genotype
`(i, j)` and transmits `cond b i j` to one offspring and, independently, `cond b' i j` to the
other; the second genes `k`, `l` come from two unrelated mates.

articles.title: Parent and offspring (Fisher 1918)
articles.statement: `Cov(P, O) = V_A / 2`.

articles.title: Parent–offspring covariance of genotypic values
articles.statement:
The covariance of the genotypic values of a parent and its offspring: the parent has
genotype `(i, j)` (frequency `p i p j`) and transmits `cond b i j` (each with probability
`1/2`), and the offspring's other gene `k` comes from an unrelated mate (frequency `p k`).

articles.title: Dominance deviation of a genotype
articles.statement: The dominance deviation `δ i j = G i j - μ - α i - α j`.

articles.title: Dominance variance at a biallelic locus (Falconer & Mackay 1996, ch. 8)
articles.statement: `V_D = (2pqd) ²`, for every real `q₁`.

articles.title: Least squares (Fisher 1918)
articles.statement:
Among all fits `c + a i + a j` of the genotypic value by
a function additive over the two genes, the additive fitted genotypic value `μ + α i + α j`
minimizes the weighted squared error `∑ p i p j (G i j - c - a i - a j) ²`; its error is `V_D`.

articles.title: Dominance variance
articles.statement: The dominance variance `V_D = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j δ i j ²`.

articles.title: Fisher's variance decomposition
articles.statement: `V_G = V_A + V_D`.

articles.title: Genetic variance under Hardy–Weinberg proportions
articles.statement: The genetic variance `V_G = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j (G i j - μ) ²`.

articles.title: Decomposition of the genotypic value
articles.statement: The decomposition `G i j = μ + α i + α j + δ i j` (an identity by definition of `δ`).

articles.title: Mean genotypic value under Hardy–Weinberg proportions
articles.statement: The mean genotypic value `μ = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j G i j` under Hardy–Weinberg proportions.

articles.title: Average effects have mean zero
articles.statement: The average effects have mean zero: `∑ i p i α i = 0`.

articles.title: Orthogonality of dominance deviations in the first allele
articles.statement:
Orthogonality of the dominance deviations for a symmetric genotypic value:
`∑ i p i δ i j = 0` for every `j`.

articles.title: Orthogonality of dominance deviations in the second allele
articles.statement: Orthogonality of the dominance deviations: `∑ j p j δ i j = 0` for every `i`.

articles.title: Genotype of an individual at a biallelic locus
articles.statement: The genotype (reference-allele count) `x_i ∈ {0, 1, 2}` of individual `i`.

articles.title: GCTA diagonal relationship estimator
articles.statement:
The diagonal estimator of GCTA (Yang et al. 2011) at one locus,
`A_ii = 1 + (x_i² - (1 + 2p) x_i + 2p²) / (2p(1 - p))`.

articles.title: Genetic relationship matrix entry
articles.statement:
The genetic relationship matrix entry of Yang et al. (2010) at one locus,
`A_ij = (x_i - 2p)(x_j - 2p) / (2p(1 - p))`.

articles.title: Symmetry of identity by descent
articles.statement: Identity by descent is symmetric.

articles.title: A gene copy is identical by descent with itself
articles.statement: A gene copy is identical by descent with itself: `ibd c c = 1`.

articles.title: Malécot's identity-by-descent model
articles.statement:
Malécot's identity-by-descent model at one biallelic locus, at the level of second
moments. The individuals are `ι`; individual `i` carries the gene copies `(i, 0)` (paternal) and
`(i, 1)` (maternal), and `allele c ∈ {0, 1}` indicates the reference allele on copy `c`. The
reference allele has frequency `p ∈ (0, 1)` (a polymorphic locus), and `ibd c d` is the
probability that the copies `c` and `d` are identical by descent: IBD copies carry the same
allele and non-IBD copies are independent draws with frequency `p` (Malécot 1948), which gives
the second moments `𝔼[a_c a_d] = p² + p (1 - p) ibd c d`. Only these first and second moments
are assumed. `ibd` is determined by the moments (`p (1 - p) ≠ 0`), and `ibd c c = 1`
(`IBDModel.ibd_self`). In Malécot's model `ibd c d ∈ [0, 1]`; the structure does not require
this, and the identities below hold for any real `ibd` (for example a correlation relative to a
reference population, which can be negative). A monomorphic locus (`p ∈ {0, 1}`) is excluded:
there the GRM denominator `2p(1 - p)` vanishes.

articles.title: Inbreeding coefficient
articles.statement:
The inbreeding coefficient `F_i`: the probability that the two copies of `i` are identical
by descent.

articles.title: Integrability of products of allele indicators
articles.statement: Products of allele indicators are integrable.

articles.title: Integrability of allele indicators
articles.statement: The allele indicators are integrable.

articles.title: Integrability of products of genotypes
articles.statement: Products of genotypes are integrable.

articles.title: Integrability of genotypes
articles.statement: Genotypes are integrable.

articles.title: The genetic relationship covariance
articles.statement:
**The genetic relationship covariance** (Yang et al. 2010):
`𝔼[(x_i - 2p)(x_j - 2p)] = 2p(1 - p) · 2 φ_ij`.

articles.title: Second moment of genotypes in terms of kinship
articles.statement: `𝔼[x_i x_j] = 4p² + 4p(1 - p) φ_ij`.

articles.title: Expected genotype equals $2p$
The GCTA diagonal estimator is unbiased for `1 + F_i`
articles.statement:
**The GCTA diagonal estimator is unbiased for `1 + F_i`** (Yang et al. 2011):
`𝔼[1 + (x_i² - (1 + 2p) x_i + 2p²) / (2p(1 - p))] = 1 + F_i`.

articles.title: Diagonal GRM entry is unbiased for $1 + F_i$
articles.statement: The diagonal GRM entry is unbiased for `1 + F_i`: `𝔼[A_ii] = 1 + F_i`.

articles.title: The GRM is unbiased for twice the kinship
articles.statement:
**The GRM is unbiased for twice the kinship** (Yang et al. 2010):
`𝔼[A_ij] = 2 φ_ij`, for every pair `i, j` (including `i = j`, where `2 φ_ii = 1 + F_i`).

articles.title: The KING moment
articles.statement:
**The KING moment** (Manichaikul et al. 2010) for two non-inbred individuals:
`𝔼[(x_i - x_j)²] = 4p(1 - p)(1 - 2φ_ij)`.

articles.title: The KING moment
articles.statement:
**The KING moment** (Manichaikul et al. 2010), general form:
`𝔼[(x_i - x_j)²] = 2p(1 - p)(1 + F_i) + 2p(1 - p)(1 + F_j) - 8p(1 - p) φ_ij`.

articles.title: Symmetry of kinship
articles.statement: Kinship is symmetric.

articles.title: Self-kinship equals $(1 + F_i)/2$
Kinship coefficient
articles.statement:
The kinship coefficient `φ_ij`: the probability that a copy drawn at random from `i` and a
copy drawn at random from `j` are identical by descent.

articles.title: Derivative of mean fitness with respect to the trait mean
articles.statement:
The derivative of mean fitness with respect to the trait mean is
`d/dμ w̄(μ) = 𝔼[(z - μ) W z] / v`, for bounded measurable fitness and `v > 0`.

articles.title: Lande's gradient of mean fitness for multivariate traits
articles.statement:
The gradient of mean fitness with respect to the vector of trait means is
`∇_μ w̄(μ) = P⁻¹ 𝔼[W z · (z - μ)]`, for positive definite `P` and bounded measurable `W`.

articles.title: Stein's lemma
articles.statement:
**Stein's lemma** for the normal law `N(μ, v)`, `v > 0`: if `g` is differentiable with
derivative `g'` and `g`, `(z - μ) g z` and `g'` are integrable, then
`𝔼[(z - μ) g z] = v 𝔼[g' z]` (Stein 1981, Lemma 1).

articles.title: Mean fitness of a multivariate normal trait
articles.statement:
The mean fitness `w̄(μ) = 𝔼[W z]` of a population whose trait vector is distributed as
`N(μ, P)`.

articles.title: Mean fitness of a normally distributed trait
articles.statement:
The mean fitness `w̄(μ) = 𝔼[W z]` of a population whose trait is distributed as
`N(μ, v)`.

articles.title: The Lande–Arnold selection gradient
articles.statement:
**The Lande–Arnold selection gradient** for one normally distributed trait: for a
differentiable bounded fitness function with integrable derivative, `β = S / v = 𝔼[W' z] / w̄`,
the average slope of relative fitness `W / w̄` (Lande–Arnold 1983).

articles.title: Lande's equation
articles.statement:
**Lande's equation** for one normally distributed trait (Lande 1979): the selection
differential is the phenotypic variance times the derivative of log mean fitness with respect
to the trait mean, `S = v · d/dμ log w̄(μ)`.

articles.title: Lande's equation
articles.statement:
**Lande's equation** (Lande 1979): for a multivariate normal trait vector, the selection
differential is the phenotypic covariance matrix applied to the gradient of log mean fitness
with respect to the trait means, `S = P ∇_μ log w̄(μ)`.

articles.title: Multivariate directional selection differential
articles.statement:
The directional selection differential `S = 𝔼[W z · (z - μ)] / w̄` of a trait vector
distributed as `N(μ, P)`: the fitness-weighted mean trait vector of the selected parents minus
the mean `μ` before selection. If `w̄ = 0` it is the junk value `0`.

articles.title: Directional selection differential
articles.statement:
The directional selection differential `S = 𝔼[(z - μ) W z] / w̄`: the mean trait of the
selected parents, weighting each individual by its fitness, minus the mean trait `μ` before
selection. If `w̄ = 0` the division returns the junk value `0`.

articles.title: The LDpred-inf posterior
articles.statement:
**The LDpred-inf posterior** (Vilhjálmsson et al. 2015; the likelihood
`β̂ | β ~ N(R β, R / N)` of Zhu and Stephens 2017): with `M` markers, `N` individuals,
heritability `h² > 0`, effects `β ~ N(0, h² / M · I)`, an LD matrix `R` that is positive definite,
and marginal estimates `β̂ = R β + ε` with `ε ~ N(0, R / N)` independent of `β`, the posterior law
of `β` given `β̂` is `N((R + M / (N h²) · I)⁻¹ β̂, (1 / N) (R + M / (N h²) · I)⁻¹)`. In particular
`𝔼[β | β̂] = (R + M / (N h²) · I)⁻¹ β̂`.

articles.title: BLUP as a conditional law
articles.statement:
**BLUP as a conditional law** (Henderson 1975; Robinson 1991): in the Gaussian mixed model
`y = X b + Z u + e` with fixed effects `b`, random effects `u ~ N(0, G)` and residuals
`e ~ N(0, R)` independent, `G` and `R` positive definite, the conditional law of `u` given `y`
is `N(G Zᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X b), G - G Zᵀ V⁻¹ Z G)` with `V = Z G Zᵀ + R` (for almost every `y`).

articles.title: BLUP is the conditional expectation
articles.statement:
**BLUP is the conditional expectation** in the Gaussian mixed model:
`𝔼[u | y] = G Zᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X b)` almost surely.

articles.title: The raw residual-product second moment of the marginal estimates
articles.statement:
**The raw residual-product second moment of the marginal estimates** (Zhu and Stephens
2017): if `𝔼[ε_i ε_i'] = σ² [i = i']`, then
`𝔼[(β̂_j - (R β)_j)(β̂_k - (R β)_k)] = σ² / N · R_jk`.

This theorem deliberately assumes neither that `P` is a probability measure nor that the noise
has mean zero, so its conclusion is not by itself a covariance or a Gaussian likelihood. With a
probability measure and mean-zero noise, `integral_marginalEffect` identifies `R β` as the mean,
and this raw second moment is the corresponding covariance.

articles.title: The mean of the marginal estimates
articles.statement:
**The mean of the marginal estimates** (Zhu and Stephens 2017): for fixed effects `β` and
noise with mean zero, `𝔼[X_jᵀ y / N] = (R β)_j` with `R = Xᵀ X / N` (`ldCorr`).

articles.title: The MME solution is the GLS estimate and the BLUP
articles.statement:
**The MME solution is the GLS estimate and the BLUP** (Henderson 1975): if moreover
`Xᵀ V⁻¹ X` is invertible, the mixed-model equations have the unique solution
`b̂ = (Xᵀ V⁻¹ X)⁻¹ Xᵀ V⁻¹ y` (the GLS estimate) and `û = G Zᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X b̂)`.

articles.title: Henderson's mixed-model equations
articles.statement:
**Henderson's mixed-model equations** (Henderson 1975; Robinson 1991): for positive definite
`G` and `R` and `V = Z G Zᵀ + R`, `(b, u)` solves the mixed-model equations if and only if `b`
solves the generalized least-squares normal equations `Xᵀ V⁻¹ X b = Xᵀ V⁻¹ y` and
`u = G Zᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X b)`.

articles.title: Solution of Henderson's mixed-model equations
articles.statement:
Henderson's mixed-model equations for `y = X b + Z u + e`, `Cov u = G`, `Cov e = R`:
`[Xᵀ R⁻¹ X, Xᵀ R⁻¹ Z; Zᵀ R⁻¹ X, Zᵀ R⁻¹ Z + G⁻¹] [b; u] = [Xᵀ R⁻¹ y; Zᵀ R⁻¹ y]`.

articles.title: Marginal association estimate of a marker
articles.statement:
The `N`-normalized marginal association estimate `β̂_j = X_jᵀ y / N` of marker `j` for the
phenotype `y = X β + ε` (fixed effects `β`, noise `ε`).

articles.title: Phenotypic covariance of a linear mixed model
articles.statement:
The phenotypic covariance `V = Z G Zᵀ + R` of the linear mixed model
`y = X b + Z u + e` with `Cov u = G`, `Cov e = R`.

articles.title: Positive definiteness of the phenotypic covariance
articles.statement: `V = Z G Zᵀ + R` is positive definite.

articles.title: Ancestral paths from an individual
articles.statement:
The ancestral paths from `i`: the lists `[i = v₀, v₁, …, v_k]` with each `v_{t+1}` a parent
of `v_t` (`k ≥ 0`; the path `[i]` has no edge).

articles.title: Gene-dropping outcome
articles.statement:
A gene-dropping outcome: `ω i k` is the Mendelian coin of the copy `(i, k)` (`k = 0` the
paternal copy, `k = 1` the maternal copy), saying which copy (`0` or `1`) of the parent `g k`
of `i` it inherits. Under gene dropping all `4 ^ n` outcomes are equally likely.

articles.title: An ancestral path returning to its start is trivial
articles.statement: A path from `i` ending at `i` is `[i]`.

articles.title: Ancestral path as its start followed by a tail
articles.statement: Every ancestral path from `i` starts with `i`.

articles.title: Symmetry of gene-dropping kinship
articles.statement: Gene-dropping kinship is symmetric.

articles.title: Malécot's recursion computes gene-dropping kinship
articles.statement:
The kinship coefficient computed by Malécot's recursion is the probability of identity by
descent under gene dropping.

articles.title: Zero kinship with an unrelated founder
articles.statement: A founder `j ≠ i` that is not an ancestor of `i` has kinship `0` with `i`.

articles.title: Malécot's recursion
articles.statement:
**Malécot's recursion** under gene dropping: if `j ≠ i` is not an ancestor of `i` and has
parents `f, m`, then `φ i j = (φ i f + φ i m) / 2`.

articles.title: Self-kinship under gene dropping
articles.statement: `φ i i = (1 + F i) / 2` under gene dropping.

articles.title: Kinship coefficient under gene dropping
articles.statement:
The kinship (coancestry) coefficient under gene dropping: the probability that a copy drawn
at random from `i` and a copy drawn at random from `j` are identical by descent.

articles.title: Ancestral paths are nonempty with the starting individual as head
articles.statement: Every path in `ancPaths i` starts at `i` and is nonempty.

articles.title: Symmetry of identity by descent
articles.statement: Identity by descent is symmetric.

articles.title: Malécot's recursion step for identity by descent
articles.statement: One step of Malécot's recursion for identity by descent.

articles.title: A gene copy is identical by descent with itself
articles.statement: Two copies are identical by descent of themselves with probability `1`.

articles.title: Probability of identity by descent under gene dropping
articles.statement:
The probability, under gene dropping (independent fair Mendelian coins), that the gene
copies `c` and `d` are identical by descent, i.e. descend from the same founder copy.

articles.title: Malécot's recursion computes the inbreeding coefficient
articles.statement:
The inbreeding coefficient computed by Malécot's recursion is the probability of identity
by descent of the two copies of `i` under gene dropping.

articles.title: Wright's path formula
articles.statement:
**Wright's path formula** for the inbreeding coefficient (Wright 1922): if `i` has parents
`f = g 0` and `m = g 1`, then `F_i = Σ (1/2) ^ (n₁ + n₂ + 1) (1 + F_A)` over common ancestors `A`
of `f` and `m` (including `f` or `m` themselves) and pairs of ancestral paths from `f` and `m`
to `A` (with `n₁` and `n₂` edges) that share only `A`. Here `F` is the gene-dropping inbreeding
coefficient.

articles.title: Founders are not inbred
articles.statement: The inbreeding coefficient of a founder is `0`.

articles.title: Malécot
articles.statement:
The inbreeding coefficient of `i` is the kinship of its parents,
`F i = φ f m`, under gene dropping.

articles.title: Inbreeding coefficient under gene dropping
articles.statement:
The inbreeding coefficient under gene dropping: the probability that the two copies of `i`
are identical by descent.

articles.title: Parents are ancestors
articles.statement: A parent is an ancestor.

articles.title: Ancestor relation in a pedigree
articles.statement: `a` is an ancestor of `b` (a parent, a parent of a parent, …).

articles.title: Parent relation in a pedigree
articles.statement: `a` is a parent of `b`.

articles.title: Symmetry of tabular kinship
articles.statement: The tabular kinship is symmetric.

articles.title: Wright's path formula
articles.statement:
**Wright's path formula** in kinship form: `φ i j` is the sum, over common ancestors `A`
(including `i` or `j` themselves) and pairs of ancestral paths `p` from `i` to `A` and `p'` from
`j` to `A` that share no individual other than `A`, of `(1/2) ^ (n₁ + n₂ + 1) * (1 + F A)`,
where `n₁ + n₂ + 1 = p.length + p'.length - 1` is the number of individuals on the loop.

articles.title: Inbreeding coefficient by Malécot's recursion
articles.statement:
The inbreeding coefficient by Malécot's recursion: `F i = φ f m` for the parents `f, m` of
`i`, and `F i = 0` for a founder.

articles.title: Tabular kinship when the first individual is a later founder
articles.statement: The tabular recursion for `j < i` with `i` a founder.

articles.title: Tabular kinship when the first individual is a later non-founder
articles.statement: The tabular recursion for `j < i` with `i` a non-founder.

articles.title: Tabular kinship when the second individual is a later founder
articles.statement: The tabular recursion for `i < j` with `j` a founder.

articles.title: Tabular kinship when the second individual is a later non-founder
articles.statement: The tabular recursion for `i < j` with `j` a non-founder.

articles.title: Tabular self-kinship of a founder
articles.statement: The tabular recursion on the diagonal for a founder: `φ i i = 1 / 2`.

articles.title: Tabular self-kinship of a non-founder
articles.statement: The tabular recursion on the diagonal for a non-founder: `φ i i = (1 + φ f m) / 2`.

articles.title: Kinship coefficient by Malécot's recursion
articles.statement:
The kinship coefficient by Malécot's recursion, computed in the order of the numbering
(the tabular method): for `i < j`, `φ i j = (φ i f + φ i m) / 2` with `f, m` the parents of `j`
and `φ i j = 0` if `j` is a founder; `φ i i = (1 + φ f m) / 2` with `f, m` the parents of `i`
and `φ i i = 1 / 2` for a founder; symmetric for `j < i`.

articles.title: Individuals on an ancestral path are its start or precede it
articles.statement: Every individual on an ancestral path from `i` is `i` or precedes it.

articles.title: Ancestors precede their descendants
articles.statement: Ancestors precede their descendants.

articles.title: Ancestral paths from a founder
articles.statement: The only ancestral path from a founder is `[i]`.

articles.title: Ancestral paths from a non-founder
articles.statement: The ancestral paths from a non-founder: `[i]` and `i :: q` for a path `q` from a parent.

articles.title: Pedigree without selfing
articles.statement:
No individual is the offspring of a selfing (father ≠ mother), as in Wright's setting of a
bisexual population.

articles.title: A founder gene copy is its own origin
articles.statement: A founder copy is its own origin.

articles.title: Origin of a gene copy of a non-founder
articles.statement: A copy of a non-founder descends from the chosen copy of the corresponding parent.

articles.title: Founder origin of a gene copy
articles.statement:
The founder copy from which the gene copy `c = (i, k)` descends under the gene-dropping
outcome `ω`: a founder copy is its own origin; a copy of a non-founder descends from the copy
`ω i k` of its parent `g k`.

articles.title: Ancestral paths ending at a given ancestor
articles.statement: The ancestral paths from `i` that end at `A`.

articles.title: Pedigree
articles.statement:
A pedigree on the individuals `Fin n`, numbered so that parents precede their children
(every finite pedigree, a finite DAG, has such a numbering). `parents i = some g` means that
`g 0` is the father and `g 1` the mother of `i`; `parents i = none` means that `i` is a founder.
Founders are unrelated and not inbred (their `2 n_F` gene copies are distinct).

articles.title: Trivial ancestral path
articles.statement: `[i]` is an ancestral path from `i`.

articles.title: Cardinality of a sorted prefix
articles.statement: A prefix of length `k ≤ card ι` has `k` elements.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of categorical configuration priors
articles.statement: Categorical configuration priors are non-negative.

articles.title: Normalized categorical colocalization prior
articles.statement: A normalized categorical prior, distinct from the cited coloc relative weights.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of configuration Bayes factors
articles.statement: A configuration Bayes factor is non-negative when both traits' Bayes factors are.

articles.title: Bayes factor of a colocalization configuration
articles.statement:
The Bayes factor of a configuration against the null: the product of the two traits' Bayes
factors, `1` for a trait without a causal variant (the two studies are independent).

articles.title: Closed-form scores for the categorical colocalization prior
articles.statement:
Closed forms for the optional normalized categorical-prior model. This differs from the cited
coloc formula only in using its remaining null mass rather than the cited H0 weight `1`.

articles.title: Posterior identity for the categorical colocalization prior
articles.statement: The normalized posterior identity for the separate categorical-prior model.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of closed-form colocalization scores
articles.statement: Cited coloc closed-form scores are non-negative on the Bayes-factor domain.

articles.title: Closed-form colocalization hypothesis scores
articles.statement:
The cited coloc closed-form algebraic scores. H0 has score `1`; H1--H4 retain the
per-configuration coefficients of Giambartolomei et al. (2014). They are unnormalized hypothesis
weights, and hence have a probability interpretation, when the Bayes factors are non-negative.

articles.title: Positivity of colocalization evidence
articles.statement:
Cited coloc evidence is strictly positive for non-negative Bayes factors because H0 has
unnormalized weight `1`.

articles.title: Colocalization hypothesis of a causal configuration
articles.statement:
The hypothesis of a configuration `(causal variant of trait 1, causal variant of trait 2)`,
`none` meaning no causal variant.

articles.title: The five colocalization hypotheses
articles.statement:
The five coloc hypotheses: no association (`h0`), trait 1 only (`h1`), trait 2 only (`h2`),
two distinct causal variants (`h3`), one shared causal variant (`h4`).

articles.title: Colocalization normalization identity
articles.statement:
The unconditional algebraic coloc normalization identity: each hypothesis's configuration
score divided by the total score equals its closed-form score divided by the closed-form total.
For arbitrary real `bf1` and `bf2` these ratios need not be probabilities. See
`colocPosterior_nonneg` and `sum_colocPosterior_eq_one` for the probability-domain results.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of colocalization posteriors
articles.statement: Normalized cited coloc hypothesis weights are non-negative for non-negative Bayes factors.

articles.title: Colocalization prior parameters
articles.statement:
Non-negative coloc configuration-weight parameters (Giambartolomei et al. 2014): `p1`, `p2`,
`p12` for a variant causal for trait 1 only, trait 2 only, and both. The cited hypothesis weights
use null weight `1`. The bound also supports a separate normalized categorical-prior model.

articles.title: The effect posterior of the single-effect regression
articles.statement:
**The effect posterior of the single-effect regression** (Wang et al. 2020): given
`y = x β + e` with `β ~ N(0, σ₀²)` independent of `e ~ N(0, σ² I)`, for almost every `y` the
effect is normal with mean `σ₀² / (σ₀² + s²) · β̂` and variance `σ₀² s² / (σ₀² + s²)`, where
`β̂ = olsEffect x y` and `s² = olsVar σ2 x`.

articles.title: Positivity of the prior-weighted marginal likelihood
articles.statement: Strictly positive evidence has a strictly positive prior-weighted marginal likelihood.

articles.title: A minimum-size credible set exists and is a sorted prefix
articles.statement:
If the total mass is at least
`ρ`, some prefix of length `k` is `ρ`-credible, has `k` elements, and every `ρ`-credible set has
at least `k` elements.

articles.title: A normalized prior gives some variant positive weight
articles.statement: A normalized non-negative finite prior assigns positive weight to some variant.

articles.title: Wakefield's Bayes factor as a density ratio of Gaussians
articles.statement:
The alternative marginal `N(0, V + W)` has density `wakefieldABF V W` with respect to the null
law `N(0, V)`.

articles.title: Credible set of variants
articles.statement: A `ρ`-credible set: its total posterior inclusion probability is at least `ρ`.

articles.title: The shortest credible prefix has minimum size
articles.statement:
**The shortest credible prefix has minimum size** (Maller et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2020): if
`σ` sorts `α` in decreasing order and no prefix shorter than `k` is `ρ`-credible, every
`ρ`-credible set has at least `k` elements.

articles.title: The marginal law of the phenotype given the causal variant
articles.statement:
If `y = x β + e` with
`β ~ N(0, σ₀²)` independent of `e ~ N(0, σ² I)`, then `y` has density
`multivariateGaussianPDFReal 0 (serCov σ2 σ02 x)`.

articles.title: The regression Bayes factor is the Wakefield ABF
articles.statement:
**The regression Bayes factor is the Wakefield ABF** (Wang et al. 2020): the
density of `y` when variant `x` carries an `N(0, σ₀²)` effect, divided by its density with no
effect, is the ABF of the summary statistics `olsEffect x y` and `olsVar σ2 x`.

articles.title: Normalized weighted evidence
articles.statement:
Algebraic normalization of arbitrary weights times evidence. This is useful even outside the
probability domain; it takes Lean's value `0` when the denominator vanishes.

articles.title: Marginal least-squares effect estimate
articles.statement:
The marginal least-squares effect estimate `xᵀ y / xᵀ x` of a variant with genotype vector
`x`.

articles.title: Sampling variance of the least-squares effect estimate
articles.statement: The sampling variance `σ² / xᵀ x` of `olsEffect x y` for residual variance `σ²`.

articles.title: Null mass of the categorical colocalization prior
articles.statement: The remaining null mass in the optional normalized categorical-prior model.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of posterior inclusion probabilities
articles.statement: Posterior inclusion probabilities are non-negative when every evidence value is positive.

articles.title: Posterior inclusion probability
articles.statement:
Posterior inclusion probability from a normalized non-negative prior and variant evidence.
When every evidence value is positive, `PriorWeights.evidence_pos` makes the denominator strictly
positive, and `pip_nonneg` and `sum_pip` prove that these values form a probability distribution.

articles.title: Single-effect regression covariance is positive definite
articles.statement: `serCov σ2 σ02 x` is positive definite for `σ² > 0`.

articles.title: Prior weights over the causal variant
articles.statement: A finite probability distribution used as the prior over the single causal variant.

articles.title: The ABF is the Bayes factor
articles.statement:
If `β ~ N(0, W)` and the sampling error `ε ~ N(0, V)` are
independent, the law of the estimate `β + ε` (alternative) has density `wakefieldABF V W` with
respect to the law of `ε` (null).

articles.title: Covariance of the single-effect regression model
articles.statement:
The covariance `σ₀² x xᵀ + σ² I` of `y = x β + e` for `β ~ N(0, σ₀²)` and
`e ~ N(0, σ² I)`.

articles.title: Single-effect likelihood-ratio identity
articles.statement:
The unconditional algebraic single-effect likelihood-ratio identity for arbitrary real
weights. Its right side is accurately named algebraic normalization, not a posterior probability.

articles.title: Posterior inclusion probabilities of the single-effect regression
articles.statement:
**Posterior inclusion probabilities of the single-effect regression** (Wang et al. 2020):
Bayes' rule for the causal variant with a normalized non-negative prior equals `pip` applied to
the strictly positive Wakefield ABFs.

articles.title: Positivity of the single-effect regression evidence
articles.statement: The prior-weighted single-effect evidence is strictly positive on the regression domain.

articles.title: Prefix of variants in a given order
articles.statement: The first `k` variants in the order `σ`.

articles.title: Categorical-prior hypothesis scores equal their closed forms
articles.statement: The corresponding closed forms for the optional normalized categorical-prior model.

articles.title: Categorical colocalization priors sum to one
articles.statement: The optional categorical configuration priors sum to one.

articles.title: Colocalization posteriors sum to one
articles.statement: Normalized cited coloc hypothesis weights sum to one for non-negative Bayes factors.

articles.title: The coloc closed forms
articles.statement:
**The coloc closed forms** (Giambartolomei et al. 2014): the sum of unnormalized configuration
weight times Bayes factor over each hypothesis equals its closed form.

articles.title: Sorted prefix carries the most posterior mass
articles.statement:
The `k` largest values carry the most mass: if `σ` sorts `α` in decreasing order, no set of
`S.card` variants has more mass than the prefix of that length.

articles.title: Posterior inclusion probabilities sum to one
articles.statement: Posterior inclusion probabilities normalize to one when every evidence value is positive.

articles.title: Wakefield's closed form
articles.statement:
With `z = b / √V`,
`ABF = √(V / (V + W)) · exp (z² W / (2 (V + W)))`.

articles.title: Positivity of Wakefield's approximate Bayes factor
articles.statement: Wakefield's ABF is strictly positive on its sampling-variance domain.

articles.title: Wakefield's approximate Bayes factor
articles.statement:
Wakefield's approximate Bayes factor: the `N(0, V + W)` density of the estimate `b` (its
marginal law under the alternative `β ~ N(0, W)`) divided by its `N(0, V)` density (the null
`β = 0`). Wakefield (2009) reports the reciprocal, null over alternative; coloc and SuSiE use
this orientation, in which large values favor association. For `V = 0` the null density is
Mathlib's junk value `0` and so is the ratio; the theorems assume `V ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of colocalization configuration weights
articles.statement: Cited coloc configuration weights are non-negative.

articles.title: Unnormalized colocalization configuration weight
articles.statement: The cited coloc unnormalized configuration weight, whose H0 weight is `1`.

articles.title: Best linear unbiased predictor of genetic effects
articles.statement:
The BLUP `ĝ = G V⁻¹ (y - X β̂)` of the genetic effects, with `G = σ_g² K`
(Henderson 1975).

articles.title: Coordinate ascent along an update schedule
articles.statement: Coordinate ascent along the update schedule `s`: at time `t` factor `s t` is updated.

articles.title: One coordinate-ascent step
articles.statement: One coordinate-ascent step: replace factor `j` by its CAVI update.

articles.title: Coordinate-ascent update of one variational factor
articles.statement:
The CAVI update of factor `j`: the prior tilted by the potential,
`qⱼ ∝ π · exp fⱼ = exp 𝔼_{q_{-j}}[log p(y, β)]`.

articles.title: Squared norm of a genotype column
articles.statement: The squared norm `‖xⱼ‖² = ∑ᵢ X i j ²` of the genotype column of SNP `j`.

articles.title: Coordinate ascent does not decrease the ELBO
articles.statement: **Coordinate ascent does not decrease the ELBO.**

articles.title: The CAVI update maximizes the ELBO over its factor, with exact gap
articles.statement:
Replacing factor
`j` by an admissible `q'` gives `ELBO(caviStep q j) - KL(q' ‖ caviUpdate q j)`.

articles.title: Mean-field evidence lower bound
articles.statement:
The mean-field evidence lower bound
`-(n/2) log (2π σ_e²) - 𝔼_q ‖y - X β‖² / (2 σ_e²) - ∑ⱼ KL(qⱼ ‖ π)`, meaningful for `σ_e² > 0`.
It is the ELBO for admissible factors (finite KL); for an inadmissible factor `toReal` would turn
an infinite divergence into `0`, so all results assume admissibility.

articles.title: The ELBO as a function of one factor
articles.statement:
With the other factors fixed, the ELBO of
`q` with factor `j` replaced by an admissible `q'` is `∫ fⱼ dq' - KL(q' ‖ π) + C`.

articles.title: Expected residual sum of squares under the variational factors
articles.statement:
The expected residual sum of squares `‖y - X μ‖² + ∑ⱼ ‖xⱼ‖² vⱼ` of the product of the
factors `q`, with means `μⱼ` and variances `vⱼ` (`integral_rss_pi`).

articles.title: Generalized least-squares estimator
articles.statement: The generalized least-squares estimator `β̂ = (Xᵀ V⁻¹ X)⁻¹ Xᵀ V⁻¹ y`.

articles.title: The score of a SNP effect
articles.statement: **The score of a SNP effect** at `γ = 0` is `xᵀ P y`.

articles.title: Information of a SNP outside the column space of $X$ is positive
articles.statement: The information `xᵀ P x` is positive when the SNP `x` is not in the column space of `X`.

articles.title: Mixture prior has finite second moment
articles.statement: The mixture prior has a finite second moment.

articles.title: The expected residual sum of squares of a product of factors
articles.statement:
For probability factors
with finite second moments, `𝔼_{∏ qⱼ} ‖y - X β‖² = ‖y - X μ‖² + ∑ⱼ ‖xⱼ‖² vⱼ`.

articles.title: Coordinate-ascent update is an admissible factor
articles.statement:
The CAVI update is an admissible factor, for a probability prior with a finite second
moment.

articles.title: Admissible variational factor
articles.statement:
An admissible variational factor for the prior `π`: a probability measure with a finite
second moment and finite KL divergence from `π` (`q ≪ π` with integrable log-likelihood
ratio).

articles.title: Stationary points of coordinate ascent
articles.statement:
No admissible change of factor `j` increases
the ELBO iff `qⱼ` is the expected-log-joint update `π · exp fⱼ / Z`.

articles.title: Henderson's mixed-model equations give the GLS estimator and the BLUP
articles.statement:
For positive
definite `K`, `σ_g² > 0` and `X` of full column rank, `(β, g)` solves the mixed-model equations
iff `β = β̂` and `g = σ_g² K V⁻¹ (y - X β̂)`. This is the specialization of
`MixedModel.isMMESolution_iff_gls` to `Z = 1`, `G = σ_g² K`, `R = σ_e² I`; the generic
theorem gives `β = glsMatrix X V *ᵥ y` and `g = G V⁻¹ (y - X β̂)`, which are `Model.gls`
and `Model.blup` by the two conversion lemmas below.

articles.title: Solution of Henderson's mixed-model equations
articles.statement:
`(β, g)` solves Henderson's mixed-model equations with `R = σ_e² I` and `G = σ_g² K`,
i.e. the specialization of `MixedModel.IsMMESolution` to `Z = 1` (every individual has its
own genetic effect), `G = σ_g² K`, `R = σ_e² I`. In unfolded form this is
`Xᵀ R⁻¹ X β + Xᵀ R⁻¹ g = Xᵀ R⁻¹ y` and `R⁻¹ X β + (R⁻¹ + G⁻¹) g = R⁻¹ y`. The equations
are meaningful when `G` is invertible (`isMMESolution_iff`); otherwise `G⁻¹` is Lean's
junk inverse `0`.

articles.title: Mixture prior is a probability measure
articles.statement: The mixture prior is a probability measure for a mixing weight `p ≤ 1`.

articles.title: The GLS maximizer is unique
articles.statement:
For `X` of full column rank, `X β` attains the maximal
marginal log-likelihood only at `β = β̂`.

articles.title: Maximal marginal log-likelihood
articles.statement: The maximal marginal log-likelihood is `-(n log 2π + log det V + yᵀ P y) / 2`.

articles.title: GLS maximizes the marginal likelihood
articles.statement:
For `X` of full column rank, every mean `X β`
has marginal log-likelihood at most that of the GLS fit `X β̂`.

articles.title: Marginal log-likelihood of the mean
articles.statement:
The marginal log-likelihood of the mean `μ`: the log of the `N(μ, V)` density at `y`,
`-(n log 2π + log det V + (y - μ)ᵀ V⁻¹ (y - μ)) / 2` (`det V > 0` by `posDef_V`).

articles.title: Mean of a variational factor
articles.statement: The mean `∫ b dq` of a factor.

articles.title: Two-Gaussian mixture prior on a SNP effect
articles.statement:
The BOLT-LMM prior on a SNP effect: the mixture `p N(0, v₁) + (1 - p) N(0, v₂)` of two
centered Gaussians with variances `v₁, v₂` (`v₂ = 0` gives the spike-and-slab prior with a point
mass at `0`).

articles.title: Variance components of the linear mixed model
articles.statement:
The variance components of the linear mixed model `y = X β + g + e` with
`g ~ N(0, σ_g² K)` and `e ~ N(0, σ_e² I)` on `n` individuals: a positive semidefinite genetic
relationship matrix `K`, a genetic variance `σ_g² ≥ 0` and an environmental variance
`σ_e² > 0`.

articles.title: The ELBO is nondecreasing along coordinate ascent
articles.statement: **The ELBO is nondecreasing along coordinate ascent**, for any update schedule.

articles.title: Partial residual of a SNP
articles.statement: The partial residual `rⱼ = y - ∑_{k ≠ j} xₖ μₖ` of the other SNPs' posterior means.

articles.title: Positive definiteness of the phenotypic covariance
articles.statement: `V = σ_g² K + σ_e² I` is positive definite.

articles.title: Coordinate-ascent potential for one SNP effect
articles.statement:
The CAVI potential `fⱼ(b) = (b xⱼᵀ rⱼ - ‖xⱼ‖² b² / 2) / σ_e²`: the part of the expected
log-likelihood `𝔼_{q_{-j}}[log p(y | β)]` that depends on `βⱼ = b`
(`exists_elbo_update_eq`).

articles.title: The profile log-likelihood of a SNP effect is an exact quadratic
articles.statement:
`ℓ(γ) = ℓ(0) + γ xᵀ P y - γ² xᵀ P x / 2`, so its score at `γ = 0` is `xᵀ P y` and its
information is `xᵀ P x`.

articles.title: Profile log-likelihood of a SNP effect
articles.statement:
The profile marginal log-likelihood of a SNP effect `γ` for the SNP genotype vector `x`:
`sup_β logLik y (X β + γ x)`.

articles.title: Identity $PVP = P$ for the residual-forming matrix
articles.statement:
`P V P = P`. With `P X = 0`, this says that under the null model `y = X β + ε` with
`Cov ε = V` the score `xᵀ P y = xᵀ P ε` has variance `xᵀ P V P x = xᵀ P x`.

articles.title: Residual-forming matrix annihilates the fixed effects
articles.statement: `P X = 0`: the residual-forming matrix annihilates the fixed effects.

articles.title: Residual-forming matrix
articles.statement: The residual-forming matrix `P = V⁻¹ - V⁻¹ X (Xᵀ V⁻¹ X)⁻¹ Xᵀ V⁻¹`.

articles.title: Score at the null generalized least-squares fit
articles.statement: The score is evaluated at the null GLS fit: `xᵀ P y = xᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X β̂)`.

articles.title: Score statistic for one SNP
articles.statement:
The score statistic `(xᵀ P y)² / (xᵀ P x)` for one SNP `x`. Its denominator is positive
when `x` is not in the column space of `X` (`info_pos`); otherwise the statistic is `0` by
the convention `a / 0 = 0` and carries no information.

articles.title: Marginal phenotypic covariance matrix
articles.statement: The marginal phenotypic covariance `V = σ_g² K + σ_e² I` of `y = X β + g + e`.

articles.title: pLI is antitone in the observed count
articles.statement:
The posterior of a class `c₀` whose rate is the
smallest is antitone in `o`, for every prior.

articles.title: Class posterior is strictly antitone in the observed count
articles.statement: Strictly antitone when some class has a strictly larger rate.

articles.title: Posterior class probability in the Poisson mixture
articles.statement:
The posterior probability of class `c` for a gene with `o` observed and `E` expected LoF
variants, in the Poisson mixture with prior weights `w` and class rates `rate`:
`w_c P(o | rate_c E) / ∑_{c'} w_{c'} P(o | rate_{c'} E)`. pLI is this at the class with the smallest
rate.

articles.title: The M-step maximizes `Q(· | w)`
articles.statement: **The M-step maximizes `Q(· | w)`** over admissible weights.

articles.title: EM update of the Poisson mixture class weights
articles.statement: The EM update `w'_z = (1/N) ∑_n P_w(z | o_n)`, for `N > 0` genes and positive rates.

articles.title: Flat-prior posterior of `γ`
articles.statement:
The likelihood `γ ↦ P(o | Poisson(γ E))` times `E` is the
Gamma density of shape `o + 1` and rate `E`. For `E > 0` that density integrates to one, so `E`
is the normalizing constant of the flat-prior posterior (the identity itself is algebraic and
holds for every real `E`).

articles.title: The flat-prior posterior quantile is Garwood's bound
articles.statement:
The Gamma(`o + 1`, `E`) posterior
puts mass exactly `1 - α` below `oeUpper α E o`.

articles.title: Loss-of-function count data for a gene
articles.statement: A gene's data: observed LoF count `o` and positive expected count `E`.

articles.title: Positivity of the Poisson mixture joint likelihood
articles.statement: The joint likelihood is positive for positive rates.

articles.title: Joint likelihood of gene data and constraint class
articles.statement: The joint likelihood of a gene's data and class `z`: `w_z P(o | rate_z E)`.

articles.title: LOEUF of a gene with no observed LoF variants
articles.statement: **LOEUF of a gene with no observed LoF variants** is `log 20 / E`.

articles.title: LOEUF
articles.statement: The upper end of the 90% interval, `oeUpper (1/20)`.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the log-likelihood along the class-weight EM iterates
articles.statement: The log-likelihood is monotone along the EM iterates.

articles.title: EM does not decrease the likelihood
articles.statement: **EM does not decrease the likelihood** of the class weights.

articles.title: Positivity of the class masses
articles.statement: The class masses are positive when there is at least one gene.

articles.title: Expected number of genes in a constraint class
articles.statement:
The expected number of genes in class `z` under the posteriors at weights `w`:
`∑_n P_w(z | o_n)`.

articles.title: Exact coverage
articles.statement:
For every true ratio `γ ≥ 0` and `E > 0`, when `o ~ Poisson(γ E)`,
`P(γ ≤ oeUpper α E o) ≥ 1 - α`.

articles.title: Observed/expected upper bound decreases with the expected count
articles.statement: The bound is strictly decreasing in the expected count `E > 0`.

articles.title: Observed/expected upper bound increases with the observed count
articles.statement: The bound is strictly increasing in the observed count.

articles.title: Observed/expected upper bound with no observed variants
articles.statement: With no observed variants the bound is `log (1 / α) / E`.

articles.title: Upper confidence bound for the observed/expected ratio
articles.statement:
The upper confidence bound for the observed/expected ratio at level `α`:
`u_α(o) / E`, with `u_α` Garwood's bound for the Poisson mean.

articles.title: Positivity of the Poisson likelihood
articles.statement: The likelihood is positive at a positive mean.

articles.title: Recursion for the Poisson likelihood
articles.statement: The likelihood recursion `P(o + 1 | μ) = P(o | μ) μ / (o + 1)`.

articles.title: Poisson likelihood of an observed count
articles.statement: The Poisson likelihood `e^{-μ} μ^o / (o!)` of an observed count `o` at mean `μ`.

articles.title: Strictly positive class weights summing to one
articles.statement: Strictly positive class weights summing to one.

articles.title: Class posteriors sum to one
articles.statement: The class posteriors sum to one.

articles.title: Class masses sum to the number of genes
articles.statement: The class masses add up to the number of genes.

articles.title: Daetwyler–Dudbridge formula
articles.statement:
With sampling variance `s² = 1 / N`,
`r²_g = N h² / (N h² + M)`.

articles.title: Polygenic-score accuracy
articles.statement:
**Polygenic-score accuracy** as a ratio of expectations: `r²_g = h² / (h² + M s²)`. (If
`h² = 0` both sides are `0`.)

articles.title: Polygenic-score accuracy in the LD-score model
articles.statement:
With orthogonal standardized training
columns, `β̂ = Xᵀ y / N` and residual variance `1 - h²`,
`r²_g = N h² / (N h² + M (1 - h²))`. The cited `N h² / (N h² + M)` takes the residual variance to
be `1`.

articles.title: Squared accuracy of a polygenic score
articles.statement:
The squared correlation of the genetic value and the polygenic score as a ratio of
expectations, `𝔼[βᵀβ̂]² / (𝔼[βᵀβ] 𝔼[β̂ᵀβ̂])`: by `integral_score_mul_score`, `βᵀβ̂`, `βᵀβ` and
`β̂ᵀβ̂` are the covariance and variances of `xᵀβ` and `xᵀβ̂` over a target population of
standardized uncorrelated markers. It is not the expectation of a squared correlation.

articles.title: Pooled allele frequency
articles.statement: The pooled frequency `p = ∑ i n_i / (2 N)` of the counted allele.

articles.title: The allelic test equals the trend test iff the pooled sample is in Hardy–Weinberg proportions
articles.statement:
**The allelic test equals the trend test iff the pooled sample is in Hardy–Weinberg
proportions** (`n₁² = 4 n₀ n₂`; Sasieni 1997), whenever the trend numerator is nonzero.

articles.title: Allelic versus trend test
articles.statement:
**Allelic versus trend test** (Sasieni 1997): with cases and controls present, a pooled
allele frequency strictly between `0` and `1` and a positive score variance,
`allelic · 2 p q = trend · Var`.

articles.title: Allelic test statistic
articles.statement:
The **allelic test**: Pearson's statistic of the `2 × 2` table of case and control allele
counts (`2N` alleles).

articles.title: Normalized score in the stratified LD-score model
articles.statement: The `N`-normalized score `β̂ j = X_jᵀ y / N`.

articles.title: Estimated marker effects
articles.statement: The estimated effects `β̂ = β + e`.

articles.title: Association statistic in the stratified LD-score model
articles.statement: The association statistic `χ² j = N β̂ j ²`.

articles.title: Joint estimate equals marginal estimates for uncorrelated markers
articles.statement:
For markers uncorrelated in the sample (`XᵀX` diagonal) without zero columns, the joint
estimate is the vector of marginal estimates.

articles.title: COJO joint estimate
articles.statement:
**COJO joint estimate** (Yang et al. 2012, eq. (5)): the joint least-squares estimate
`(XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ y` equals `(XᵀX)⁻¹ D β̂` in terms of the marginal estimates `β̂`, so it can be
computed from summary statistics and `XᵀX`. (Stated for every `X`; it is the least-squares
estimate when `XᵀX` is invertible.)

articles.title: Conditional estimate as a fit to the first-block residual
articles.statement:
Unconditionally, the conditional formula equals the nonsingular-inverse formula applied to
the algebraic residual `y - X₁ ((X₁ᵀX₁)⁻¹ X₁ᵀ y)`. If both Gram determinants are units, these
are the successive least-squares fits on blocks 1 and 2. With a singular Gram matrix they need
not minimize residual error. This is in general not the block-2 part of the joint formula on
both blocks (the formulas agree when `X₂ᵀX₁ = 0`).

articles.title: COJO conditional algebraic formula from summary statistics
articles.statement:
**COJO conditional algebraic formula from summary statistics** (Yang et al. 2012, eq. (17)):
`b̂₂|b̂₁ = (X₂ᵀX₂)⁻¹ D₂ β̂₂ - (X₂ᵀX₂)⁻¹ X₂ᵀX₁ (X₁ᵀX₁)⁻¹ D₁ β̂₁`.

articles.title: Conditional estimate of second-block effects (COJO)
articles.statement:
The unconditional algebraic formula from Yang et al. 2012, eq. (15):
`(X₂ᵀX₂)⁻¹ X₂ᵀ y - (X₂ᵀX₂)⁻¹ X₂ᵀX₁ (X₁ᵀX₁)⁻¹ X₁ᵀ y`. When both Gram determinants are units,
this has the usual interpretation as the block-2 fit conditional on the block-1 fit. For a
singular Gram matrix, Mathlib's nonsingular inverse is zero and the value can be a junk value.

articles.title: Squared correlation of case status and genotype score
articles.statement:
The squared sample correlation of case status (`1` for cases, `0` for controls) and the
genotype score over the `N` individuals of the table.

articles.title: Bivariate LD-score model
articles.statement:
The bivariate LD-score model (Bulik-Sullivan et al. 2015b), at the level of the cross
second moments that enter `𝔼[z₁ z₂]`: a pool of `n` genotyped individuals with genotype matrix
`X`, two GWAS samples `S₁`, `S₂` of the pool (possibly overlapping), effects `β₁`, `β₂` with
`∫ β₁ k β₂ l = (ρ_g / M) [k = l]` (genetic covariance `ρ_g`), noises `ε₁`, `ε₂` with
`∫ ε₁ i ε₂ i' = ρ_e [i = i']` (residual cross-moment `ρ_e` within an individual), effects of
each trait orthogonal to the noise of the other. The structure intentionally does not impose
within-trait moments or phenotype normalization, so it does not identify `ρ_e` with phenotypic
correlation or establish that the scaled scores below are standardized z-scores.

articles.title: Diagonal of the genotype Gram matrix
articles.statement: The diagonal `D = diag(XᵀX)` of the Gram matrix.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of heritability in the effect-estimate model
articles.statement: The model forces `h² ≥ 0` when there is at least one marker.

articles.title: Training genotype matrix with orthogonal standardized columns
articles.statement:
The training genotype matrix has orthogonal columns with sum of squares `N`,
`∑ i, X i k * X i l = N [k = l]`; for centered columns this says that the markers are
uncorrelated, with unit sample variance, in the training sample.

articles.title: Expected squared norm of the estimated effects
articles.statement: `𝔼[β̂ᵀβ̂] = h² + M s²` (for at least one marker).

articles.title: Expected cross product of true and estimated effects
articles.statement: `𝔼[βᵀβ̂] = h²` (for at least one marker).

articles.title: Expected squared norm of the true effects
articles.statement: `𝔼[βᵀβ] = h²` (for at least one marker).

articles.title: Stratified LD-score regression
articles.statement:
**Stratified LD-score regression** (Finucane et al. 2015): for a standardized genotype
matrix and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_c τ_c ℓ(j, cat c) + σ²_e`. Full-matrix standardization makes
every normalized cross product in `stratLDScore` a sample correlation.

articles.title: One causal variant
articles.statement:
**One causal variant** (the LD-proxy noncentrality; Pritchard & Przeworski 2001): if the
genotype matrix is standardized and the only category is the single causal marker `c` with
variance `τ`, then for a marker `m` and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² m] = N τ r m c ² + σ²_e`.

articles.title: Expected association statistic in the stratified LD-score model
articles.statement:
The exact expectation of the association statistic in the stratified model, for any
genotype matrix: `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_c τ_c ℓ(j, cat c) + σ²_e (∑ i, X i j ²) / N`.

articles.title: Cross moment of two polygenic scores
articles.statement:
In a target population whose marker genotypes `x j` have raw second moments
`∫ x j * x k = [j = k]` (standardized, uncorrelated markers), the scores `xᵀ a` and `xᵀ b` of two
effect vectors have raw cross moment `aᵀ b`. With mean-zero genotypes and a probability measure
this is the covariance of the genetic value `xᵀ β` and the polygenic score `xᵀ β̂`.

articles.title: Equal normalized-cross-product specialization of the residual cross-moment identity
articles.statement:
If
the two samples have the same normalized cross products with marker `j` and the overlap marker
is standardized at `j`
(`∑_{i ∈ S₁ ∩ S₂} X i j ² = N_s`), then
`𝔼[z₁ j z₂ j] = √(N₁ N₂) ρ_g ℓ_j / M + ρ_e N_s / √(N₁ N₂)`. Here `ρ_e` is only the residual
cross-moment specified by `CrossTraitModel`; this theorem does not state the Bulik-Sullivan
phenotypic-correlation overlap formula or establish z-score normalization.

articles.title: Cross-trait scaled-score identity, exact form
articles.statement:
With `N₁ = |S₁|`, `N₂ = |S₂|`,
`𝔼[z₁ j z₂ j] = √(N₁ N₂) (ρ_g / M) ∑_k r¹ j k r² j k + ρ_e (∑_{i ∈ S₁ ∩ S₂} X i j ²) / √(N₁ N₂)`,
with the in-sample normalized cross products `r¹`, `r²` (`sampleCorr`).

articles.title: Marginal least-squares estimate of a marker effect
articles.statement:
The marginal least-squares estimate `x_jᵀ y / x_jᵀ x_j` of marker `j` (single-marker
regression without intercept, on centered genotypes and phenotype as in Yang et al. 2012).

articles.title: Numerator of the Cochran–Armitage trend statistic
articles.statement: The trend numerator `U = ∑ i, i (r i S - s i R)` with `R = ∑ r`, `S = ∑ s`.

articles.title: Estimates of the derived model are normalized scores
articles.statement: The estimates of `ofLDScore` are the normalized scores `Xᵀ y / N` of the LD-score model.

articles.title: Effect-estimate model derived from the LD-score model
articles.statement:
The effect-estimate model obtained from the LD-score model when the effects are estimated by
the normalized scores `β̂ = Xᵀ y / N` on a training matrix with orthogonal standardized columns:
the error is `e k = ∑ i, X i k ε i / N` and its sampling variance is `(1 - h²) / N`.

articles.title: Pearson's chi-squared statistic of a 2 × 2 table
articles.statement:
Pearson's statistic `n (a d - b c)² / ((a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d))` of a `2 × 2` table
`[[a, b], [c, d]]` with `n = a + b + c + d`.

articles.title: Phenotype in the stratified LD-score model
articles.statement: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.

articles.title: Effect-estimate model for polygenic score accuracy
articles.statement:
The effect-estimate model behind polygenic-score accuracy (Daetwyler et al. 2008;
Dudbridge 2013), at the level of raw second moments, for `M` independent markers: true effects
`beta k` with `∫ β k β l = (h² / M) [k = l]`, estimation errors `err k` with
`∫ e k e l = s² [k = l]`, orthogonal to the effects. The estimates are `β̂ = β + e`
(`betaHat`). For a probability measure and mean-zero effects and errors these are the
covariance conditions of the cited model; `s²` is the sampling variance of each estimate
(`1 / N` in the cited papers, `(1 - h²) / N` in `ofLDScore`).

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the sampling error variance of effect estimates
articles.statement: The model forces `s² ≥ 0` when there is at least one marker.

articles.title: In-sample LD correlation
articles.statement:
The in-sample normalized cross product `∑_{i ∈ S} X i j X i k / |S|` of markers `j`, `k` in
the sample `S` of a pool of individuals (the sample LD correlation for a matrix standardized
within `S`).

articles.title: Departure of the genotype-score variance from Hardy–Weinberg
articles.statement:
The observed score variance minus the Hardy–Weinberg score variance `2 p q`:
`Var - 2 p (1 - p) = (4 n₀ n₂ - n₁²) / (2 N²)`.

articles.title: Pooled genotype-score variance
articles.statement: The pooled genotype-score variance `∑ i² n_i / N - (∑ i n_i / N)²`, `n_i = r i + s i`.

articles.title: Stratified LD score
articles.statement:
The stratified normalized-cross-product score
`ℓ(j, C) = ∑_{k ∈ C} (X_jᵀ X_k / N)²`. For a standardized genotype matrix this is the stratified
LD score of marker `j` with respect to annotation category `C` (Finucane et al. 2015).

articles.title: Stratified LD-score model
articles.statement:
The stratified LD-score model (Finucane et al. 2015), at the level of raw second moments:
annotation categories `cat c ⊆ {markers}` (possibly overlapping), per-category contributions
`tau c`, effects with `∫ β k β l = [k = l] ∑_c τ_c [k ∈ cat c]`, noise with
`∫ ε i ε i' = σ²_e [i = i']`, effects orthogonal to noise. The cited model normalizes the
phenotypic variance so that `σ²_e ≈ 1`; the confounding term `N a` is not modeled.

articles.title: Number of individuals in a case-control genotype table
articles.statement: The number of individuals `N = ∑ (r i + s i)`.

articles.title: Genotype-phenotype cross products from marginal estimates
articles.statement:
`Xᵀ y = D β̂` for the marginal estimates `β̂` (Yang et al. 2012). This holds for every
genotype matrix: a column with `x_jᵀ x_j = 0` is zero, so both sides vanish there.

articles.title: The trend test is `N r²`
articles.statement:
**The trend test is `N r²`** (Armitage 1955): the Cochran–Armitage statistic is `N` times
the squared sample correlation of case status and genotype score. (In degenerate tables, where a
denominator vanishes, both sides are `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.)

articles.title: Cochran–Armitage trend statistic
articles.statement:
The **Cochran–Armitage trend statistic** with scores `0, 1, 2` (Armitage 1955):
`N U² / (R S (N ∑ i² n_i - (∑ i n_i)²))`.

articles.title: Scaled marginal score for the first trait
articles.statement:
The scaled marginal score `z₁ j = √N₁ X_jᵀ y₁ / N₁` of marker `j` for trait 1, computed on
`S₁` with `y₁ = X β₁ + ε₁`. The model does not assert the normalization needed for a z-score.

articles.title: Scaled marginal score for the second trait
articles.statement: The analogous scaled marginal score `z₂ j` of marker `j` for trait 2, computed on `S₂`.

articles.title: Imputed summary statistic
articles.statement: The imputed statistic `ẑ = wᵀ z_o` with weights `w`.

articles.title: Excess error of a linear imputation
articles.statement:
If `Σ_oo w = Σ_ot`, then for any weights `w'`,
`𝔼 (z_t - w'ᵀ z_o)² = 𝔼 (z_t - wᵀ z_o)² + (w' - w)ᵀ Σ_oo (w' - w)`.

articles.title: ImpG is the best linear imputation
articles.statement:
The weights solving `Σ_oo w = Σ_ot` minimize the mean
squared error `𝔼 (z_t - w'ᵀ z_o)²` over all weights `w'`.

articles.title: Mean squared error of imputation with ImpG weights
articles.statement:
For the ImpG weights (`Σ_oo w = Σ_ot`) the mean squared imputation error is
`Σ_tt - wᵀ Σ_ot = Σ_tt - Σ_to Σ_oo⁻¹ Σ_ot`, the linear-prediction residual variance
(the conditional variance only under the Gaussian ImpG model).

articles.title: Mean squared imputation error
articles.statement: The mean squared imputation error: `𝔼 (z_t - ẑ)² = Σ_tt - 2 wᵀ Σ_ot + wᵀ Σ_oo w`.

articles.title: Cross moment of the imputed and untyped statistics
articles.statement: `𝔼 ẑ z_t = wᵀ Σ_ot`.

articles.title: Second moment of the statistic imputed with ImpG weights
articles.statement:
For the ImpG weights (`Σ_oo w = Σ_ot`, i.e. `w = Σ_oo⁻¹ Σ_ot` when `Σ_oo` is invertible) the
imputed statistic has second moment `wᵀ Σ_ot = Σ_to Σ_oo⁻¹ Σ_ot`; for `Σ_tt = 1` this is
`1 -` the linear-prediction residual variance, ImpG's `r²_pred`.

articles.title: Second moment of the imputed statistic
articles.statement: `𝔼 ẑ² = wᵀ Σ_oo w`.

articles.title: Normalized imputed statistic
articles.statement:
For any weights `w` with `wᵀ Σ_oo w > 0` (for example the
ridge weights solving `(Σ_oo + λ I) w = Σ_ot`), the statistic `ẑ / √(wᵀ Σ_oo w)` has second
moment `1`, so it has unit variance under the centred null.

articles.title: Second-moment model for summary-statistic imputation
articles.statement:
Square-integrable statistics `z_t` (untyped marker) and `z_o` (typed markers) with raw second
moments `𝔼 z_o z_oᵀ = Σ_oo`, `𝔼 z_t z_o = Σ_ot`, `𝔼 z_t² = Σ_tt`. These are the covariances of
the ImpG null model when the statistics are centred.

articles.title: Symmetry of the typed-marker moment matrix
articles.statement: The moment matrix `Σ_oo` is symmetric.

articles.title: The centred moments order `q₁²` and `q₂²`
articles.statement:
If `κ_π ≠ 0` and `ρ_g = q₁ q₂ ≠ 0`, then
`|E(α₁ α₂³) - 3 ρ_g| ≤ |E(α₁³ α₂) - 3 ρ_g|` iff `q₂² ≤ q₁²`.

articles.title: The uncentred comparison is reversed when `κ_π < 0`
articles.statement:
If `κ_π < 0` and `ρ_g ≠ 0`, then
`|E(α₁ α₂³)| ≤ |E(α₁³ α₂)|` iff `q₁² ≤ q₂²`. So the paper's uncentred criterion needs
`κ_π > 0`; the centred criterion `abs_centredMoment_le_iff` does not.

articles.title: The paper's uncentred comparison, under its sign condition
articles.statement:
If `κ_π > 0` and
`ρ_g ≠ 0`, then `|E(α₁ α₂³)| ≤ |E(α₁³ α₂)|` iff `q₂² ≤ q₁²` (O'Connor and Price 2018, after
Equation 2, which states the forward implication).

articles.title: Marginal effect on the first trait in the latent causal variable model
articles.statement: The marginal effect `α₁ = q₁ π + γ₁` on trait 1.

articles.title: Marginal effect on the second trait in the latent causal variable model
articles.statement: The marginal effect `α₂ = q₂ π + γ₂` on trait 2.

articles.title: Centred mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1^3 \alpha_2)$
articles.statement: The centred mixed fourth moment: `E(α₁³ α₂) - 3 ρ_g = κ_π q₁³ q₂`.

articles.title: Centred mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1 \alpha_2^3)$
articles.statement: The centred mixed fourth moment: `E(α₁ α₂³) - 3 ρ_g = κ_π q₁ q₂³`.

articles.title: Genetic causality proportion is at most 1
articles.statement: `gcp ≤ 1` when `q₁² ≤ 1` (for nonzero `q₁, q₂` with `ρ_g² < 1`).

articles.title: Sign of the genetic causality proportion
articles.statement: `gcp ≥ 0` iff `q₂² ≤ q₁²`, for nonzero `q₁, q₂` with `ρ_g² = (q₁ q₂)² < 1`.

articles.title: The paper's criterion for `gcp ≥ 0`
articles.statement:
**The paper's criterion for `gcp ≥ 0`** (O'Connor and Price 2018, after Equation 2), under
the sign condition `κ_π > 0` that it needs: if `ρ_g ≠ 0`, `ρ_g² < 1` and
`|E(α₁ α₂³)| ≤ |E(α₁³ α₂)|`, then `gcp ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Genetic causality proportion
articles.statement:
The genetic causality proportion `gcp = (log|q₂| - log|q₁|) / (log|q₂| + log|q₁|)`
(O'Connor and Price 2018, Equation 4). Meaningful for `0 < |q₁|, |q₂| ≤ 1` and `ρ_g² < 1`; for
`|q₁| = |q₂| = 1` the denominator vanishes and the value is `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.

articles.title: Mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1 \alpha_2^3)$
articles.statement: The mirror image of Equation 2: `E(α₁ α₂³) = κ_π q₁ q₂³ + 3 q₁ q₂`.

articles.title: Genetic correlation in the latent causal variable model
articles.statement: The genetic correlation is `E(α₁ α₂) = q₁ q₂` (O'Connor and Price 2018, after Equation 1).

articles.title: Mixed fourth moment
articles.statement:
**Mixed fourth moment** (O'Connor and Price 2018, Equation 2):
`E(α₁³ α₂) = κ_π q₁³ q₂ + 3 q₁ q₂`.

articles.title: Excess kurtosis of the latent effect
articles.statement: The excess kurtosis `κ_π = E(π⁴) - 3` of the effect on the latent variable.

articles.title: Latent causal variable model
articles.statement:
The latent causal variable model of O'Connor and Price (2018, Equation 3) on a probability
space: `α_k = q_k π + γ_k` with `π` independent of `(γ₁, γ₂)`, the law of `(γ₁, γ₂)` invariant
under each sign flip, `π` of mean zero and unit variance, and both `α_k` of unit second moment.
Fourth moments are assumed finite.

articles.title: Genetic causality proportion is at least −1
articles.statement: `-1 ≤ gcp` when `q₂² ≤ 1` (for nonzero `q₁, q₂` with `ρ_g² < 1`).

articles.title: Excess kurtosis of the latent effect is at least −2
Fourth moment of the latent effect is at least one
articles.statement: `E(π⁴) ≥ (E π²)² = 1`, so the excess kurtosis is at least `-2`.

articles.title: Mediated coefficient of the first trait is at most one in size
articles.statement: Unit variance of `α₁` forces `q₁² ≤ 1` (the non-mediated part has variance `1 - q₁²`).

articles.title: Mediated coefficient of the second trait is at most one in size
articles.statement: Unit variance of `α₂` forces `q₂² ≤ 1`.

articles.title: Genetic causality proportion solves the defining equation
articles.statement:
The genetic causality proportion solves the paper's Equation 1:
`q₂² / q₁² = (ρ_g²) ^ gcp` with `ρ_g = q₁ q₂`, for nonzero `q₁, q₂` with `ρ_g² < 1`.

articles.title: Attenuation ratio under constant stratification
articles.statement:
With a constant stratification term `N a`, the attenuation ratio of the exact intercept
`1 - h² + N a` and the mean expected statistic is `(N a - h²) / (N h² ℓ̄ / M + N a - h²)`.

articles.title: Attenuation ratio
articles.statement: The attenuation ratio `(intercept - 1) / (mean χ² - 1)` of Loh et al. (2018).

articles.title: Normalized score under stratification
articles.statement: The `N`-normalized score of marker `j` under stratification, `X_jᵀ y / N`.

articles.title: Normalized marginal score in the LD-score model
Association statistic under stratification
articles.statement: The association statistic `N * β̂ j ^ 2` under stratification.

articles.title: Association statistic in the LD-score model
articles.statement: The association statistic `χ² j = N * β̂ j ^ 2` of marker `j`.

articles.title: Confounding share lies between 0 and 1
articles.statement:
The confounding share `N a / (N a + N h² ℓ̄ / M)` lies in `[0, 1]` when `a`, `h²` and `ℓ̄`
are nonnegative (as they are in the model: `a` is a square, `h² ≥ 0` by `Model.h2_nonneg`,
LD scores are sums of squares).

articles.title: Confounding share of inflation under constant stratification
articles.statement:
With a constant stratification term `N a`, the share of the mean inflation above the exact
null level `1 - h²` that is due to stratification is `N a / (N a + N h² ℓ̄ / M)`.

articles.title: Heritability is at most one in the LD-score model
articles.statement: The heritability is at most `1` when there is at least one individual.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of heritability in the LD-score model
articles.statement: The heritability is nonnegative when there is at least one marker.

articles.title: LD-score regression
articles.statement:
LD-score regression (Bulik-Sullivan et al. 2015): for a standardized genotype matrix
(`IsStandardized`, so that `ldCorr` is the sample correlation and `ldScore` the LD score) and
`N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² j] = N h² / M * ℓ j + (1 - h²)`. The expected association statistic is affine in
the LD score, with slope `N h² / M` and intercept `1 - h²`. The proof uses only that column `j`
has sum of squares `N`; the rest of the standardization is what makes `ℓ j` an LD score.

articles.title: LD-score regression with constant stratification
articles.statement:
With a constant stratification term (`s² (X_jᵀ c / N)² = a` for every marker), the expected
statistic is exactly affine in the LD score, with slope `N h² / M` and intercept
`1 - h² + N a`.

articles.title: Expected statistic under stratification for standardized genotypes
articles.statement:
Stratification inflation for a standardized genotype matrix and `N ≠ 0`:
`𝔼[χ² j] = N h² / M * ℓ j + (1 - h²) + N s² (X_jᵀ c / N)²`.

articles.title: Expected association statistic under stratification
articles.statement:
Stratification inflation: for a probability measure and mean-zero effects and noise,
`𝔼[χ² j] = N h² / M * ℓ j + (1 - h²) (∑ i, X i j ^ 2) / N + N s² (X_jᵀ c / N)²`.

articles.title: Expected association statistic for an arbitrary genotype matrix
articles.statement:
The exact expectation of the association statistic built from the `N`-normalized score,
for an arbitrary genotype matrix:
`𝔼[χ² j] = N h² / M * ℓ j + (1 - h²) * (∑ i, X i j ^ 2) / N`. (For `N = 0` both sides are `0`
by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.)

articles.title: Standardized genotype matrix
articles.statement:
The genotype matrix is standardized: every marker column has mean `0` and sum of squares
`N` (unit sample variance).

articles.title: A standardized marker has correlation one with itself
articles.statement: For a standardized matrix each marker has correlation `1` with itself.

articles.title: Correlations of standardized markers lie in (-1, 1)
articles.statement: For a standardized matrix the correlations lie in `[-1, 1]` (Cauchy–Schwarz).

articles.title: Normalized cross product of genotype markers
articles.statement:
The normalized cross product `r j k = X_jᵀ X_k / N` of markers `j` and `k`. For a
standardized genotype matrix (`IsStandardized`) it is the sample correlation of the two
markers; for other matrices it is only a scale-dependent dot product.

articles.title: LD score of a marker
articles.statement:
The LD score `ℓ j = ∑ k, r j k ^ 2` of marker `j` (an LD score in the sense of the cited
paper for a standardized genotype matrix).

articles.title: Mean association statistic with constant stratification
articles.statement:
With a constant stratification term `N a`, the mean expected statistic is
`N h² ℓ̄ / M + (1 - h² + N a)`.

articles.title: Polygenic inflation of the mean association statistic
articles.statement:
Polygenic inflation: for a standardized genotype matrix with `N, M ≠ 0`, the mean expected
association statistic is `1 - h² + N h² ℓ̄ / M`.

articles.title: Mean LD score
articles.statement: The mean LD score `ℓ̄ = (1 / M) ∑ j, ℓ j`.

articles.title: Random-effects model of LD-score regression
articles.statement:
The random-effects model of LD-score regression (Bulik-Sullivan et al. 2015), stated at
the level of raw second moments, for `N` individuals and `M` markers with heritability `h2`.

* `beta k` is the (random) effect of marker `k`, with `∫ β k * β l = h2 / M * [k = l]`;
* `eps i` is the environmental noise of individual `i`, with
  `∫ ε i * ε i' = (1 - h2) * [i = i']`;
* effects and noise are orthogonal in `L²`.

The measure is arbitrary and no means are assumed; for a probability measure and mean-zero
effects and noise these are the covariance conditions of the cited model. The genotype matrix is
not part of the model: all expectations are conditional on it.

articles.title: Phenotype with population stratification
articles.statement: The phenotype with a stratification shift: `y i = (X β) i + ε i + s * c i`.

articles.title: Phenotype in the LD-score model
articles.statement: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.

articles.title: Reduced form: outcome difference is the complier-weighted effect
articles.statement:
The reduced form (Imbens & Angrist 1994): under independence, exclusion and monotonicity,
with integrable potential outcomes and both arms of positive probability, the difference in
mean outcomes between the arms is `𝔼[(Y(z, 1) - Y(z, 0)) 1_complier]`, for either `z`.

articles.title: First stage: treatment-rate difference equals complier share
articles.statement:
The first stage (Imbens & Angrist 1994): under independence and monotonicity, with both
arms of positive probability, the difference in treatment rates between the arms is the
proportion of compliers.

articles.title: Mean of a variable within an instrument arm
articles.statement:
The mean of `f` in the arm `Z = z`, `𝔼[f | Z = z]`, the expectation under the conditional
measure. It is the junk value `0` when `P(Z = z) = 0`.

articles.title: Compliance type of a pair of potential treatments
articles.statement: The compliance type of the potential treatments `(D(0), D(1)) = (d₀, d₁)`.

articles.title: Compliance types of Angrist, Imbens and Rubin
articles.statement:
The four compliance types of Angrist, Imbens & Rubin (1996), determined by the pair of
potential treatments `(D(0), D(1))`.

articles.title: Compliers in a potential-outcomes model
articles.statement: The compliers, `D(0) = 0` and `D(1) = 1`.

articles.title: Wald ratio identity for an instrument independent of the residual
articles.statement: The Wald covariance identity when the instrument is independent of the residual.

articles.title: Wald ratio identity
articles.statement:
The Wald covariance identity: if `Cov(Z, U) = 0` and `Cov(Z, X) ≠ 0`, then
`Cov(Z, Y) / Cov(Z, X) = β`. For a two-valued `Z` the ratio is the grouping estimator of Wald
(1940), the difference of the group means of `Y` over that of `X`. This is a moment-condition
identity, not a formal causal-identification result.

articles.title: Wald ratio as a ratio of regression slopes
articles.statement:
The Wald ratio as a ratio of regression slopes: the slope of `Y` on `Z` divided by the slope
of `X` on `Z` (the form used with SNP–outcome and SNP–exposure associations) is `β`. This is
again an observational moment identity.

articles.title: Bias of the ordinary least-squares coefficient under confounding
articles.statement:
The ordinary least-squares coefficient identity for `Y` on `X` is
`β + Cov(X, U) / Var(X)`, which differs from `β` exactly when `Cov(X, U) ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Covariance with the outcome in a linear moment model
articles.statement:
The covariance of any square-integrable variable with the outcome splits along the
observational decomposition: `Cov(V, Y) = β Cov(V, X) + Cov(V, U)`.

articles.title: MR-Egger intercept under pleiotropy
articles.statement:
The MR-Egger intercept under pleiotropy: it is the weighted mean pleiotropic effect
`ᾱ_v` minus `Cov_v(γ, α) / Var_v(γ) · γ̄_v`.

articles.title: MR-Egger intercept
articles.statement: The MR-Egger intercept `β̂̄_Y - slope · β̂̄_X` (weighted means).

articles.title: InSIDE identity for MR-Egger
articles.statement:
The finite-sample InSIDE identity (Bowden, Davey Smith & Burgess 2015): if the pleiotropic
terms are uncorrelated with the instrument strengths in the weighted sense,
`Cov_v(α, γ) = 0`, the MR-Egger slope is the coefficient `β` and the intercept is the weighted
mean pleiotropic term `ᾱ_v`. This identity alone does not encode a causal interpretation.

articles.title: MR-Egger slope under pleiotropy
articles.statement:
The MR-Egger slope under pleiotropy (Bowden, Davey Smith & Burgess 2015): if the SNP–outcome
associations are `Γ_j = α_j + β γ_j`, with pleiotropic terms `α_j` and SNP–exposure
associations `γ_j`, the Egger slope of `Γ` on `γ` is `β + Cov_v(γ, α) / Var_v(γ)`.

articles.title: MR-Egger slope
articles.statement:
The MR-Egger slope (Bowden, Davey Smith & Burgess 2015): the slope of the weighted linear
regression of `β̂_{Yj}` on `β̂_{Xj}` with an intercept, `Cov_v(β̂_X, β̂_Y) / Var_v(β̂_X)`. The
paper's weights are `v_j = σ_j⁻²`.

articles.title: MR-Egger line is the weighted least-squares line
articles.statement:
The MR-Egger line is the weighted least-squares line: for nonnegative weights and `β̂_X`
of nonzero weighted variance (so the total weight is positive and `β̂_X` is not constant on the
support of the weights), it minimizes the weighted residual sum of squares.

articles.title: Weighted residual sum of squares of a line
articles.statement:
The weighted residual sum of squares `∑ v_j (β̂_{Yj} - a - b β̂_{Xj})²` of the line with
intercept `a` and slope `b`.

articles.title: Exclusion restriction for an instrument
articles.statement:
Exclusion: the instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment,
`Y(0, d) = Y(1, d)`.

articles.title: Independence assumption for an instrument
articles.statement:
Independence (random assignment): the instrument is independent of the vector of all
potential treatments and potential outcomes.

articles.title: Unbiasedness of the IVW estimator
articles.statement:
Unbiasedness of IVW (Burgess, Butterworth & Thompson 2013), with the SNP–exposure
associations `β̂_{Xj}` treated as fixed: if `β̂_{Yj} = β β̂_{Xj} + ε_j` with integrable
mean-zero errors, the IVW estimator has mean `β`.

articles.title: IVW estimator as a weighted mean of ratio estimates
articles.statement:
The IVW estimator is the weighted mean of the ratio estimates with weights
`w_j = β̂_{Xj}² / σ_j²`. This holds for all data: a SNP with `β̂_{Xj} = 0` has weight `0` and
contributes nothing to either side.

articles.title: IVW estimator minimizes the weighted residual sum of squares
articles.statement:
The IVW estimator is the weighted least-squares slope through the origin: it minimizes
the weighted residual sum of squares. This holds for all data: if every `β̂_{Xj} = 0` the sum
does not depend on the slope (and `ivw` is the junk value `0`), and a SNP with `σ_j = 0` has
weight `0` on both sides by Lean's `x / 0 = 0`.

articles.title: Directional pleiotropy biases the IVW estimator
articles.statement:
Directional pleiotropy biases IVW: if `Γ_j = α_j + β γ_j`, the IVW estimate is
`β + ∑ γ_j α_j σ_j⁻² / ∑ γ_j² σ_j⁻²`. For example a common pleiotropic term `α_j = α ≠ 0`
biases IVW whenever `∑ γ_j σ_j⁻² ≠ 0`, whereas a constant `α` satisfies InSIDE, so
`eggerSlope_eq_of_inside` gives MR-Egger slope `β` and intercept `α`.

articles.title: IVW recovers an exact proportionality coefficient
articles.statement:
Without error, IVW recovers the proportionality coefficient: if
`β̂_{Yj} = β β̂_{Xj}` for all `j` and some `β̂_{Xj} ≠ 0`, then the IVW estimate is `β`.
This algebraic statement does not itself give `β` a causal interpretation.

articles.title: Inverse-variance weight of a ratio estimate
articles.statement:
The first-order inverse-variance weight `w_j = β̂_{Xj}² / σ_j²` of the ratio estimate of SNP
`j`, where `σ_j` is the standard error of `β̂_{Yj}` (Burgess, Butterworth & Thompson 2013).

articles.title: Inverse-variance-weighted estimator
articles.statement:
The inverse-variance-weighted (IVW) estimator
`∑ β̂_{Xj} β̂_{Yj} σ_j⁻² / ∑ β̂_{Xj}² σ_j⁻²` (Burgess, Butterworth & Thompson 2013). The
standard errors are positive in the model; it is the junk value `0` if every `β̂_{Xj} = 0`.

articles.title: Linear moment model for instrumental variables
articles.statement:
An observational linear moment model: variables `Z`, `X`, `Y` and `U` on a probability
space, all square integrable, with the algebraic decomposition `Y = α + β X + U`.
The residual `U` is an arbitrary observed-variable function. Consequently `outcome_eq` does not
exclude direct effects of `Z` under interventions, and `β` is only the coefficient in this
decomposition. Orthogonality (`Cov(Z, U) = 0`) and nonzero first stage (`Cov(Z, X) ≠ 0`) are
hypotheses of the covariance identities that use them.

articles.title: Ratio with a Gaussian denominator has infinite first moment
articles.statement:
