A ratio with a Gaussian denominator has no first moment (a classical fact, recalled in the
weak-instrument analysis of Burgess & Thompson 2011): if `D ~ N(m, v)` with `v > 0` and `N` is
independent of `D` and not almost surely `0`, then `𝔼|N / D| = ∞`. Applied to the ratio
estimator `β̂_Y / β̂_X` with a normally distributed SNP–exposure estimate `β̂_X`.

articles.title: Monotonicity assumption (no defiers)
articles.statement:
Monotonicity: assignment never decreases the treatment, `D(0) ≤ D(1)`; there are no
defiers.

articles.title: Ratio of independent normal variables is not integrable
articles.statement:
The ratio of two independent normal variables, the denominator with positive variance and
the numerator not almost surely zero (`(mN, vN) ≠ (0, 0)`), is not integrable.

articles.title: Observed outcome in a potential-outcomes model
articles.statement: The observed outcome `Y = Y(Z, D(Z))`.

articles.title: Observed treatment in a potential-outcomes model
articles.statement: The observed treatment `D = D(Z)`.

articles.title: Potential-outcomes model with binary instrument and treatment
articles.statement:
A potential-outcomes model with a binary instrument and a binary treatment (Imbens &
Angrist 1994; Angrist, Imbens & Rubin 1996): the assigned instrument `Z`, the potential
treatments `D(z)` and the potential outcomes `Y(z, d)`, all measurable. The observed treatment
is `D(Z)` and the observed outcome `Y(Z, D(Z))`. The identifying assumptions (independence,
exclusion, monotonicity, relevance) are separate predicates.

articles.title: Ratio estimate of a single SNP
articles.statement:
The ratio estimate `β̂_{Yj} / β̂_{Xj}` of SNP `j` (Lean's `x / 0 = 0` gives `0` when
`β̂_{Xj} = 0`; such SNPs carry weight `0` in `ivwWeight`).

articles.title: Positivity of the total IVW weight
articles.statement: The total weight is positive as soon as some SNP has `β̂_{Xj} ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Observed treatment as a 0-1 real variable
articles.statement: The observed treatment as a `0`/`1` real variable.

articles.title: Compliance type of a unit
articles.statement: The compliance type of a unit.

articles.title: Variance of the IVW estimator
articles.statement:
The first-order variance of IVW (Burgess, Butterworth & Thompson 2013): with the
`β̂_{Xj}` fixed and `β̂_{Yj} = β β̂_{Xj} + ε_j`, where the errors are square integrable,
pairwise uncorrelated (for instance independent) and `Var(ε_j) = σ_j²`, the IVW estimator has
variance `(∑ w_j)⁻¹ = (∑ β̂_{Xj}² / σ_j²)⁻¹`.

articles.title: Unrestricted algebraic identity behind the LATE theorem
articles.statement:
The unrestricted algebraic identity behind LATE. If the complier set has measure zero, both
sides totalize to `0`; therefore this theorem is not an identification or complier-average claim
at that boundary. Use `waldEstimand_eq_late` for the source-faithful result with relevance.

articles.title: Local average treatment effect theorem
articles.statement:
The local average treatment effect theorem (Imbens & Angrist 1994, Theorem 1; Angrist,
Imbens & Rubin 1996): under independence, exclusion, monotonicity and relevance, with integrable
potential outcomes and both arms of positive probability, the Wald estimand is the average
treatment effect among compliers, `𝔼[Y(1) - Y(0) | complier]` (read at either instrument value
`z`, which exclusion makes irrelevant). Relevance is the nonzero complier mass hypothesis; by
`armMean_treated_sub`, it is equivalent here to a nonzero Wald denominator.

articles.title: Wald instrumental-variable estimand
articles.statement:
The Wald (instrumental-variable) estimand
`(𝔼[Y | Z = 1] - 𝔼[Y | Z = 0]) / (𝔼[D | Z = 1] - 𝔼[D | Z = 0])`.

articles.title: Weighted covariance
articles.statement:
The weighted covariance `∑ v_j (a_j - ā_v)(b_j - b̄_v) / ∑ v_j`, where `ā_v` and `b̄_v` are
weighted means.

articles.title: Weighted mean
articles.statement: The weighted mean `∑ v_j a_j / ∑ v_j`.

articles.title: Weighted residual sum of squares through the origin
articles.statement:
The weighted residual sum of squares `∑ (β̂_{Yj} - b β̂_{Xj})² / σ_j²` of the regression
through the origin with slope `b`.

articles.title: Balance mean is decreasing in the selection coefficient
articles.statement: The balance mean is antitone in `s > 0` for `n U ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Mean PTV count at mutation-selection balance
articles.statement:
Mean PTV allele count `n U / s` at deterministic mutation–selection balance, for `n`
sampled chromosomes, PTV mutation rate `U` and heterozygous selection coefficient `s > 0`.

articles.title: Posterior of `s_het` is stochastically nonincreasing in the PTV count, any antitone mean
articles.statement:
**Posterior of `s_het` is stochastically nonincreasing in the PTV count, any antitone
mean**: for a prior `μ` on `s_het` concentrated on `(0, ∞)`, a Poisson count with mean `λ`
nonnegative and antitone on `(0, ∞)`, integrable likelihoods and positive marginal likelihoods,
`P(s_het > t ∣ k') ≤ P(s_het > t ∣ k)` whenever `k ≤ k'`.

articles.title: Cassa et al. (2017) model
articles.statement:
With the balance mean `n U / s_het` (`n, U > 0`) and any
probability prior on `s_het ∈ (0, ∞)`, the posterior probability `P(s_het > t ∣ k)` is
nonincreasing in the observed PTV count `k`.

articles.title: Stratification within the axis span does not change the residual
articles.statement:
Adding a vector of the subspace (stratification lying in the axis span) does not change the
residual.

articles.title: Additivity of residualization
articles.statement: Residualization is additive.

articles.title: Residual as projection onto the orthogonal complement
articles.statement: The residual is the orthogonal projection onto `Vᗮ`.

articles.title: Residual vanishes exactly on the subspace
articles.statement: The residual vanishes exactly on the subspace.

articles.title: Residuals lie in the orthogonal complement
articles.statement: Residuals are orthogonal to the adjustment subspace.

articles.title: Vectors orthogonal to the subspace are their own residuals
articles.statement:
Vectors orthogonal to the subspace are their own residuals: stratification outside the axis
span is not removed.

articles.title: Homogeneity of residualization
articles.statement: Residualization is homogeneous.

articles.title: Residual with respect to an orthonormal family of axes
articles.statement:
Regressing on an orthonormal family of axes one axis at a time gives the joint residual:
`y - ∑ₖ ⟪aₖ, y⟫ aₖ`.

articles.title: Residualized vector after adjustment for a subspace
articles.statement:
The adjusted (residualized) `y`: the residual of the least-squares regression of `y` on the
subspace `V` (`y` minus its orthogonal projection onto `V`).

articles.title: Allele-frequency estimate of a marker
articles.statement:
The allele-frequency estimate `p̂ⱼ = μⱼ / 2` of marker `j`, where `μⱼ` is the mean
variant-allele count of column `j` (autosomal diploid data, counts in `{0, 1, 2}`).

articles.title: Each top axis lies in the span of the top axes
articles.statement: Each of the top `K` axes lies in their span.

articles.title: Axes of variation
articles.statement: The axes of variation: an orthonormal eigenbasis of `Ψ`, in decreasing eigenvalue order.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of the axes of variation
articles.statement: The eigenvalues of `Ψ` in decreasing order, matching `axes`.

articles.title: Stratification in the axis span is removed
articles.statement:
Adding vectors of `V` to the phenotype and
the genotype does not change the EIGENSTRAT statistic.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the EIGENSTRAT statistic
articles.statement: The EIGENSTRAT statistic is nonnegative when `K + 1 ≤ N`.

articles.title: Genotypes in the axis span carry no signal after adjustment
articles.statement:
A genotype lying in the axis span carries no signal after adjustment (its residual is zero,
and the statistic is the junk value `0` of the zero denominator).

articles.title: EIGENSTRAT association statistic
articles.statement:
The EIGENSTRAT association statistic `(N - K - 1) ⟪r_g, r_y⟫² / (‖r_g‖² ‖r_y‖²)` of the
adjusted genotype `r_g` and adjusted phenotype `r_y`: `(N - K - 1)` times their squared cosine,
which is their squared sample correlation when both are centered (Price et al. 2006). When either
adjusted vector is zero the ratio is the junk value `0`.

articles.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, existence
articles.statement:
Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, existence: the coefficient of the residual-on-residual regression
gives a least-squares decomposition of `y` on `V ⊔ span {g}`.

articles.title: Dimension of the span of the top axes
articles.statement: The top `K` axes span a `K`-dimensional subspace.

articles.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, uniqueness
articles.statement:
Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, uniqueness: in any least-squares decomposition
`y = c + β g + e` with `c ∈ V` and `e ⊥ V ⊔ span {g}`, the coefficient `β` is the
coefficient of the regression of the residualized `y` on the residualized `g`, and the
residual `e` is the residual of that regression.

articles.title: Residuals are orthogonal to every axis
articles.statement: Residuals are orthogonal to every vector of the subspace, in particular to every axis.

articles.title: Characterization of the axes counted as significant
articles.statement:
The first `numSignificant stat t K` indices are exactly those `k < K` whose statistics and
all earlier ones exceed the threshold.

articles.title: Significant axes have statistics above the threshold
articles.statement: Every axis counted as significant has a statistic above the threshold.

articles.title: Conditional error bound
articles.statement:
If, under the null hypothesis, the `k`-th statistic exceeds `t`
with probability at most `1 - F t` (the Tracy–Widom approximation with `F` the TW₁ distribution
function, taken here as a hypothesis), then the rule declares more than `k` significant axes with
probability at most `1 - F t`.

articles.title: Patterson's normalized genotype matrix
Count of significant axes decreases with the threshold
articles.statement: A higher threshold declares no more axes significant.

articles.title: Significant-axis count for decreasing statistics
articles.statement:
For decreasing statistics (such as ordered eigenvalues compared with a fixed threshold) the
sequential count is the number of statistics above the threshold.

articles.title: At most K axes are declared significant
articles.statement: At most `K` axes are declared significant.

articles.title: Criterion for at least one significant axis
articles.statement: At least one axis is significant iff the leading statistic exceeds the threshold.

articles.title: Sequential count of significant axes
articles.statement:
Patterson's sequential count of significant axes: among the first `K` statistics, the
length of the leading run of statistics exceeding the threshold `t` (testing stops at the first
non-significant one).

articles.title: All-ones vector lies in the kernel of the relatedness matrix
articles.statement:
The all-ones vector is in the kernel of `Ψ` (columns of the normalized matrix are centered),
so at most `N - 1` eigenvalues are nonzero.

articles.title: Patterson's relatedness matrix is positive semidefinite
articles.statement: Patterson's matrix `Ψ` is positive semidefinite.

articles.title: Patterson's relatedness matrix
articles.statement:
Patterson's `N × N` matrix `Ψ = M Mᵀ / (number of markers)` of the normalized genotypes,
whose top eigenvectors are the axes of variation.

articles.title: Span of the top axes of variation
articles.statement: The span of the top `K` axes of variation, the subspace EIGENSTRAT adjusts for.

articles.title: Sherman–Morrison applied to the candidate marker
articles.statement:
For positive definite `V₀` and
`c ≥ 0`, `(V₀ + c x xᵀ)⁻¹ x = (1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x)⁻¹ • V₀⁻¹ x`.

articles.title: Including the marker in the covariance never increases the statistic
articles.statement:
Including the candidate marker in the covariance never increases the mixed-model
statistic: `χ²(V₀ + c x xᵀ) ≤ χ²(V₀)` for positive definite `V₀` and `c ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Proximal contamination
articles.statement:
Including the candidate marker `x` in the covariance,
`V = V₀ + c x xᵀ` with `V₀` positive definite and `c ≥ 0`, divides the mixed-model statistic by
`1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x`, for every phenotype vector `y`:
`χ²(V₀ + c x xᵀ) = χ²(V₀) / (1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x)`.

articles.title: Mixed-model association chi-squared statistic
articles.statement:
The mixed-model (generalized-least-squares score) statistic
`χ²(V) = (xᵀ V⁻¹ y)² / (xᵀ V⁻¹ x)` of the marker `x` for the phenotype `y` under the phenotypic
covariance `V`. For positive definite `V` and `x ≠ 0` the denominator is positive.

articles.title: Marginal marker-phenotype correlations in SLDP regression
articles.statement:
The vector `α̂ = Xᵀ y / N` of marginal correlations between the (standardized) markers and
the phenotype.

articles.title: SLDP first-moment identity
articles.statement:
**SLDP first-moment identity** (Reshef et al. 2018, Methods, Equation 5): if the true effects
have mean `μ v`, then `𝔼 α̂ = μ R̂ v`, a multiple of the signed LD profile `R̂ v` of `v`.

articles.title: First-moment identity, exact in-sample form
articles.statement:
Conditional on the genotype matrix,
`𝔼 α̂ = R̂ 𝔼 β` with `R̂ = Xᵀ X / N`.

articles.title: Unbiasedness with covariates
articles.statement:
**Unbiasedness with covariates** (the signed background model): suppose the true effects
have mean `μ v + U γ` for background annotations `U` (columns `u_b`) with arbitrary coefficients
`γ`, let `A = R̂ U` be their signed LD profiles, and let `z⊥ = R̂ v - A w` be the weighted residual
of the signed LD profile of `v` on `A` (`Aᵀ W z⊥ = 0`) for a symmetric weight matrix `W`. If
`⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W ≠ 0`, then `𝔼 [⟪z⊥, α̂⟫_W / ⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W] = μ`. By `Matrix.frischWaughLovell` this
estimator equals the coefficient of `R̂ v` in the joint weighted regression of `α̂` on
`[A | R̂ v]`, and the same as regressing the residualized `α̂` on `z⊥`.

articles.title: Unbiasedness of the weighted least-squares estimator
articles.statement:
For any weight matrix `W` and
signed LD profile `s = R̂ v` with `⟪s, s⟫_W = sᵀ W s ≠ 0`, if `𝔼 β = μ v` then
`𝔼 [⟪s, α̂⟫_W / ⟪s, s⟫_W] = μ`, where `⟪a, b⟫_W = aᵀ W b`. SLDP uses the inverse of
`Ω = σ² R² + R / N` as `W`.

articles.title: In-sample LD matrix
articles.statement: The in-sample LD matrix `R̂ = Xᵀ X / N`, with entries `ldCorr X j k`.

articles.title: First-moment phenotype model of SLDP regression
articles.statement:
The linear phenotype model of SLDP regression at the level of first moments: integrable
random effects `β` with means `meanBeta` and integrable noise `ε` of mean zero. (SLDP's model
takes `meanBeta = μ v` for a signed annotation `v`; second moments are not needed for the
first-moment identity.)

articles.title: Phenotype in the SLDP regression model
articles.statement: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.

articles.title: Annotation LD score of a marker
articles.statement:
The LD score of marker `j` with respect to annotation `C`:
`ℓ(j, C) = ∑_k a_{kC} r_jk²` (Finucane et al. 2015 for binary annotations; Gazal et al. 2017 for
continuous ones).

articles.title: Normalized marker score in stratified LD-score regression
articles.statement: The `N`-normalized score `β̂ j = X_jᵀ y / N` of marker `j` (as in `LDScore.Model.betaHat`).

articles.title: Heritability of a marker category
articles.statement:
The heritability `h²(C) = ∑_{k ∈ C} σ²_k` of category `C`, for a labeling `cat` of the
markers by categories.

articles.title: Number of markers in a category
articles.statement: The number `M_C` of markers in category `C`.

articles.title: Stratified statistic agrees with the LD-score statistic
articles.statement: The stratified statistic of `ofLDScore D` is the statistic of `LDScore`.

articles.title: Association chi-squared statistic in stratified LD-score regression
articles.statement: The association statistic `χ² j = N * β̂ j ^ 2` of marker `j`.

articles.title: Design matrix of stratified LD-score regression
articles.statement:
The design matrix `[1 | N ℓ(·, C)]` of stratified LD-score regression with a free intercept;
column `none` is the intercept and column `some C` the scaled annotation LD score.

articles.title: Heritability enrichment of a category
articles.statement:
The enrichment of category `C`: its proportion of heritability divided by its proportion of
markers, `(h²(C) / h²) / (M_C / M)` with `h² = ∑_k σ²_k` (Finucane et al. 2015).

articles.title: Injective matrix action iff full column rank
articles.statement: A real matrix has injective `mulVec` iff it has full column rank.

articles.title: Expected statistics are the design matrix times the parameters
articles.statement:
Under the annotation model, the vector of expected statistics is the design matrix applied
to the parameter vector `(σ²_e, τ)` (intercept first). Hence the parameters are determined by
the expected statistics of all markers, whatever their values, iff
`(design X a).rank = Fintype.card (Option ι)` (`injective_mulVec_iff_rank_eq_card`).

articles.title: Frequency-dependent architecture
articles.statement:
**Frequency-dependent architecture** (the α model of Schoech et al. 2019): if the per-allele
effect variance of marker `k` with allele frequency `p_k` is proportional to `[p_k (1 - p_k)]^α`,
the variance of the effect of the standardized genotype is `σ²_k = c [p_k (1 - p_k)]^(1 + α)`,
and then, for a standardized genotype matrix and `N ≠ 0`,
`𝔼[χ² j] = N c ∑_k [p_k (1 - p_k)]^(1 + α) r_jk² + σ²_e`. (The real power is meaningful for
`0 < p_k < 1`.)

articles.title: Stratified LD-score regression
articles.statement:
**Stratified LD-score regression** (Finucane et al. 2015; continuous annotations, Gazal et
al. 2017): if the per-marker variances are linear in the annotations, `σ²_k = ∑_C τ_C a_{kC}`,
then for a standardized genotype matrix and `N ≠ 0`,
`𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_C τ_C ℓ(j, C) + σ²_e`.

articles.title: Expected chi-squared statistic of a standardized marker
articles.statement:
For a column with sum of squares `N` (a standardized marker) and `N ≠ 0`:
`𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_k r_jk² σ²_k + σ²_e`.

articles.title: Expected statistic with per-marker variances
articles.statement:
**Expected statistic with per-marker variances**, for an arbitrary genotype matrix:
`𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_k r_jk² σ²_k + σ²_e (∑_i X_ij²) / N`. (For `N = 0` both sides are `0`.)

articles.title: Random-effects model of stratified LD-score regression
articles.statement:
The random-effects model of stratified LD-score regression at the level of raw second
moments: marker `k` has effect variance `sigma2 k`, the noise has variance `sigmaE2`, and
effects and noise are orthogonal in `L²`. As in `LDScore.Model`, the measure is arbitrary, no
means are assumed, and all statements are conditional on the genotype matrix.

articles.title: LD-score regression model as a stratified model
articles.statement:
The LD-score regression model of `LDScore` is the stratified model with equal per-marker
variances `h² / M` and noise variance `1 - h²`.

articles.title: Phenotype in the stratified LD-score model
articles.statement: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.

articles.title: LDSC-SEG contrast
articles.statement:
**LDSC-SEG contrast** (Finucane et al. 2018): for per-SNP variances
`σ²_k = ∑_C τ_C a_{kC}`, two SNPs `k`, `k'` whose annotations agree except on annotation `cS`
differ in per-SNP variance by `τ_{cS} (a_{k cS} - a_{k' cS})`. With `cS` the indicator of a gene
set `S` contained in the control gene set `G` (whose indicator is one of the other annotations),
`k ∈ S` and `k' ∈ G ∖ S` with equal values of all other annotations give
`σ²_k - σ²_{k'} = τ_S`.

articles.title: Marker-proportion-weighted enrichments sum to one
articles.statement:
For a partition of the markers into categories (a labeling `cat`) and nonzero total
heritability, the marker-proportion-weighted enrichments sum to one:
`∑_C (M_C / M) * Enrichment(C) = 1`. Empty categories contribute `0` on both sides of each
term.

articles.title: Zero-mean criterion for the DENTIST difference
articles.statement:
The standardized DENTIST difference has mean zero iff the reference correlation equals the
true correlation or the lead variant has mean zero (for `r ^ 2 < 1`).

articles.title: Mean of the standardized DENTIST difference
articles.statement:
The mean `(ρ - r) λ / √(1 - r²)` of the standardized DENTIST difference when the true
correlation is `ρ`, the reference correlation is `r` and the lead variant has mean `λ`.

articles.title: DENTIST-S statistic
articles.statement:
The DENTIST-S statistic `(z_i - r z_c) ^ 2 / (1 - r ^ 2)` of a variant with `z`-score `zi`,
given the `z`-score `zc` of the lead (putative causal) variant and the reference correlation `r`
between them (Kanai et al. 2022, Equation 1). Meaningful for `r ^ 2 < 1`; for `r ^ 2 = 1` it is
`0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.

articles.title: Unit-variance criterion for the DENTIST difference
articles.statement:
The standardized DENTIST difference has unit variance iff the reference correlation is `0`
or equals the true correlation (for `r ^ 2 < 1`).

articles.title: Variance of the standardized DENTIST difference
articles.statement:
The variance `(1 - 2 r ρ + r²) / (1 - r²)` of the standardized DENTIST difference when the
true correlation is `ρ` and the reference correlation is `r`.

articles.title: DENTIST-S is exactly `χ²₁` when the reference LD is right
articles.statement:
Under the model of
`map_standardized_eq_gaussianReal` with reference correlation equal to the true correlation
`ρ` (`ρ ^ 2 < 1`), the DENTIST-S statistic has the `chiSquareMeasure 1` law, for every value
`λ` of the lead variant's mean.

articles.title: DENTIST-S is chi-squared with one degree of freedom under correct LD
articles.statement:
When the reference correlation equals the true correlation `ρ` (`ρ ^ 2 < 1`), the DENTIST-S
statistic has the law of the square of a standard normal variable.

articles.title: Exact law of the standardized DENTIST difference
articles.statement:
Let `(z_i, z_c)` be jointly Gaussian
with unit variances, correlation `ρ` (the covariance, as the variances are `1`), and means
`ρ λ` and `λ`. For a reference correlation `r` with `r ^ 2 < 1`, the standardized difference
`(z_i - r z_c) / √(1 - r²)` is Gaussian with mean `dentistMean ρ r λ` and variance
`dentistVariance ρ r`.

articles.title: AND-gate production rate in the logic approximation
articles.statement:
AND-gate production in the logic approximation: rate `β` when `K_x < x` and `K_y < y`,
else `0`.

articles.title: No OFF delay
articles.statement:
For a nonnegative threshold `K_xz`, whatever `Y` does, the FFL and simple
regulation decay identically after an OFF step: `Z(t) = z₀ e^{-α_z t}`.

articles.title: Feed-forward loop target after an OFF step
articles.statement:
The FFL target after `Sx` is removed at `t = 0` (`X* = 0`), starting from `Z(0) = z₀`, for
an arbitrary trajectory `Y` of the intermediate factor.

articles.title: ON delay
articles.statement: The FFL target stays at `0` until `T_on`.

articles.title: Delayed rise
articles.statement:
After `T_on` the FFL target relaxes from `0` towards `β_z/α_z`:
`Z(t) = (β_z/α_z)(1 - e^{-α_z (t - T_on)})` (for `α_z > 0`, `K_xz < 1`).

articles.title: Feed-forward loop target after an ON step
articles.statement:
The FFL target after an ON step of `Sx` at `t = 0` from `Y(0) = Z(0) = 0`, with `X* = 1`
and `K_xz < 1`.

articles.title: Relaxation solution satisfies its differential equation
articles.statement:
The relaxation solves `z' = P - α z` at every time where the (locally integrable) production
rate `P` is continuous.

articles.title: Intermediate factor solves its production–decay equation
articles.statement:
`yOn` solves `Y' = β_y - α_y Y` with `Y(0) = 0` (for `α_y ≠ 0`; at `α_y = 0` Lean's
`β_y / 0 = 0` makes `yOn` identically `0`, which is not a solution).

articles.title: Positivity of the ON delay
articles.statement: The ON delay is positive.

articles.title: ON-step delay of the feed-forward loop
articles.statement:
The ON-step delay `T_on = (1/α_y) log(1 / (1 - K_yz / Y_st))`, `Y_st = β_y/α_y`: the time
at which `Y` crosses the activation threshold `K_yz` of `Z`. Meaningful for
`0 < K_yz < Y_st`.

articles.title: Variation-of-constants solution of a linear relaxation equation
articles.statement:
The variation-of-constants solution of `z' = P(t) - α z`, `z(0) = z₀`:
`z(t) = z₀ e^{-α t} + ∫₀ᵗ e^{-α (t - s)} P(s) ds`. Used for `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Single-input production rate in the logic approximation
articles.statement: Single-input production in the logic approximation: rate `β` when `K_x < x`, else `0`.

articles.title: Simple-regulation target after an OFF step
articles.statement: The simple-regulation target after `Sx` is removed at `t = 0`, from `Z(0) = z₀`.

articles.title: Simple regulation responds without delay
articles.statement:
Simple regulation responds without delay: `Z(t) = (β_z/α_z)(1 - e^{-α_z t}) > 0` for all
`t > 0`.

articles.title: Simple-regulation target after an ON step
articles.statement: The simple-regulation target after an ON step of `Sx` at `t = 0` from `Z(0) = 0`.

articles.title: Intermediate factor exceeds the threshold exactly after the ON delay
articles.statement: `Y` exceeds `K_yz` exactly after the ON delay: `K_yz < Y(t) ↔ T_on < t`.

articles.title: Intermediate factor after an ON step
articles.statement: `Y` after an ON step of `Sx` from `Y(0) = 0`: `Y(t) = (β_y/α_y)(1 - e^{-α_y t})`.

articles.title: The pseudo-Helmholtz function does not increase along solutions
articles.statement:
Along a solution of a
mass-action system with positive rate constants and a positive complex-balanced equilibrium
`c*`, positive and differentiable (two-sided) at every `t ≥ 0`, `G(x t)` is nonincreasing on
`[0, ∞)`.

## Sources

- Horn & Jackson (1972).

articles.title: Complexes of a chemical reaction network
articles.statement: The complexes of the network: the sources and products of its reactions.

articles.title: Deficiency of a chemical reaction network
articles.statement:
The deficiency `δ = n - ℓ - s` (number of complexes, linkage classes, dimension of the
stoichiometric subspace) of a network with finitely many complexes.

articles.title: Birch's theorem, uniqueness
articles.statement:
Two positive vectors whose difference lies in a subspace
`W` and whose logarithms differ by a vector orthogonal to `W` are equal.

## Sources

- Birch (1963); Horn & Jackson (1972).

articles.title: Horn–Feinberg: complex balancing for every choice of rate constants
articles.statement:
A weakly
reversible mass-action network of deficiency zero has, for any positive rate constants, a
positive complex-balanced equilibrium. Together with
`existsUnique_equilibrium_of_isComplexBalanced` this gives `existsUnique_equilibrium`.

## Sources

- Horn (1972); Feinberg (1972); Feinberg (1987).

articles.title: Birch's theorem, existence
articles.statement:
For any subspace `W` of `S → ℝ` and positive `a`, `b`
there is a positive `c` with `c - b ∈ W` and `log c - log a` orthogonal to `W` (for the dot
product). Source: Birch (1963); Horn & Jackson (1972).

articles.title: Horn–Jackson: one equilibrium per compatibility class
articles.statement:
If a mass-action system with
positive rate constants has a positive complex-balanced equilibrium, then each positive
stoichiometric compatibility class `(x₀ + 𝒮) ∩ ℝ_{>0}^S`, `x₀ > 0`, contains exactly one
positive equilibrium. Source: Horn & Jackson (1972); Feinberg (2019), ch. 15.

articles.title: Deficiency-zero theorem, weakly reversible case
articles.statement:
A weakly reversible mass-action
network of deficiency zero has, for any positive rate constants, exactly one equilibrium in
each positive stoichiometric compatibility class.

## Sources

- Horn (1972); Horn & Jackson (1972); Feinberg (1987).

articles.title: Pseudo-Helmholtz function along positive mass-action solutions
articles.statement:
The pseudo-Helmholtz function has time derivative `helmholtzRate` along a solution of the
mass-action system, at any time where the solution is positive.

articles.title: Equality in the Horn–Jackson inequality
articles.statement:
Under the hypotheses of
`helmholtzRate_nonpos`, the rate of change of the pseudo-Helmholtz function vanishes at a
positive `c` exactly when `c` is an equilibrium. Source: Horn & Jackson (1972).

articles.title: Horn–Jackson inequality
articles.statement:
If `c*` is a positive complex-balanced equilibrium for
positive rate constants, the pseudo-Helmholtz function does not increase along the
mass-action vector field at any positive `c`. Source: Horn & Jackson (1972);
Feinberg (2019), ch. 15.

articles.title: Rate of change of the pseudo-Helmholtz function
articles.statement:
The rate of change of the pseudo-Helmholtz function along the mass-action vector field,
`∑_s (log c_s - log c*_s) f_s(c)`: the derivative of `pseudoHelmholtz cstar` at `c > 0`
applied to `massActionField k c` (`hasDerivAt_pseudoHelmholtz`).

articles.title: Horn–Jackson
articles.statement:
If a mass-action system with positive rate constants has a positive
complex-balanced equilibrium, then every positive equilibrium is complex balanced.

## Sources

- Horn & Jackson (1972); Feinberg (2019), ch. 15.

articles.title: Complex-balanced concentrations
articles.statement:
Concentrations `c` are complex balanced for the rate constants `k`: at every complex `z`,
the total rate of the reactions with source `z` equals the total rate of the reactions with
product `z`. (Complexes that occur in no reaction give `0 = 0`.)

## Sources

- Horn & Jackson (1972); Feinberg (2019), ch. 15.

articles.title: Weakly reversible reaction network
articles.statement:
The network is weakly reversible: for every reaction `y → y'` there is a directed path of
reactions from `y'` back to `y`.

articles.title: Linkage graph of a reaction network
articles.statement:
The undirected reaction graph on the complexes: distinct complexes are adjacent when one
reacts to the other.

articles.title: Complex-balanced states are equilibria
articles.statement:
A complex-balanced state is an equilibrium of the mass-action system (for all real `c`
and `k`). Source: Horn & Jackson (1972).

articles.title: Mass-action vector field
articles.statement:
The mass-action vector field with rate constants `k`:
`x ↦ ∑_r k r (∏_s x_s ^ (src r s)) (prod r - src r)`.

articles.title: Deficiency-zero theorem, non-weakly-reversible case
articles.statement:
A mass-action network of
deficiency zero that is not weakly reversible has no positive equilibrium for any positive
rate constants.

## Sources

- Feinberg (1987).

articles.title: Number of linkage classes of a reaction network
articles.statement:
The number of linkage classes of a network with finitely many complexes: connected
components of the undirected reaction graph.

articles.title: Horn–Jackson: the positive equilibria
articles.statement:
If `c*` is a positive complex-balanced
equilibrium for positive rate constants, the positive equilibria are exactly the positive
`c` whose `log c - log c*` is orthogonal (for the dot product) to the stoichiometric
subspace. Source: Horn & Jackson (1972); Feinberg (2019), ch. 15.

articles.title: Pseudo-Helmholtz function
articles.statement:
The pseudo-Helmholtz function `G(c) = ∑_s c_s (log c_s - log c*_s - 1)` relative to the
reference concentrations `cstar` (Horn & Jackson 1972). It is meaningful for positive `c`
and `cstar`; elsewhere `Real.log` takes junk values.

articles.title: Mass-action reaction rate
articles.statement: The mass-action rate `k r * ∏_s c_s ^ (src r s)` of reaction `r` at concentrations `c`.

articles.title: Chemical reaction network
articles.statement:
A chemical reaction network on the species `S` with reactions indexed by `ρ`: reaction `r`
turns the source complex `src r` into the product complex `prod r` (stoichiometric
coefficients).

articles.title: Directed reaction relation on complexes
articles.statement:
The directed reaction relation on complexes: `y ⟶ y'` if some reaction has source `y` and
product `y'`.

articles.title: Stoichiometric subspace
articles.statement: The stoichiometric subspace: the span of the reaction vectors `prod r - src r`.

articles.title: Complex balance exchanges source and product sums
articles.statement:
Complex balance at `c` rewrites the rate-weighted sum of any function of the products as
the same sum over the sources (for all real `c` and `k`).

articles.title: Uniqueness of the steady state
articles.statement:
**Uniqueness of the steady state** (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7). For `K₁, K₂ > 0`, if
`0 < W < 1` and `rateRatio K₁ K₂ W = v` with `v > 0`, then `W` is the Goldbeter–Koshland
function.

articles.title: Goldbeter–Koshland function lies strictly between 0 and 1
articles.statement: For `v, K₁, K₂ > 0` the Goldbeter–Koshland function lies in `(0, 1)`.

articles.title: Equal maximal rates
articles.statement:
**Equal maximal rates** (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 9): for `V₁ = V₂` and `K₁, K₂ > 0`
the steady-state modified fraction is `K₂ / (K₁ + K₂)`.

articles.title: Goldbeter–Koshland function
articles.statement:
The **Goldbeter–Koshland function**: the steady-state mole fraction of modified protein
when `V₁ / V₂ = v` (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7, rationalized so that it also covers
`v = 1`, Eq. 9). Meaningful for `v, K₁, K₂ > 0`.

articles.title: Hill response coefficient
articles.statement:
**Hill response coefficient** (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 11). For a Hill response with
`n > 0` and `K > 0`, if `S₉, S₁ > 0` give 90% and 10% response, then
`S₉ / S₁ = 81 ^ (1 / n)`.

articles.title: Hill response function
articles.statement:
The fraction of a Hill response `Sⁿ / (Kⁿ + Sⁿ)` with half-saturation constant `K` and
Hill coefficient `n` (meaningful for `S, K > 0`, `n > 0`).

articles.title: Michaelis–Menten response
articles.statement:
**Michaelis–Menten response** (`n = 1`): going from 10% to 90% of the response takes an
81-fold increase of the stimulus.

articles.title: Response coefficient exceeds 1
articles.statement:
For `K₁, K₂ > 0` the response coefficient exceeds `1`: the switch is never infinitely
sharp.

articles.title: The Goldbeter–Koshland function is a steady state
articles.statement:
**The Goldbeter–Koshland function is a steady state** (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7):
for `v, K₁, K₂ > 0`, `rateRatio K₁ K₂ (goldbeterKoshland v K₁ K₂) = v`.

articles.title: Rate ratio at a given steady-state modified fraction
articles.statement:
The value of `V₁ / V₂` for which the mole fraction `W` of modified protein is at steady
state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 8): `W (1 - W + K₁) / ((1 - W) (W + K₂))`. Meaningful for
`0 < W < 1` and `K₁, K₂ > 0`; at `W = 1` Lean's `a / 0 = 0` gives the junk value `0`.

articles.title: The response coefficient
articles.statement:
**The response coefficient** (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 10): for `K₁, K₂ > -0.1`,
`R_v = 81 (K₁ + 0.1)(K₂ + 0.1) / ((K₁ + 0.9)(K₂ + 0.9))`.

articles.title: Response coefficient is below the Michaelis–Menten value 81
articles.statement: For `K₁, K₂ > 0` the response coefficient is below the Michaelis–Menten value `81`.

articles.title: Response coefficient of a covalent modification cycle
articles.statement:
The **response coefficient** `R_v`: the ratio of the values of `V₁ / V₂` giving 90% and 10%
modified protein at steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981).

articles.title: Steady state of the modification cycle
articles.statement:
**Steady state of the modification cycle** (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 8). For
`V₂ > 0`, `K₁, K₂ > 0` and `0 < W < 1`, modification and demodification balance,
`V₁ (1 - W) / (K₁ + 1 - W) = V₂ W / (K₂ + W)`, iff `V₁ / V₂ = rateRatio K₁ K₂ W`.

articles.title: Rate ratio is strictly increasing in the modified fraction
articles.statement:
`rateRatio K₁ K₂` is strictly increasing on `(0, 1)` for `K₁, K₂ > 0`: it is the product
of the positive increasing functions `W / (W + K₂)` and `1 + K₁ / (1 - W)`.

articles.title: First-order limit
articles.statement:
As both `K₁, K₂ → ∞` the response coefficient tends to `81`, the
value of a Michaelis–Menten response.

articles.title: Zero-order ultrasensitivity
articles.statement:
As both `K₁, K₂ → 0` the response coefficient tends to
`1`.

articles.title: Steady-state (DC) gain of a linear system
articles.statement:
The steady-state (DC) gain `d - c ⬝ A⁻¹ b`; for nonsingular `A` the output at the
equilibrium for input `u` is `dcGain * u`.

articles.title: Unique equilibrium of a nonsingular linear system
articles.statement: For nonsingular `A`, the unique equilibrium for input `u` is `x = -u • A⁻¹ b`.

articles.title: Vector field of a linear time-invariant system
articles.statement: The vector field `A x + u b` at state `x` and input `u`.

articles.title: Integral-feedback functional is the time integral of the output
articles.statement:
Along a trajectory `ẋ(t) = A x(t) + u(t) b`, the functional `k ⬝ x(t)` of an
integral-feedback system has derivative `y(t) = c ⬝ x(t) + d u(t)`: it is the time integral of
the output.

articles.title: Integral feedback is necessary
articles.statement:
**Integral feedback is necessary** (linear systems with nonsingular `A`): perfect
adaptation holds iff some linear functional of the state integrates the output; one such
functional is `k = c A⁻¹`.

articles.title: Integral feedback
articles.statement:
A linear functional `z = k ⬝ x` of the state integrates the output,
`ż = k ⬝ (A x + u b) = y`, for every state and input.

articles.title: Perfect adaptation iff the DC gain vanishes
articles.statement: For nonsingular `A`, perfect adaptation holds iff the steady-state gain vanishes.

articles.title: Integral feedback implies perfect adaptation
articles.statement: Integral feedback implies perfect adaptation.

articles.title: Perfect adaptation
articles.statement:
For every constant input `u`, the output vanishes at every
equilibrium.

articles.title: Single-input single-output linear time-invariant system
articles.statement:
A single-input single-output linear time-invariant system `ẋ = A x + u b`,
`y = c ⬝ x + d u` with state space `n → ℝ`.

articles.title: Integral feedback gives robust perfect adaptation
articles.statement:
**Integral feedback gives robust perfect adaptation** (nonlinear form). Let `F p` be the
vector field and `y p` the output of a system with parameters `p`, and let `z` be a
differentiable state function with derivative `z' x` satisfying
`z' x (F p x) = y p x` for all `p`, `x` (so `ż = y` along every trajectory, for
every parameter). Then the output vanishes at every equilibrium of every `F p`.

articles.title: Output at equilibrium equals DC gain times input
articles.statement: For nonsingular `A`, the output at the equilibrium for input `u` is `dcGain * u`.

articles.title: Output of a linear time-invariant system
articles.statement: The output `c ⬝ x + d u`, measured from its adapted value.

articles.title: Covariance of identical reporters equals extrinsic variance
articles.statement:
For identical reporters the covariance is the extrinsic variance:
`Cov(X, Y) = Var(E[X | m])`.

articles.title: Two-reporter formula for extrinsic noise
articles.statement: The two-reporter extrinsic noise is `Var(E[X | m]) / ⟨X⟩²` (Swain et al. Eq. 8).

articles.title: Extrinsic noise strength
articles.statement: Two-reporter extrinsic noise strength `η_ext² = (⟨X Y⟩ - ⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩) / (⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩)`.

articles.title: Identical reporters have equal means
articles.statement: Identical reporters have the same mean.

articles.title: Half mean squared reporter difference equals intrinsic variance
articles.statement:
For identical reporters half the mean squared difference is the intrinsic variance:
`⟨(X - Y)²⟩ / 2 = ⟨Var(X | m)⟩`.

articles.title: Two-reporter formula for intrinsic noise
articles.statement: The two-reporter intrinsic noise is `⟨Var(X | m)⟩ / ⟨X⟩²` (Swain et al. Eq. 8).

articles.title: Intrinsic noise strength
articles.statement: Two-reporter intrinsic noise strength `η_int² = ⟨(X - Y)²⟩ / (2 ⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩)`.

articles.title: Identical reporter pair
articles.statement:
Two reporters of the same gene given the extrinsic σ-algebra `m`: equal conditional means,
equal conditional second moments, and conditionally uncorrelated. Conditional independence with
identical conditional laws given `m` implies these three conditions.

articles.title: Two-reporter decomposition
articles.statement:
**Two-reporter decomposition** (Swain et al. 2002; Elowitz et al. 2002): for any
square-integrable reporters, `η_tot² = η_int² + η_ext²`.

articles.title: Total noise splits into intrinsic and extrinsic parts
articles.statement:
The two-reporter total noise is `Var(X) / ⟨X⟩²`, and it splits into the intrinsic and
extrinsic parts by the law of total variance.

articles.title: Total noise strength
articles.statement: Two-reporter total noise strength `η_tot² = (⟨X² + Y²⟩ / 2 - ⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩) / (⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩)`.

articles.title: Rigorous QSSA
articles.statement:
**Rigorous QSSA** (Tikhonov 1952; Heineken–Tsuchiya–Aris 1967). On the slow time scale
`τ = e₀ t`, the substrate of the full Michaelis–Menten system with `s(0) = s₀`, `c(0) = 0`,
`e(0) = e₀` stays within `C e₀` of the solution `S̄` of the reduced equation
`dS̄/dτ = -k₂ S̄ / (K_M + S̄)`, `S̄(0) = s₀`, uniformly on `[0, T]`.

articles.title: Quasi-steady-state manifold
articles.statement:
With total enzyme `e₀` (so `e = e₀ - c`), `k₁ > 0` and
`K_M + s ≠ 0`, the complex is stationary iff `c = e₀ s / (K_M + s)`.

articles.title: Mass-action rate of the enzyme–substrate complex
articles.statement: The mass-action rate of the complex, `c' = k₁ e s - (kb + k₂) c`.

articles.title: Enzyme conservation
Fast transient of the complex with frozen substrate
articles.statement:
The fast transient of the complex with the substrate frozen at `s̄`:
`c(t) = c* + (c₀ - c*) e^{-k₁ (s̄ + K_M) t}`, where `c* = e₀ s̄ / (K_M + s̄)`.

articles.title: Fast transient solves the boundary-layer equation
articles.statement:
The fast transient solves the boundary-layer equation `c' = k₁ (e₀ - c) s̄ - (kb + k₂) c`
for `k₁ > 0` and `K_M + s̄ ≠ 0`.

articles.title: Solution of the Michaelis–Menten mass-action system
articles.statement:
A solution of the Michaelis–Menten mass-action system on `[0, ∞)`:
`s' = -k₁ e s + kb c`, `c' = k₁ e s - (kb + k₂) c`, `e' = -c'`, `p' = k₂ c`.

articles.title: Michaelis constant
articles.statement: The Michaelis constant `K_M = (kb + k₂)/k₁` (Briggs–Haldane). Meaningful for `k₁ > 0`.

articles.title: Michaelis–Menten rate stays below its maximum
articles.statement: The rate law is below its maximum: `v(s) < V_max` for `s ≥ 0`, `V_max, K_M > 0`.

articles.title: Michaelis constant is the half-saturation substrate level
articles.statement: The Michaelis constant is the half-saturation substrate level: `v(K_M) = V_max / 2`.

articles.title: Michaelis–Menten rate is strictly increasing
articles.statement: The rate law is strictly increasing on `s ≥ 0` for `V_max, K_M > 0`.

articles.title: Michaelis–Menten rate law
articles.statement: The Michaelis–Menten rate law `v(s) = V_max s / (K_M + s)`.

articles.title: Briggs–Haldane rate law
articles.statement:
On the quasi-steady-state manifold the product forms at rate
`k₂ c = V_max s / (K_M + s)`, `V_max = k₂ e₀`.

articles.title: Quasi-steady-state value of the complex
articles.statement: The quasi-steady-state value of the complex, `c = e₀ s / (K_M + s)`.

articles.title: Mass conservation
Substrate consumption at the Michaelis–Menten rate under QSSA
articles.statement:
On the quasi-steady-state manifold the substrate is consumed at the Michaelis–Menten rate:
`s' = -V_max s / (K_M + s)`.

articles.title: Mass-action rate of the substrate
articles.statement: The mass-action rate of the substrate, `s' = -k₁ e s + kb c`.

articles.title: Fast transient converges to the quasi-steady state
articles.statement:
The fast transient converges to the quasi-steady-state value for `k₁ > 0` and
`s̄ + K_M > 0`.

articles.title: Saturation of the Michaelis–Menten rate
articles.statement: Saturation: `v(s) → V_max` as `s → ∞`.

articles.title: Generator of the mass-action chain on a finite state class
articles.statement:
The generator of the stochastic mass-action chain restricted to a finite set `Ω` of
states: `Q x y = ∑_r λ_r(x) ([fire r x = y] - [x = y])`. It is a rate matrix when `Ω` is
closed under firing (`isRateMatrix_classGenerator`).

articles.title: Stationary law of the stochastic mass-action chain on a finite class
articles.statement:
**Stationary law of the stochastic mass-action chain on a finite class** (Anderson,
Craciun & Kurtz 2010, Thm 4.1–4.2). Let the rate constants be nonnegative, `c > 0` complex
balanced, and `Ω` a nonempty finite set of states closed under the reactions in both
directions. Then the restricted generator is a rate matrix, and the normalized product-form
Poisson law `π(x) ∝ ∏_s c_s^{x_s} e^{-c_s} / Nat.factorial x_s` on `Ω` is a positive
probability vector invariant under the transition semigroup: `π P(t) = π` for every `t`.

articles.title: Normalized Poisson stationary law on a finite state class
articles.statement: The Poisson weights normalized on a finite set `Ω` of states.

articles.title: Concentration control coefficient
articles.statement:
The concentration control coefficient `C^{s_m}_{e_i} = (e_i / s_m) ∂s_m/∂e_i`, meaningful
for a positive concentration `s_m` and a steady state differentiable at `e`.

articles.title: Weak duality for flux balance analysis
articles.statement: Weak duality for flux balance analysis.

articles.title: Elasticity of a reaction rate
articles.statement:
The elasticity `ε^{v_i}_{s_m} = (s_m / v_i) ∂v_i/∂s_m`, meaningful for a nonzero rate
`v_i` and a rate law differentiable at `s`.

articles.title: Uniqueness in the Markov chain tree theorem
articles.statement:
For an irreducible rate matrix every invariant vector is a multiple of the in-tree weights:
the stationary law is proportional, at each state, to the weight of the spanning in-trees
rooted there.

articles.title: Strong duality for flux balance analysis
articles.statement:
Strong duality for flux balance analysis: a feasible problem has a dual feasible point
whose value is the optimal value.

articles.title: Feasible flux balance problem attains its optimum
articles.statement: A feasible flux balance problem attains its optimum.

articles.title: The FBA value is piecewise linear
articles.statement:
There are finitely many affine functions
`b ↦ y ⬝ᵥ b + κ` whose minimum is the optimal value at every feasible right-hand side `b`.

## Sources

- Rockafellar (1970), Thm 19.3; Orth, Thiele & Palsson (2010).

articles.title: Finitely many dual solutions suffice
articles.statement:
There is a finite set `T` of pairs
`(y, u ⬝ᵥ α - l ⬝ᵥ β)` with `(y, α, β)` dual feasible, such that for every feasible `b` some
pair in `T` is optimal: `y ⬝ᵥ b + κ = fbaValue S l u c b`.

articles.title: Regular steady states exist by the implicit function theorem
articles.statement:
If `s₀` is a steady state
at enzyme levels `e₀`, the rate laws are continuously differentiable at `s₀`, and the Jacobian
`δ ↦ N (e₀ ⊙ f'(s₀) δ)` is injective, then the steady state continues to a map `σ` with
`σ e₀ = s₀` satisfying `IsRegularSteadyState`.

articles.title: Shadow prices
articles.statement:
**Shadow prices** (Orth, Thiele & Palsson 2010): at a feasible `b`, the metabolite prices
`y` of the optimal dual solutions are exactly the supergradients of the optimal value:
`fbaValue b' ≤ fbaValue b + y ⬝ᵥ (b' - b)` for every feasible `b'`.

articles.title: Symmetric matrix balancing
articles.statement:
**Symmetric matrix balancing** (Sinkhorn 1964; the "equal visibility" normalization of
Imakaev et al. 2012): a symmetric matrix with positive entries has a unique positive vector
`d` with `diag(d) A diag(d)` doubly stochastic.

articles.title: Dual feasibility for flux balance analysis
articles.statement:
Dual feasibility for flux balance analysis: `y` prices the metabolites, `α, β ≥ 0` the
upper and lower flux bounds, and `Sᵀ y + α - β = c`.

articles.title: Dual objective of flux balance analysis
articles.statement: The dual objective `b ⬝ᵥ y + u ⬝ᵥ α - l ⬝ᵥ β`.

articles.title: Feasible fluxes of flux balance analysis
articles.statement: The feasible fluxes of flux balance analysis: `S v = b`, `l ≤ v ≤ u`.

articles.title: Concavity of the flux balance optimum in the right-hand side
articles.statement: The optimal value is concave in the right-hand side `b` on the set of feasible `b`.

articles.title: Optimal value of flux balance analysis
articles.statement:
The optimal value `max {c ⬝ᵥ v | S v = b, l ≤ v ≤ u}` of flux balance analysis
(the supremum; it is `0` by convention when the problem is infeasible).

articles.title: State after one reaction firing
articles.statement:
The state reached from `x` by one firing of reaction `r`, `x - src r + prod r`
(meaningful when `src r ≤ x`, the only case in which the propensity is nonzero).

articles.title: Flux control coefficient
articles.statement:
The flux control coefficient `C^{J_j}_{e_i} = (e_i / J_j) ∂J_j/∂e_i`. It is meaningful
when `J_j ≠ 0` and the steady-state flux is differentiable at `e`; otherwise Lean's `x / 0 = 0`
and `fderiv` of a non-differentiable map, `0`, give junk values.

articles.title: Reaction fluxes proportional to enzyme levels
articles.statement: Reaction rates `v_i(e, s) = e_i f_i(s)` proportional to enzyme levels `e`.

articles.title: Shadow prices are derivatives when unique
articles.statement:
If `b` is an interior point of the set of
feasible right-hand sides and `y` is the only metabolite price vector of an optimal dual
solution, then the optimal value is differentiable at `b` with derivative `b' ↦ y ⬝ᵥ b'`.

## Sources

- Rockafellar (1970), Thm 25.1; Orth, Thiele & Palsson (2010).

articles.title: Necessity of total support
articles.statement:
**Necessity of total support** (Sinkhorn & Knopp 1967; Csima & Datta 1972): if a positive
diagonal scaling `diag(d) A diag(d)` is doubly stochastic, then `A` has total support. The proof
uses Birkhoff's theorem. The converse for symmetric nonnegative `A` is
`exists_symmetric_balancing_of_hasTotalSupport`.

articles.title: Total support of a square matrix
articles.statement:
A square matrix has **total support** if it is nonzero and every positive entry lies on a
positive diagonal: for `A i j > 0` there is a permutation `σ` with `σ i = j` and
`A k (σ k) > 0` for all `k` (Sinkhorn & Knopp 1967; Csima & Datta 1972).

articles.title: Interaction graph of a Boolean network
articles.statement:
In the interaction graph of `f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1}ⁿ` there is an edge `j → i` when the
`i`-th coordinate of `f` depends on the `j`-th variable.

articles.title: Acyclic interaction graph
articles.statement: The interaction graph of `f` has no directed cycle (loops included).

articles.title: Spanning in-tree rooted at a state
articles.statement:
`t : ι → ι` is a spanning in-tree rooted at `r` (each `i ≠ r` points to its parent
`t i`): `t r = r` and iterating `t` from any state reaches `r`.

articles.title: Irreducible rate matrix
articles.statement:
A rate matrix is irreducible if every state reaches every other state through positive
jump rates.

articles.title: Restricted mass-action generator is a rate matrix
articles.statement:
The restricted generator is a rate matrix when the rate constants are nonnegative and
`Ω` is closed under the reactions.

articles.title: Regular steady state of a metabolic network
articles.statement:
A regular steady state at enzyme levels `e₀`: `σ` is differentiable at `e₀`, the rate
laws are differentiable at `σ e₀`, `N v(e, σ e) = 0` for `e` near `e₀`, and the Jacobian
`δ ↦ N ∂_s v(e₀, σ e₀) δ` is injective (it is square, so this is its invertibility).

articles.title: Global balance of the product-form Poisson weights
articles.statement:
**Global balance of the product-form Poisson weights** (Anderson, Craciun & Kurtz 2010,
Thm 4.1): if `c` is complex balanced for the deterministic mass-action system with rate
constants `k`, then at every state `x` the total outflow `π(x) ∑_r λ_r(x)` equals the total
inflow `∑_{r : prod r ≤ x} π(x - prod r + src r) λ_r(x - prod r + src r)` for
`π = poissonWeight c`. This is an algebraic identity valid for all real `k` and `c`.

articles.title: Anderson–Craciun–Kurtz on a finite class
articles.statement:
**Anderson–Craciun–Kurtz on a finite class** (Anderson, Craciun & Kurtz 2010,
Thm 4.1–4.2): if `c` is complex balanced and every state of `Ω` from which a reaction leads
into `Ω` lies in `Ω` (`hbwd`), the Poisson weights restricted to `Ω` are invariant for the
restricted generator: `π Q = 0`, for all real `k` and `c`. For a closed communicating class of
a weakly reversible network with positive rate constants `hbwd` holds (the reverse reaction
path leads back).

articles.title: Product-form Poisson weight of a state
articles.statement:
The product-form Poisson weight `∏_s c_s ^ x_s e^{-c_s} / Nat.factorial x_s` of a
state `x`.

articles.title: Stochastic mass-action propensity
articles.statement:
The stochastic mass-action propensity of reaction `r` in state `x` (molecule counts):
`k r * ∏_s x_s (x_s - 1) ⋯ (x_s - src_s + 1)`, the falling factorial
`Nat.descFactorial x_s src_s` (it vanishes when `x_s < src_s`). Anderson, Craciun & Kurtz
(2010), §2.

articles.title: Robert's theorem
articles.statement:
**Robert's theorem** (Robert 1980): if the interaction graph of `f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1}ⁿ`
is acyclic, `f` has a unique fixed point `p`, and every synchronous trajectory reaches it
within `n` steps.

articles.title: Uniqueness of Sinkhorn scaling
articles.statement:
Two diagonal scalings of a positive matrix to doubly
stochastic form differ by a positive scalar.

articles.title: Steady-state fluxes along a steady-state map
articles.statement: The steady-state fluxes `J(e) = v(e, σ(e))` along a steady-state map `σ`.

articles.title: Concentration summation theorem
articles.statement:
**Concentration summation theorem** (Heinrich & Rapoport 1974): for a positive
steady-state concentration `s_m`, `∑_i C^{s_m}_{e_i} = 0`. The positivity hypothesis is the
domain on which the scaled concentration control coefficients have their biological meaning.

articles.title: Flux connectivity theorem
articles.statement:
**Flux connectivity theorem** (Kacser & Burns 1973): when all steady-state fluxes are
nonzero, `∑_i C^{J_j}_{e_i} ε^{v_i}_{s_m} = 0` for every flux `J_j` and metabolite `s_m`.

articles.title: Flux summation theorem
articles.statement:
**Flux summation theorem** (Kacser & Burns 1973; Heinrich & Rapoport 1974): for a
nonzero steady-state flux `J_j`, `∑_i C^{J_j}_{e_i} = 1`.

articles.title: In-tree weights of an irreducible rate matrix are positive
articles.statement: For an irreducible rate matrix every in-tree weight is positive.

articles.title: Markov chain tree theorem
articles.statement:
**Markov chain tree theorem** (King & Altman 1956; Hill 1966): the in-tree weights are
invariant for every matrix with zero row sums, `w Q = 0`. The proof matches both sides with the
maps `g : ι → ι` whose functional graph has its cycle through `j` (Anantharam & Tsoucas 1989).

articles.title: Total weight of spanning in-trees
articles.statement: The total weight `∑_t ∏_{i ≠ r} Q i (t i)` of the spanning in-trees rooted at `r`.

articles.title: State before one reaction firing
articles.statement:
The state from which one firing of reaction `r` leads to `x`, `x - prod r + src r`
(meaningful when `prod r ≤ x`).
